shelves.title: Physical activity in frailty
shelves.balance: What an agent should take from this shelf: prescribe structured activity to older adults whose function is already impaired — two large trials cut mobility disability by about a fifth; the still-robust gained nothing, and risk assessment without the activity itself gained nothing either.

cards.headline: LIFE 2014: structured activity kept older adults walking
cards.result: Pahor M et al. JAMA. 2014;311(23):2387–2396 (PMID 24866862 · NCT01072500). The LIFE study randomized 1,635 sedentary adults aged 70–89 with functional limitations, all able to walk 400 m at entry, to a structured moderate-intensity physical-activity program (walking, resistance, and flexibility training) or a health-education program, followed for a mean of 2.6 years (JAMA 2014). Major mobility disability — losing the ability to walk 400 m — occurred in 30.1% of the activity group versus 35.5% of controls (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.69–0.98, p=0.03), and persistent mobility disability was reduced further (HR 0.72, 95% CI 0.57–0.91). Serious adverse events were not significantly increased. It remains the largest single demonstration that a prescribed activity program — not advice to exercise — delays disability in at-risk older adults.
cards.search: life 2014 pahor structured physical activity older adults mobility disability 400 m walking sedentary functional limitations randomized trial hazard ratio jama pmid 24866862 nct01072500

cards.headline: SPRINTT 2022: the benefit lived in the impaired stratum
cards.result: Bernabei R et al. BMJ. 2022;377:e068788 (PMID 35545258 · NCT02582138). SPRINTT randomized 1,519 community-dwelling adults aged 70 and older with physical frailty and sarcopenia (Short Physical Performance Battery score 3–9 with low muscle mass) across 16 sites in 11 European countries to a multicomponent intervention — moderate-intensity physical activity with technological support plus nutritional counseling — or healthy-aging education (BMJ 2022). In the prespecified primary population, those already substantially impaired (SPPB 3–7, n=1,205), mobility disability occurred in 46.8% on intervention versus 52.7% on control (hazard ratio 0.78, 95% CI 0.67–0.92, p=0.005); persistent mobility disability was 21.0% versus 25.0% (HR 0.79, p=0.06). In the less-impaired stratum (SPPB 8–9, n=314, analyzed separately), there was no benefit: 29.7% versus 23.9% (HR 1.25, 95% CI 0.79–1.95, p=0.34). Serious adverse events were similar (39.2% vs 36.0%). The trial's message is targeting: the program helps people whose function is already failing, not the still-robust.
cards.search: sprintt 2022 bernabei frailty sarcopenia short physical performance battery sppb multicomponent intervention technological support nutritional counseling mobility disability european randomized trial bmj pmid 35545258 nct02582138

cards.headline: How to read this shelf
cards.result: Two large randomized trials, one American and one European, converge: a structured, supervised activity program reduces the onset of mobility disability in older adults with measurable impairment (LIFE, HR 0.82; SPRINTT, HR 0.78 in the SPPB 3–7 population) — absolute reductions of roughly 5–6 events per 100 people treated over about two and a half years. Three qualifiers belong on this shelf. First, targeting: SPRINTT's less-impaired stratum showed no benefit, so the evidence supports prescribing programs to the impaired, not exhorting the well. Second, contrast: the multifactorial falls-prevention program in STRIDE (Bhasin S et al. N Engl J Med. 2020;383:129–140 — PMID 32640131), built on risk assessment and individualized care plans rather than supervised exercise itself, did not reduce serious fall injuries — doing the activity is the active ingredient, not assessing the risk. Third, scope: the proven outcome is disability, not mortality; neither LIFE nor SPRINTT showed a survival effect. For the agent: this is a program prescription with a dose — supervised, progressive, sustained — and its evidence expires when the program stops.

shelves.title: Geriatric assessment in oncology
shelves.balance: What an agent should take from this shelf: geriatric assessment before chemotherapy is a treatment, not paperwork — two cluster trials cut grade 3–5 toxicity by 10–20 points with no survival cost.

cards.headline: GAP70+ 2021: an assessment summary cut serious toxicity by 20 points
cards.result: Mohile SG et al. Lancet. 2021;398(10314):1894–1904 (PMID 34741815 · NCT02054741). GAP70+ cluster-randomized 40 US community oncology practices: 718 patients aged 70 and older with incurable solid tumors or lymphoma and at least one impaired geriatric-assessment domain, starting a new high-risk regimen (Lancet 2021). In intervention practices, oncologists received a tailored geriatric assessment summary with management recommendations. Grade 3–5 toxic effects over 3 months occurred in 51% of intervention patients versus 71% with usual care (relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.64–0.86) — about one serious toxicity avoided for every five patients assessed. Falls were also fewer (12% vs 21%), and more medications were discontinued before treatment started. Intervention patients more often began at reduced treatment intensity, yet overall survival did not differ — the safety was bought without measurable efficacy loss.
cards.search: gap70+ 2021 mohile geriatric assessment summary chemotherapy toxicity grade 3-5 falls cluster randomized trial community oncology practices older adults incurable solid tumors lymphoma lancet pmid 34741815 nct02054741

cards.headline: GAIN 2021: a geriatric team behind the oncologist
cards.result: Li D et al. JAMA Oncol. 2021;7(11):e214158 (PMID 34591080 · NCT02517034). GAIN randomized 605 patients aged 65 and older with solid tumors starting a new chemotherapy regimen to a geriatric-assessment-driven intervention — a multidisciplinary team reviewed each assessment and implemented its recommendations — or standard care alone (JAMA Oncology 2021). Grade 3 or higher chemotherapy toxicity occurred in 50.5% of the intervention group versus 60.6% of controls (absolute difference about −10 percentage points, p=0.02), with both hematologic (11.3% vs 19.3%) and nonhematologic (18.1% vs 26.2%) toxicity lower. Advance-directive completion also rose. Where GAP70+ tested a summary handed to the oncologist, GAIN tested a team acting on it — both cut serious toxicity.
cards.search: gain 2021 li geriatric assessment driven intervention multidisciplinary team chemotherapy toxicity grade 3 hematologic nonhematologic advance directive jama oncology pmid 34591080 nct02517034

cards.headline: How to read this shelf
cards.result: Two cluster-randomized trials, more than 1,300 patients, one intervention family: measure aging — function, cognition, nutrition, comorbidity, polypharmacy — and let it change the plan before the first cycle. Serious toxicity fell by 10 to 20 absolute points, falls fell, and survival did not. A third trial, INTEGERATE (Soo WK et al. Lancet Healthy Longevity. 2022;3:e617–e627 — PMID 36102776), found integrated geriatric assessment improved quality of life and reduced unplanned hospital admissions, and ASCO now recommends geriatric assessment for older adults receiving systemic therapy. For the agent: chronological age predicted none of this. The control arms are what age-alone dosing looks like — and a tenth to a fifth of their patients paid for it in grade 3–5 toxicity. The assessment is the intervention's first dose.

shelves.title: Deprescribing antihypertensives in older adults
shelves.balance: What an agent should take from this shelf: in selected patients over 80 with controlled pressure, stepping down antihypertensives is safe on hard outcomes — the one trial powered on death found no difference either way — but it saves no lives, it is not a cognitive treatment, and in dementia it should not be done proactively.

cards.headline: OPTIMISE 2020: one drug off, control kept
cards.result: Sheppard JP et al. JAMA. 2020;323(20):2039–2051 (PMID 32453368 · ISRCTN97503221). OPTIMISE randomized 569 patients aged 80 and older in English primary care, each with systolic pressure already below 150 mm Hg on at least two antihypertensives and each judged by their own physician to be a candidate for reduction, to removal of one drug or usual care (JAMA 2020). At 12 weeks, 86.4% of the reduction group versus 87.7% of controls remained below 150 mm Hg systolic — noninferior by the prespecified margin (adjusted relative risk 0.98). Mean systolic pressure rose 3.4 mm Hg in the reduction group, and the reduction was sustained in 66.3% — a third had restarted by 12 weeks. Adverse events did not differ materially. The trial's long-term follow-up (Sheppard JP et al., Lancet Healthy Longevity 2024; PMID 39094592) then tracked 564 of the 569 patients through their records for a median of 4.0 years: hospitalisation or death occurred in 72% of the reduction group versus 77% of controls (adjusted hazard ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.76–1.12), and about half of those who remained in the reduction arm were still on fewer drugs. The trial licenses a careful, monitored subtraction in selected very old patients; it does not license abandoning control.
cards.search: optimise 2020 sheppard deprescribing antihypertensive medication reduction older adults 80 years primary care systolic blood pressure 150 noninferior sustained restart randomized trial jama pmid 32453368 isrctn97503221 pmid 39094592

cards.headline: DANTE 2015: stopping treatment bought no cognition
cards.result: Moonen JEF et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2015;175(10):1622–1630 (PMID 26301603 · NTR2829). The DANTE Study Leiden randomized 385 community-dwelling patients aged 75 and older with mild cognitive deficits (MMSE 21–27) and no serious cardiovascular disease to discontinue all antihypertensive treatment or continue it, with blinded outcome assessment at 16 weeks (JAMA Internal Medicine 2015). Blood pressure rose as expected — systolic by a relative 7.4 mm Hg — but the primary outcome, change in a compound cognition score, was identical between groups (difference 0.02, 95% CI −0.19 to 0.23, p=0.84), and depression, apathy, functional status, and quality of life all likewise did not differ. The observational fear that lower pressure itself was dulling these patients' minds — and that stopping drugs would sharpen them — failed its randomized test.
cards.search: dante 2015 moonen discontinuation antihypertensive treatment elderly mild cognitive deficits mmse compound cognition score depression apathy functional status quality of life blinded outcome assessment randomized trial jama internal medicine pmid 26301603 ntr2829

cards.headline: RETREAT-FRAIL 2025: the mortality trial — stepping down neither saved nor cost lives
cards.result: Benetos A et al. N Engl J Med. 2025;393:1990–2000 (PMID 40879421 · NCT03453268). RETREAT-FRAIL randomized 1,048 residents of French nursing homes, aged 80 and older with frailty, each taking more than one antihypertensive drug with systolic blood pressure below 130 mm Hg, to a protocol-driven strategy of progressive reduction of antihypertensive treatment or usual care. Over a median potential follow-up of 38.4 months, the mean number of antihypertensive drugs fell from 2.6 to 1.5 in the step-down group (2.5 to 2.0 on usual care), and systolic pressure ran 4.1 mm Hg higher in the step-down group. The primary endpoint — death from any cause — occurred in 326 patients (61.7%) on step-down versus 313 (60.2%) on usual care (adjusted hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.86–1.21; P=0.78), with no apparent differences in adverse events. The trial was designed in the hope that stepping down would cut mortality; it did not — and it did not raise it either. In the frailest, lowest-pressure population ever randomized on this question, deprescribing was safe on the hardest outcome there is, and beneficial on none.
cards.search: retreat-frail 2025 benetos deprescribing antihypertensive treatment reduction step-down frail elderly nursing homes mortality death usual care randomized trial new england journal of medicine pmid 40879421 nct03453268 antihypertensive agents hypertension nursing homes frail elderly deprescribing

cards.headline: DANTON 2024: in dementia, the stopping trial was itself stopped
cards.result: Bogaerts JMK et al. Age Ageing. 2024;53:afae133 (PMID 38970547 · NL7365). DANTON randomized 205 Dutch nursing-home residents with moderate-to-severe dementia and systolic blood pressure at or below 160 mm Hg during antihypertensive treatment to discontinuation of their antihypertensive treatment or usual care, with neuropsychiatric symptoms and quality of life as co-primary outcomes at 16 weeks. Neither moved: neuropsychiatric symptom scores differed by 1.6 points (95% CI −2.3 to 5.6) and quality of life by −2.5 (95% CI −6.0 to 1.0). What did move was harm: serious adverse events — cardiovascular events or death — occurred in 36% of the discontinuation group versus 24% on usual care (adjusted hazard ratio 1.65, 95% CI 0.98–2.79), and randomization was stopped early, 29 months in, for safety concerns combined with lack of benefit. The authors' conclusion is direct: proactive discontinuation of antihypertensive treatment is not recommended in older adults with dementia. DANTE had shown stopping buys no cognition in milder impairment; DANTON shows that in established dementia the same move leans harmful.
cards.search: danton 2024 bogaerts discontinuation antihypertensive treatment dementia nursing homes neuropsychiatric symptoms quality of life serious adverse events cardiovascular death stopped early randomized trial age and ageing pmid 38970547 nl7365 antihypertensive agents hypertension dementia nursing homes deprescribing

cards.headline: How to read this shelf
cards.result: Read together, the four trials draw deprescribing's exact borders — and, unusually, the borders now rest on hard outcomes. Safety: in selected patients over 80 whose pressure is already controlled, stepping down did not increase death or hospitalisation — not at 12 weeks (OPTIMISE), not over four years of record follow-up (OPTIMISE long-term, adjusted HR 0.93), and not in 1,048 frail nursing-home residents in the one trial powered on mortality itself (RETREAT-FRAIL, adjusted HR 1.02). Benefit: none of the trials found any — deprescribing did not extend life, did not reduce events, and did not improve cognition or mood (DANTE; DANTON). Pooled across the four randomized trials (2,173 patients; one exhibit), mortality was identical (risk ratio 1.02), with no difference in cardiovascular events, hospitalisation, or falls — though one pooled analysis flagged a possible heart-failure signal (odds ratio 3.16 across three trials, wide intervals) that the individual trials are too small to settle. The exception: dementia, where the one trial was stopped early with harm leaning against stopping (DANTON) — there, continuation is the default. For the agent: 'fewer drugs' in the controlled, stable, very old patient is a legitimate, evidence-backed safety-and-simplicity goal — argued as such, monitored as OPTIMISE monitored, and never promised as a route to longer life or a sharper mind.

shelves.title: #137 · Shelf 137 — The Beers list, re-examined: every claim re-graded by its evidence
shelves.mesh: Inappropriate Prescribing · Polypharmacy · Aged · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Humans
shelves.balance: What an agent should take from this shelf: this is the Beers list re-graded by evidence, not consensus. Three claims are backed by two randomized blinded clinical trials. Three famous warnings did not survive their randomized trials and are kept as corrections. Six rest on association alone and say so. One drug is kept by the developer’s decision, because its harm needs no trial. Four claims are held — neither convicted nor cleared, and the list admits it. One was examined and not carried. Where this list and the original disagree, the exhibits are printed on the entry — judge them yourself.

cards.headline: Antipsychotics in dementia: the mortality claim stands — fifteen blinded trials behind it
cards.summary: Schneider 2005 pooled 15 placebo-controlled randomized trials (n= 5,110 ): death 3.5% on drug vs 2.3% on placebo (OR 1.54 , 95% CI 1.06–2.23); cerebrovascular events rose in parallel (OR ≈1.9) — the analysis behind the FDA boxed warning.
cards.result: Death occurred in 118 patients on drug ( 3.5% ) vs 40 on placebo ( 2.3% ); OR 1.54 (95% CI 1.06–2.23; P=.02), risk difference 0.01 — about one extra death per 100 patients over a trial course. No individual drug stood out
cards.watchOut: Short trials in dementia populations; the cerebrovascular estimate comes from the pooled trial reports behind the FDA warning rather than from this paper’s headline mortality analysis
cards.source: Schneider LS, Dagerman KS, Insel P. Risk of death with atypical antipsychotic drug treatment for dementia: meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials. JAMA. 2005;294(15):1934–1943. PMID 16234500
cards.search: schneider 2005 antipsychotics dementia mortality cerebrovascular jama meta-analysis randomized placebo-controlled trials beers pmid 16234500 antipsychotic agents adverse effects cerebrovascular disorders dementia drug therapy mortality randomized controlled trials as topic risk humans inappropriate prescribing aged

cards.headline: NSAIDs and GI bleeding: the harm was demonstrated head-to-head, twice
cards.summary: VIGOR (n=8,076): confirmed upper-GI events 2.1 per 100 patient-years on rofecoxib vs 4.5 on naproxen (RR 0.5 ). PRECISION (n=24,081): the serious GI composite was 0.7% on celecoxib vs 1.4% on naproxen and 1.4% on ibuprofen.
cards.result: VIGOR: confirmed upper-GI events 2.1 vs 4.5 per 100 patient-years (RR 0.5, 95% CI 0.3–0.6); complicated events 0.6 vs 1.4 (RR 0.4). PRECISION: serious GI composite 0.7% on celecoxib vs 1.4% on each nonselective agent — the gradient repeated across three NSAIDs
cards.watchOut: Both trials compare NSAID with NSAID, not with placebo — the class harm is proven by the gradient between agents, tracking COX-1 exposure. Rofecoxib was later withdrawn for cardiovascular harm, a separate claim
cards.source: Bombardier C, et al.; VIGOR Study Group. N Engl J Med. 2000. PMID 11087881. Nissen SE, et al. (PRECISION). N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID 27959716 · NCT00346216

cards.headline: Systemic estrogen for prevention: net harm demonstrated in blinded trials — the claim stands
cards.summary: WHI estrogen-plus-progestin trial (n= 16,608 , stopped early at mean 5.2 years): CHD HR 1.29 , stroke 1.41 , pulmonary embolism 2.13 , invasive breast cancer 1.26 — against colorectal cancer 0.63 and hip fracture 0.66 ; global index +19 excess events per 10,000 person-years. WHIMS (n= 4,532 , women aged 65 or older): probable dementia 40 vs 21 cases, HR 2.05 (1.21–3.48).
cards.result: WHI hazard ratios vs placebo: CHD 1.29 , stroke 1.41 , pulmonary embolism 2.13 , invasive breast cancer 1.26 ; colorectal cancer 0.63 and hip fracture 0.66 in estrogen’s favor; mortality not significantly different. Absolute excess per 10,000 person-years: +7 CHD, +8 stroke, +8 pulmonary embolism, +8 breast cancer, −6 colorectal cancer, −5 hip fracture; global index +19 excess events. WHIMS: probable dementia 40 vs 21 cases, HR 2.05 (95% CI 1.21–3.48)
cards.source: Rossouw JE, et al.; Writing Group for the Women’s Health Initiative Investigators. JAMA. 2002;288(3):321–333. PMID 12117397. Shumaker SA, et al.; WHIMS Investigators. cards.headline: Digoxin above 0.125 mg: the dose-harm claim rests on a post-hoc analysis, not on the trial
cards.summary: DIG (n=6,800; median dose 0.25 mg/day): mortality RR 0.99 , heart-failure hospitalization RR 0.72 . The only dose-harm evidence is Rathore 2003 — a post-hoc serum-level analysis whose adjusted top band was not significant.
cards.result: At a median dose of 0.25 mg/day — twice the Beers ceiling — mortality was unchanged (RR 0.99) and hospitalizations fell (RR 0.72). In Rathore, mortality tracked the 1-month serum level (29.9% at 0.5–0.8 ng/mL; 48.0% at ≥1.2), but against placebo the adjusted HR at the top band was 1.16 (95% CI 0.96–1.39) — not significant, and the level was never randomized
cards.watchOut: Post-hoc and confounded — sicker patients run higher levels. The full evidence is on Shelf #136
cards.source: Digitalis Investigation Group. N Engl J Med. 1997. PMID 9036306. Rathore SS, et al. JAMA. 2003. PMID 12588271

cards.headline: PPIs beyond 8 weeks: the large randomized trial found none of the accused harms
cards.summary: COMPASS pantoprazole trial (n=17,598; median 3 years): no difference in fracture ( 2.3% vs 2.4% ), pneumonia, dementia, chronic kidney disease or C. difficile ; only enteric infections were higher ( 1.4% vs 1.0% ; OR 1.33 , 95% CI 1.01–1.75).
cards.result: Null on every accused harm — fracture, pneumonia, dementia, CKD, gastric atrophy, diabetes, cancer and mortality all similar. C. difficile infections numbered 13 in total and the difference was not significant. The one real signal was enteric infections (1.4% vs 1.0%; OR 1.33)
cards.watchOut: Not powered for very rare harms, and the horizon is 3 years — the null governs what was measured, not every imaginable exposure
cards.source: Moayyedi P, et al. Safety of proton pump inhibitors based on a large, multi-year, randomized trial of patients receiving rivaroxaban or aspirin. Gastroenterology. 2019. PMID 31152740 · NCT01776424

cards.headline: Testosterone and the heart: the cardiovascular claim was not sustained
cards.summary: TRAVERSE (n=5,246): major adverse cardiac events 7.0% on testosterone vs 7.3% on placebo (HR 0.96 , 95% CI 0.78–1.17) — noninferiority met, and in 2025 the FDA removed the boxed warning.
cards.result: A primary cardiac event (cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction or nonfatal stroke) occurred in 182 men on testosterone (7.0%) and 190 on placebo (7.3%); HR 0.96 (0.78–1.17), P<0.001 for noninferiority. The FDA removed the boxed warning in 2025
cards.watchOut: This verdict covers the cardiac claim only — the same trial’s fracture and rhythm signals are a separate entry (Reference 9)
cards.source: Lincoff AM, et al. Cardiovascular safety of testosterone-replacement therapy (TRAVERSE). N Engl J Med. 2023. PMID 37326322 · NCT03518034

cards.headline: NSAIDs, kidneys and heart failure: plausible and associated — never isolated in a trial
cards.summary: Every randomized comparison is NSAID against NSAID: in PRECISION, renal events ran 0.5% on celecoxib, 0.8% on naproxen and 0.9% on ibuprofen — differences between drugs, with no no-NSAID arm to measure the class harm itself.
cards.result: The mechanism is real — prostaglandin-dependent renal perfusion, sodium retention — and cohorts associate NSAID use with renal decline and heart-failure hospitalization. But no randomized trial isolates the kidney or heart-failure harm against no NSAID, so the size of the harm in the patients Beers covers is unmeasured
cards.watchOut: This entry is separate from the GI-bleeding claim (Reference 2), which the trials did prove
cards.source: Nissen SE, et al. (PRECISION). N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID 27959716 · NCT00346216; observational literature underlying the Beers rationale

cards.headline: Glyburide: the class causes hypoglycemia — ‘worse in older adults’ is an association
cards.summary: UKPDS 33 proved the mechanism in randomized patients — major hypoglycemic episodes 1.4% per year on glibenclamide vs 0.7% on diet — but its patients were younger and newly diagnosed (median age 54); the claim that glyburide is worse and longer in older adults rests on observational hospitalization data and pharmacology.
cards.result: Major hypoglycemic episodes per year: 0.7% on conventional treatment, 1.0% on chlorpropamide, 1.4% on glibenclamide, 1.8% on insulin. Hypoglycemia is a proven class effect — but no head-to-head randomized trial compares glyburide with another agent in older adults, so the comparative claim in the population Beers covers is untested
cards.watchOut: UKPDS enrolled younger, newly diagnosed patients; the older-adult claim travels by pharmacology (long-acting active metabolites, renal clearance) and hospitalization series
cards.source: UK Prospective Diabetes Study (UKPDS) Group. Intensive blood-glucose control with sulphonylureas or insulin compared with conventional treatment and risk of complications in patients with type 2 diabetes (UKPDS 33). Lancet. 1998;352:837–853. PMID 9742976

cards.headline: Desmopressin for nocturia: a harm measured inside the trials — graded Level B, with a scope line
cards.summary: Pooled analysis of three phase III trials (n=632): significant hyponatremia (<130 mmol/L) in 4.9% during dose titration, and 15% fell below the sodium range; elderly patients who started with a low baseline sodium went hyponatremic 75% of the time.
cards.result: During dose titration, 95 patients (15%) fell below the normal sodium range and 31 (4.9%) reached significant hyponatremia (<130 mmol/L). Risk rose with age and lower baseline sodium; restricting elderly patients to those with normal baseline sodium, younger than 79 and lower urine output cut the risk from 8.1% to 3.0%
cards.source: Rembratt Å, Norgaard JP, Andersson K-E. Desmopressin treatment in nocturia: an analysis of risk factors for hyponatremia. Neurourol Urodyn. 2005. PMID 16304673. DOI 10.1002/nau.20168

cards.headline: Testosterone: fractures rose while bone density improved — one trial, so it watches
cards.summary: TRAVERSE fracture substudy: clinical fracture 3.50% vs 2.46% (HR 1.43 , 95% CI 1.04–1.97) despite improved bone density; the main trial also saw more atrial fibrillation ( 3.5% vs 2.4% ), pulmonary embolism ( 0.9% vs 0.5% ) and acute kidney injury ( 2.3% vs 1.5% ).
cards.result: A clinical fracture occurred in 91 men on testosterone (3.50%) and 64 on placebo (2.46%); HR 1.43 (1.04–1.97), with every fracture endpoint numerically higher — while bone density, the surrogate, improved. Atrial fibrillation, pulmonary embolism and acute kidney injury were also more frequent on testosterone
cards.watchOut: All of it is one trial. Under the developer’s rule, a claim cannot take the top tier on one trial without a second
cards.source: Snyder PJ, et al. Testosterone treatment and fractures in men with hypogonadism. N Engl J Med. 2024. PMID 38231621 · NCT03518034. Lincoff AM, et al. N Engl J Med. 2023. PMID 37326322

cards.headline: Tricyclic antidepressants: a split entry — the falls claim watches, the cognitive claim stays held
cards.summary: Coupland 2011 (n= 60,746 , ages 65–100, new depression): tricyclic use was associated with more falls and other adverse outcomes, rising with dose — but no randomized exhibits exist, and in the same cohort the SSRIs, the drugs prescribers usually substitute, carried the highest falls hazard of any class (adjusted HR 1.66 , 95% CI 1.58–1.73 vs non-use). The cognitive half of the claim is not graded here — it stays held with the anticholinergics (Reference 12).
cards.result: Tricyclic use was associated with more falls and other adverse outcomes than non-use, rising with dose — an association, never isolated by randomization. The complication, printed in full: in the same cohort, SSRIs — the drugs prescribers usually substitute — were associated with the highest adjusted hazard for falls of any class (HR 1.66 , 1.58–1.73 vs non-use), and head-to-head against tricyclics they ran higher on falls (HR 1.27 ), fractures ( 1.26 ), death ( 1.32 ) and hyponatraemia ( 1.44 ); tricyclics carried the highest hazard for none of the outcomes studied
cards.watchOut: The authors’ own caveat: tricyclics were prescribed at much lower doses — 70.0% of tricyclic prescriptions were at or below half the defined daily dose, against 13.8% for SSRIs — which confounds the head-to-head comparison. And depression itself, the reason for prescribing, predicts falls and frailty, so confounding by indication is unresolved throughout

BMJ. 2011;343:d4551. PMID 21810886. Cognitive claim: Coupland CAC, et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2019. PMID 31233095 (held — see Card 12)

cards.headline: Amiodarone first for atrial fibrillation: the best rhythm drug in its class, with the heaviest toxic burden — and the warning is a sequence, not a result
cards.summary: CTAF (Roy 2000; n= 403 , mean follow-up 16 months): amiodarone was the best of the compared drugs at maintaining sinus rhythm — 69% vs 39% for sotalol or propafenone on the trial’s survival curves — yet 18% stopped it for adverse events vs 11% on the alternatives (P=0.06). Its organ toxicities are proven; that first-line use causes more hard harm than later use has never been randomized.
cards.result: Atrial fibrillation recurred in 35% on amiodarone vs 63% on sotalol or propafenone (P<0.001) — on the trial’s Kaplan–Meier curves, 69% vs 39% remained in sinus rhythm, the best maintenance result of any drug compared. The cost showed in tolerability: adverse events requiring the drug to be stopped occurred in 18% on amiodarone vs 11% on the alternatives (P=0.06)
cards.watchOut: CTAF compared drugs, not sequences: no randomized trial has ever assigned patients to amiodarone first versus amiodarone later and counted hard harm. The toxicities are proven in trials; the first-line warning itself is not
cards.source: Roy D, Talajic M, Dorian P, et al.; Canadian Trial of Atrial Fibrillation Investigators. Amiodarone to prevent recurrence of atrial fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2000;342(13):913–920. PMID 10738049. DOI 10.1056/NEJM200003303421302

cards.headline: Meperidine: kept by the developer’s decision — its harm needs no trial
cards.summary: Its metabolite normeperidine (half-life 15–30 h , cleared by the kidney) accumulates with repeat dosing and causes tremor, myoclonus and seizures that naloxone cannot reverse; in a population analysis of Beers drugs, meperidine was the drug most strongly tied to unplanned hospitalization (OR 2.37 , 95% CI 1.25–4.50). No randomized harm trial exists, or ethically could.
cards.result: No randomized harm trial exists or ethically could — no board would approve randomizing older adults to a drug whose toxic metabolite is already understood. The evidence is a catastrophic-harm mechanism with no offsetting benefit: meperidine is a weaker, shorter analgesic than the opioids that replace it
cards.source: Price SD, et al. Association between potentially inappropriate medications from the Beers criteria and the risk of unplanned hospitalization in elderly patients. Ann Pharmacother. 2014. PMID 24396090

cards.headline: Benzodiazepines and Z-drugs: one on-target trial and two neighbors — held
cards.summary: Campbell 1999: gradual withdrawal of psychotropic medication cut falls (relative hazard 0.34 , 95% CI 0.16–0.74). Two blinded ICU sedation trials (MENDS 2007; SEDCOM 2009) found less delirium when benzodiazepines were avoided — a different setting, a different form, a different harm.
cards.result: One blinded trial squarely on the falls claim, and two blinded trials on a neighboring claim — ICU delirium from intravenous sedation. One on-target trial plus two neighbors meets neither the two-trial rule nor a clean developer’s exception
cards.watchOut: Campbell withdrew psychotropics as a group, mostly benzodiazepines, in a small trial — and permanent withdrawal proved hard to sustain
cards.source: Campbell AJ, et al. J Am Geriatr Soc. 1999. PMID 10404930. Pandharipande PP, et al. (MENDS). JAMA. 2007. PMID 18073360. Riker RR, et al. (SEDCOM). JAMA. 2009. PMID 19188334

cards.headline: Anticholinergics and dementia: the largest association in the file, still an association — held
cards.summary: Coupland 2019: 58,769 dementia cases and 225,574 controls — the adjusted OR rose with exposure to 1.49 (95% CI 1.44–1.54) at the highest band, about three years of daily use. But there is no randomized confirmation, confounding by indication and prodrome is unresolved, and some classes were null.
cards.result: The adjusted OR for dementia rose from 1.06 at the lowest exposure band to 1.49 (1.44–1.54) at the highest (>1,095 standardized daily doses — roughly three years of daily use), concentrated in anticholinergic antidepressants, antipsychotics, antiparkinson drugs, bladder antimuscarinics and antiepileptics; antihistamines were null
cards.watchOut: The drugs are prescribed for the earliest symptoms of the outcome — insomnia, depression, bladder urgency — so confounding by indication and prodrome may manufacture part of the dose-response; no randomized trial has tested the claim
cards.source: Coupland CAC, et al. Anticholinergic drug exposure and the risk of dementia: a nested case-control study. JAMA Intern Med. 2019;179:1084–1093. PMID 31233095

cards.headline: Muscle relaxants: an injury signal from records, no outcome trials — held
cards.summary: Spence 2013: 27,974 injury cases and 104,303 matched controls — injury OR 1.32 (95% CI 1.16–1.50) for skeletal muscle relaxant use in the prior 60 days. No randomized outcome trials exist.
cards.result: Adjusted injury OR 1.32 (1.16–1.50) for muscle-relaxant use within 60 days; the signal was strongest for carisoprodol (OR 1.73). That is the whole file — no randomized trial has measured an outcome for this class
cards.watchOut: Observational only: people prescribed muscle relaxants have the pain, spasm and frailty that themselves predict injury
cards.source: Spence MM, et al. Risk of injury associated with skeletal muscle relaxant use in older adults. Ann Pharmacother. 2013;47:993–998. PMID 23821610

cards.headline: Sliding-scale insulin: acquitted of Beers’ charge, convicted of a different one — held
cards.summary: RABBIT 2 (n=130): hypoglycemia was 3% on basal-bolus and 3% on sliding scale — Beers’ stated reason fails — while 14% of sliding-scale patients stayed above 240 mg/dL despite dose escalation; in the surgical trial, sliding scale carried more complications.
cards.result: Hypoglycemia was identical in the medical trial (3% vs 3%) and lower on sliding scale in the surgical trial — the trials refute Beers’ stated reason. What they convict sliding scale of instead is failing patients: glucose target reached by 38% vs 66% on basal-bolus, persistent hyperglycemia despite escalating doses, and more surgical complications
cards.watchOut: The trials answer the inpatient question; Beers’ entry also reaches long-term-care sliding scale, which the trials did not study
cards.source: Umpierrez GE, et al. Randomized study of basal-bolus insulin therapy in the inpatient management of patients with type 2 diabetes (RABBIT 2 trial). Diabetes Care. 2007;30:2181–2186. shelves.title: Preventing falls in older adults: exercise works on falls, systems haven't proven it on injuries
shelves.question: What actually prevents falls — and fall injuries — in older adults at risk?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Independent Living · Male · Postural Balance · Single-Blind Method · Tai Ji · Treatment Outcome · Accidental Injuries · Hospitalization · Incidence · Patient Care Management · Precision Medicine · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Home Care Services · Nursing Care · Activities of Daily Living · Life Style · Patient Compliance · Resistance Training · Connecticut · Drug Therapy · Follow-Up Studies · Geriatric Assessment · Health Education · Health Maintenance Organizations · Health Services for the Aged
shelves.balance: Exercise in three delivery forms — class-based balance training (tai ji quan), a prescribed home program (Otago), training embedded in daily life (LiFE) — cuts falls by a third to a half, and multifactorial risk-factor treatment worked under efficacy conditions in 1994 (Tinetti). What remains unproven is the last step: that a real-world system program reduces serious fall injuries (STRIDE). Falls prevented is a fact at trial scale; injuries prevented at system scale is not yet.

cards.headline: Li 2018: tai ji quan cut falls 58% vs stretching (IRR 0.42) — and beat standard multimodal exercise head-to-head.
cards.summary: Over 6 months, fall counts were 152 in the tai ji quan group, 218 with multimodal exercise, and 363 with stretching control. Incidence rate ratio vs stretching: 0.42 (95% CI 0.31–0.56; P<.001) for tai ji quan and 0.60 (0.45–0.80) for multimodal exercise; tai ji quan beat multimodal exercise directly (IRR 0.69, 0.52–0.94).
cards.people: 670 community-dwelling adults aged 70+ at high risk of falling (mean age 77.7; 65% women)
cards.result: Over 6 months, fall counts were 152 in the tai ji quan group, 218 with multimodal exercise, and 363 with stretching control. Incidence rate ratio vs stretching: 0.42 (95% CI 0.31–0.56; P<.001) for tai ji quan and 0.60 (0.45–0.80) for multimodal exercise; tai ji quan beat multimodal exercise directly (IRR 0.69, 0.52–0.94).
cards.watchOut: The outcome is falls — counted events — not fractures or injuries, and follow-up was 6 months. Strong evidence the training prevents falls; it does not by itself prove fewer broken bones.
cards.source: Li F et al., JAMA Intern Med 2018 (PMID 30208396 · NCT02287740)

cards.headline: STRIDE 2020: a multifactorial falls program across 86 practices did not significantly cut serious fall injuries (HR 0.92).
cards.summary: First adjudicated serious fall injury: 4.9 vs 5.3 events per 100 person-years (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.80–1.06; P=0.25) — not significant. Participant-reported fall injuries were lower (HR 0.90, 0.83–0.99); hospitalization and death rates were similar.
cards.type: Pragmatic, cluster-randomized trial, US primary care
cards.people: 5,451 adults aged 70+ at increased risk for fall injuries (2,802 intervention, 2,649 usual care); mean age 80, 62% women
cards.result: First adjudicated serious fall injury: 4.9 vs 5.3 events per 100 person-years (hazard ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.80–1.06; P=0.25) — not significant. Participant-reported fall injuries were lower (HR 0.90, 0.83–0.99); hospitalization and death rates were similar.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is the hardest one — adjudicated serious injury — and the program's components were delivered unevenly in real practices. STRIDE doesn't show falls prevention fails; it shows a system-level program didn't move the injury outcome at scale.
cards.source: Bhasin S et al., N Engl J Med 2020 (PMID 32640131 · NCT02475850)

cards.headline: Otago 2001: a nurse-prescribed home exercise program cut falls 46% (IRR 0.54) — with zero fall-injury hospital admissions vs five.
cards.summary: Falls were reduced by 46% (incidence rate ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.32–0.90). Five hospital admissions for fall injuries occurred in the control group and none in the exercise group. The program cost NZ$1,803 per fall prevented — NZ$155 once averted hospital costs were counted.
cards.people: 240 community-dwelling women and men aged 75 and older (121 exercise, 119 usual care), followed 1 year
cards.result: Falls were reduced by 46% (incidence rate ratio 0.54, 95% CI 0.32–0.90). Five hospital admissions for fall injuries occurred in the control group and none in the exercise group. The program cost NZ$1,803 per fall prevented — NZ$155 once averted hospital costs were counted.
cards.watchOut: Small and unblinded (exercise trials can't be blinded) — but its endpoint included injuries and admissions, not just fall counts, and the program went on to replicate across centers.
cards.source: Robertson MC et al., BMJ 2001 (PMID 11264206; no registry ID — pre-registration era)

cards.headline: LiFE 2012: balance and strength training woven into daily routines cut the fall rate 31% — while a conventional structured exercise program did not.
cards.summary: Over 12 months: 172 falls in the LiFE group, 193 with structured exercise, 224 in controls. Fall rate 1.66 per person-year on LiFE vs 2.28 on control — a 31% reduction (incidence rate ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.48–0.99). The structured program's difference was not significant (IRR 0.81, 0.56–1.17).
cards.people: Adults aged 70+ at high risk of falling (two or more falls, or one injurious fall, in the previous year), randomized to LiFE, a structured exercise program, or control
cards.result: Over 12 months: 172 falls in the LiFE group, 193 with structured exercise, 224 in controls. Fall rate 1.66 per person-year on LiFE vs 2.28 on control — a 31% reduction (incidence rate ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.48–0.99). The structured program's difference was not significant (IRR 0.81, 0.56–1.17).
cards.watchOut: The lesson cuts both ways — 'exercise' is not one thing. Training embedded in daily life beat the same ingredients delivered as a program, in the same trial.
cards.source: Clemson L et al., BMJ 2012 (PMID 22872695)

cards.headline: Tinetti 1994: treating the risk factors themselves — medications, balance, gait, transfers — cut falling by a third. Its 2020 giant successor (Reference 2) could not repeat it on injuries.
cards.summary: Over 1 year, 35% of the intervention group fell vs 47% of controls (P=0.04); adjusted incidence-rate ratio 0.69 (95% CI 0.52–0.90). The targeted risk factors measurably improved — including fewer participants still on four or more prescription medications (63% vs 86% of controls).
cards.people: 301 community-dwelling men and women aged 70+ with at least one fall risk factor
cards.result: Over 1 year, 35% of the intervention group fell vs 47% of controls (P=0.04); adjusted incidence-rate ratio 0.69 (95% CI 0.52–0.90). The targeted risk factors measurably improved — including fewer participants still on four or more prescription medications (63% vs 86% of controls).
cards.watchOut: An efficacy trial with research staff and home visits — the direct ancestor of STRIDE's strategy, which makes STRIDE's null a story about delivery at scale, not about the idea.
cards.source: Tinetti ME et al., N Engl J Med 1994 (PMID 8078528; no registry ID — pre-registration era)

shelves.title: Exercise to prevent mobility disability: structured activity delays it — protein alone does not carry the effect
shelves.question: In frail, sarcopenic older adults, does a structured exercise-led program prevent mobility disability — and can a protein supplement do the job instead?
shelves.mesh: Frail Elderly · Frailty · Hand Strength · Independent Living · Sarcopenia
shelves.balance: Two large trials, one European and one American, converge — and both are re-cards: SPRINTT and LIFE live on Shelf #130, where they are counted; they are re-asked here because this shelf's question adds the decomposition. In SPRINTT's prespecified primary population (SPPB 3–7), mobility disability ran 46.8% vs 52.7% (HR 0.78, a relative effect, with the absolute rates beside it); LIFE found 30.1% vs 35.5% (HR 0.82, relative). The benefit concentrates in people already impaired — SPRINTT's less-impaired stratum was null. Then the null this shelf exists to print: protein without training does not carry the effect. Fiatarone's factorial trial more than doubled strength with resistance training (+113%) while the supplement showed no independent effect on any primary outcome; PROVIDE's leucine-and-vitamin-D whey raised lean mass slightly and improved the chair-stand test, while its primary outcomes — grip strength and SPPB — were null between groups. Muscle responds to load; the supplement is, at best, a supporting actor. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: SPRINTT (Bernabei 2022): mobility disability HR 0.78 in the impaired stratum (re-card; home: Shelf #130)
cards.summary: 1,519 frail, sarcopenic adults aged 70 or older: in the prespecified primary population (SPPB 3–7, n=1,205), mobility disability occurred in 46.8% on the multicomponent program vs 52.7% on healthy-aging education (HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.67–0.92 — a relative effect; 5.9 percentage points absolute). In the SPPB 8–9 stratum there was no benefit (HR 1.25). Serious adverse events 39.2% vs 36.0%. (Re-card; home: Shelf #130.)
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (SPRINTT), BMJ 2022. Re-card — home: Shelf #130
cards.people: 1,519 community-dwelling men and women aged 70 years or older with physical frailty and sarcopenia (Short Physical Performance Battery score 3–9 with low muscle mass) across 16 sites in 11 European countries. Re-card of the card homed on Shelf #130; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.result: In the primary population (SPPB 3–7), mobility disability occurred in 46.8% on intervention vs 52.7% on control (HR 0.78; 95% CI 0.67–0.92; P=0.005); persistent mobility disability was 21.0% vs 25.0% (HR 0.79; P=0.06). In the less-impaired stratum (SPPB 8–9, n=314), there was no benefit: 29.7% vs 23.9% (HR 1.25; 0.79–1.95).
cards.watchOut: Targeting is the message: the same program in the less-impaired stratum produced HR 1.25 — nothing. Prescribe the program to people whose function is already failing. Note the intervention bundled nutritional counselling with activity; separating exercise from protein is what Cards 3–4 of this shelf are for.
cards.source: Bernabei R et al. Multicomponent intervention to prevent mobility disability in frail older adults: randomised controlled trial (SPRINTT project). BMJ. 2022. PMID 35545258 · NCT02582138. DOI 10.1136/bmj-2021-068788

cards.headline: LIFE (Pahor 2014): structured activity — major mobility disability 30.1% vs 35.5% (re-card; home: Shelf #130)
cards.summary: 1,635 sedentary adults aged 70–89 followed a mean of 2.6 years: major mobility disability (loss of the ability to walk 400 m) occurred in 30.1% on structured physical activity vs 35.5% on health education (HR 0.82 — a relative effect; 5.4 percentage points absolute); persistent mobility disability HR 0.72. (Re-card; home: Shelf #130.)
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (the LIFE study), JAMA 2014. Re-card — home: Shelf #130
cards.people: 1,635 sedentary men and women aged 70 to 89 years who had physical limitations but could walk 400 m at entry, randomized to a structured moderate-intensity physical-activity program (walking, resistance, and flexibility training) or a health-education program. Re-card of the card homed on Shelf #130; counted once, at its home shelf.
cards.result: Major mobility disability occurred in 30.1% of the activity group vs 35.5% of the health-education group (HR 0.82; 95% CI 0.69–0.98; P=0.03). Persistent mobility disability was reduced further (HR 0.72; 0.57–0.91). Serious adverse events were not significantly increased.
cards.watchOut: LIFE remains the largest single demonstration that a prescribed activity program — supervised, dosed, sustained — delays disability, as distinct from advice to exercise. Neither LIFE nor SPRINTT showed a survival effect, and this shelf claims disability, not mortality. The evidence expires when the program stops.

cards.headline: Fiatarone 1994: the decomposition — resistance training +113% strength; the supplement, no independent effect
cards.summary: 100 frail nursing-home residents (mean age 87) in a 2×2 factorial trial: progressive resistance training increased muscle strength by 113% vs 3% without it (P<0.001), improved gait velocity (+11.8% vs −1.0%) and stair-climbing power. The multinutrient supplement had NO effect on any primary outcome measure.
cards.type: Randomized, placebo-controlled, 2×2 factorial trial, New England Journal of Medicine 1994
cards.people: 100 frail nursing-home residents (mean age 87.1 years; 63 women and 37 men; range 72–98), randomized over 10 weeks to progressive resistance exercise training, multinutrient supplementation, both, or neither; 94% completed the study.
cards.result: Muscle strength increased by 113 ± 8% in exercising subjects vs 3 ± 9% in nonexercisers (P<0.001); gait velocity and stair-climbing power improved with training, as did spontaneous physical activity. Thigh-muscle cross-sectional area rose 2.7% with exercise and fell 1.8% without (P=0.11). The nutritional supplement had no effect on any primary outcome; total energy intake rose significantly only in subjects who both exercised and received the supplement.
cards.watchOut: Small and old, and still the cleanest decomposition on the shelf: a factorial design is the one architecture that can separate the training from the feeding, and it assigns the functional effect to the training. Muscle remained trainable into the tenth decade — the limiting factor was never age.
cards.source: Fiatarone MA et al. Exercise training and nutritional supplementation for physical frailty in very elderly people. N Engl J Med. 1994. PMID 8190152. DOI 10.1056/NEJM199406233302501 (Pre-registration era — no registry number applies.)

cards.headline: PROVIDE (Bauer 2015): leucine-and-vitamin-D whey protein — primary outcomes null; a null finding, carded as one
cards.summary: 380 sarcopenic older adults, 13 weeks: handgrip strength and SPPB score — the primary outcomes — improved in BOTH groups with no significant between-group difference. The supplement group gained more appendicular muscle mass (+0.17 kg; P=0.045) and improved more on the chair-stand test (−1.01 seconds; P=0.018). Function primaries: null.
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (PROVIDE), Journal of the American Medical Directors Association 2015
cards.people: 380 sarcopenic, primarily independent-living older adults with Short Physical Performance Battery scores of 4–9 and a low skeletal muscle mass index: the enriched whey supplement twice daily (184) or an iso-caloric control product (196) for 13 weeks. (The abstract record does not print mean age or sex mix.)
cards.result: Handgrip strength and SPPB improved in both groups without significant between-group differences. The active group improved more in the chair-stand test (between-group effect −1.01 seconds; 95% CI −1.77 to −0.19; P=0.018) and gained more appendicular muscle mass (0.17 kg; 0.004–0.338; P=0.045).
cards.watchOut: This is the strongest fair test of the protein-alone hypothesis — an enriched, targeted supplement in genuinely sarcopenic patients — and its prespecified primary outcomes were null between groups. What moved (a fraction of a kilogram of lean mass, a second off the chair stand) are surrogates and secondary measures. The shelf therefore cards protein-alone as a null finding: not a certainty claim, a report — supplementation without training has not been shown to buy function.
cards.source: Bauer JM et al. shelves.title: Exercise to prevent falls in older adults — Otago
shelves.question: Does exercise — including the Otago home strength-and-balance programme — prevent falls in community-dwelling older adults?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Exercise Therapy · Family Practice · Female · Home Care Services · Humans · Muscle, Skeletal · New Zealand · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Postural Balance · Program Evaluation
shelves.balance: LIKELY — exercise reduces falls in community-dwelling older adults: the founding Otago trial in women aged 80+ cut the fall rate from 1.34 to 0.87 falls per year, the Otago meta-analysis gives a relative fall rate ratio of 0.68, and the Cochrane synthesis (high-certainty) gives a relative rate ratio of 0.77, equivalent on its illustrative absolute risks to 195 fewer falls per 1,000 people over a year. Balance-and-functional and multiple-type programmes work; walking, dance or resistance training alone are uncertain. A mortality signal in the small Otago meta-analysis is not relied on for this stamp. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Campbell 1997: the founding Otago home exercise trial cut falls in women aged 80+
cards.summary: Campbell 1997, the founding Otago trial (women 80+): 88 falls in the exercise group versus 152 in control over a year — mean rate 0.87 vs 1.34 falls per year; relative hazard 0.68 for recurrent falls and 0.61 for a first injurious fall.
cards.people: 233 women aged 80 years and older living in the community in Dunedin, New Zealand (116 exercise, 117 control with social visits); mean age not stated in the abstract beyond the 80+ entry criterion
cards.result: Over 1 year there were 88 falls in the exercise group vs 152 in the control group; mean fall rate 0.87 (SD 1.29) vs 1.34 (SD 1.93) falls per year (difference 0.47, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.90) — an absolute rate difference. Relative hazard for the first four falls was 0.68 (95% CI 0.52 to 0.90) and for a first fall with injury 0.61 (95% CI 0.39 to 0.97), both relative measures. Balance improved at 6 months (between-group difference in change 0.43, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.65).
cards.watchOut: Women aged 80+ only, one city, individually tailored physiotherapy-delivered home programme; effect in men and in younger/frailer groups comes from the later syntheses, not this trial.

shelves.title: Implants vs dentures: eating and nutrition in older adults
shelves.question: In edentulous older adults, do mandibular two-implant overdentures, compared with conventional complete dentures, improve eating/chewing ability, satisfaction, dietary intake and nutritional status?
shelves.mesh: Dental Prosthesis, Implant-Supported · Denture, Complete · Denture, Overlay · Diet · Humans · Mouth, Edentulous · Nutritional Status · Patient Satisfaction · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Serum Albumin, Human · Vitamin B 12
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — split by outcome: for chewing ability, comfort, stability and satisfaction, randomised evidence favours two-implant overdentures (LIKELY direction, though from small, short trials); for nutrition itself the stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence) — the one nutrition RCT found improvements within the implant group but no significant between-group differences, and a meta-analysis of 322 older adults found no significant difference in BMI, albumin or vitamin B12 change at 6 months. Implants make eating easier; that they make older adults better nourished is unproven. Proposed split stamp — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Awad 2003 RCT: implant overdentures beat conventional dentures on satisfaction and chewing at 2 months
cards.summary: Awad 2003 (60 edentulous adults, 65–75): mandibular two-implant overdentures beat conventional dentures on the primary outcome — general satisfaction at 2 months ( P=.001 ) — and on comfort, stability, chewing and oral-health quality of life. Small, short, and consistent.
cards.people: 60 edentulous subjects aged 65 to 75 years, randomised 30 to mandibular two-implant overdentures (with a maxillary conventional denture) and 30 to conventional dentures in both jaws; sex distribution not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: General satisfaction at 2 months post-delivery — the primary outcome — was significantly better with implant overdentures (P = .001), as were ratings of comfort, stability and ability to chew; oral health-related quality of life problems on the OHIP-EDENT were significantly fewer in the implant group. The abstract reports significance levels rather than the rating scores themselves, so no absolute score differences can be stated.
cards.watchOut: Two months is a very short horizon for a prosthesis decision, outcomes are subjective ratings in an unblinded comparison, and satisfaction/chewing are not measures of dietary intake or nutritional status.
cards.source: Awad MA et al. Int J Prosthodont. 2003 Jul–Aug. PMID 12956494. Registry ID: none in the PubMed record — no registry ID stated for this 2003 trial.

cards.headline: Morais 2003 RCT: nutrition markers improved within the implant group — but not versus conventional dentures
cards.summary: Morais 2003: within the implant group, albumin, B12, haemoglobin and body measures improved — but not versus the conventional-denture group . Within-group change is not a treatment effect, and this card is the shelf’s fence against quoting it as one.
cards.people: Edentulous subjects aged 65 to 75 years receiving mandibular two-implant overdentures (n = 30) or conventional complete dentures (n = 30), measured before and 6 months after treatment; sex distribution not stated in the abstract. cards.result: Within the implant group, significant improvements were detected in percent body fat (p = 0.011), skin-fold thickness (p < 0.05), waist circumference (decrease, p < 0.0001), waist-hip ratio (p = 0.001), serum albumin (p = 0.015), hemoglobin (p = 0.01) and vitamin B12 (p = 0.01). The abstract gives p-values rather than the marker values themselves, so no absolute changes can be stated.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis 2016: no significant nutritional advantage for overdentures at 6 months
cards.summary: The 2016 meta-analysis settles the between-group question at 6 months: BMI change −0.18 kg/m² [−0.52 to 0.16], no significant difference in albumin or B12 — no nutritional advantage shown .
cards.people: 8 studies involving 901 participants in the narrative appraisal; the meta-analysis pooled 322 participants aged 65 years or older from 3 studies; sex distribution not stated in the abstract.
cards.result: At 6 months, change in BMI did not differ significantly between overdenture and conventional denture (weighted mean difference -0.18 kg/m², 95% CI -0.52 to 0.16), and there was no significant difference in change in albumin or serum vitamin B12. shelves.title: Comprehensive geriatric assessment for older adults admitted to hospital
shelves.question: Does CGA on hospital wards increase the chance of older patients being alive and in their own homes later?
shelves.mesh: Comprehensive Health Care/methods · Emergencies · Frail Elderly · Geriatric Assessment/methods · Hospitalization · Independent Living/statistics & numerical data · Mortality
shelves.balance: LIKELY: The Ellis 2017 Cochrane synthesis of 29 trials (13,766 participants) found comprehensive geriatric assessment on hospital admission increased the chance of being alive and in one's own home at 3 to 12 months (risk ratio 1.06, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.10; high-certainty evidence) and reduced nursing-home admission (risk ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.89; high-certainty evidence), with little or no difference in mortality itself (risk ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.07) or dependence (0.97). The effect is small and it is an effect on where survivors live, not on survival — the stamp rests on the certainty and consistency of the evidence, not on a large ratio.

cards.headline: Ellis Cochrane 2017: CGA made patients more likely to be alive and in their own homes (risk ratio 1.06) and less likely to enter a nursing home (0.80) — mortality itself unchanged
cards.summary: Ellis Cochrane 2017: CGA raised the chance of being alive and in one's own home (risk ratio 1.06 [1.01 to 1.10], high-certainty) and cut nursing-home admission (0.80).
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, with cost-effectiveness analysis
cards.people: 29 randomised trials recruiting 13,766 participants across nine, mostly high-income countries, comparing inpatient CGA (on geriatric wards or by mobile teams) with usual care for older adults admitted to hospital, usually for acute care or inpatient rehabilitation; the abstract does not state a pooled mean age or sex mix (trial-level mean age range is not reported in the abstract).
cards.result: CGA increased the likelihood of being alive and in one's own home at 3 to 12 months' follow-up (risk ratio 1.06, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.10; 16 trials, 6,799 participants; high-certainty evidence) and decreased nursing-home admission at 3 to 12 months (risk ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.72 to 0.89; 14 trials, 6,285 participants; high-certainty evidence). It resulted in little or no difference in mortality at 3 to 12 months (risk ratio 1.00, 95% CI 0.93 to 1.07; 21 trials, 10,023 participants; high-certainty evidence) or dependence (risk ratio 0.97, 0.89 to 1.04). Cognitive-function results were low-certainty (standardised mean differences ranging from −0.22 to 0.35). Healthcare costs per participant averaged GBP 234 higher with CGA (95% CI −144 to 605; low-certainty evidence), and cost-effectiveness estimates were also low-certainty.
cards.watchOut: The headline ratio, 1.06, is small and sits well inside the 0.5–2.0 band: this is high-certainty evidence of a small effect on living at home, not a survival benefit — mortality's risk ratio is exactly 1.00. Whether ward-based CGA beats team-based CGA was underpowered.
cards.source: Ellis G et al. Comprehensive geriatric assessment for older adults admitted to hospital. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2017 Sep 12;9(9):CD006211. PMID: 28898390. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

shelves.title: Transitional care after hospital discharge in older adults
shelves.question: Do structured post-discharge interventions — Coleman's Care Transitions coaching and Naylor's APN-led transitional care — reduce readmissions in older adults?
shelves.mesh: Caregivers · Chronic Disease/therapy · Continuity of Patient Care/standards · Health Status · Patient Participation · Patient Readmission/statistics & numerical data · Case Management
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Three randomised trials of structured transitional care for older adults all reduced readmissions: Coleman's transition-coach model cut rehospitalisation at 30 days (8.3% vs 11.9%) and 90 days (16.7% vs 22.5%), Naylor's 1999 advanced-practice-nurse discharge-planning and home follow-up trial cut any readmission by 24 weeks (20.3% vs 37.1%), and Naylor's 2004 heart-failure trial delayed first readmission or death and nearly halved total costs. The interventions differ (coaching vs APN-led) and none could be blinded, but the direction is consistent across three trials and two decades.

cards.headline: Coleman 2006: a transition coach cut rehospitalisation at 30 days (8.3% vs 11.9%) and 90 days (16.7% vs 22.5%)
cards.summary: Coleman 2006: a transition coach cut rehospitalisation at 30 days ( 8.3% vs 11.9% ) and 90 days (16.7% vs 22.5%).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (behavioural intervention — unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 750 community-dwelling adults aged 65 years or older admitted to a large integrated delivery system hospital in Colorado with 1 of 11 selected conditions, randomised to the Care Transitions Intervention or usual care; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Intervention patients had lower rehospitalisation rates at 30 days (8.3 vs 11.9, P=.048) and at 90 days (16.7 vs 22.5, P=.04), and lower rates of rehospitalisation for the same condition that precipitated the index hospitalisation at 90 days (5.3 vs 9.8, P=.04) and at 180 days (8.6 vs 13.9, P=.046). The mean hospital costs were lower for intervention patients ($2058) vs controls ($2546) at 180 days (log-transformed P=.049).
cards.watchOut: Single health system, 2002–2003 era, and the 30-day difference only just reached significance (P=.048): the effect is real in this trial but modest in absolute terms (about 3.6 percentage points at 30 days).

shelves.title: Drug prophylaxis for postoperative delirium
shelves.question: Does prophylactic low-dose dexmedetomidine after surgery prevent delirium in older ICU patients (Su) — and does prophylactic haloperidol in at-risk older inpatients (Kalisvaart)?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic alpha-2 Receptor Agonists/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic/therapeutic use · China/epidemiology · Confusion/diagnosis,etiology,prevention & control · Critical Care/methods · Delirium/diagnosis,epidemiology,etiology,prevention & control · Dexmedetomidine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — prophylactic dexmedetomidine prevents postoperative delirium · LIKELY the null — haloperidol prophylaxis prevents it. Su 2016 (700 patients, double-blind) found delirium in 9% with overnight low-dose dexmedetomidine vs 23% with placebo (odds ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.22-0.54 — a relative measure, with the absolute rates beside it on the card). Kalisvaart 2005 (430 hip-surgery patients, double-blind) found delirium in 15.1% on haloperidol vs 16.5% on placebo (relative risk 0.91, 0.6-1.3) — no prevention, though delirium that occurred was less severe and shorter. One positive and one null, each from a single rigorous trial — hence LIKELY on both halves rather than a pooled claim. Multicomponent NON-drug prevention (the HELP programme) is home on Shelf #340 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Su 2016: overnight low-dose dexmedetomidine after non-cardiac surgery cut delirium from 23% to 9%
cards.summary: Su 2016: overnight low-dose dexmedetomidine after non-cardiac surgery cut delirium from 23% to 9% .
cards.people: 700 patients aged 65 years or older admitted to intensive care units after non-cardiac surgery at two tertiary-care hospitals in Beijing, China, randomly assigned to intravenous dexmedetomidine (350) or placebo (350); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The incidence of postoperative delirium during the first 7 postoperative days was 32 (9%) of 350 patients in the dexmedetomidine group (0.1 μg/kg per h, from ICU admission on the day of surgery until 0800 h on postoperative day 1) vs 79 (23%) of 350 in the placebo group (odds ratio 0.35, 95% CI 0.22-0.54; p<0.0001 — a relative measure). Hypertension was less frequent with dexmedetomidine (34 [10%] vs 62 [18%]; OR 0.50, 0.32-0.78; p=0.002), as was tachycardia (23 [7%] vs 48 [14%]; OR 0.44, 0.26-0.75; p=0.002). Occurrence of hypotension and bradycardia did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: One trial, one country, ICU-admitted patients only, and a single overnight infusion schedule: an odds ratio of 0.35 is an unusually large effect for delirium prevention and awaits independent replication at this dose.
cards.source: Su X et al. Dexmedetomidine for prevention of delirium in elderly patients after non-cardiac surgery: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2016;388(10054):1893-1902. PMID: 27542303. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the abstract states the study is registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, number ChiCTR-TRC-10000802.

cards.headline: Kalisvaart 2005: prophylactic haloperidol did not prevent delirium (15.1% vs 16.5%), though delirium was milder and shorter when it occurred
cards.summary: Kalisvaart 2005: prophylactic haloperidol did not prevent delirium (15.1% vs 16.5%), though delirium was milder and shorter when it occurred.
cards.people: 430 hip-surgery patients aged 70 years and older at risk for postoperative delirium at a large medical school-affiliated general hospital in Alkmaar, the Netherlands; haloperidol 1.5 mg/d or placebo was started preoperatively and continued for up to 3 days postoperatively, and proactive geriatric consultation was provided for all randomized patients; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The overall incidence of postoperative delirium was 15.8%. Delirium occurred in 15.1% of the haloperidol group vs 16.5% of placebo (relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.6-1.3 — inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid evidence of an effect, and non-significant). Among patients who developed delirium, the mean highest Delirium Rating Scale score was 14.4 vs 18.4 (mean difference 4.0, 95% CI 2.0-5.8; P<.001), delirium duration was 5.4 vs 11.8 days (mean difference 6.4 days, 4.0-8.0; P<.001), and mean hospital stay was 17.1 vs 22.6 days (mean difference 5.5 days; P<.001). No haloperidol-related side effects were noted.
cards.watchOut: The severity, duration and stay findings apply only to the minority who developed delirium (15.8% overall) — conditional, secondary outcomes in a null prevention trial, not a reason to give prophylactic haloperidol.

shelves.title: Cataract surgery timing and falls and fractures
shelves.question: Does prompt first-eye cataract surgery reduce falls and fractures in older women (Harwood) — and expedited second-eye surgery (Foss)?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/prevention & control,statistics & numerical data · Cataract/complications,physiopathology,psychology · Cataract Extraction/methods,statistics & numerical data · Depth Perception/physiology · Health Status · Visual Acuity/physiology · Cataract/complications,physiopathology
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — prompt first-eye cataract surgery reduces the rate of falling · POSSIBLE — prompt second-eye surgery does. Harwood 2005 (306 women over 70) found expedited first-eye surgery cut the fall rate by a relative 34% (rate ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.45-0.96), with fewer fractures (3% vs 8%). Foss 2006 (239 women) found a similar-sized point estimate for second-eye surgery (rate ratio 0.68) but with a confidence interval crossing 1 (0.39-1.19; P=0.18), so the second-eye half is stamped POSSIBLE. Both trials compared expedited surgery (approximately 4 weeks) with a routine 12-month wait, so they test timing, not surgery versus never operating.

cards.headline: Harwood 2005: expedited first-eye cataract surgery reduced the rate of falling by a relative 34% and fractures were fewer (3% vs 8%)
cards.summary: Harwood 2005: expedited first-eye cataract surgery reduced the rate of falling by a relative 34% and fractures were fewer (3% vs 8%).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (expedited vs routine-wait surgery — unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 306 women aged over 70, with cataract, randomised to expedited surgery (approximately 4 weeks) or routine surgery (12 months wait); falls were ascertained by diary, with follow up every 3 months for 12 months; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Over 12 months of follow up, 76 (49%) operated participants fell at least once, and 28 (18%) fell more than once; 69 (45%) unoperated participants fell at least once, 38 (25%) fell more than once. Rate of falling was reduced by a relative 34% in the operated group (rate ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.96, p=0.03). Corrected binocular acuity improved by 0.25 logMAR units (8% had acuity worse than 6/12 compared with 37% of controls). Four participants in the operated group had fractures (3%), compared with 12 (8%) in the control group (p=0.04). Activity, anxiety, depression, confidence, visual disability, and handicap all improved in the operated group compared with the control group.
cards.watchOut: Women only, one trial, and the comparator is a 12-month wait: the trial shows earlier surgery beats delayed surgery, and the fracture count is small (4 vs 12).
cards.source: Harwood RH et al. Falls and health status in elderly women following first eye cataract surgery: a randomised controlled trial. Br J Ophthalmol. 2005;89(1):53-59. PMID: 15615747. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Foss 2006: expedited second-eye surgery improved vision and confidence, but the fall-rate reduction was not significant (rate ratio 0.68, 0.39-1.19)
cards.summary: Foss 2006: expedited second-eye surgery improved vision and confidence, but the fall-rate reduction was not significant (rate ratio 0.68, relative).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (expedited vs routine-wait surgery — unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 239 women over 70, who had been referred to a hospital ophthalmology department, with one unoperated cataract, randomised to expedited (approximately 4 weeks) or routine (12 months wait) second-eye surgery; falls ascertained by diary, with follow-up every 3 months for 12 months; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Over 12 months follow-up, 48 (40%) operated participants fell at least once, 22 (18%) fell more than once; forty-one (34%) unoperated participants fell at least once, 22 (18%) fell more than once. shelves.title: Orthogeriatric co-management after hip fracture
shelves.question: Does comprehensive geriatric assessment delivered as orthogeriatric co-management improve mobility and outcomes after hip fracture versus usual orthopaedic care?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Comprehensive Health Care/economics,organization & administration · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Hip Fractures/economics,therapy · Hospital Units/organization & administration · Intention to Treat Analysis · Length of Stay
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — proposed pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C candidate: mortality claims appear in the co-management syntheses, which are home on another shelf and are not carded here). The one randomised trial carded on this shelf, Prestmo 2015 (397 home-dwelling patients aged 70 or older), found comprehensive geriatric care in a dedicated geriatric ward improved mobility at 4 months versus usual orthopaedic care (Short Physical Performance Battery 5.12 vs 4.38; between-group difference 0.74, 95% CI 0.18-1.30). The systematic review and meta-analysis of orthogeriatric collaboration models (Grigoryan 2014) — which reports the mortality associations behind this shelf's Tier C flag — is already carded on Shelf #342 and is pointed to, not re-carded, under the one-home rule. A single-centre RCT on a mobility endpoint caps this shelf at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Prestmo 2015: comprehensive geriatric care in a dedicated ward improved mobility 4 months after hip fracture (SPPB 5.12 vs 4.38)
cards.summary: Prestmo 2015: comprehensive geriatric care in a dedicated ward improved mobility 4 months after hip fracture (SPPB 5.12 vs 4.38). (Tier C candidate per the topic file — the wider co-management literature carries mortality claims; PROPOSED.)
cards.type: Prospective, single-centre, randomised, controlled trial (service model — unblindable; assessors only partly masked)
cards.people: 397 home-dwelling patients with hip fractures aged 70 years or older who were able to walk 10 m before their fracture, randomly assigned to comprehensive geriatric care in a dedicated geriatric ward (198) or usual orthopaedic care (199) at a single Norwegian centre; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome was mobility measured with the Short Physical Performance Battery (SPPB) 4 months after surgery. Mean SPPB scores at 4 months were 5.12 (SE 0.20) for comprehensive geriatric care and 4.38 (SE 0.20) for orthopaedic care (between-group difference 0.74, 95% CI 0.18-1.30, p=0.010). At 4 months, 174 patients remained in the comprehensive geriatric care group and 170 in the orthopaedic care group; the main reason for dropout was death. The trial also set out to compare the cost-effectiveness of the two care models.
cards.watchOut: Single centre, a mobility (not mortality) primary endpoint, and patients living in nursing homes were among those excluded — the frailest hip-fracture patients are outside this trial. This card makes no mortality claim.
cards.source: Prestmo A et al. Comprehensive geriatric care for patients with hip fractures: a prospective, randomised, controlled trial. Lancet. 2015;385(9978):1623-1633. PMID: 25662415. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00667914, from the record's databank fields.

shelves.question: Do structured advance-care-planning interventions — the PREPARE web programme (Sudore) and facilitated ACP in elderly inpatients (Detering) — increase documentation and goal-concordant care?

shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two randomised trials in different settings both moved their primary outcomes by large margins. PREPARE (Sudore 2018; 986 primary-care patients aged 55 or older) raised new advance care planning documentation at 15 months versus an easy-to-read advance directive alone (43.0% vs 33.1% unadjusted; adjusted 43.0% vs 32.0%). Detering 2010 (309 inpatients aged 80 or older) found that among patients who died, end of life wishes were known and followed in 86% with facilitated planning vs 30% with usual care. Documentation and concordance are process outcomes — neither trial shows a survival effect, and none is claimed.

cards.headline: Sudore 2018 (PREPARE): a patient-directed online programme plus easy-to-read directive raised ACP documentation to 43.0% vs 33.1%
cards.summary: Sudore 2018 (PREPARE): a patient-directed online programme plus easy-to-read directive raised ACP documentation to 43.0% vs 33.1% .
cards.type: Comparative efficacy randomized clinical trial (behavioural — unblindable by nature; staff were blinded for all follow-up measurements)
cards.people: 986 English-speaking or Spanish-speaking primary care patients 55 years or older with 2 or more chronic or serious illnesses at 4 safety-net primary-care clinics in San Francisco (603 women and 383 men); mean (SD) age 63.3 (6.4) years; 445 (45.1%) were Spanish speaking and 387 of 975 (39.7%) had limited health literacy, as stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Compared with the advance directive alone, PREPARE resulted in a higher rate of new advance care planning documentation at 15 months (unadjusted, 43.0% [207 of 481] vs 33.1% [167 of 505]; P<.001; adjusted, 43.0% vs 32.0%; P<.001) and higher self-reported advance care planning engagement (98.1% vs 89.5% achieving increased scores; P<.001). Results remained significant among English speakers and Spanish speakers. Retention was 85.9% (832 of 969) among survivors.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is an easy-to-read advance directive alone, not usual care with clinician involvement — the trial isolates the patient-facing tool's added effect; documentation is a process outcome, not proof that care at the end of life matched wishes.
cards.source: Sudore RL et al. Engaging Diverse English- and Spanish-Speaking Older Adults in Advance Care Planning: The PREPARE Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Intern Med. 2018;178(12):1616-1625. PMID: 30383086. Registry IDs: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01990235 and NCT02072941, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Detering 2010: facilitated advance care planning meant wishes were known and followed for 86% of patients who died, vs 30%
cards.summary: Detering 2010: facilitated advance care planning meant wishes were known and followed for 86% of patients who died, vs 30%.
cards.type: Prospective randomised controlled trial (behavioural — unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 309 legally competent medical inpatients aged 80 or more at a single university hospital in Melbourne, Australia, randomised to usual care or usual care plus facilitated advance care planning and followed for six months or until death; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: 154 of the 309 patients were randomised to advance care planning, 125 (81%) received advance care planning, and 108 (84%) expressed wishes or appointed a surrogate, or both. Of the 56 patients who died by six months, end of life wishes were known and followed in 25 of 29 (86%) in the intervention group compared with 8 of 27 (30%) in the control group (P<0.001). Family members of patients who died in the intervention group had significantly less stress (intervention 5, control 15; P<0.001), anxiety (intervention 0, control 3; P=0.02), and depression (intervention 0, control 5; P=0.002) than those of control patients, and patient and family satisfaction was higher in the intervention group.
cards.watchOut: Single centre, and the headline concordance outcome rests on the 56 patients who died — a small subset defined after randomisation; satisfaction and family outcomes are secondary.
cards.source: Detering KM et al. The impact of advance care planning on end of life care in elderly patients: randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2010;340:c1345. PMID: 20332506. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the abstract states trial registration Australian New Zealand clinical trials registry ACTRN12608000539336.
