cards.headline: Synthesis: getting wishes recorded and honoured works by both routes tested — LIKELY
cards.summary: Getting wishes recorded and honoured works by both routes tested — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Sudore 2018 (986 primary-care patients) and Detering 2010 (309 hospital inpatients aged 80 or older).
cards.result: Documentation: 43.0% vs 33.1% (PREPARE, against an active comparator). Concordance among patients who died: 86% vs 30% (Detering, against usual care). Two different interventions (a self-directed web programme; a trained facilitator) in two different populations (primary care, 55 or older; hospital inpatients, 80 or older) point the same way on getting wishes recorded and honoured — hence LIKELY on the process claim, with no claim about survival or quality of dying beyond the family-satisfaction findings on the Detering card.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was powered for, or reports, mortality or place-of-death outcomes; do not cite this shelf for those.

shelves.title: Supporting dementia caregivers
shelves.question: Do multicomponent caregiver interventions reduce burden and depression (REACH II) and delay nursing-home placement (Mittelman NYU)?
shelves.mesh: Caregivers/psychology · Cost of Illness · Dementia/nursing · Depression/etiology,prevention & control · Ethnicity · Institutionalization/statistics & numerical data · Self Care/psychology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two large randomised trials of multicomponent caregiver support, in different designs and populations, both met their primary aims. REACH II (642 caregivers across three ethnic groups) improved a composite quality-of-life indicator versus control calls (P<0.001 in Hispanic or Latino caregivers and P=0.037 in white caregivers, with a significant effect also in Black or African-American spouse caregivers) and lowered clinical depression prevalence (12.6% vs 22.7%). The NYU intervention (406 spouse caregivers) reduced the rate of nursing-home placement by a relative 28.3% (adjusted hazard ratio 0.717), a model-predicted median delay of 557 days. Behavioural interventions cannot be blinded, but two independent trials with concordant benefit support LIKELY.

cards.headline: Belle 2006 (REACH II): a structured multicomponent intervention improved caregiver quality of life and cut clinical depression (12.6% vs 22.7%)
cards.summary: Belle 2006 (REACH II): a structured multicomponent intervention improved caregiver quality of life and cut clinical depression (12.6% vs 22.7%).
cards.type: Randomized, controlled trial (behavioural — unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 642 in-home caregivers in 5 US cities — 212 Hispanic or Latino, 219 white or Caucasian, and 211 Black or African-American caregivers — and their care recipients with Alzheimer disease or related disorders, randomised within each racial or ethnic group to a structured multicomponent intervention (12 in-home and telephone sessions over 6 months) or to 2 brief check-in telephone calls; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome was a quality-of-life indicator comprising 6-month caregiver depression, burden, self-care, and social support and care recipient problem behaviors. Hispanic or Latino and white or Caucasian caregivers in the intervention group experienced significantly greater improvement in quality of life than those in the control group (P<0.001 and P=0.037, respectively); Black or African-American spouse caregivers also improved significantly more (P=0.003). Prevalence of clinical depression was lower among caregivers in the intervention group (12.6% vs 22.7%; P=0.001). There were no statistically significant differences in institutionalization at 6 months.
cards.watchOut: A single 6-month follow-up assessment and a composite primary outcome: the shelf claims quality-of-life and depression benefit, not delayed placement — that claim belongs to the NYU trial below.
cards.source: Belle SH et al. Enhancing the quality of life of dementia caregivers from different ethnic or racial groups: a randomized, controlled trial. Ann Intern Med. 2006;145(10):727-738. PMID: 17116917. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00177489, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Mittelman 2006 (NYU): counselling and support for spouse caregivers delayed nursing home placement — relative rate reduction 28.3%, model-predicted median 557 days
cards.summary: Mittelman 2006 (NYU): counselling and support for spouse caregivers delayed nursing home placement — relative rate reduction 28.3%.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (behavioural — unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 406 spouse caregivers of community-dwelling patients with Alzheimer disease, a referred volunteer sample enrolled over a 9.5-year period, randomised to an enhanced counseling and support intervention (six sessions of individual and family counseling, support group participation, and continuous availability of ad hoc telephone counseling) or usual care; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Patients whose spouses received the intervention experienced a 28.3% reduction in the rate of nursing home placement compared with usual care controls — a relative reduction (hazard ratio 0.717 after covariate adjustment, p=0.025; the abstract gives no absolute placement rates). The difference in model-predicted median time to placement was 557 days. Improvements in caregivers' satisfaction with social support, response to patient behavior problems, and symptoms of depression collectively accounted for 61.2% of the intervention's beneficial impact on placement.
cards.watchOut: Volunteer spouse caregivers at a single academic programme, enrolled over 9.5 years: motivated participants and an intensive, continuously available intervention limit how far the 557-day figure generalises. The hazard ratio of 0.717 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 band this library does not treat as solid evidence on its own, so the claim rests on the trial's design and the concordant REACH II result, not on the ratio alone.
cards.source: Mittelman MS et al. Improving caregiver well-being delays nursing home placement of patients with Alzheimer disease. Neurology. 2006;67(9):1592-1599. PMID: 17101889. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: support the caregiver and both caregiver health and time at home improve — LIKELY
cards.summary: Support the caregiver and both caregiver health and time at home improve — LIKELY.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Belle 2006 (REACH II, 642 caregivers) and Mittelman 2006 (NYU, 406 spouse caregivers).
cards.result: REACH II: better caregiver quality of life and less clinical depression at 6 months (12.6% vs 22.7%), no placement effect at 6 months. NYU: placement delayed over long follow-up (hazard ratio 0.717 after adjustment; model-predicted median difference 557 days). Together they support support-first care for dementia caregivers — benefit to the caregiver in both trials, and delayed institutionalisation where follow-up was long enough to see it. Patient-directed dementia drug and cognition shelves are a different question and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate current dementia-care models; the interventions are staff-intensive, and effects depend on actually delivering the sessions.
cards.source: Synthesis of Belle SH et al. Ann Intern Med. 2006;145(10):727-738. PMID: 17116917; Mittelman MS et al. Neurology. 2006;67(9):1592-1599. PMID: 17101889. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Preventing pressure injuries: repositioning and support surfaces
shelves.question: Can nursing-home residents at moderate/high risk be repositioned every 4 hours instead of 2 (TURN) — and do alternating-pressure mattresses beat overlays in hospital (PRESSURE 2)?
shelves.mesh: Beds/adverse effects,standards · Equipment Design · Equipment Failure · Incidence · Nursing Homes/supply & distribution · Ontario/epidemiology · Pressure Ulcer/epidemiology,etiology,nursing
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — repositioning every 3–4 hours is as safe as every 2 hours on a high-density foam mattress · MAYBE (weak evidence) — alternating-pressure mattresses prevent pressure ulcers better than high-specification foam. TURN (942 nursing-home residents) found pressure-ulcer incidence of 2.5%, 0.6% and 3.1% on 2-, 3- and 4-hourly schedules with no significant difference (P=.68) — one large trial, hence POSSIBLE for the no-difference claim. PRESSURE 2 (2,029 hospital patients) found insufficient evidence of a difference in time to a new category 2 or worse ulcer (hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.56-1.04; P=0.089 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, non-significant on its primary analysis), with a small benefit only in a treatment-phase sensitivity analysis — hence MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Bergstrom 2013 (TURN): on high-density foam mattresses, repositioning every 3 or 4 hours caused no more pressure ulcers than every 2 hours
cards.summary: Bergstrom 2013 (TURN): on high-density foam mattresses, repositioning every 3 or 4 hours caused no more pressure ulcers than every 2 hours.
cards.type: Multisite, randomized clinical trial (nursing schedule — blinded outcome assessors)
cards.people: 942 consenting residents aged 65 years or older without pressure ulcers, at moderate (Braden scores 13-14) or high (scores 10-12) risk of pressure ulcers, in 20 nursing homes in the United States and 7 in Canada using high-density foam mattresses, randomly allocated to a repositioning schedule (2, 3, or 4 hour) for 3 weeks; participants were mostly female (77.6%) and Caucasian (80.5%) and had a mean age of 85.1 (SD 7.7) years, as stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Nineteen (2.0%) participants developed superficial pressure ulcers. There was no significant difference in pressure-ulcer incidence according to repositioning group (2 hour, 8/321, 2.5%; 3 hour, 2/326, 0.6%; 4 hour, 9/295, 3.1%; P=.68), nor between the high and moderate-risk groups (P=.79); incidence also did not differ significantly by schedule within the high-risk participants (P=.90) or the moderate-risk participants (P=.68). Blinded assessors assessed skin weekly.
cards.watchOut: Only 19 events over 3 weeks: the trial rules out a large penalty for longer intervals on these mattresses, but cannot exclude small differences, and it does not apply to residents on other support surfaces.
cards.source: Bergstrom N et al. Turning for Ulcer ReductioN: a multisite randomized clinical trial in nursing homes. J Am Geriatr Soc. 2013;61(10):1705-1713. PMID: 24050454. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Nixon 2019 (PRESSURE 2): alternating-pressure mattresses vs high-specification foam — primary analysis inconclusive (HR 0.76, 0.56-1.04)
cards.summary: Nixon 2019 (PRESSURE 2): alternating-pressure mattresses vs high-specification foam — primary analysis inconclusive (hazard ratio 0.76, relative).
cards.type: Multicentre, Phase III, open, prospective, parallel group, randomised controlled trial with health economic evaluation
cards.people: 2,029 high risk (acutely ill, bedfast/chairfast and/or Category 1 pressure ulcer or pain at a pressure-ulcer site) adult in-patients in 42 UK secondary/community in-patient facilities, randomised (1:1) to alternating pressure mattresses (1,016) or high specification foam (1,013) for a maximum treatment phase of 60 days; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Of the 2,029 patients, 160 (7.9%) developed new pressure ulcers. For the primary outcome — time to development of a new pressure ulcer of Category 2 or worse, to 30 days post-treatment — there was insufficient evidence of a difference between groups (Fine and Gray hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.56-1.04; P=0.0890; absolute difference 2%; the hazard ratio is a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band). A treatment-phase time-to-event sensitivity analysis did reach significance (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.46-0.93; P=0.0176; 2.6% absolute difference). Economic analyses indicate that alternating pressure mattresses are cost-effective. There were no safety concerns.
cards.watchOut: Open trial, a low event rate limiting power, and the significant result is a sensitivity analysis rather than the primary endpoint — the honest headline is 'not proven on the primary analysis', which is why this half of the shelf is MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.source: Nixon J et al. Pressure Relieving Support Surfaces for Pressure Ulcer Prevention (PRESSURE 2): Clinical and Health Economic Results of a Randomised Controlled Trial. EClinicalMedicine. 2019;14:42-52. PMID: 31709401. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the abstract states trial registration ISRCTN 01151335.

cards.headline: Synthesis: turning dogma and mattress dogma both outrun their trial evidence
cards.summary: Turning dogma and mattress dogma both outrun their trial evidence — split POSSIBLE / MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Bergstrom 2013 (TURN, 942 nursing-home residents) and Nixon 2019 (PRESSURE 2, 2,029 hospital inpatients).
cards.result: Repositioning: 2-hourly turning is not supported as necessary on high-density foam — incidence 2.5% (2-hourly), 0.6% (3-hourly), 3.1% (4-hourly), no significant difference (TURN). Surfaces: alternating-pressure mattresses are not proven superior to high-specification foam on the primary analysis (hazard ratio 0.76, 0.56-1.04; PRESSURE 2). The practical reading is that schedule and surface dogma both outrun their trial evidence.
cards.watchOut: TURN's residents were all on high-density foam; combining 'turn less often' with an untested surface goes beyond either trial.

shelves.title: Screening for osteoporosis with FRAX
shelves.question: Does community screening with FRAX (with DXA for the high-risk band) reduce hip fractures versus usual care (SCOOP; ROSE)?
shelves.mesh: Community Health Services · Hip Fractures/diagnosis,epidemiology,prevention & control · Mass Screening · Osteoporotic Fractures/diagnosis,epidemiology,prevention & control · Proportional Hazards Models · Risk Assessment · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — FRAX-based community screening reduces hip fractures (SCOOP) · POSSIBLE the null — two-step FRAX screening reduces fractures overall (ROSE). SCOOP (12,483 women aged 70-85) missed its primary outcome (all osteoporosis-related fractures: hazard ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.85-1.03) but reduced hip fractures (HR 0.72, 0.59-0.89 — a relative measure; the abstract gives no absolute hip-fracture rates). ROSE (34,229 women aged 65-80) found no significant overall reduction in fractures on intention-to-treat analysis, with benefit only in per-protocol analyses of women who were FRAX-positive and accepted DXA (hip fracture adjusted subhazard ratio 0.741). Two large trials, discordant at the whole-population level — each half is stamped POSSIBLE. Treatment of established osteoporosis is a different question and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Shepstone 2018 (SCOOP): FRAX-based community screening did not reduce all fractures (HR 0.94) but did reduce hip fractures (HR 0.72)
cards.summary: Shepstone 2018 (SCOOP): FRAX-based community screening did not reduce all fractures (hazard ratio 0.94, relative) but did reduce hip fractures (hazard ratio 0.72, relative).
cards.type: Two-arm randomised controlled trial (screening strategy — unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 12,483 women aged 70-85 years recruited from 100 general practitioner (GP) practices in seven regions of the UK and randomly assigned to a screening programme using the Fracture Risk Assessment Tool (FRAX) (6,233 women) or usual management, excluding women currently on prescription anti-osteoporotic drugs; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Over a 5-year period, screening did not reduce the primary outcome of one or more osteoporosis-related fractures (hazard ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.85-1.03, p=0.178), nor the overall incidence of all clinical fractures (0.94, 0.86-1.03, p=0.183), but screening reduced the incidence of hip fractures (0.72, 0.59-0.89, p=0.002 — relative measures throughout). Treatment was recommended in 898 (14%) of 6,233 women in the screening group; use of osteoporosis medication was higher at the end of year 1 in the screening group compared with controls (15% vs 4%), with uptake of 78% at 6 months in the screening high-risk subgroup. There was no evidence of differences in mortality, anxiety levels, or quality of life.
cards.watchOut: The hip-fracture result is a prespecified secondary outcome under a null primary endpoint, and the abstract reports no absolute hip-fracture rates — read 0.72 as a relative effect of a screening-and-treatment pathway, not of FRAX alone.
cards.source: Shepstone L et al. Screening in the community to reduce fractures in older women (SCOOP): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2018;391(10122):741-747. PMID: 29254858. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the abstract states the trial is registered with the International Standard Randomised Controlled Trial registry, number ISRCTN 55814835.

cards.headline: Rubin 2018 (ROSE): two-step FRAX screening showed no overall fracture reduction; benefit appeared only in women who completed DXA
cards.summary: Rubin 2018 (ROSE): two-step FRAX screening showed no overall fracture reduction; benefit appeared only in women who completed DXA.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (screening strategy — unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 34,229 women aged 65-80 years in Denmark included in intention-to-treat analyses, randomized to a two-step screening program (self-administered FRAX questionnaire, with women scoring 15% or more for major osteoporotic fractures invited to a DXA scan, then standard osteoporosis management) or to an office-based case-finding control strategy; a total of 3,416 fractures were observed during a median follow-up of 5 years; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: No significant differences were found in the intention-to-treat analyses for incident clinical fractures. The per-protocol analyses showed a risk reduction in the group that underwent DXA scanning compared to women in the control group with a FRAX of 15% or more, with regard to major osteoporotic fractures, hip fractures, and all fractures; the risk reduction was most pronounced for hip fractures (adjusted subhazard ratio 0.741, p=0.007 — a relative measure).
cards.watchOut: Per-protocol analyses compare women who complied with DXA against the whole control group and are subject to healthy-complier bias: they show the pathway can work in women who complete it, not that offering it reduces fractures — the intention-to-treat null governs the shelf.
cards.source: Rubin KH et al. Effectiveness of a two-step population-based osteoporosis screening program using FRAX: the randomized Risk-stratified Osteoporosis Strategy Evaluation (ROSE) study. Osteoporos Int. 2018;29(3):567-578. PMID: 29218381. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

shelves.title: Preventing falls in care homes
shelves.question: Does a multifactorial falls-prevention programme (staff training, assessment, exercise components) reduce falls in care-home residents — the FinCH trial?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/economics,prevention & control,statistics & numerical data · Activities of Daily Living · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Health Plan Implementation/economics,organization & administration,statistics & numerical data · Homes for the Aged/economics,organization & administration,statistics & numerical data · Quality-Adjusted Life Years · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — the GtACH programme reduced falls in UK care homes · POSSIBLE the null — care-facility falls interventions in general. FinCH (1,657 residents, 84 care homes, cluster randomised) found the Guide to Action for Care Homes programme cut the fall rate in its primary window (91-180 days after randomisation) to an unadjusted incidence rate ratio of 0.57 (95% CI 0.45-0.71 — a relative measure; rates were six falls per 1,000 residents vs 10 per 1,000). The wider trial base is weaker: the Cameron 2018 Cochrane review of 95 trials found multifactorial interventions in care facilities uncertain for rate of falls (rate ratio 0.88, 0.66-1.18, very low-quality evidence) and exercise uncertain (0.93, 0.72-1.20). One well-run large programme trial against an uncertain class literature — the programme earns LIKELY, the class only POSSIBLE the null. Community falls prevention is home on Shelf #161 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Logan 2021 (FinCH): the GtACH multifactorial programme cut care-home falls (rate ratio 0.57; six vs ten falls per 1,000 residents)
cards.summary: Logan 2021 (FinCH): the GtACH multifactorial programme cut care-home falls (rate ratio 0.57, relative; six vs ten falls per 1,000 residents).
cards.type: Multicentre, parallel, cluster randomised controlled trial with economic evaluation (programme — unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 1,657 consenting residents in 84 UK long term care homes registered to care for older people or those with dementia (39 homes randomised to the intervention and 45 to usual care); mean age of residents was 85 years and 32% were men, as stated in the abstract.
cards.result: The primary outcome was fall rate at 91-180 days after randomisation; primary outcome data were available for 630 participants in the GtACH group and 712 in the usual care group. The unadjusted incidence rate ratio for falls between 91 and 180 days was 0.57 (95% CI 0.45 to 0.71, P<0.001) in favour of the GtACH programme — a relative measure — with rates of six falls/1000 residents in the GtACH group vs ten falls/1000 residents with usual care. GtACH training was delivered to 1,051 of 1,480 staff (71%). Barthel index scores and Physical Activity Measure-Residential Care Homes scores were similar between groups at all time points. The incremental cost was £108 (95% CI -£271.06 to 487.58); incremental cost per QALY was £4,544 (EQ-5D-5L-P based) and £20,889 (DEMQOL-P-U based).
cards.watchOut: The primary window is days 91-180 specifically (an effect measured after training bedded in), training reached 71% of staff, and results come from UK care homes with consenting residents.
cards.source: Logan PA et al. Multifactorial falls prevention programme compared with usual care in UK care homes for older people: multicentre cluster randomised controlled trial with economic evaluation. BMJ. 2021;375:e066991. PMID: 34876412. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the abstract states ISRCTN34353836.

cards.headline: Cameron 2018 (Cochrane): across 95 trials, exercise and multifactorial interventions in care facilities were uncertain for fall rates
cards.summary: Cameron 2018 (Cochrane, pinned at build): across 95 trials, exercise and multifactorial interventions in care facilities were uncertain for fall rates.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Cochrane review)
cards.people: 95 trials (138,164 participants) — 71 trials (40,374 participants; mean age 84 years; 75% women) in care facilities and 24 trials (97,790 participants; mean age 78 years; 52% women) in hospitals, searched to August 2017, as stated in the abstract.
cards.result: In care facilities, exercise was uncertain for rate of falls (rate ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.20; 2,002 participants, 10 studies; I²=76%; very low-quality evidence) and may make little or no difference to the risk of falling (risk ratio 1.02, 0.88 to 1.18; 2,090 participants, 10 studies; low-quality evidence). Multifactorial interventions were uncertain for rate of falls (rate ratio 0.88, 0.66 to 1.18; 3,439 participants, 10 studies; I²=84%; very low-quality evidence) and may make little or no difference to the risk of falling (risk ratio 0.92, 0.81 to 1.05; 3,153 participants, 9 studies; low-quality evidence). Vitamin D supplementation probably reduced the rate of falls (rate ratio 0.72, 0.55 to 0.95; 4,512 participants, 4 studies; moderate-quality evidence) in a population with low vitamin D levels, but probably made little or no difference to the risk of falling (0.92, 0.76 to 1.12). The majority of trials were at high risk of bias in one or more domains, mostly relating to lack of blinding.
cards.watchOut: A 2018 review of mostly small, high-bias-risk trials: its uncertainty is about the class as tested then — it predates FinCH and does not contradict a single well-implemented programme working.
cards.source: Cameron ID et al. Interventions for preventing falls in older people in care facilities and hospitals. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018;9(9):CD005465. PMID: 30191554. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a specific trained programme worked in care homes; the generic class evidence stays uncertain
cards.summary: A specific trained programme worked in care homes (LIKELY); the generic class evidence stays uncertain (POSSIBLE the null).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Logan 2021 (FinCH, 1,657 residents, 84 care homes) and Cameron 2018 (Cochrane review, 95 trials).
cards.result: FinCH's GtACH programme: fall rate ratio 0.57 (95% CI 0.45-0.71) in its primary window, cost-effective on the EQ-5D-5L-P measure, with no decrease in activity or increase in dependency. The pre-FinCH class literature (Cameron): rate ratios of 0.88-0.93 with wide intervals and low or very low quality ratings. The shelf's claim is narrow — a specific, trained, multifactorial programme worked in UK care homes — not that any falls bundle works anywhere. Community-dwelling falls prevention (exercise and the STRIDE-era multifactorial trials) is home on Shelf #161 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: FinCH is one trial of one programme; a second trial of the GtACH programme itself would be needed before the class claim could rise.

shelves.title: Geriatric assessment before surgery
shelves.question: Does preoperative comprehensive geriatric assessment and optimization (POPS) reduce complications and length of stay in older patients undergoing elective surgery?
shelves.mesh: Geriatric Assessment/methods · Length of Stay · Postoperative Complications/mortality,prevention & control · Preoperative Care/methods,mortality · Vascular Surgical Procedures/methods,mortality · Delirium/diagnosis,epidemiology,prevention & control · Elective Surgical Procedures
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — preoperative comprehensive geriatric assessment and optimisation shortens hospital stay · POSSIBLE the null — a geriatric liaison intervention prevents postoperative delirium. Partridge 2017 (POPS; 176 vascular-surgery patients) found geometric mean length of stay 3.32 vs 5.53 days (ratio of geometric means 0.60, 95% CI 0.46-0.79) with fewer delirium, cardiac and bladder/bowel complications — one single-centre trial, so POSSIBLE. Hempenius 2013 (260 frail older cancer-surgery patients, multicentre) found no significant delirium prevention from a geriatric liaison intervention (9.4% vs 14.3%; odds ratio 0.63, 0.29-1.35) — a null from a modest-sized trial, so POSSIBLE the null. Comprehensive geriatric assessment for medical admissions is home on Shelf #605 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Partridge 2017 (POPS): preoperative CGA and optimisation cut geometric mean stay from 5.53 to 3.32 days in older vascular-surgery patients
cards.summary: Partridge 2017 (POPS): preoperative CGA and optimisation cut geometric mean stay from 5.53 to 3.32 days in older vascular-surgery patients.
cards.type: Randomized clinical trial (service intervention — unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 176 patients aged at least 65 years scheduled for elective aortic aneurysm repair or lower-limb arterial surgery included in the final analysis (control 91, intervention 85), enrolled in an RCT of standard preoperative assessment or preoperative comprehensive geriatric assessment and optimization, with randomization stratified by sex and surgical site; the abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Geometric mean length of hospital stay was 5.53 days in the control group and 3.32 days in the intervention group (ratio of geometric means 0.60, 95% CI 0.46 to 0.79; P<0.001). There was a lower incidence of delirium (11 vs 24 per cent; P=0.018), cardiac complications (8 vs 27 per cent; P=0.001) and bladder/bowel complications (33 vs 55 per cent; P=0.003) in the intervention group compared with the control group. Patients in the intervention group were less likely to require discharge to a higher level of dependency (4 of 85 vs 12 of 91; P=0.051).
cards.watchOut: Single-centre, 176 patients, vascular surgery only, and several secondary outcomes: the length-of-stay result is the primary endpoint and is solid for this population; the complication differences are secondary.
cards.source: Partridge JS et al. Randomized clinical trial of comprehensive geriatric assessment and optimization in vascular surgery. Br J Surg. 2017;104(6):679-687. PMID: 28198997. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the abstract states Registration number: ISRCTN23142588.

cards.headline: Hempenius 2013: a geriatric liaison intervention did not significantly prevent postoperative delirium in frail elderly cancer patients (9.4% vs 14.3%)
cards.summary: Hempenius 2013 (pinned at build): a geriatric liaison intervention did not significantly prevent postoperative delirium in frail elderly cancer patients (9.4% vs 14.3%).
cards.type: Multicentre, prospective, randomized, controlled trial (service intervention — unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 260 patients over 65 years of age undergoing elective surgery for a solid tumour, recruited to a multicentre, prospective, randomized, controlled trial of standard treatment versus a geriatric liaison intervention (preoperative geriatric consultation, an individual treatment plan targeted at risk factors for delirium, daily visits by a geriatric nurse, and advice on managing problems); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Data of 260 patients were analysed. Delirium occurred in 31 patients (11.9%), and there was no significant difference between the incidence of delirium in the intervention group and the usual-care group (9.4% vs 14.3%, odds ratio 0.63, 95% CI 0.29-1.35 — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band and non-significant). Secondary outcome measures were the severity of delirium, length of hospital stay, complications, mortality, care dependency, quality of life, return to an independent preoperative living situation and additional care at home.
cards.watchOut: Only 31 delirium events: the trial cannot exclude a moderate preventive effect, which is why the null is stamped POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY.
cards.source: Hempenius L et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: preoperative optimisation shortened stay; liaison for delirium prevention did not significantly prevent delirium
cards.summary: Preoperative optimisation shortened stay (POSSIBLE); liaison for delirium prevention did not significantly prevent delirium (POSSIBLE the null).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Partridge 2017 (POPS, 176 vascular-surgery patients) and Hempenius 2013 (260 frail elderly cancer-surgery patients).
cards.result: Assessment-and-optimisation before vascular surgery shortened stay (ratio of geometric means 0.60, 0.46-0.79) and cut complications (POPS); a liaison model aimed chiefly at delirium prevention in cancer surgery did not significantly prevent delirium (odds ratio 0.63, 0.29-1.35; Hempenius). shelves.title: Structured medication review for older adults with polypharmacy (OPERAM and SPPiRE)
shelves.question: In multimorbid older adults taking many medicines, does a structured, team-based medication review reduce drug-related hospital admissions versus usual care — and what did the primary-care SPPiRE programme find on potentially inappropriate prescribing?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/statistics & numerical data · Cluster Analysis · Europe · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Inappropriate Prescribing/adverse effects,prevention & control · Multimorbidity · Polypharmacy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference on admissions, with only small prescribing effects): The large hospital-based OPERAM cluster trial (2,008 inpatients aged 70 or older) found no effect of structured pharmacotherapy optimisation on first drug-related hospital admission (21.9% vs 22.4%; hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.17), and no effect on falls or death. The primary-care SPPiRE cluster trial (404 patients on 15 or more medicines) trimmed the number of medicines slightly (incidence rate ratio 0.95) but showed no significant effect on having at least one potentially inappropriate prescription. Structured review tidies prescribing a little; on this evidence it does not keep people out of hospital.

cards.headline: OPERAM 2021: structured pharmacotherapy optimisation did not reduce drug-related hospital admissions (21.9% vs 22.4%; HR 0.95)
cards.summary: OPERAM (2021): structured pharmacotherapy optimisation did not reduce drug-related hospital admissions ( 21.9% vs 22.4% ; HR 0.95), despite inappropriate prescribing in 86.1% of participants.
cards.type: Cluster randomised controlled trial (110 inpatient-ward clusters, four European countries)
cards.people: 2,008 older adults aged 70 years or older with multimorbidity (at least 3 chronic conditions) and polypharmacy (at least 5 long-term drugs; median nine drugs), randomised by ward cluster in university hospitals in Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium and Ireland: 963 participants in 54 intervention clusters and 1,045 in 56 usual-care clusters. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Inappropriate prescribing was present in 86.1% of intervention participants (mean 2.75 STOPP/START recommendations each), and 62.2% had at least one recommendation implemented by two months. Despite that, a first drug-related hospital admission occurred in 211 participants (21.9%) in the intervention group versus 234 (22.4%) in the control group; the hazard ratio for first drug-related hospital admission was 0.95 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.17) in the intention-to-treat analysis censored for death, and 0.91 (0.69 to 1.19) per protocol. The hazard ratio for first fall was 0.96 (0.79 to 1.15; 237 vs 263 first falls) and for death 0.90 (0.71 to 1.13; 172 vs 203 deaths) — neither significant. The hazard ratios all sit inside the 0.5–2.0 band and are not solid evidence of benefit on their own; here they are also null.
cards.watchOut: A hospital-inpatient intervention at discharge, with only about three-fifths of recommendations implemented: it tests this optimisation package as delivered, not every possible medication-review model.
cards.source: Blum MR et al. Optimizing Therapy to Prevent Avoidable Hospital Admissions in Multimorbid Older Adults (OPERAM): cluster randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2021;374:n1585. PMID: 34257088. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02986425, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: SPPiRE 2022: GP-delivered medication review cut medicine counts slightly (IRR 0.95) but did not significantly reduce potentially inappropriate prescriptions
cards.summary: SPPiRE (2022): GP-delivered medication review cut medicine counts slightly (IRR 0.95 ) but did not significantly reduce potentially inappropriate prescribing.
cards.type: Cluster randomised controlled trial (51 general practices, Ireland)
cards.people: 404 community-dwelling patients aged 65 years or older with complex multimorbidity, defined as being prescribed 15 or more regular medicines (mean 17.37, SD 3.50, at baseline), recruited across 51 GP practices in the Republic of Ireland (26 intervention, 25 control) and followed to six months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At six months both groups had fewer medicines, with a small but significantly greater reduction in the intervention group (incidence rate ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.899 to 0.999; P=0.045). There was no significant effect on the odds of having at least one potentially inappropriate prescription (odds ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.140 to 1.064; P=0.066 — a relative figure whose confidence interval crosses 1). There was no evidence of harm: adverse events recorded included mortality, emergency-department presentations and adverse drug withdrawal events, and fewer than 2% of drug withdrawals in the intervention group led to a reported withdrawal event.
cards.watchOut: Primary outcomes were measured at just two time points because data could not be extracted electronically — the authors name this the main limitation. The medicine-count effect (5% relative) is small at individual level.
cards.source: McCarthy C et al. GP-delivered medication review of polypharmacy, deprescribing, and patient priorities in older people with multimorbidity in Irish primary care (SPPiRE Study): A cluster randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Synthesis: review improves the prescription list a little, not the admission count — LIKELY no admission benefit
cards.summary: Review improves the prescription list a little, not the admission count — LIKELY (no admission benefit).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: OPERAM (2,008 hospital inpatients aged 70 or older, four European countries) and SPPiRE (404 primary-care patients aged 65 or older on 15 or more medicines, Ireland).
cards.result: The two settings agree on the shape of the answer: these programmes find a great deal of inappropriate prescribing (86.1% of OPERAM participants) and can reduce it somewhat, and SPPiRE trimmed total medicine counts by a relative 5%, yet OPERAM's patient-level outcome — drug-related hospital admission, 21.9% vs 22.4% — did not move, and SPPiRE's inappropriate-prescription endpoint was not significant. That is why the stamp is LIKELY for the null on admissions rather than a benefit claim built on process measures. This shelf is about structured review as the intervention: antihypertensive deprescribing lives on Shelf #132 and benzodiazepine deprescribing on Shelf #500, and neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial was powered or designed to test mortality, and neither showed a mortality difference; do not cite this shelf for or against a survival effect of medication review.

shelves.title: Droxidopa for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
shelves.question: Does droxidopa improve orthostatic symptoms and standing blood pressure in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (Parkinson disease, autonomic failure) versus placebo — in the pivotal phase 3 trial and in the randomised withdrawal study of responders?
shelves.mesh: Autonomic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Autonomic Nervous System Diseases/complications,drug therapy · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Dizziness/drug therapy · Droxidopa/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Hypotension, Orthostatic/drug therapy,etiology · Multiple System Atrophy/complications,drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: In the pivotal phase 3 trial, patients who had already responded to open-label droxidopa improved more on droxidopa than placebo over seven days on the Orthostatic Hypotension Questionnaire composite (by 0.90 units, P=0.003), with standing systolic pressure up 11.2 vs 3.9 mm Hg. But the randomised withdrawal study in responders failed its primary endpoint — dizziness/lightheadedness worsened by 1.9 units on placebo vs 1.3 on continued droxidopa (P=0.509) — with only secondary and post-hoc composite scores favouring the drug. Short-term symptomatic benefit in selected responders is plausible; durability is unproven, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Kaufmann 2014: in open-label responders, droxidopa beat placebo over 7 days on symptoms (OHQ composite by 0.90 units) and standing systolic pressure
cards.summary: Droxidopa trial (2014): in open-label responders, droxidopa beat placebo over 7 days on symptoms (OHQ composite by 0.90 units ) and standing systolic pressure.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial with open-label dose optimisation and washout before randomisation (enriched responder design)
cards.people: 162 patients with symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension due to Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, pure autonomic failure or nondiabetic autonomic neuropathy were randomised after open-label droxidopa titration (100–600 mg three times daily) and a 7-day washout, to 7 days of droxidopa or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Improvement in mean Orthostatic Hypotension Questionnaire (OHQ) composite score favoured droxidopa over placebo by 0.90 units (P=0.003); the symptom subscore favoured droxidopa by 0.73 units (P=0.010, largest change in dizziness/lightheadedness) and the symptom-impact subscore by 1.06 units (P=0.003, largest change for standing a long time). Mean standing systolic blood pressure increased by 11.2 vs 3.9 mm Hg (P<0.001), and mean supine systolic pressure by 7.6 vs 0.8 mm Hg (P<0.001). At endpoint, supine systolic pressure above 180 mm Hg was seen in 4.9% of droxidopa and 2.5% of placebo recipients. Adverse events in at least 3% of droxidopa recipients were headache (7.4%) and dizziness (3.7%); no patient discontinued double-blind treatment because of adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Enriched design: only patients who responded to open-label droxidopa were randomised, and the double-blind phase lasted seven days — the result does not describe unselected patients or long-term benefit, and the drug raises supine blood pressure as well as standing pressure.
cards.source: Kaufmann H et al. Droxidopa for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: a randomized, placebo-controlled, phase 3 trial. Neurology. 2014;83(4):328-335. PMID: 24944260. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Hauser/Biaggioni 2015: the randomised withdrawal study failed its primary endpoint (P=0.509) — only secondary scores favoured droxidopa
cards.summary: Randomised withdrawal study (2015): failed its primary endpoint (P=0.509) — only secondary scores favoured droxidopa.
cards.type: Randomised withdrawal study (responders to open-label droxidopa randomised to continue or switch to placebo for 14 days)
cards.people: 101 patients with symptomatic neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and Parkinson disease, multiple system atrophy, pure autonomic failure or nondiabetic autonomic neuropathy, who had responded to open-label droxidopa titration (100–600 mg three times daily) plus a further 7 days of open-label treatment, were randomised to continue droxidopa or withdraw to placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome — mean worsening of the OHQ dizziness/lightheadedness score from randomisation to end of study — was 1.9 (SD 3.2) units with placebo and 1.3 (SD 2.8) units with droxidopa (P=0.509), so the study failed its primary efficacy endpoint. Four of the other five OHQ symptom scores and all four symptom-impact scores favoured droxidopa, with significance for the ability to perform activities requiring standing a short time (P=0.033) and a long time (P=0.028); a post-hoc analysis of a predefined composite of all symptoms also favoured droxidopa (P=0.013). There was no significant difference between groups for standing systolic blood pressure (P=0.680). Droxidopa was well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A failed primary endpoint with positive secondary and post-hoc analyses is hypothesis-supporting, not confirmatory — the authors themselves state that additional trials are needed. Fourteen days of withdrawal in known responders is also a narrow test.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a real short-term signal in responders, an unproven maintenance effect — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: A real short-term signal in responders, an unproven maintenance effect — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Kaufmann 2014 (162 randomised responders, 7-day double-blind phase) and the 2015 randomised withdrawal study (101 responders, 14 days).
cards.result: Both trials study people already known to respond to droxidopa, so the shelf's claim is narrow from the start. Within that frame, the phase 3 trial is positive on symptoms and standing pressure, while the withdrawal trial — the design that tests whether benefit persists — missed its primary endpoint (P=0.509) and found no standing-pressure difference. That combination supports POSSIBLE for short-term symptom relief in responders and no stronger claim. The 2024–2026 currency sweep found a randomised withdrawal trial of a different agent, ampreloxetine, in multiple system atrophy (PMID 42475649): a competitor drug's trial, not droxidopa evidence, and it is not carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the phase 3 result without the withdrawal trial beside it, and do not generalise either result to patients who have never taken droxidopa.

shelves.title: High-intensity resistance and impact training for bone in older adults (LIFTMOR and LIFTMOR-M)
shelves.question: Is supervised high-intensity resistance and impact training safe — and does it improve bone mineral density and function — in postmenopausal women with low bone mass (LIFTMOR) and in middle-aged and older men (LIFTMOR-M), against the long-standing fear that heavy loading fractures osteoporotic spines?
shelves.mesh: Body Composition · Bone Density/physiology · Bone Diseases, Metabolic/physiopathology · Life Style · Osteoporosis, Postmenopausal/physiopathology · Physical Functional Performance · Resistance Training/adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised programmes — LIFTMOR in 101 postmenopausal women and LIFTMOR-M in 93 men — found that supervised twice-weekly high-intensity resistance and impact training improved lumbar spine bone mineral density by about 3–4 percentage points more than control over eight months, improved function, and produced only minor adverse events (one back spasm in the women's trial; five minor events in the men's). The stamp is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY, because both trials are small, bone density is a surrogate — neither trial measured fractures — and the safety record comes from closely supervised, screened volunteers.

cards.headline: LIFTMOR (Watson 2018): high-intensity resistance and impact training improved spine BMD by 2.9% vs −1.2% in postmenopausal women, with one minor adverse event
cards.summary: LIFTMOR (2018): high-intensity resistance and impact training improved spine BMD by 2.9% vs −1.2% in postmenopausal women, and no fractures occurred.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (supervised high-intensity resistance and impact training vs home-based low-intensity exercise, 8 months)
cards.people: 101 postmenopausal women with low bone mass (T-score below −1.0), screened for conditions and medications affecting bone and function, randomised to eight months of twice-weekly 30-minute supervised high-intensity resistance and impact training (HiRIT, n=49; five sets of five repetitions above 85% of one-repetition maximum) or a home-based low-intensity exercise programme (n=52). Mean age 65 (SD 5) years; all participants were women.
cards.result: HiRIT was superior to control for lumbar spine bone mineral density (2.9% [SD 2.8] vs −1.2% [SD 2.8]; P<0.001), femoral neck bone mineral density (0.3% [2.6] vs −1.9% [2.6]; P=0.004), femoral neck cortical thickness (13.6% [16.6] vs 6.3% [16.6]; P=0.014), height (0.2 [0.5] cm vs −0.2 [0.5] cm; P=0.004), and all functional performance measures (P<0.001). Compliance was high (92% [11] vs 85% [24]). Only one adverse event was reported: a minor lower back spasm in the HiRIT group, causing 2 of 70 missed training sessions.
cards.watchOut: Bone density and strength indices are surrogates: the trial was not powered for, and did not report, fractures. Participants were otherwise healthy, screened volunteers training under close supervision — not a licence for unsupervised heavy loading in frail patients.
cards.source: Watson SL et al. High-Intensity Resistance and Impact Training Improves Bone Mineral Density and Physical Function in Postmenopausal Women With Osteopenia and Osteoporosis: The LIFTMOR Randomized Controlled Trial. J Bone Miner Res. 2018;33(2):211-220. PMID: 28975661. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: LIFTMOR-M (Harding 2020): the same training improved spine BMD in older men (4.1% vs 0.9%) versus a non-randomised matched control
cards.summary: LIFTMOR-M (2020): the same training improved spine BMD in older men ( 4.1% vs 0.9% ) versus a non-randomised matched control.
cards.type: Semi-randomised controlled trial (HiRIT vs isometric axial compression randomised; control group non-randomised and matched)
cards.people: 93 middle-aged and older men with low hip and/or lumbar spine bone mineral density (mean age 67.1 [SD 7.5] years; femoral neck T-score −1.6 [0.6]) were randomised to high-intensity progressive resistance and impact training (HiRIT, n=34) or machine-based isometric axial compression (IAC, n=33), or allocated to a non-randomised matched control group (n=26), for eight months.
cards.result: Compared with control, HiRIT improved trochanteric bone mineral density (2.8% [0.8] vs −0.1% [0.9]; P=0.024), lumbar spine bone mineral density (4.1% [0.7] vs 0.9% [0.8]; P=0.003), calcaneal broadband ultrasound attenuation and stiffness index, lean mass (1.5% [0.8] vs −2.4% [0.9]; P=0.002), and timed up-and-go, sit-to-stand, back and leg strength (all P<0.05). HiRIT also beat IAC on lumbar spine BMD (4.1% vs 2.0%; P=0.039). Compliance was high (HiRIT 77.8% [16.6]; IAC 78.5% [14.8]). There were five minor adverse events (HiRIT 2; IAC 3).
cards.watchOut: The control group was not randomised, so the HiRIT-versus-control comparison carries allocation-bias risk the women's trial does not; and as in LIFTMOR, outcomes are density and function, not fractures.
cards.source: Harding AT et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: heavy supervised loading helped bone density in both sexes and did not fracture anyone — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Heavy supervised loading helped bone density in both sexes and did not fracture anyone — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: LIFTMOR (101 postmenopausal women) and LIFTMOR-M (93 older men), each eight months of supervised high-intensity resistance and impact training.
cards.result: The two programmes point the same way: lumbar spine bone mineral density gains of roughly 3–4 percentage points over control, better function and strength, high compliance, and no fractures or serious adverse events under supervision — one minor back spasm in women, five minor events in men. What neither trial can say is whether fractures fall, because neither measured them, and the men's control group was not randomised. The shelf therefore stamps the bone-density and safety-under-supervision claim POSSIBLE. Bone drugs live on Shelves #91 and #92 and exercise for osteoarthritis pain on Shelf #683; none is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Safety here means screened, supervised, progressive training. Extrapolating to unsupervised heavy lifting in people with vertebral fractures or frailty goes beyond either trial.

shelves.title: Home-based dementia care: the COPE programme and the Tailored Activity Program
shelves.question: Do structured home-based programmes for people with dementia and their caregivers — occupational-therapy-led COPE, and the Tailored Activity Program (TAP) — improve patient function and behaviour and caregiver well-being versus control?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Behavior Therapy · Caregivers · Dementia/complications,nursing,physiopathology,therapy · Health Status · Home Care Services · Interpersonal Relations
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: COPE (237 randomised dementia–caregiver dyads) produced small improvements at four months in patient functional dependence and engagement and in caregiver well-being and confidence, which were no longer present for patients at nine months. TAP (250 dyads) missed its primary outcome — agitation/aggression did not improve (P=0.43) — but reduced the help patients needed with daily activities, improved caregiver well-being and confidence, and was followed by fewer health-related events at six months (15 vs 28 dyads). Real but small, partly secondary-outcome benefits from two single trials: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: COPE (Gitlin 2010): a home-based biobehavioral programme improved patient function and caregiver well-being at 4 months, not at 9 months
cards.summary: COPE (2010): a home-based biobehavioral programme improved patient function and caregiver well-being at 4 months, not at 9 months.
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (two-group, home-based intervention vs telephone-call control)
cards.people: 237 community-living dyads of a patient with dementia and a family caregiver (of 270 eligible of 284 screened; recruited in Pennsylvania, 2006–2008) were randomised to COPE — up to 12 home or telephone contacts over four months assessing patient capabilities, checking blood and urine samples, and training families in home safety, task simplification and stress reduction — or to a control of three telephone calls and educational materials. Outcomes were collected in 209 dyads (88%) at four months and 173 (73%) at nine months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At four months, COPE patients had less functional dependence than controls (adjusted mean difference 0.24, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.44; P=.02; Cohen d=0.21), less dependence in instrumental activities of daily living (0.32, 0.09 to 0.55; P=.007; d=0.43), and improved engagement (0.12, 0.07 to 0.22; P=.03; d=0.26). COPE caregivers improved in well-being (Perceived Change Index difference 0.22, 0.08 to 0.36; P=.002; d=0.30) and confidence using activities (0.81, 0.30 to 1.32; P=.002; d=0.54). By four months, 64 COPE dyads (62.7%) vs 48 control dyads (44.9%) had eliminated at least one caregiver-identified problem (P=.01). At nine months there were no group differences for patients, though caregivers still perceived greater benefits.
cards.watchOut: Effects are small (Cohen d 0.21–0.54), the patient benefits did not persist to nine months, and nearly a third of dyads were missing by nine months. A four-month programme, not a disease-modifying treatment.
cards.source: Gitlin LN et al. A biobehavioral home-based intervention and the well-being of patients with dementia and their caregivers: the COPE randomized trial. JAMA. 2010;304(9):983-991. PMID: 20810376. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00259454, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: TAP (Gitlin 2021): the Tailored Activity Program missed its primary outcome (agitation/aggression, P=0.43) but reduced care needs and improved caregiver outcomes
cards.summary: TAP (2021): the Tailored Activity Program missed its primary outcome (agitation/aggression, P=0.43) but reduced care needs and improved caregiver outcomes.
cards.type: Single-blind randomised controlled trial (home-based tailored activity programme vs attention control)
cards.people: 250 dyads of a person living with dementia (clinically significant agitation/aggression) and a caregiver, recruited in the Baltimore–Washington DC area (2012–2016), randomised to TAP (n=124) — up to eight home visits over three months assessing abilities and interests and teaching caregivers to use prescribed activities, plus dementia education and stress reduction — or attention control (n=126). Caregivers: mean age 65.4 (SD 12.6) years, 81.2% female. Patients: mean age 81.4 (SD 7.9) years, 63.2% female, mean MMSE 14.3 (SD 7.8).
cards.result: At three months, TAP conferred no benefit on the primary outcome of agitation/aggression frequency-by-severity (P=0.43; d=0.11). It did result in less assistance needed with instrumental activities of daily living (P=0.02; d=−0.33) and activities of daily living (P=0.04; d=−0.30), improved caregiver well-being (P=0.01; d=0.39) and confidence using activities (P=0.02; d=0.32). By six months, 15 patients in TAP had at least one health-related event versus 28 in control — reported as a 48.8% improvement (P=0.03), a relative figure for a composite of death, hospitalisations and caregiver events. Prescribed activities were well tolerated, and TAP caregivers were more likely to perceive study benefits.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome was null; the positive findings are secondary outcomes in a single trial, and the health-events composite mixes patient death and hospitalisation with caregiver outcomes. Enrolled patients had significant agitation/aggression at entry, which is the population the null primary result describes.
cards.source: Gitlin LN et al. Effects of the tailored activity program (TAP) on dementia-related symptoms, health events and caregiver wellbeing: a randomized controlled trial. BMC Geriatr. 2021;21(1):581. PMID: 34670502. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01892579, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: dyad programmes help function and caregivers modestly; the behaviour claim failed its own primary test — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Dyad programmes help function and caregivers modestly; the behaviour claim failed its own primary test — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: COPE (237 dyads) and TAP (250 dyads), both occupational-therapy-led home programmes for the patient–caregiver dyad.
cards.result: Across both trials the consistent findings are modest functional gains for patients (COPE dependence difference 0.24 at four months; TAP less help needed with daily activities) and better caregiver well-being and confidence — while TAP's headline behaviour outcome, agitation/aggression, was not improved (P=0.43), and COPE's patient gains faded by nine months. The shelf stamps the dyad-benefit claim POSSIBLE and makes no claim that these programmes treat agitation. Caregiver-only support programmes (REACH II, NYU) are a different question, drafted as Shelf #795; nothing from that shelf is carded here.

shelves.title: Stopping antipsychotics in dementia: the DART-AD withdrawal trial
shelves.question: In people with Alzheimer's disease already taking antipsychotics, does continuing them beat switching to placebo — acutely, and on survival and cognition over long-term follow-up (DART-AD)?
shelves.mesh: Alzheimer Disease/drug therapy,psychology · Antipsychotic Agents/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Dementia/drug therapy,psychology · Alzheimer Disease/drug therapy,mortality,psychology · Antipsychotic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Dementia/drug therapy,mortality,psychology · Kaplan-Meier Estimate
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the long-term report carries a survival difference). Stopping antipsychotics had no overall detrimental effect on cognition or neuropsychiatric symptoms at 6–12 months in DART-AD (165 randomised; differences −0.4 points on the Severe Impairment Battery and −2.4 on the Neuropsychiatric Inventory, both non-significant). On long-term follow-up, survival was lower in patients who continued antipsychotics (24-month survival 46% vs 71%; hazard ratio for death 0.58 favouring the switch-to-placebo group) — a mortality claim from a single small trial programme, which is why this stamp is proposed, not settled, and sits in the Tier C slow lane.

cards.headline: DART-AD short term (Ballard 2008): stopping antipsychotics did not worsen cognition or neuropsychiatric symptoms overall at 6 months
cards.summary: DART-AD, short term (2008): stopping antipsychotics did not worsen cognition or neuropsychiatric symptoms overall at 6 months.
cards.people: 165 patients with Alzheimer's disease in the UK who had been prescribed an antipsychotic (thioridazine, chlorpromazine, haloperidol, trifluoperazine or risperidone) for behavioural or psychiatric disturbance for at least three months were randomised to continue the drug for 12 months (n=83) or switch to identical placebo (n=82); 128 (78%) commenced treatment (64 per arm) and 51 per arm were analysed for the primary outcome. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: There was no significant difference between the continue and placebo groups in estimated mean change in Severe Impairment Battery scores between baseline and six months (estimated mean difference in deterioration −0.4, 95% CI −6.4 to 5.5, favouring placebo; P=0.9), nor in Neuropsychiatric Inventory scores (n=56 and 53; difference −2.4, −8.2 to 3.5, favouring continue treatment; P=0.4). Both results became more pronounced at 12 months. There was some evidence that patients with an initial Neuropsychiatric Inventory score of 15 or more benefited on neuropsychiatric symptoms from continuing treatment.
cards.watchOut: Only 128 of 165 randomised patients started treatment and 102 were analysed for the primary outcome; the trial is small for the symptom subgroups it explores, and the suggestion of benefit from continuing in severe symptoms (NPI at least 15) is subgroup evidence, not a randomised comparison of its own.
cards.source: Ballard C et al. A randomised, blinded, placebo-controlled trial in dementia patients continuing or stopping neuroleptics (the DART-AD trial). PLoS Med. 2008;5(4):e76. PMID: 18384230. Registry ID: ISRCTN33368770, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: DART-AD long term (Ballard 2009): continuing antipsychotics was associated with lower survival (24-month survival 46% vs 71%; HR 0.58)
cards.summary: DART-AD, long term (2009): continuing antipsychotics was associated with lower survival (24-month survival 46% vs 71% ).
cards.type: Long-term follow-up of the DART-AD randomised placebo-controlled discontinuation trial
cards.people: The same DART-AD cohort: 165 patients with Alzheimer's disease living in UK care facilities, randomised (83 continue antipsychotic, 82 switch to placebo), of whom 128 (78%) started treatment (64 per arm); mortality was assessed at 12 months and by telephone follow-up out to 24–54 months after enrolment of the last participant. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Cumulative probability of survival during the first 12 months was 70% (95% CI 58 to 80%) in the continue-treatment group versus 77% (64 to 85%) in the placebo group (modified intention-to-treat). cards.watchOut: One trial of 165 randomised patients, with survival differences that grow at time points beyond the 12-month randomised treatment period; causes of death came from death certificates. shelves.title: Protein supplementation in frail older adults: the Tieland programme
shelves.question: Does protein supplementation improve physical performance and muscle mass in frail older people — alone, and added to resistance-type exercise training?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Dietary Proteins/administration & dosage,metabolism · Dietary Supplements · Frail Elderly · Muscle, Skeletal/anatomy & histology,physiology · Physical Fitness · Sarcopenia/diet therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small Dutch trial programme, two reports. Protein supplementation alone (15 g twice daily, 24 weeks; 65 frail older people) improved short physical performance battery scores (8.9 to 10.0 points vs 7.8 to 7.9 on placebo; interaction P=.02) but did not increase muscle mass or fibre size. Added to twice-weekly resistance training (62 frail older people), protein did allow lean mass to rise (47.2 to 48.5 kg vs no change on placebo; interaction P=.006), while strength and performance improved with training in both groups. Single-programme, small-n evidence for a performance effect and a training-dependent mass effect: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Tieland 2012 (performance): protein supplementation improved physical performance (SPPB 8.9 to 10.0) but not muscle mass in frail older people
cards.summary: Protein supplementation trial (2012): improved physical performance (SPPB 8.9 to 10.0 ) but not muscle mass in frail older people.
cards.people: 65 frail elderly people randomised to daily protein supplementation (15 g protein at breakfast and lunch) or placebo for 24 weeks, with skeletal muscle mass (DXA), muscle fibre size (biopsy), strength (one-repetition maximum) and physical performance (short physical performance battery, SPPB) assessed at baseline and at 12 and 24 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Skeletal muscle mass did not change in either group over 24 weeks (protein 45.8 [SE 1.7] to 45.8 [1.7] kg; placebo 46.7 [1.7] to 46.6 [1.7] kg; P>.05), and type I and II muscle fibre size did not change (P>.05). Muscle strength increased in both groups (P<.01), with leg extension strength tending to increase more with protein (57 [5] to 68 [5] kg) than placebo (57 [5] to 63 [5] kg; interaction P=.059). Physical performance improved significantly in the protein group (SPPB 8.9 [0.6] to 10.0 [0.6] points) and did not change on placebo (7.8 [0.6] to 7.9 [0.6]; interaction P=.02).
cards.watchOut: Small (65 participants) and from a single research programme; the baseline SPPB gap between groups (8.9 vs 7.8 points) is large for a randomised trial of this size, and the headline outcome improved while the proposed mechanism — more muscle — did not.

shelves.title: Prehabilitation for frail patients before colorectal surgery
shelves.question: In frail patients awaiting colorectal cancer resection, does multimodal prehabilitation (exercise, nutrition, anxiety reduction) cut postoperative complications versus starting rehabilitation after surgery — and does the larger PREHAB trial in a broader surgical population agree?
shelves.mesh: Colorectal Neoplasms/complications,surgery · Enhanced Recovery After Surgery · Exercise Therapy · Frailty/complications · Nutrition Therapy · Postoperative Care/rehabilitation · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — prehabilitation reduces severe complications in the broader colorectal-surgery population (PREHAB) · MAYBE (weak evidence) — benefit in frail patients specifically, where the one frail-only trial was null. In PREHAB (251 adults with colorectal cancer, not selected for frailty), severe complications (Comprehensive Complication Index above 20) occurred in 17.1% with prehabilitation vs 29.7% with standard care (odds ratio 0.47). In the frail-only trial (110 frail patients), starting the same kind of programme before rather than after surgery changed nothing (Complication Index difference −3.2, P=.45). The frail-specific claim the shelf was drafted for is the weaker half.

cards.headline: Carli 2020: in frail patients, prehabilitation before colorectal resection did not reduce 30-day complications versus rehabilitation after surgery (CCI difference −3.2, P=.45)
cards.summary: Frail-patient prehabilitation trial (2020): prehabilitation before colorectal resection did not reduce 30-day complications versus rehabilitation after surgery (adjusted difference −3.2; P=.45).
cards.type: Single-blind, parallel-arm randomised clinical trial (prehabilitation vs postoperative rehabilitation — an active comparator)
cards.people: 110 frail patients (Fried Frailty Index at least 2) undergoing colorectal cancer resection at two university-affiliated tertiary hospitals, randomised from 120 frail patients (of 418 assessed, 290 excluded as not frail) to a multimodal programme of exercise, nutrition and psychological support started four weeks before surgery, or the same programme started after surgery; all within a standardised enhanced recovery pathway. Mean age 78 (SD 7) years; 47.3% men; 79.1% had minimally invasive surgery.
cards.result: There was no between-group difference in the primary outcome, the 30-day Comprehensive Complications Index (adjusted mean difference −3.2, 95% CI −11.8 to 5.3; P=.45). Secondary outcomes — 30-day overall and severe complications, length of stay, emergency-department visits, readmissions, recovery of walking capacity and patient-reported outcomes — were also not different between groups.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was the same programme delivered after surgery, not no rehabilitation, and most surgery was minimally invasive inside an enhanced-recovery pathway — a high standard of usual care against which a pre-surgery head start may add little. It remains the only trial restricted to frail patients.
cards.source: Carli F et al. Effect of Multimodal Prehabilitation vs Postoperative Rehabilitation on 30-Day Postoperative Complications for Frail Patients Undergoing Resection of Colorectal Cancer: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Surg. 2020;155(3):233-242. PMID: 31968063. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02502760, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PREHAB (Molenaar 2023): prehabilitation cut severe complications in a broader colorectal population (17.1% vs 29.7%; OR 0.47)
cards.summary: PREHAB (2023): prehabilitation cut severe complications in a broader colorectal population ( 17.1% vs 29.7% ; OR 0.47).
cards.type: International multicentre randomised clinical trial (prehabilitation vs standard care)
cards.people: 251 adults with non-metastasised colorectal cancer in teaching hospitals with enhanced-recovery programmes (international, multicentre), randomised to a four-week in-hospital supervised multimodal prehabilitation programme (high-intensity exercise three times weekly, nutrition, psychological support, smoking cessation when needed) or standard care. Median age 69 (IQR 60–76) years; 55% male; 93% had laparoscopic or robotic surgery. The trial stopped early because of the COVID-19 pandemic.
cards.result: Severe complications (Comprehensive Complication Index score above 20) were significantly fewer with prehabilitation: 21 of 123 (17.1%) vs 38 of 128 (29.7%); odds ratio 0.47 (95% CI 0.26 to 0.87; P=.02) — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it here. Medical complications were also fewer (19 of 123 [15.4%] vs 35 of 128 [27.3%]; odds ratio 0.48, 0.26 to 0.89; P=.02). Four weeks after surgery, six-minute walking distance did not differ significantly between groups versus baseline (mean difference 15.6 m, 95% CI −1.4 to 32.6; P=.07), though other functional-capacity measures generally favoured prehabilitation.
cards.watchOut: Stopped early for COVID-19 before its planned size, and the population was not selected for frailty — its positive result cannot be imported into the frail population where the direct trial was null.

cards.headline: Synthesis: benefit shown where frailty was not required, absent where it was — a split stamp
cards.summary: Benefit shown where frailty was not required, absent where it was — Split: POSSIBLE · MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Carli 2020 (110 frail patients, prehabilitation vs postoperative rehabilitation) and PREHAB 2023 (251 unselected colorectal patients, prehabilitation vs standard care).
cards.result: The discordance is the finding: severe complications fell by a relative half in the broader trial (17.1% vs 29.7%) while the frail-only trial's complication index was unchanged (−3.2 points, P=.45) against an active rehabilitation comparator. Differences in comparator (standard care vs the same programme later), population and early stopping could each explain part of the gap; none is resolved by these two trials. Hence the split: POSSIBLE for the broader colorectal population, MAYBE (weak evidence) for benefit in frail patients specifically. Geriatric assessment before surgery (POPS) is an assessment model, drafted as Shelf #799, and is not carded here. The 2024–2026 sweep returned further prehabilitation trials in colorectal and other surgery (including new multicentre frailty prehabilitation reports) — none yet large enough in frail colorectal patients to supersede the frail-only trial, and none is carded here.
cards.watchOut: Surgical and behavioural interventions cannot be blinded to patients or treating teams; complication indices were, however, collected on standardised scales in both trials.

shelves.title: Vaccinating care-home staff against influenza to protect residents
shelves.question: Does vaccinating health-care workers in long-term care against influenza reduce deaths and influenza-like illness among the residents they care for — the Potter trial and the Hayward cluster trial?
shelves.mesh: Cluster Analysis · Frail Elderly/statistics & numerical data · Health Personnel · Hospitals, Chronic Disease · Influenza Vaccines · Influenza, Human/mortality · Long-Term Care
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruled at build: the claimed beneficiary outcome is resident mortality). Two cluster trials from the 1990s–2000s found lower resident mortality where staff were vaccinated: Potter 1997 (total patient mortality 10% vs 17%; odds ratio 0.56) and Hayward 2006 (five fewer deaths per 100 residents during the 2003–4 influenza-activity period — but no significant difference in the low-influenza 2004–5 season or outside influenza-activity periods). A mortality benefit that appears only in influenza-active periods, from two older cluster trials with staff uptake under two-thirds, is a Tier C claim: proposed, not settled.

cards.headline: Potter 1997: vaccinating long-term-care staff was associated with resident mortality of 10% vs 17% (OR 0.56)
cards.summary: Care-home staff vaccination study (1997): vaccinating long-term-care staff was associated with resident mortality of 10% vs 17% (OR 0.56).
cards.type: Cluster randomised trial (12 long-term-care sites randomised for staff vaccination)
cards.people: 1,059 patients in 12 geriatric medical long-term-care sites, randomised by site for vaccination of their health-care workers, studied over the winter of 1994–95. In hospitals where vaccination was offered, 653 (61%) of 1,078 health-care workers were vaccinated. The abstract does not state residents' mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Vaccination of health-care workers was associated with a reduction in total patient mortality from 17% to 10% (odds ratio 0.56, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.80 — a relative figure, with the absolute rates beside it here) and in influenza-like illness (odds ratio 0.57, 0.34 to 0.94). Vaccination of the patients themselves was not associated with a significant effect on mortality (odds ratio 1.15, 0.81 to 1.64).
cards.watchOut: A 1990s trial with only 12 clusters and 61% staff uptake; the striking patient-vaccination null beside the staff-vaccination result is part of the finding, and later debate about healthy-vaccinee and cluster effects applies to a mortality claim of this size.
cards.source: Potter J et al. Influenza vaccination of health care workers in long-term-care hospitals reduces the mortality of elderly patients. J Infect Dis. 1997;175(1):1-6. PMID: 8985189. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (1994–95).

cards.headline: Hayward 2006: staff vaccination cut resident deaths in the 2003–4 influenza season (−5.0 per 100 residents) but not in the quiet 2004–5 season
cards.summary: Staff vaccination trial (2006): cut resident deaths in the 2003–4 influenza season ( −5.0 per 100 residents ) but not in the quiet 2004–5 season.
cards.type: Pair-matched cluster randomised controlled trial (44 care homes, two influenza seasons)
cards.people: Residents (n=2,604) and staff (n=1,703) in 44 UK care homes (22 intervention, 22 matched control) in a large private chain, over the winters of 2003–4 and 2004–5. Staff vaccine coverage in intervention homes was 48.2% (407/884) of full-time staff in 2003–4 and 43.2% (365/844) in 2004–5, versus 5.9% and 3.5% in control homes; national influenza rates were substantially below average in 2004–5.
cards.result: The primary outcome was all-cause resident mortality. In the 2003–4 period of influenza activity, significant decreases were found in resident mortality in intervention homes versus control homes (rate difference −5.0 per 100 residents, 95% CI −7.0 to −2.0), in influenza-like illness (P=0.004), in GP consultations for influenza-like illness (P=0.008) and in hospital admissions with influenza-like illness (P=0.009). No significant differences were found in 2004–5, or during periods of no influenza activity in 2003–4.
cards.watchOut: The effect is season-conditional: it appeared only when influenza was circulating at moderate levels, and staff uptake never reached half of full-time staff in the second season. Two seasons, one of them very quiet, is a thin base for a standing mortality claim.
cards.source: Hayward AC et al. Effectiveness of an influenza vaccine programme for care home staff to prevent death, morbidity, and health service use among residents: cluster randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2006;333(7581):1241.
