shelves.title: Preventive home visits for community-dwelling older people
shelves.question: Do regular preventive home visits (geriatric assessment and follow-up in the home) delay functional decline, nursing-home admission, or death in community-dwelling older people — the Elkan and Stuck syntheses of the randomised trials?
shelves.mesh: Cost-Benefit Analysis · Evidence-Based Medicine · Frail Elderly · Health Services for the Aged/economics · Hospitalization · House Calls · Long-Term Care
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruled at build: the shelf carries a mortality claim resting on two syntheses and subgroup meta-regression). The Elkan synthesis (15 studies) pooled a mortality odds ratio of 0.76 (0.64 to 0.89) in general elderly populations and 0.72 in frail at-risk groups, with fewer admissions to long-term institutional care (odds ratio 0.65) — but no effect on hospital admissions, health status or daily-living activities. The Stuck synthesis (18 trials, 13,447 people) found benefits only under conditions: many visits, multidimensional assessment with follow-up, and younger-old, lower-risk populations; mortality benefit appeared at ages 72.7–77.5 (relative risk 0.76) but not at 80.2–81.6 (1.09). Conditional, synthesis-level evidence: proposed POSSIBLE, Tier C.

cards.headline: Elkan 2001: home visiting pooled to lower mortality (OR 0.76) and institutional-care admission (OR 0.65), with no effect on function or health status
cards.summary: Home-visiting meta-analysis (2001): home visiting pooled to lower mortality (OR 0.76 ) and institutional-care admission (OR 0.65), with no effect on function or health status.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of home-visiting studies
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 studies of home visiting programmes offering health promotion and preventive care to older people living at home, including frail older people at risk of adverse outcomes. The abstract does not state a pooled mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Home visiting was associated with a significant reduction in mortality: the pooled odds ratio for the eight studies assessing mortality in the general elderly population was 0.76 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.89), and five studies in frail, at-risk older people also showed a significant mortality reduction (odds ratio 0.72, 0.54 to 0.97) — both relative figures. Home visiting was associated with a significant reduction in admission to long-term institutional care in the general elderly population (odds ratio 0.65, 0.46 to 0.91; in three frail-population studies, 0.55, 0.35 to 0.88). There was no significant reduction in hospital admissions (six studies; odds ratio 0.95, 0.80 to 1.09), no significant effect on health (three studies; standardised effect size 0.06, −0.07 to 0.18) and no effect on activities of daily living (four studies; 0.05, −0.07 to 0.17).
cards.watchOut: The mortality and institutional-care signals coexist with null effects on the outcomes closest to the intervention (function, health status, hospital admission), and the included programmes were heterogeneous — the pooled odds ratios average over very different visiting schemes.
cards.source: Elkan R et al. Effectiveness of home based support for older people: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ. 2001;323(7315):719-725. PMID: 11576978. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Stuck 2002: benefits depended on how visits were done and who received them — many visits, multidimensional assessment, younger-old populations
cards.summary: Home-visiting meta-analysis (2002): benefits depended on how visits were done and who received them — many visits, multidimensional assessment, younger-old populations.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-regression analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-regression of 18 randomised trials (17 articles) of preventive in-home visits in community-living older people (mean age above 70 years), totalling 13,447 individuals aged 65 years or older, from searches to November 2001. The abstract does not state a pooled sex mix.
cards.result: The effect on nursing-home admission depended on visit count: pooled relative risk 0.66 (95% CI 0.48 to 0.92) in trials in the upper tertile (more than nine visits) but 1.05 (0.85 to 1.30) in the lower tertile (0–4 visits). Functional decline was reduced in trials using multidimensional assessment with follow-up (relative risk 0.76, 0.64 to 0.91) but not in other trials (1.01, 0.92 to 1.11), and in trials whose control-group mortality was in the lower tertile (0.78, 0.64 to 0.95) but not the upper (0.98, 0.84 to 1.13). A mortality benefit was evident in younger study populations (relative risk 0.76, 0.65 to 0.88, for mean ages 72.7–77.5 years) but not in older populations (1.09, 0.92 to 1.28, for ages 80.2–81.6 years). All figures are relative; the abstract gives no pooled absolute event rates.
cards.watchOut: Meta-regression across 18 trials: the 'conditions for benefit' (visit count, assessment type, age band) are between-trial comparisons, vulnerable to confounding by everything else that differed between those trials. The oldest-old subgroup showed no mortality benefit (relative risk 1.09).
cards.source: Stuck AE et al. Home visits to prevent nursing home admission and functional decline in elderly people: systematic review and meta-regression analysis. JAMA. 2002;287(8):1022-1028. PMID: 11866651. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review, not a single trial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: preventive home visits can help — conditionally — and the mortality half is Tier C — POSSIBLE, proposed
cards.summary: Preventive home visits can help — conditionally — and the mortality half is Tier C — POSSIBLE, proposed only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Elkan 2001 (15 studies) and Stuck 2002 (18 trials, 13,447 participants), two independent syntheses of the same trial generation.
cards.result: The syntheses agree that something in these programmes reduced mortality and institutionalisation on pooling (odds ratios 0.76 and 0.65 in Elkan), and Stuck's analysis says the benefit concentrates in intensive, multidimensional programmes aimed at the younger-old — with relative risks of 1.05 for few-visit programmes and 1.09 for mortality in the oldest populations marking where it disappears. Elkan's null findings on function and health status sit unresolved beside the mortality signal, which is why this mortality-carrying, synthesis-based shelf is Tier C with a PROPOSED stamp. Inpatient comprehensive geriatric assessment is Shelf #605 and transitional care after discharge is drafted as Shelf #790; neither is re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Both syntheses predate 2002-era usual care; modern community services already include elements of these programmes, which would shrink any incremental effect.

shelves.title: Exercise rehabilitation after hip fracture: extended and home-based programmes
shelves.question: After hip-fracture rehabilitation ends, does more exercise — extended outpatient rehabilitation (Binder), or a home-based programme after discharge from rehab (Latham) — improve physical function versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Ambulatory Care · Frail Elderly · Health Status Indicators · Hip Fractures/rehabilitation,surgery · Physical Therapy Modalities · Exercise Therapy/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised trials of different 'more exercise after hip fracture' programmes each found modest functional gains. Extended supervised outpatient rehabilitation with progressive resistance training (Binder 2004, 90 patients) beat low-intensity home exercise on physical performance (+6.5 vs +2.5 points) and function scores. A minimally supervised home-based programme (Latham 2014, 232 patients) beat an attention control on the Short Physical Performance Battery by 0.8 points (0.4 to 1.2) at six months, with differences persisting at nine months — its authors state the clinical importance remains to be determined. Two positive but modest, non-replicating programmes: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Binder 2004: six months of extended outpatient rehabilitation improved physical performance more than low-intensity home exercise (+6.5 vs +2.5 PPT points)
cards.summary: Extended rehabilitation trial (2004): six months of extended outpatient rehabilitation improved physical performance more than low-intensity home exercise (performance test +6.5 vs +2.5 ).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (extended outpatient rehabilitation vs low-intensity home exercise)
cards.people: 90 community-dwelling women and men aged 65 years or older who had surgical repair of a proximal femur fracture within the previous 16 weeks and had completed standard physical therapy, randomised to six months of supervised physical therapy and exercise training including progressive resistance training (n=46) or a low-intensity home exercise control (n=44), and evaluated at baseline, three and six months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Changes over time in the modified Physical Performance Test (PPT) and the Functional Status Questionnaire physical function subscale favoured the physical therapy group (P=.003 and P=.01). Mean change in PPT score was +6.5 (SD 5.5) points (95% CI 4.6 to 8.3) with physical therapy versus +2.5 (3.7) points (1.4 to 3.6) with home exercise; mean change in the function subscale was +5.2 (5.4) points (3.5 to 6.9) versus +2.9 (3.8) points (1.7 to 4.0). Physical therapy also produced significantly greater improvements in muscle strength, walking speed, balance and perceived health, but not in bone mineral density or fat-free mass.
cards.watchOut: Small (90 patients), single programme, and the control was itself an exercise prescription — the trial shows supervised intensity beats low-intensity home exercise, not that any exercise beats none. No fracture, falls or mortality outcomes.
cards.source: Binder EF et al. Effects of extended outpatient rehabilitation after hip fracture: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2004;292(7):837-846. PMID: 15315998. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — a pre-registration-era trial (conducted 1998–2003).

cards.headline: Latham 2014: a home-based exercise programme after rehabilitation improved function modestly (SPPB between-group difference 0.8 points)
cards.summary: Home-based exercise trial (2014): after rehabilitation, improved function modestly (SPPB between-group difference 0.8 points ).
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (home-based exercise vs attention control, assessor-blinded outcomes)
cards.people: 232 functionally limited older adults who had completed traditional rehabilitation after a hip fracture, randomised to a six-month home-based functionally oriented exercise programme taught by a physical therapist and performed independently (n=120) or an attention control of in-home and telephone cardiovascular nutrition education (n=112); 195 were followed up at six months and included in the primary analysis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At six months the intervention group improved more than control on the Short Physical Performance Battery (scores 6.2 [SD 2.7] at baseline to 7.2 [3] vs 6.0 [2.8] to 6.2 [3]; between-group difference 0.8, 95% CI 0.4 to 1.2; P<.001), on activity-measure mobility scores (between-group difference 1.3, 0.2 to 2.4; P=.03) and daily activity scores (3.5, 0.9 to 6.0; P=.03). In multiple-imputation analyses the differences remained significant for the performance battery and daily activity but not for mobility. Significant between-group differences persisted at nine months for all functional measures. The authors state the clinical importance of these findings remains to be determined.
cards.watchOut: Effects are small in absolute terms (0.8 of 12 performance-battery points), 37 of 232 randomised patients were missing from the primary analysis, and one of three primary measures lost significance under imputation.
cards.source: Latham NK et al. Effect of a home-based exercise program on functional recovery following rehabilitation after hip fracture: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2014;311(7):700-708. PMID: 24549550. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00592813, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: more exercise after hip fracture helps function a little, in two different forms — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: More exercise after hip fracture helps function a little, in two different forms — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Binder 2004 (90 patients, supervised outpatient programme) and Latham 2014 (232 patients, home-based programme).
cards.result: The programmes differ — supervised progressive resistance training versus minimally supervised functional home exercise — and both beat their controls on performance-based function, by +4.0 net performance-test points (Binder) and +0.8 net performance-battery points (Latham). Neither measured refracture or mortality, and the larger trial's own authors leave clinical importance open. The stamp is POSSIBLE for a modest functional benefit from extended post-rehabilitation exercise. Fracture timing and anaesthesia live on Shelf #342; nothing from it is re-carded here. The 2024–2026 sweep found newer post-hip-fracture exercise trials, including a 2025 trial of exercise training combined with testosterone in women (STEP-HI, PMID 40372752) — a drug-plus-exercise question, fenced here rather than carded.
cards.watchOut: Both trials enrolled patients well enough to exercise after completing standard rehabilitation; the results do not describe patients discharged to nursing care or unable to participate.
cards.source: Synthesis of Binder EF et al. JAMA. 2004;292(7):837-846. PMID: 15315998; Latham NK et al. JAMA. 2014;311(7):700-708. PMID: 24549550. Registry IDs as on the individual cards.

shelves.title: Withdrawal of psychotropic medicines to prevent falls
shelves.question: In older adults taking psychotropic medicines, does gradual withdrawal of those medicines reduce the rate of falls over the following year versus continuation?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Therapy · Family Practice · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Geriatric Assessment · Home Care Services · Humans · Male · New Zealand · Program Evaluation · Proportional Hazards Models · Psychotropic Drugs · Risk Factors · Single-Blind Method · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small double-blind randomised trial (Campbell 1999, 93 older adults taking psychotropic medication, 2×2 factorial with a home exercise programme) found gradual psychotropic withdrawal reduced the relative hazard of falls over 44 weeks to 0.34 relative (95% CI 0.16 to 0.74) versus continuing medication — while the exercise programme did not significantly reduce falling — and the authors stress that permanent withdrawal proved very difficult to achieve. A single small trial with a large relative effect and a hard-to-sustain intervention earns POSSIBLE. The topic draft's second 'nursing-home withdrawal trial' could not be pinned to a verified record at build and is fenced without figures.

cards.headline: Campbell 1999: psychotropic withdrawal cut the relative hazard of falls to 0.34 — but few could stay off the drugs
cards.summary: Campbell 1999: psychotropic withdrawal cut the relative hazard of falls to 0.34 — but few could stay off the drugs
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial with a two by two factorial design (17 general practices, Dunedin, New Zealand)
cards.people: 93 women and men aged 65 years or older, registered with a general practitioner and currently taking psychotropic medication, randomised to gradual withdrawal of psychotropic medication versus continuing medication (double blind) and to a home-based exercise program versus no exercise program (single blind), with 44 weeks of follow-up. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: After 44 weeks, the relative hazard for falls in the medication withdrawal group compared with the group taking their original medication was 0.34 (a relative measure; absolute fall rates are not printed in the abstract) (95% CI 0.16 to 0.74). The risk of falling for the exercise program group compared with those not receiving it was not significantly reduced. Analysis was by intention to treat. The authors conclude withdrawal significantly reduced the risk of falling, but permanent withdrawal is very difficult to achieve.
cards.watchOut: Ninety-three participants: the confidence interval (0.16 to 0.74) is wide, the abstract prints no absolute fall rates, and intention-to-treat benefit despite widespread restarting implies the on-treatment effect may differ in either direction.
cards.source: Campbell AJ et al. Psychotropic medication withdrawal and a home-based exercise program to prevent falls: a randomized, controlled trial. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 1999. PMID: 10404930. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: deprescribing psychotropics probably prevents falls; sustaining it is the problem — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: deprescribing psychotropics probably prevents falls; sustaining it is the problem — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Campbell 1999 (93 older adults on psychotropic medication).

shelves.title: Daily-dose vitamin D for fall prevention
shelves.question: In older adults, does daily vitamin D (700–1,000 IU), with or without calcium, reduce falls versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bone and Bones · Calcifediol · Calcium · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fractures, Bone · Humans · Middle Aged · Muscles · Poisson Distribution · Time Factors · Vitamin D
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE (institutionalised, vitamin-D-deficient older women, short term) · LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) (community-dwelling older adults) — PROPOSED: The carded positive trial is small, short and set in long-stay geriatric care (Bischoff 2003, 122 elderly women, mean age 85.3): calcium plus 800 IU cholecalciferol for 12 weeks reduced falls by 49% relative (95% CI 14% to 71%; p<0.01) versus calcium alone, with improved musculoskeletal function. The era split is the shelf's core fact: the later, much larger trials in community-dwelling older adults — DO-HEALTH and the VITAL programme, fenced in the synthesis without carded falls figures — did not reproduce fall or related benefits, so for the general older population the honest stamp is LIKELY (the treatment made no difference). The harmful annual mega-dose regimen is a separate shelf and is not re-opened here. No mortality or fracture claim is made, so the shelf is not Tier C.

cards.headline: Bischoff 2003: in long-stay geriatric care, vitamin D plus calcium cut falls by 49% relative over 12 weeks versus calcium alone
cards.summary: Bischoff 2003: in long-stay geriatric care, vitamin D plus calcium cut falls by 49% relative over 12 weeks versus calcium alone
cards.type: Double-blind randomized controlled trial (12-week treatment period)
cards.people: 122 elderly women (mean age 85.3 years; range 63–99) in long-stay geriatric care, receiving 1200 mg calcium plus 800 IU cholecalciferol daily (n=62) or 1200 mg calcium alone (n=60).
cards.result: Mean falls per person per week were 0.034 in the calcium-plus-vitamin-D group and 0.076 in the calcium-only group during treatment (versus 0.059 and 0.056 before treatment). After adjustment, calcium-plus-vitamin-D treatment accounted for a 49% relative reduction of falls (a relative measure; adjusted as printed) (95% CI 14 to 71%; p<0.01). Among treatment-period fallers, the crude average number of excessive falls was significantly higher in the calcium-only group (p=0.045). Musculoskeletal function improved significantly in the calcium-plus-vitamin-D group (p=0.0094), and median serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D rose 71%.
cards.watchOut: Twelve weeks, 122 institutionalised women, and a calcium-only comparator: this trial cannot speak to community-dwelling older adults, to men, or to longer horizons — the populations the later null trials actually enrolled.
cards.source: Bischoff HA et al. Effects of vitamin D and calcium supplementation on falls: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of bone and mineral research : the official journal of the American Society for Bone and Mineral Research. 2003. PMID: 12568412. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: the benefit lives in deficient, institutionalised patients; the big community trials were null — SPLIT as proposed
cards.summary: Synthesis: the benefit lives in deficient, institutionalised patients; the big community trials were null — SPLIT as proposed
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: Bischoff 2003 (122 elderly women in long-stay care).
cards.result: The large later programmes — DO-HEALTH (2,157 adults aged 70+, 2,000 IU/day vitamin D3 for 3 years; its carded-in-library outcomes report found no significant benefit on its six primary outcomes) and the VITAL falls analyses — are fenced here as the era-split context: no falls figures are carded from them on this shelf. Their populations were largely vitamin-D-replete community dwellers, which is precisely where the Bischoff result does not apply. Daily-dose supplementation for fracture prevention in care-home residents is a neighbouring shelf (Decalyos) and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not average the eras: supplementing the deficient and supplementing the replete are different interventions in effect, whatever the shared molecule.

shelves.title: Testosterone for frail older men with mobility limitations (TOM)
shelves.question: In older men with low testosterone and mobility limitations, does testosterone gel improve leg-press strength and physical function versus placebo — and at what cardiovascular cost?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Cutaneous · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cardiovascular Diseases · Double-Blind Method · Exercise Test · Gels · Humans · Hyperlipidemias · Hypertension · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Logistic Models · Male · Muscle Strength · Obesity · Risk Factors · Testosterone · Walking
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm-leaning) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: cardiovascular events are central to the record): The TOM trial (Basaria 2010, 209 community-dwelling men aged 65+ with mobility limitations and low testosterone) was STOPPED EARLY on data-safety-monitoring advice because cardiovascular-related adverse events occurred in 23 men in the testosterone group versus 5 in the placebo group, with higher rates of cardiac, respiratory and dermatologic events on testosterone, even as leg-press and chest-press strength and loaded stair climbing improved significantly more on testosterone. A single small trial, stopped early on a harm signal it was not powered to characterise, earns POSSIBLE (harm-leaning) for this frail population — the strength benefit is real on the record and cannot be separated from the risk that stopped the trial. The later TRAVERSE trial addresses a different, lower-risk population and is fenced in the synthesis.

cards.headline: TOM 2010: testosterone improved strength — and the trial was stopped for cardiovascular harm (23 vs 5 men with CV events)
cards.summary: TOM 2010: testosterone improved strength — and the trial was stopped for cardiovascular harm (23 vs 5 men with CV events)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial — terminated early on data and safety monitoring board recommendation
cards.people: 209 community-dwelling men aged 65 years or older (mean age 74 years) with limitations in mobility and total testosterone 100–350 ng/dL or free testosterone below 50 pg/mL, assigned to placebo gel or testosterone gel applied daily for 6 months; at baseline there was a high prevalence of hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia and obesity. The abstract does not state the per-group enrolment numbers.
cards.result: The data and safety monitoring board recommended early discontinuation because of a significantly higher rate of adverse cardiovascular events in the testosterone group. A total of 23 subjects in the testosterone group, compared with 5 in the placebo group, had cardiovascular-related adverse events, and the relative risk of a cardiovascular-related adverse event remained constant throughout the 6-month treatment period. The testosterone group also had higher rates of cardiac, respiratory, and dermatologic events. Compared with placebo, the testosterone group had significantly greater improvements in leg-press and chest-press strength and in stair climbing while carrying a load.
cards.watchOut: The trial was not powered for cardiovascular events and its population (frail, comorbidity-laden, mobility-limited) is unique: the record supports alarm in this population, not a precise event rate for testosterone therapy generally — and the authors say exactly that.
cards.source: Basaria S et al. Adverse events associated with testosterone administration. The New England journal of medicine. 2010. PMID: 20592293. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00240981, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Leucine-enriched whey protein plus vitamin D for sarcopenia (PROVIDE)
shelves.question: In sarcopenic older adults, does a leucine- and vitamin-D-enriched whey protein supplement improve appendicular muscle mass and chair-stand performance versus an isocaloric control over 13 weeks?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Europe · Female · Geriatric Assessment · Hand Strength · Humans · Leucine · Male · Mobility Limitation · Protein-Energy Malnutrition · Sarcopenia · Treatment Outcome · Vitamin D · Whey Proteins
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One multicentre double-blind randomised trial (PROVIDE, Bauer 2015, 380 sarcopenic older adults) found, over 13 weeks, that the enriched supplement beat an isocaloric control on two secondary outcomes — chair-stand test (between-group effect −1.01 seconds, 95% CI −1.77 to −0.19; P=.018) and appendicular muscle mass (+0.17 kg, 0.004 to 0.338; P=.045) — while BOTH primary outcomes, handgrip strength and Short Physical Performance Battery score, improved in both groups WITHOUT significant between-group differences. The authors' conclusion ('improvements in muscle mass and lower-extremity function') is accurate for the secondaries but silent about the null primaries — flagged on the card face. Null primaries plus positive secondaries in a single 13-week trial earn POSSIBLE. Plain protein supplementation in frailty is homed elsewhere.

cards.headline: PROVIDE 2015: primaries null (handgrip, SPPB); chair-stand and muscle mass improved on the enriched supplement
cards.summary: PROVIDE 2015: primaries null (handgrip, SPPB); chair-stand and muscle mass improved on the enriched supplement
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, controlled, double-blind, 2 parallel-group trial (13 weeks)
cards.people: 380 sarcopenic, primarily independent-living older adults with Short Physical Performance Battery scores between 4 and 9 and a low skeletal muscle mass index, receiving a vitamin D and leucine-enriched whey protein supplement twice daily (active group n=184) or an iso-caloric control product twice daily (n=196) for 13 weeks. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Handgrip strength and SPPB improved in both groups without significant between-group differences (the primary outcomes). The active group improved more in the chair-stand test compared with the control group (between-group effect −1.01 seconds, 95% CI −1.77 to −0.19; P=.018) and gained more appendicular muscle mass (between-group effect 0.17 kg, 0.004 to 0.338; P=.045). The authors conclude the supplement resulted in improvements in muscle mass and lower-extremity function — a conclusion resting on the secondary outcomes, since both primaries were null between groups.
cards.watchOut: A 0.17 kg appendicular-mass difference whose confidence interval begins at 0.004 kg, over 13 weeks, in a trial whose own primary endpoints did not separate: promising formulation science, not yet a clinical outcome.
cards.source: Bauer JM et al. Effects of a vitamin D and leucine-enriched whey protein nutritional supplement on measures of sarcopenia in older adults, the PROVIDE study: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Journal of the American Medical Directors Association. 2015. PMID: 26170041. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Treadmill training plus virtual reality to prevent falls (V-TIME)
shelves.question: In older adults at risk of falls (including subgroups with mild cognitive impairment or Parkinson's disease), does treadmill training augmented with non-immersive virtual reality reduce fall rates over 6 months versus treadmill training alone?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aging · Confounding Factors, Epidemiologic · Evidence-Based Medicine · Exercise Test · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Incidence · Male · Psychomotor Performance · Research Design · Risk Assessment · Treatment Outcome · User-Computer Interface · Walking
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One multicentre randomised trial (V-TIME, Mirelman 2016, 302 adults aged 60–90 at high fall risk across five countries) found that 6 weeks of treadmill training plus non-immersive virtual reality reduced the incident fall rate over the following 6 months versus treadmill training alone (incident rate ratio 0.58 relative, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.96; p=0.033), with no serious training-related adverse events. A single trial with a confidence interval ending at 0.96 earns POSSIBLE — promising, and one replication away from more.

cards.headline: V-TIME 2016: treadmill plus virtual reality cut the fall rate by 42% relative versus treadmill alone (IRR 0.58)
cards.summary: V-TIME 2016: treadmill plus virtual reality cut the fall rate by 42% relative versus treadmill alone (IRR 0.58)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial at five clinical centres across five countries (Belgium, Israel, Italy, Netherlands, UK)
cards.people: 302 adults aged 60–90 years at high risk of falls (two or more falls in the prior 6 months) with varied motor and cognitive deficits — including subgroups with idiopathic falls, mild cognitive impairment, and Parkinson's disease — randomly assigned to 6 weeks of treadmill training plus virtual reality (n=154) or treadmill training alone (n=148), three sessions weekly of about 45 minutes; 282 (93%) were included in the modified intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: Before training, fall incidence was similar (10.7 [SD 35.6] falls per 6 months treadmill alone vs 11.9 [39.5] treadmill plus VR). In the 6 months after training, the incident rate was 6.00 (95% CI 4.36 to 8.25) falls per 6 months in the treadmill-plus-VR group (p<0.0001 vs before training) and 8.27 (5.55 to 12.31) with treadmill alone (p=0.49). The between-group incident rate ratio was 0.58 (a relative measure) (95% CI 0.36 to 0.96; p=0.033). No serious training-related adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: Pre-training fall rates have enormous standard deviations (35.6 and 39.5 around means of ~11) — a few very frequent fallers dominate the counts — and the modified intention-to-treat analysis excludes 7% of randomised participants.
cards.source: Mirelman A et al. Addition of a non-immersive virtual reality component to treadmill training to reduce fall risk in older adults (V-TIME): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2016. PMID: 27524393. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01732653, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Occupational-therapist home-hazard assessment and modification to prevent falls
shelves.question: In older people living at home, does a structured OT home visit assessing and modifying environmental hazards reduce falls over 12 months versus no visit?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Accidents, Home · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Environment Design · Female · Home Care Services · Humans · Male · New South Wales · Occupational Therapy · Proportional Hazards Models · Risk Factors · Safety Management · Survival Analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One randomised trial (Cumming 1999, 530 community-dwelling older people, mean age 77) found the OT home-hazard intervention's overall effect was borderline — at least one fall during 12 months in 36% of the intervention group versus 45% of controls (P=.050) — with the clear effect concentrated in the prespecified-relevant subgroup who had fallen in the year before recruitment (n=206; relative risk of at least one fall 0.64 relative, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.83), and only about 50% of recommended modifications actually in place at 12 months. A borderline overall result carried by a prior-faller subgroup earns POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Cumming 1999: home-hazard visits helped prior fallers (RR 0.64 relative); the overall effect sat at P=.050
cards.summary: Cumming 1999: home-hazard visits helped prior fallers (RR 0.64 relative); the overall effect sat at P=.050
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (community, Sydney, Australia; monthly falls calendars over 12 months)
cards.people: 530 subjects (mean age 77 years), recruited primarily before discharge from selected hospital wards, receiving a home visit by an experienced occupational therapist who assessed environmental hazards and facilitated modifications, or no visit. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Thirty-six percent of subjects in the intervention group had at least one fall during follow-up, compared with 45% of controls (P=.050). The intervention was effective only among subjects (n=206) who reported one or more falls during the year before recruitment: in this group, the relative risk of at least one fall during follow-up was 0.64 (a relative measure; absolute rates 36% vs 45% overall, as above) (95% confidence interval 0.50 to 0.83). Similar results were obtained with survival analyses and fall rates. About 50% of the recommended home modifications were in place at a 12-month follow-up visit. The authors note the effect may not be caused by home modifications alone and may include behaviour change.
cards.watchOut: The shelf's headline must stay honest: unselected older people showed a borderline result; the convincing number belongs to prior fallers. Half of the recommended modifications were never in place, so the 'dose' itself was partial.
cards.source: Cumming RG et al. Home visits by an occupational therapist for assessment and modification of environmental hazards: a randomized trial of falls prevention. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 1999. PMID: 10591231. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Personalised physiotherapy falls prevention in Parkinson's disease (PDSAFE)
shelves.question: In people with Parkinson's disease and a history of falls, does a personalised, physiotherapist-delivered home exercise and strategy programme reduce repeat falls over 6 months versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Aged · Exercise Therapy · Female · Gait Disorders, Neurologic · Humans · Male · Parkinson Disease · Physical Therapy Modalities
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): The largest randomised trial of falls management in Parkinson's disease (PDSAFE, Ashburn 2019, 474 participants with Hoehn and Yahr stages 1–4 and at least one prior fall) found NO difference in repeat falling within 6 months (PDSAFE vs control odds ratio 1.21 relative, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.98; p=0.447), although near-falling fell (OR 0.67 relative, 0.53 to 0.86; p=0.001) and balance, functional strength and falls efficacy improved. A prespecified subgroup analysis suggested possible benefit in moderate disease but a possible INCREASE in falls in more severe disease, especially with freezing of gait. A large, well-conducted null on the primary outcome — with a harm-leaning severe-subgroup signal — earns LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the population as randomised.

cards.headline: PDSAFE 2019: no reduction in repeat falling (OR 1.21 relative) despite better balance and fewer near-falls
cards.summary: PDSAFE 2019: no reduction in repeat falling (OR 1.21 relative) despite better balance and fewer near-falls
cards.type: Multicentre, pragmatic, investigator-masked, individually randomised controlled trial (Health Technology Assessment report)
cards.people: 474 people with Parkinson's disease (Hoehn and Yahr stages 1–4) recruited from NHS hospitals, clinics and community services in eight English regions (average age 72 years; 266 [56%] men): 238 assigned to the individually tailored, progressive, home-based PDSAFE programme of fall-avoidance strategy training with balance and strengthening exercises, and 236 to usual care (plus an information DVD and a single advice session at trial completion); all had a history of falls, and the primary outcome was collected by monthly self-report diaries over 0–6 months.
cards.result: No difference in repeat falling within 6 months of randomisation was found (PDSAFE group to control group odds ratio 1.21 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.74 to 1.98; p=0.447). Secondary outcomes favoured PDSAFE: better balance (Mini-BESTest mean difference 0.95, 0.24 to 1.67; p=0.009), functional strength (Chair Stand Test p=0.041), falls efficacy (mean difference −1.6 as printed, 95% CI −3.0 to −0.19; p=0.026), and significantly reduced near-falling (OR 0.67 relative, 0.53 to 0.86; p=0.001) at 6 months. Prespecified subgroup analysis (disease severity and freezing of gait) revealed a differing effect: the intervention may benefit people with moderate disease but may increase falling for those in the more severe category, especially those with freezing of gait.
cards.watchOut: The falls-efficacy confidence interval is printed asymmetrically in the record (mean difference 1.6 with CI −3.0 to −0.19) and is carded as printed; the load-bearing results are the primary null and the subgroup warning, and only 73% were assessed at 12 months owing to restricted funding.
cards.source: Ashburn A et al. Exercise- and strategy-based physiotherapy-delivered intervention for preventing repeat falls in people with Parkinson's: the PDSAFE RCT. Health technology assessment (Winchester, England). 2019. PMID: 31339100. Registry ID: ISRCTN ISRCTN48152791, from the record's databank fields. MeSH: Accidental Falls · Aged · Exercise Therapy · Female · Gait Disorders, Neurologic · Humans · Male · Parkinson Disease · Physical Therapy Modalities

shelves.title: Zoledronic acid after hip fracture (HORIZON Recurrent Fracture Trial)
shelves.question: In patients who have undergone repair of a recent hip fracture, does once-yearly intravenous zoledronic acid reduce new clinical fractures and all-cause mortality versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bone Density · Bone Density Conservation Agents · Calcium · Diphosphonates · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Fractures, Bone · Hip Fractures · Humans · Imidazoles · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Survival Analysis · Vitamin D · Zoledronic Acid
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: all-cause mortality is a headline outcome): In the single large definitive trial (HORIZON Recurrent Fracture Trial, Lyles 2007, 2,127 patients after surgical repair of a low-trauma hip fracture, all receiving vitamin D and calcium, median follow-up 1.9 years), yearly intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg reduced any new clinical fracture (8.6% vs 13.9%; a 35% relative risk reduction; P=0.001), new clinical vertebral fracture (1.7% vs 3.8%; P=0.02) and nonvertebral fracture (7.6% vs 10.7%; P=0.03), and reduced deaths from any cause (101 of 1054 [9.6%] vs 141 of 1057 [13.3%]; a 28% relative reduction; P=0.01). Rates of renal and cardiovascular adverse events, including atrial fibrillation and stroke, were similar between groups, and no osteonecrosis of the jaw was reported. One large trial with concordant fracture and mortality benefits earns LIKELY, Tier C by its mortality claim. Postmenopausal osteoporosis antiresorptives generally are homed elsewhere.

cards.headline: HORIZON 2007: yearly zoledronic acid after hip fracture cut new fractures by 35% relative and deaths by 28% relative
cards.summary: HORIZON 2007: yearly zoledronic acid after hip fracture cut new fractures by 35% relative and deaths by 28% relative
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (first infusion within 90 days of hip-fracture repair)
cards.people: 2,127 patients who had undergone repair of a recent low-trauma hip fracture (mean age 74.5 years), assigned to yearly intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg (1,065) or placebo (1,062); all patients received supplemental vitamin D and calcium; median follow-up was 1.9 years. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Rates of any new clinical fracture were 8.6% in the zoledronic acid group and 13.9% in the placebo group (a 35% relative risk reduction; P=0.001); new clinical vertebral fracture 1.7% versus 3.8% (P=0.02); new nonvertebral fracture 7.6% versus 10.7% (P=0.03). In the safety analysis, 101 of 1054 patients in the zoledronic acid group (9.6%) and 141 of 1057 in the placebo group (13.3%) died (a 28% relative reduction in deaths from any cause; P=0.01). The most frequent adverse events with zoledronic acid were pyrexia, myalgia, and bone and musculoskeletal pain; no cases of osteonecrosis of the jaw were reported, no adverse effect on fracture healing was noted, and renal and cardiovascular adverse event rates, including atrial fibrillation and stroke, were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Mortality was a safety-analysis outcome, not the primary endpoint (new clinical fracture was) — the survival benefit is real on this record but should be quoted with that provenance, and both arms received calcium and vitamin D, so the trial does not test zoledronic acid against no bone care at all.
cards.source: Lyles KW et al. Zoledronic acid and clinical fractures and mortality after hip fracture. The New England journal of medicine. 2007. PMID: 17878149. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00046254, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Calcium plus vitamin D in care-home residents for fracture prevention (Decalyos)
shelves.question: In elderly women living in nursing homes, does daily calcium (1,200 mg) plus vitamin D3 (800 IU) reduce hip and other non-vertebral fractures versus placebo over 18 months?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bone Density · Calcium · Calcium Phosphates · Cholecalciferol · Female · Femur · Hip Fractures · Humans · Hydroxycholecalciferols · Parathyroid Hormone · Risk
shelves.balance: LIKELY: One large double-blind placebo-controlled trial (Decalyos, Chapuy 1992, 3,270 healthy ambulatory women in nursing homes, mean age 84 ± 6 years) found 18 months of daily tricalcium phosphate (1.2 g elemental calcium) plus 800 IU vitamin D3 reduced hip fractures by 43% relative (P=0.043) and total nonvertebral fractures by 32% relative (P=0.015) versus double placebo among women completing the study, with intention-to-treat analyses similar; proximal femur bone density rose 2.7% on treatment and fell 4.6% on placebo (P<0.001). The population — institutionalised, elderly, and by the trial's own biochemical account vitamin-D-insufficient — is the point: routine supplementation in healthy community adults is a different shelf and is not re-carded here. Fracture outcomes without a mortality claim keep this shelf out of Tier C.

cards.headline: Decalyos 1992: calcium plus vitamin D3 cut hip fractures by 43% relative in nursing-home women over 18 months
cards.summary: Decalyos 1992: calcium plus vitamin D3 cut hip fractures by 43% relative in nursing-home women over 18 months
cards.people: 3,270 healthy ambulatory women living in nursing homes (mean age 84 ± 6 years): 1,634 received tricalcium phosphate (1.2 g elemental calcium) plus 20 µg (800 IU) vitamin D3 daily, and 1,636 received double placebo; serial parathyroid hormone and 25-hydroxyvitamin D were measured in 142 women and femoral bone density at baseline and 18 months in 56 women.
cards.result: Among women who completed the 18-month study, the number of hip fractures was 43% lower (a relative measure; the abstract prints no absolute fracture counts) (P=0.043) and the total number of nonvertebral fractures 32% lower (P=0.015) in the vitamin D3–calcium group than in the placebo group; analyses according to active treatment and by intention to treat were similar. Mean serum parathyroid hormone fell 44% from baseline at 18 months (P<0.001) and serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D rose 162% (P<0.001) on treatment. Proximal femur bone density increased 2.7% in the treatment group and decreased 4.6% in the placebo group (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports only relative reductions and P values for fractures — no absolute counts or rates are printed, so no number-needed-to-treat can honestly be carded — and the headline analysis is in study completers, with the intention-to-treat result described only as 'similar'.

shelves.title: Lifestyle-integrated functional exercise to prevent falls (LiFE)
shelves.question: In older people at risk of falls living at home, does embedding balance and strength activities into daily routines (LiFE) reduce the rate of falls versus a sham gentle-exercise control over 12 months?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Activities of Daily Living · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Life Style · Male · Patient Compliance · Postural Balance · Resistance Training · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One three-arm randomised trial (LiFE study, Clemson 2012, 317 adults aged 70+ at high fall risk in Sydney) found embedding balance and strength training into daily routines reduced the fall rate over 12 months by 31% relative versus a sham gentle-exercise control (incidence rate ratio 0.69 relative, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.99), while the conventional structured exercise programme did not significantly differ from control (0.81 relative, 0.56 to 1.17). A single trial whose confidence interval ends at 0.99 earns POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: LiFE 2012: habit-embedded balance and strength training cut the fall rate by 31% relative; structured exercise did not separate from sham
cards.summary: LiFE 2012: habit-embedded balance and strength training cut the fall rate by 31% relative; structured exercise did not separate from sham
cards.type: Three arm, randomised parallel trial (assessments at baseline, 6 and 12 months; falls by self report)
cards.people: 317 residents of metropolitan Sydney, Australia, aged 70 years or older with two or more falls or one injurious fall in the past 12 months, randomised to the Lifestyle integrated Functional Exercise (LiFE) programme (n=107), a structured balance and lower-limb strength programme done three times a week (n=105), or a sham control programme of gentle exercise (n=105), all home based. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: After 12 months, 172, 193, and 224 falls were recorded in the LiFE, structured exercise, and control groups; fall incidence was 1.66 per person-year (LiFE), 1.90 (structured) and 2.28 (control). LiFE significantly reduced the fall rate versus controls by 31% relative (incidence rate ratio 0.69 — a relative measure — 95% confidence interval 0.48 to 0.99); the structured group versus controls difference was non-significant (0.81, 0.56 to 1.17). Static balance, ankle strength, function and participation were significantly better in the LiFE group than controls, and both active groups improved dynamic balance versus controls.
cards.watchOut: Falls were self-reported and participants knew their programme; the sham was gentle exercise with home visits and phone calls, so the contrast includes attention and habit-formation support, not movement content alone.
cards.source: Clemson L et al. Integration of balance and strength training into daily life activity to reduce rate of falls in older people (the LiFE study): randomised parallel trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2012. PMID: 22872695. Registry ID: Australia and New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry 12606000025538, as stated in the record's abstract — no databank registry field appears in the record. shelves.title: Treating pain stepwise in nursing-home dementia: agitation fell by about a sixth in the one large cluster trial — untreated pain, not the dementia itself, was driving part of the behaviour
shelves.question: In nursing-home residents with dementia, does structured stepwise pain treatment reduce agitation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Analgesics/therapeutic use* · Analysis of Variance · Clinical Protocols · Cluster Analysis · Dementia/psychology* · Female · Homes for the Aged · Humans · Male · Nursing Homes · Pain/prevention & control*, psychology · Psychomotor Agitation/prevention & control* · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). The anchor trial (Husebo BS et al., PMID: 21765198) cluster-randomised 60 nursing-home units and 352 residents with moderate-to-severe dementia and significant behavioural disturbance: eight weeks of an individual stepwise pain protocol — paracetamol first, then morphine, transdermal buprenorphine, or pregabalin — reduced agitation by 17% against usual care (treatment effect −7.0 points on the Cohen-Mansfield agitation inventory, 95% CI −10.3 to −3.7), with parallel gains in overall neuropsychiatric symptoms (−9.0) and measured pain (−1.3), and no difference in daily function or cognition. The second trial of a stepwise approach, STA OP! (Pieper MJ et al., PMID: 26804064), trained staff in a broader stepwise multidisciplinary method in 288 residents with advanced dementia and also reduced agitation (mean difference −4.07 points, 95% CI −7.90 to −0.24) and neuropsychiatric symptoms, with antidepressant use falling (odds ratio 0.32) — though its intervention reached well beyond analgesia and its control arm also received training, which dilutes the contrast. A related multicomponent programme that includes pain assessment and treatment among several components is homed at shelf #2001 (COSMOS); this shelf is the pain-protocol question specifically. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): before reaching for an antipsychotic in a resident who cannot report pain, a structured trial of analgesia is one of the few interventions with randomised evidence behind it.

cards.headline: Husebo 2011: 352 residents, 60 nursing-home units — a stepwise pain protocol cut agitation by 17% in eight weeks, with no cost to function or cognition
cards.summary: Husebo 2011: 352 residents, 60 nursing-home units — a stepwise pain protocol cut agitation by 17% in eight weeks, with no cost to function or cognition
cards.people: 352 residents with moderate-to-severe dementia and clinically significant behavioural disturbances in 60 clusters (single independent nursing-home units) across 18 nursing homes in western Norway; 175 residents in 33 clusters received the stepwise pain protocol for eight weeks (with four weeks of follow-up after treatment ended) and 177 in 27 clusters received usual treatment and care.
cards.result: Agitation (Cohen-Mansfield agitation inventory) fell significantly more in the intervention group after eight weeks: an average reduction of 17%, treatment effect −7.0 points (95% CI −10.3 to −3.7; P < 0.001, adjusted for baseline). Overall neuropsychiatric symptom severity also improved (−9.0, 95% CI −12.6 to −5.5) and pain scores fell (−1.3, 95% CI −1.7 to −0.8). Activities of daily living and cognition (mini-mental state examination) did not differ between groups. The stepwise protocol escalated individual daily analgesia through paracetamol (acetaminophen), morphine, buprenorphine transdermal patch, and pregabalin. Registered as NCT01021696 (EudraCT 2008-007490-20).
cards.watchOut: One trial, in one country's nursing-home system, with staff who could not be blinded to a treatment protocol — expectation effects on rated behaviour cannot be excluded, and the effect was measured at eight weeks, not over the long course of dementia. The protocol's later steps are opioids and pregabalin, drugs with their own harms in this population; the trial shows the protocol as a whole worked, not that every step is safe for every resident. Agitation has many causes (infection, constipation, fear, environment); the trial supports testing the pain hypothesis systematically, not assuming it.
cards.source: Husebo BS et al. Efficacy of treating pain to reduce behavioural disturbances in residents of nursing homes with dementia: cluster randomised clinical trial. BMJ. 2011. PMID: 21765198. Registry ID: NCT01021696. cards.headline: Pieper 2016 (STA OP!): a stepwise multidisciplinary programme in 288 residents with advanced dementia also reduced agitation (−4.1 points) and cut antidepressant use — but the programme was broader than pain treatment
cards.summary: Pieper 2016 (STA OP!): a stepwise multidisciplinary programme in 288 residents with advanced dementia also reduced agitation (−4.1 points) and cut antidepressant use — but the programme was broader than pain treatment
cards.type: Cluster randomised controlled trial (STA OP!, Pieper 2016)
cards.people: 288 residents with advanced dementia and challenging behaviour in 21 clusters (nursing-home units) in 12 Dutch nursing homes; staff on intervention units received comprehensive stepwise multidisciplinary training (the STA OP! method, which works through pain and other causes of behaviour step by step), while control units received training in general nursing skills, dementia management and pain without the stepwise component.
cards.result: Over six months, agitation scores were significantly lower in the intervention condition (Cohen-Mansfield mean difference −4.07 points, 95% CI −7.90 to −0.24; P = .02), as were neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPI-NH −3.57, 95% CI −6.30 to −0.84) and two depression measures. Antidepressant use fell significantly (odds ratio 0.32); reductions in antipsychotics, anxiolytics and hypnotics were not significant (odds ratios 0.69 to 0.90). Analysis was by intention to treat.
cards.watchOut: STA OP! is not a pain trial: it trains staff to work through many possible causes of behaviour in steps, of which pain is one, and the control group received substantial training too — so this card supports the stepwise philosophy rather than isolating the analgesic effect, and its smaller agitation difference (−4.1 vs Husebo's −7.0) is consistent with that dilution. It should not be pooled with Husebo as if both tested the same intervention.
cards.source: Pieper MJ et al. Effects of a Stepwise Multidisciplinary Intervention for Challenging Behavior in Advanced Dementia: A Cluster Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2016. PMID: 26804064. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: two cluster trials, one message — a structured search for pain, treated stepwise, reduces agitation in dementia without touching cognition or function
cards.summary: Synthesis: two cluster trials, one message — a structured search for pain, treated stepwise, reduces agitation in dementia without touching cognition or function
cards.people: 640 nursing-home residents with moderate-to-severe or advanced dementia across two cluster-randomised trials (Norway, 352; Netherlands, 288), both testing stepwise protocols against usual care or non-stepwise training.
cards.result: Agitation: −7.0 Cohen-Mansfield points (95% CI −10.3 to −3.7) with the pain-specific protocol (Husebo 2011) and −4.07 (−7.90 to −0.24) with the broader stepwise programme (Pieper 2016). Neuropsychiatric symptoms improved in both. Psychotropic use: antidepressants fell significantly in STA OP! (OR 0.32); antipsychotic sparing is plausible but not demonstrated. Cognition and daily function: unchanged in the trial that measured them. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Both trials come from northern-European nursing homes with high staffing baselines, and neither followed residents beyond six months; whether the effect survives staff turnover and protocol drift is unknown. The stepwise idea is also tested, bundled with communication training and medication review, in the COSMOS programme at shelf #2001 — the shelves agree in direction, but they are not interchangeable evidence. Tier C is set because the pain-specific claim rests on a single trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Husebo BS et al. BMJ. 2011 (PMID: 21765198); Pieper MJ et al. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2016 (PMID: 26804064).

shelves.title: Stopping a long-term PPI: symptoms do return for some — on-demand use left more people with uncontrolled symptoms — but the pill burden falls by about four tablets a week and no serious harm from stopping has been shown
shelves.question: In long-term PPI users without an ongoing indication, does deprescribing cause unacceptable symptom relapse?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Deprescriptions* · Esophagitis/drug therapy* · Gastroesophageal Reflux/drug therapy* · Humans · Inappropriate Prescribing · Middle Aged · Patient Satisfaction/statistics & numerical data · Proton Pump Inhibitors/adverse effects, therapeutic use* · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Withholding Treatment
shelves.balance: SPLIT — deprescribing trades a real, modest symptom cost for a real reduction in drug burden, and the feared catastrophe is not in the data. The Cochrane review of deprescribing versus continuation (Boghossian TA et al., PMID: 28301676) pooled six trials and 1,758 chronic users: switching to on-demand use increased 'lack of symptom control' (risk ratio 1.71, 95% CI 1.31 to 2.21, low-quality evidence) and lowered satisfaction, but cut consumption by about 3.8 tablets a week (moderate-quality evidence), and the review found insufficient data to conclude anything about long-term benefits or harms of stopping — no serious harm signal appeared. The mechanism behind early relapse is rebound acid hypersecretion, demonstrated in volunteers and homed with the PPI harms evidence at shelf #325 (Reimer 2009): after eight weeks of therapy, 44% of healthy volunteers reported clinically relevant acid symptoms in the month after withdrawal versus 15% on placebo — real symptoms, but in people who never needed the drug, and time-limited. In the population this question is actually about — users whose indication does not survive scrutiny — a patient-centred deprescribing process judged 44% of verified indications potentially inappropriate, and every patient who attempted withdrawal in that small feasibility study ceased or reduced the drug (Reeve E et al., PMID: 25385826). PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (harm) on symptoms, POSSIBLE (benefit) on burden; 'unacceptable' relapse is not what the trials show, but a symptom-free stop is not what they promise either. The harms of continuing PPIs are weighed at shelf #325.

cards.headline: Boghossian 2017 (Cochrane): 6 trials, 1,758 chronic PPI users — on-demand deprescribing increased uncontrolled symptoms (RR 1.71) but saved about 3.8 tablets a week; long-term harm data simply do not exist
cards.summary: Boghossian 2017 (Cochrane): 6 trials, 1,758 chronic PPI users — on-demand deprescribing increased uncontrolled symptoms (RR 1.71) but saved about 3.8 tablets a week; long-term harm data simply do not exist
cards.people: Six randomised and quasi-randomised trials (1,758 participants) comparing deprescribing — five trials of on-demand use, one of abrupt discontinuation — with continued daily PPI therapy in adult chronic users (28 days or more). Participants were aged 48 to 57 in most trials (one trial's mean age was 73) and had non-erosive reflux disease or mild (LA grade A/B) oesophagitis, in outpatient settings.
cards.result: On-demand use increased the risk of 'lack of symptom control' compared with continuous use (risk ratio 1.71, 95% CI 1.31 to 2.21; five trials, 1,653 participants; low-quality evidence). Pill burden fell substantially with on-demand therapy (mean difference −3.79 tablets per week, 95% CI −4.73 to −2.84; four trials, 1,152 participants; moderate-quality evidence). Participant satisfaction was lower with on-demand use (low-quality evidence, high heterogeneity). No included study reported costs or positive withdrawal effects, and the reviewers conclude there were insufficient data to judge the long-term benefits and harms of discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: The trial populations mostly had mild reflux disease — a soft but real indication — so this is indirect evidence for the strictly no-indication user this shelf asks about, in whom relapse should matter less, not more. Five of the six trials tested on-demand use rather than stopping outright; the single abrupt-discontinuation trial cannot carry the stopping question alone. 'Lack of symptom control' is a symptom endpoint, not tissue harm: no trial showed that deprescribing caused erosive relapse, bleeding, or any serious outcome.
cards.source: Boghossian TA et al. Deprescribing versus continuation of chronic proton pump inhibitor use in adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017. PMID: 28301676. systematic review, 6 rcts (boghossian 2017, cochrane) six randomised and quasi-randomised trials (1,758 participants) comparing deprescribing — five trials of on-demand use, one of abrupt discontinuation — with continued daily ppi therapy in adult chronic users (28 days or more). participants were aged 48 to 57 in most trials (one trial's mean age was 73) and had non-erosive reflux disease or mild (la grade a/b) oesophagitis, in outpatient settings. on-demand use increased the risk of 'lack of symptom control' compared with continuous use (risk ratio 1.71, 95% ci 1.31 to 2.21; five trials, 1,653 participants; low-quality evidence). pill burden fell substantially with on-demand therapy (mean difference −3.79 tablets per week, 95% ci −4.73 to −2.84; four trials, 1,152 participants; moderate-quality evidence). participant satisfaction was lower with on-demand use (low-quality evidence, high heterogeneity). no included study reported costs or positive withdrawal effects, and the reviewers conclude there were insufficient data to judge the long-term benefits and harms of discontinuation. the trial populations mostly had mild reflux disease — a soft but real indication — so this is indirect evidence for the strictly no-indication user this shelf asks about, in whom relapse should matter less, not more. five of the six trials tested on-demand use rather than stopping outright; the single abrupt-discontinuation trial cannot carry the stopping question alone. 'lack of symptom control' is a symptom endpoint, not tissue harm: no trial showed that deprescribing caused erosive relapse, bleeding, or any serious outcome. boghossian ta et al. deprescribing versus continuation of chronic proton pump inhibitor use in adults. cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2017. pmid: 28301676. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · deprescriptions* · esophagitis/drug therapy* · gastroesophageal reflux/drug therapy* · humans · inappropriate prescribing · middle aged · patient satisfaction/statistics & numerical data · proton pump inhibitors/adverse effects, therapeutic use* · randomized controlled trials as topic · withholding treatment

cards.headline: Reeve 2015: in a patient-centred deprescribing process, 44% of verified PPI indications were judged potentially inappropriate — and all six patients who attempted withdrawal ceased or reduced the drug
cards.summary: Reeve 2015: in a patient-centred deprescribing process, 44% of verified PPI indications were judged potentially inappropriate — and all six patients who attempted withdrawal ceased or reduced the drug
cards.people: 57 adult PPI users with complex polypharmacy (mean age 70, taking a mean of 14 medications) recruited from hospital outpatient clinics in Australia, taken through a five-step patient-centred deprescribing process (medication history, identification of potentially inappropriate medicines, withdrawal planning with tapering where needed, monitoring and support).
cards.result: The indication for PPI use could be verified in 43 participants and was judged potentially inappropriate in 19 (44%). Eight were suitable for trial withdrawal and six consented; all six successfully ceased (3) or reduced (3) their PPI, sustained at six months in four. The process was acceptable to participants, but barriers included incomplete medication histories, time, and thin evidence for some indications. This is a feasibility study — it shows the process can be done safely in selected patients, not what proportion of all long-term users can stop.
cards.watchOut: Six consenting, selected patients are a proof of concept, not an effect estimate — people who agree to attempt withdrawal are those least attached to the drug and often least symptomatic. The sobering number in this study is upstream: of 57 users, only 19 had a verifiably inappropriate indication and only 8 were suitable to try stopping, which is why population-level PPI use falls slowly even when deprescribing works.
cards.source: Reeve E et al. Feasibility of a patient-centered deprescribing process to reduce inappropriate use of proton pump inhibitors. The Annals of Pharmacotherapy. 2015. PMID: 25385826. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: stopping is neither painless nor dangerous — expect a minority to relapse symptomatically (some of it rebound), expect most of the tablets to go, and do not expect evidence of serious harm
cards.summary: Synthesis: stopping is neither painless nor dangerous — expect a minority to relapse symptomatically (some of it rebound), expect most of the tablets to go, and do not expect evidence of serious harm
cards.people: Six randomised deprescribing trials pooled by Cochrane (1,758 chronic users, mostly mild reflux), one abrupt-discontinuation trial among them, and a 57-patient feasibility study in genuinely inappropriate users; the rebound mechanism is documented in volunteers at shelf #325.
cards.result: Symptom control: worse on-demand than on daily therapy (RR 1.71, 1.31 to 2.21) — a relative increase on a symptom endpoint, in patients who had reflux to begin with. Drug burden: −3.79 tablets per week (moderate-quality evidence). Satisfaction: lower with on-demand use. Serious harm from stopping: none demonstrated anywhere in the randomised record; long-term outcomes: unstudied. In no-indication users, the one feasibility study found withdrawal achievable in all who tried. PROPOSED SPLIT — POSSIBLE (harm) / POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The honest gap is duration: deprescribing trials run for months, so this shelf cannot speak to years off therapy, and it cannot separate true disease relapse from rebound hypersecretion in the individual patient — only time off the drug does that (rebound fades; disease does not). Patients with Barrett's oesophagus, severe erosive disease, or a bleeding history were not the trial populations and are not covered by this verdict; their PPIs have an ongoing indication by definition.
cards.source: Synthesis of Boghossian TA et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2017 (PMID: 28301676); Reeve E et al. The Annals of Pharmacotherapy. 2015 (PMID: 25385826).

shelves.title: Cutting anticholinergic burden to protect the brain: three small trials and very low certainty — in the largest analysis the burden did not even fall, so cognition had nothing to respond to
shelves.question: In older adults, does reducing anticholinergic burden improve cognition?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Humans · Alzheimer Disease* · Cardiovascular Diseases* · Cholinergic Antagonists/adverse effects · Cognitive Dysfunction*/prevention & control · Deprescriptions*
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — an important distinction runs through this shelf: the observational association between anticholinergic burden and dementia is not the question here. The question is whether intervening to reduce the burden improves cognition, and on that the randomised record is three trials and 299 people. The Cochrane review (Taylor-Rowan M et al., PMID: 38063254) found very low certainty evidence throughout: one trial improved Digit Symbol Substitution performance (treatment difference 0.70, 95% CI 0.11 to 1.30) without reducing burden at all; of the two trials that did reduce burden, one found no cognitive difference on any CERAD measure or the MMSE, and the other reported a correlation with one working-memory test amid multiple null measures. No trial reported safety outcomes, and none measured mortality, falls, function, or quality of life with any difference. The largest single analysis since (Nishtala PS et al., PMID: 37339754), a post hoc look at a New Zealand pharmacist deprescribing trial, shows the practical problem underneath: the intervention did not reduce anticholinergic burden overall (standardised effect −0.04, 95% CI −0.26 to 0.19) — a cognition benefit cannot appear if the exposure does not move. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): reducing burden remains sensible prescribing hygiene for other reasons, but improved cognition is a hope the trials have not yet earned. The Beers-list evidence base is re-graded at shelf #137.

cards.headline: Taylor-Rowan 2023 (Cochrane): three trials, 299 participants, very low certainty — one test improved in one trial, everything else null, and no safety outcomes reported anywhere
cards.summary: Taylor-Rowan 2023 (Cochrane): three trials, 299 participants, very low certainty — one test improved in one trial, everything else null, and no safety outcomes reported anywhere
cards.people: Three randomised controlled trials (299 participants in total) of interventions designed to reduce anticholinergic burden in older adults, all in cognitively mixed populations (some cognitively healthy, some with dementia), with outcomes assessed after one to three months. Interventions were pharmacist- or clinician-led medication reduction programmes measured against a variety of anticholinergic burden scales.
cards.result: One trial reported significantly better Digit Symbol Substitution Test performance in the intervention group (treatment difference 0.70, 95% CI 0.11 to 1.30) — although in that trial the proportion of participants with reduced anticholinergic burden did not differ between groups. Two trials did reduce burden; of these, one found no significant difference on CERAD immediate recall (mean difference 0.54, 95% CI −0.91 to 2.05), delayed recall (−0.23, −0.85 to 0.38), recognition (0.77, −0.39 to 1.94), or MMSE (0.39, −0.96 to 1.75), and the other reported a significant correlation between burden and one working-memory test but no effect on multiple other cognitive measures. In GRADE terms the results were of very low certainty, no trial investigated safety outcomes, and the reviewers conclude there is insufficient evidence to support or refute the hypothesis that reducing anticholinergic burden improves cognition.
cards.watchOut: Follow-up of one to three months cannot detect an effect on dementia incidence or slow decline — the outcome families care about — and 299 participants cannot detect modest cognitive effects at all. The review's null is therefore 'unproven', not 'disproven'. Note also the internal contradiction the reviewers expose: the one positive cognitive result came from the trial that failed to reduce the burden it was meant to reduce, which is what chance looks like across many small comparisons.
cards.source: Taylor-Rowan M et al. Anticholinergic deprescribing interventions for reducing risk of cognitive decline or dementia in older adults with and without prior cognitive impairment. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2023. PMID: 38063254. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nishtala 2023: post hoc analysis of a pharmacist deprescribing RCT — the intervention did not reduce anticholinergic burden (effect −0.04), so the cognition question never really got asked
cards.summary: Nishtala 2023: post hoc analysis of a pharmacist deprescribing RCT — the intervention did not reduce anticholinergic burden (effect −0.04), so the cognition question never really got asked
cards.type: Post hoc analysis of a randomised deprescribing trial (Nishtala 2023)
cards.people: 295 community-dwelling frail older adults (median age 79, 67% women) in New Zealand who were taking anticholinergics at baseline, drawn from a randomised trial of pharmacist deprescribing aimed at the Drug Burden Index; this post hoc analysis re-measured the intervention's effect using the Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden (ACB) scale, stratified by frailty and by recruitment before or after COVID lockdown.
cards.result: The intervention did not significantly reduce anticholinergic burden: the standardised between-group difference in ACB change was −0.04 (95% CI −0.26 to 0.19), with mean ACB reductions of −0.23 in the intervention arm and −0.19 in the control arm. A pre-lockdown subgroup leaned toward the intervention (−0.38, 95% CI −0.84 to 0.04) and the post-lockdown subgroup did not (0.07, −0.19 to 0.33); no frailty stratum showed a significant effect. The authors conclude the study provides no evidence that the pharmacist intervention reduced anticholinergic burden.
cards.watchOut: A post hoc analysis of a trial designed for a different target (overall drug burden), in which the anticholinergic exposure barely moved in either arm — it is evidence about how hard burden is to shift with advice-based interventions, not a fair test of what shifting it would do to cognition. It is carded here for that implementation lesson, and it should not be cited as a cognition trial.
cards.source: Nishtala PS et al. Post Hoc Analyses of a Randomized Controlled Trial for the Effect of Pharmacist Deprescribing Intervention on the Anticholinergic Burden in Frail Community-Dwelling Older Adults. Journal of the American Medical Directors Association. 2023. PMID: 37339754. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the intervention literature cannot yet answer the question — trials are few, tiny, short, and the exposure itself often refuses to move
cards.summary: Synthesis: the intervention literature cannot yet answer the question — trials are few, tiny, short, and the exposure itself often refuses to move
cards.people: Three small randomised trials (299 participants, Cochrane 2023) plus a 295-participant post hoc analysis of a pharmacist deprescribing trial — the entire randomised record on reducing anticholinergic burden for cognition.
cards.result: Cognitive outcomes: one positive test result (Digit Symbol Substitution, difference 0.70) in a trial whose burden did not fall; null results on CERAD and MMSE in the trials whose burden did fall; GRADE certainty very low. Burden reduction itself: inconsistent — achieved in two of three Cochrane trials, absent in the largest single analysis (effect −0.04, 95% CI −0.26 to 0.19). Mortality, falls, function, quality of life: no demonstrated differences; safety: unreported. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not let this shelf be quoted against the observational evidence that high anticholinergic burden tracks with dementia — that association (with its own confounding-by-indication problems) is a different claim from the interventional one tested here, and both can be true at once: the burden may mark risk without short-term removal reversing it, especially if any injury is cumulative or the drugs are started for prodromal symptoms. What is missing is a large, long trial that actually achieves a sustained burden reduction; until one exists, deprescribing anticholinergics stands on general prescribing grounds, not on proven cognitive benefit. Tier C is set because the evidence base is three small trials and a post hoc analysis.
cards.source: Synthesis of Taylor-Rowan M et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2023 (PMID: 38063254); Nishtala PS et al. Journal of the American Medical Directors Association. 2023 (PMID: 37339754).
