shelves.title: SENATOR: computer-generated prescribing advice changed almost nothing — ADRs 24.5% versus 24.8%, because clinicians acted on only ~15% of it
shelves.question: In hospitalised multimorbid older adults, does software-generated STOPP/START medication optimisation (SENATOR) reduce adverse drug reactions versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions*/diagnosis, epidemiology, prevention & control · Hospitalization · Humans · Multimorbidity · Polypharmacy* · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life
shelves.balance: SENATOR asked whether software can do what medication-review teams do: generate STOPP/START-based optimisation advice for older, multimorbid hospital patients and thereby prevent adverse drug reactions (ADRs). The results paper (O'Mahony D et al., PMID: 32484850) randomised 1,537 patients at six European centres and found no difference at all in the primary outcome — probable or certain ADRs within 14 days occurred in 24.5% of the intervention group versus 24.8% of controls (odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.24) — and no differences in mortality, rehospitalisation or quality of life. The trial's own explanation is in the same record: attending clinicians implemented only about 15% of the software-generated advice points, so SENATOR tested advice that was mostly never acted on. The protocol paper (Lavan AH et al., PMID: 30760204) shows the design was sound — blinded endpoint adjudication, a defined primary outcome — which makes the null a finding about implementation, not about whether optimising these prescriptions would help if actually done. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): as delivered, software-generated advice did not reduce ADRs; whether the same advice, implemented, would work remains untested by this trial.

cards.headline: SENATOR results (O'Mahony 2020): no reduction in adverse drug reactions (24.5% versus 24.8%; odds ratio 0.98) — and clinicians implemented only about 15% of the software's advice
cards.summary: SENATOR results (O'Mahony 2020): no reduction in adverse drug reactions (24.5% versus 24.8%; odds ratio 0.98) — and clinicians implemented only about 15% of the software's advice
cards.type: Multinational randomised controlled trial, results paper (SENATOR, O'Mahony 2020)
cards.people: 1,537 older medical and surgical patients with multimorbidity and polypharmacy admitted to six European medical centres, randomised 1:1 to SENATOR software-guided medication optimisation plus standard care (772 patients, mean 9.34 daily medications) or standard care alone (765 patients, mean 9.23 daily medications). In the intervention arm, attending clinicians received SENATOR-generated advice at a single time point and could adopt or ignore each recommendation. The trial used a prospective randomised open-label, blinded-endpoint (PROBE) design.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — occurrence of probable or certain adverse drug reactions within 14 days of randomisation — did not differ between groups: 24.5% in the intervention group versus 24.8% in the control group (odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.24; p=0.88). Secondary and tertiary endpoints, including all-cause mortality, rehospitalisation, composite healthcare utilisation and health-related quality of life, likewise showed no significant differences. Implementation of SENATOR software-generated advice points by attending clinicians was poor, at approximately 15%. The authors conclude that uptake of software-generated medication advice was poor and did not reduce ADR incidence during the index hospitalisation.
cards.watchOut: A null result with 15% implementation cannot distinguish 'the advice was wrong' from 'the advice was ignored' — and the single-time-point delivery (one report placed in the record) is a weak form of the intervention compared with a pharmacist or team who follows through. The trial should not be cited as evidence that STOPP/START optimisation does not work; it is evidence that generating a report does not, by itself, change prescribing.
cards.source: O'Mahony D et al. Prevention of adverse drug reactions in hospitalized older patients with multi-morbidity and polypharmacy: the SENATOR* randomized controlled clinical trial. Age and Ageing. 2020. PMID: 32484850. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: SENATOR protocol (Lavan 2019): the design behind the null — STOPP/START software advice placed in the chart, with blinded adjudication of adverse drug reactions at 14 days
cards.summary: SENATOR protocol (Lavan 2019): the design behind the null — STOPP/START software advice placed in the chart, with blinded adjudication of adverse drug reactions at 14 days
cards.people: Protocol for the multinational, pragmatic, parallel-arm PROBE trial in older patients with acute illness screened within 48 hours of hospital arrival: clinical and medication data entered into the SENATOR software, which applied STOPP and START criteria, flagged drug–drug and drug–disease interactions, and added non-pharmacological recommendations aimed at reducing delirium risk. Intervention-arm reports were placed in the medical record for a senior clinician to review and adopt as judged appropriate; both arms received routine pharmaceutical care.
cards.result: The protocol pre-specified the primary outcome as the proportion of patients experiencing at least one adjudicated probable or certain, non-trivial ADR during the index hospitalisation, assessed at 14 days post-randomisation or discharge if earlier, with potential ADRs identified retrospectively and adjudicated by a blinded expert committee; twelve pre-specified event types representing the majority of ADRs were reported to the committee. Follow-up at twelve weeks post-discharge assessed medication quality and healthcare utilisation. No outcome results are reported in this protocol record; the results are carded above (PMID: 32484850).
cards.watchOut: Carded for design transparency only — a protocol contains no results and must never be quoted as evidence of effect. Its value here is showing that the null result was not a design accident: the endpoint was pre-specified and blindly adjudicated, and the weak link the protocol itself reveals is the delivery mechanism — advice placed in the record for a busy clinician to act on, or not.

cards.result: Adverse drug reactions within 14 days: 24.5% versus 24.8% (odds ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.24). Mortality, rehospitalisation, quality of life: no significant differences. shelves.title: VISIBLE: swapping multifocals for single-lens glasses outdoors cut falls in active wearers (rate ratio 0.60) — and raised them in the least active
shelves.question: In older multifocal-glasses wearers who take part in regular outdoor activities, does switching to single-lens distance glasses reduce falls versus continuing multifocals?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/prevention & control, statistics & numerical data · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Counseling · Exercise/physiology · Eyeglasses* · Female · Humans · Male · New South Wales · Patient Compliance · Presbyopia/therapy · Quality of Life · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome · Walking/physiology
shelves.balance: The VISIBLE trial (Haran MJ et al., PMID: 20501583) randomised 606 regular multifocal-glasses wearers (mean age 80, all at increased falls risk) to receive single-lens distance glasses with advice to wear them for walking and outdoor activities, or usual care. Overall, the result was null: an 8% relative reduction in falls that was not significant (incidence rate ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.16), with the absolute fall counts not printed in the record. The pre-planned subgroup analyses split cleanly by behaviour: in people who regularly took part in outside activities, the intervention significantly reduced all falls (incidence rate ratio 0.60, 0.42 to 0.87), outside falls and injurious falls; in people with little outdoor activity, outside falls significantly increased. Only 54% of the intervention group used the distance glasses satisfactorily for at least seven of twelve months, so even the positive subgroup result was achieved with partial adherence. PROPOSED SPLIT: single-lens distance glasses for outdoor use help active multifocal wearers and may harm inactive ones — the right prescription depends on how much the person actually goes out.

cards.headline: VISIBLE 2010: single-lens distance glasses — no overall fall reduction (rate ratio 0.92), a clear benefit in regular outdoor-goers (0.60), and more outside falls in the least active
cards.summary: VISIBLE 2010: single-lens distance glasses — no overall fall reduction (rate ratio 0.92), a clear benefit in regular outdoor-goers (0.60), and more outside falls in the least active
cards.people: 606 regular wearers of multifocal glasses (mean age 80, SD 7) in Sydney and the Illawarra, Australia, all at increased risk of falls (a fall in the previous year or a timed up-and-go over 15 seconds) who used multifocals outdoors at least three times a week. 305 were randomised to provision of single-lens distance glasses with recommendations to wear them for walking and outdoor activities, and 301 to usual care, with 13 months of follow-up and blinded outcome assessors; 299 intervention and 298 control participants were available to follow-up.
cards.result: Single-lens glasses were provided to 275 (90%) of the intervention group within two months; 162 (54%) reported satisfactory use for walking and outdoor activities for at least seven of the twelve months after dispensing. Overall, the intervention resulted in an 8% relative reduction in falls that was not statistically significant (incidence rate ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.16). Pre-planned subgroup analyses showed the intervention significantly reduced all falls (incidence rate ratio 0.60, 0.42 to 0.87), outside falls and injurious falls in people who regularly took part in outside activities — while a significant increase in outside falls occurred in intervention participants who took part in little outside activity.
cards.watchOut: The headline depends on a subgroup defined by outdoor activity level: pre-planned, which earns it credibility, but still a subgroup of a trial whose overall result was null, and the harm signal in inactive wearers rests on the same analysis. Adherence was incomplete (54% satisfactory use), the record's abstract prints rate ratios without absolute fall counts, and the mechanism cuts both ways — a new pair of glasses changes depth judgement and step-edge perception until the wearer adapts, which may be exactly why infrequent outdoor walkers fell more.
cards.source: Haran MJ et al. Effect on falls of providing single lens distance vision glasses to multifocal glasses wearers: VISIBLE randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2010. PMID: 20501583. Registry ID: NCT00350389. cards.headline: Synthesis: the same glasses help or harm depending on the wearer's life — prescribe by activity level, not by age
cards.summary: Synthesis: the same glasses help or harm depending on the wearer's life — prescribe by activity level, not by age
cards.people: One randomised trial, 606 multifocal wearers at increased falls risk (VISIBLE). General falls-prevention and cataract-surgery questions are carded at shelves #161 and #792.
cards.result: All falls overall: incidence rate ratio 0.92 (95% CI 0.73 to 1.16). Regular outdoor activity subgroup: 0.60 (0.42 to 0.87), with fewer outside and injurious falls. Low outdoor activity subgroup: significantly increased outside falls. Satisfactory adherence: 54%. PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit in regular outdoor-goers, possible harm in the least active.
cards.watchOut: SPLIT here is a subgroup split from a single trial, not two bodies of evidence pointing opposite ways; replication in an activity-stratified trial would settle it. Until then, the practical rule the trial supports is narrow: offer single-lens distance glasses for outdoor walking to multifocal wearers who go out regularly, counsel them through the adaptation period, and do not press the swap on people who rarely leave home. Tier C is set because the decisive findings are subgroup findings.
cards.source: Synthesis of Haran MJ et al. BMJ. 2010 (PMID: 20501583).

shelves.title: Podiatry against falls: a multifaceted foot intervention cut the fall rate by a relative 36% in older people with disabling foot pain
shelves.question: In community-dwelling older people with foot pain/disability, does a multifaceted podiatry intervention prevent falls versus routine podiatry care?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/prevention & control · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Persons with Disabilities* · Female · Foot* · Humans · Male · Pain/complications · Patient Compliance · Podiatry* · Queensland
shelves.balance: Spink 2011 (PMID: 21680622) randomised 305 community-dwelling older people with disabling foot pain and increased falls risk to a multifaceted podiatry intervention or routine podiatry care for twelve months. The intervention group had a 36% relative reduction in the rate of falls (incidence rate ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.91; p=0.01), with the record printing 264 falls in total across both groups rather than arm-specific counts. The proportion of people who fell did not differ significantly (relative risk 0.85, 0.66 to 1.08), nor did multiple fallers (0.63, 0.38 to 1.04), and fractures were too few to judge (one versus seven; 0.14, 0.02 to 1.15). Strength, ankle range of motion and balance measures improved. Adherence was moderate: about half completed at least three-quarters of the requested exercise sessions. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single, well-conducted trial shows fewer falls per person-year from a cheap, low-risk podiatry package in people whose feet hurt — without yet showing fewer people falling or fewer fractures.

cards.headline: Spink 2011: multifaceted podiatry cut the fall rate by a relative 36% (rate ratio 0.64) in older people with disabling foot pain — but the proportion who fell did not significantly change
cards.summary: Spink 2011: multifaceted podiatry cut the fall rate by a relative 36% (rate ratio 0.64) in older people with disabling foot pain — but the proportion who fell did not significantly change
cards.people: 305 community-dwelling men and women (mean age 74, SD 6) with disabling foot pain and an increased risk of falling, recruited at a university health sciences clinic in Melbourne, Australia. 153 were allocated to a multifaceted podiatry intervention and 152 to routine podiatry care, with twelve months of follow-up; 296 participants returned all twelve monthly falls calendars.
cards.result: 264 falls occurred during the study. Participants in the intervention group experienced 36% fewer falls in relative terms than the control group (incidence rate ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.45 to 0.91; p=0.01). The proportion of fallers did not differ significantly (relative risk 0.85, 0.66 to 1.08; p=0.19), nor did multiple fallers (0.63, 0.38 to 1.04; p=0.07). One fracture occurred in the intervention group and seven in the control group (0.14, 0.02 to 1.15; p=0.07). Adherence was good but incomplete: 52% of participants completed 75% or more of the requested three exercise sessions weekly, and 55% of those issued orthoses wore them most of the time. Ankle eversion strength, ankle range of motion and balance measures improved significantly in the intervention group.
cards.watchOut: The significant outcome is the fall rate, not the risk of being a faller — the intervention may work mainly by reducing repeat falls in people who fall anyway, and the trial cannot prove even that. Fractures (one versus seven) look dramatic and mean almost nothing at these numbers. The population is specific: community-dwelling people with disabling foot pain who attended a podiatry clinic — not all older people, and not people whose falls are driven by syncope, medication or neurological disease.
cards.source: Spink MJ et al. Effectiveness of a multifaceted podiatry intervention to prevent falls in community dwelling older people with disabling foot pain: randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2011. PMID: 21680622. Registry ID: ACTRN12608000065392, stated in the record's abstract. shelves.title: Home intervention teams against falls: 163 versus 204 falls in frail elders — and Cochrane agrees, but only for people selected as high-risk
shelves.question: In community-dwelling frail older people, does a home intervention team assessment and intervention programme prevent falls versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/prevention & control · Accidents, Home/prevention & control · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Frail Elderly* · Home Care Services, Hospital-Based · Humans · Male
shelves.balance: Two layers of evidence agree, with the same condition attached: home intervention works in people selected for high falls risk. The Falls-HIT trial (Nikolaus T et al., PMID: 12588572) randomised 360 frail older people (mean age 81.5) discharged from a geriatric hospital to a home intervention team — diagnostic home visit, hazard assessment, facilitated modifications, training in technical and mobility aids, and a reinforcement visit — versus assessment with recommendations and usual care. Over one year there were 163 falls in the intervention group versus 204 in controls, a 31% relative reduction (incidence rate ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.97), concentrated in those with two or more falls in the prior year (rate ratio 0.63, 0.43 to 0.94). The Cochrane review of environmental interventions (Clemson L et al., PMID: 36893804) generalises the pattern across 22 studies: home fall-hazard interventions reduced the fall rate by a relative 26% overall (rate ratio 0.74, 0.61 to 0.91) and by a relative 38% in higher-risk selected populations (0.62, 0.56 to 0.70, high-certainty evidence), with no effect in unselected populations (1.05, 0.96 to 1.16). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): targeted home assessment and modification reduces falls in frail, high-risk older people; offered indiscriminately, it does not.

cards.headline: Nikolaus 2003 (Falls-HIT): a home intervention team produced 31% relatively fewer falls over one year (163 versus 204 falls; rate ratio 0.69), with the benefit concentrated in prior recurrent fallers
cards.summary: Nikolaus 2003 (Falls-HIT): a home intervention team produced 31% relatively fewer falls over one year (163 versus 204 falls; rate ratio 0.69), with the benefit concentrated in prior recurrent fallers
cards.people: 360 community-dwelling frail older people (mean age 81.5, SD 6.4) admitted from home to a university-affiliated geriatric hospital with functional decline, especially in mobility. All received comprehensive geriatric assessment; the intervention group additionally received a diagnostic home visit assessing environmental hazards, advice on changes, facilitation of home modifications, training in the use of technical and mobility aids, and a reinforcement visit at three months. Controls received assessment with recommendations and usual care at home. Follow-up was one year.
cards.result: After one year there were 163 falls in the intervention group and 204 in the control group — a 31% relative reduction (incidence rate ratio 0.69, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.97), with the absolute fall counts as printed. The intervention was most effective in participants who reported two or more falls in the year before recruitment: in that subgroup, recurrent fallers numbered 21 in the intervention group versus 36 in controls (p=0.009) and the fall rate was significantly reduced (incidence rate ratio 0.63, 0.43 to 0.94). Compliance with recommended changes varied by type of change, from 83% down to 33% at twelve months.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial from 2003 in a selected post-hospital frail population; the overall confidence interval (0.51 to 0.97) only just excludes no effect, and the persuasive result is the recurrent-faller subgroup. Compliance with some recommended changes fell to 33%, so the tested intervention is 'assessment plus facilitation plus follow-up', not a leaflet of recommendations — services that only advise should expect less.
cards.source: Nikolaus T et al. Preventing falls in community-dwelling frail older people using a home intervention team (HIT): results from the randomized Falls-HIT trial. cards.headline: Clemson 2023 (Cochrane): home fall-hazard interventions reduced fall rates by a relative 26% overall and 38% in higher-risk people — and not at all in unselected populations
cards.summary: Clemson 2023 (Cochrane): home fall-hazard interventions reduced fall rates by a relative 26% overall and 38% in higher-risk people — and not at all in unselected populations
cards.people: 22 randomised studies from ten countries involving 8,463 community-residing older people (average age 78; 65% women), covering home fall-hazard reduction, assistive technology, and education interventions; the home fall-hazard analysis included 14 studies and 5,830 participants.
cards.result: Home fall-hazard interventions probably reduced the overall rate of falls by a relative 26% (rate ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.91; 12 studies, 5,293 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) — 343 fewer falls per 1,000 people a year against a control risk of 1,319. In people selected for higher risk of falling, the relative reduction was 38% (rate ratio 0.62, 0.56 to 0.70; nine studies, 1,513 participants; high-certainty evidence), and the risk of being a faller fell by a relative 26% (risk ratio 0.74, 0.65 to 0.85). In people not selected for fall risk there was no reduction (rate ratio 1.05, 0.96 to 1.16; high-certainty evidence). Vision-improvement interventions may make little or no difference to fall rates (rate ratio 1.12, 0.84 to 1.50; low-certainty evidence), and effects on fractures and hospitalisations were small or absent.
cards.watchOut: The pooled 'home hazard' category bundles different programmes, and the high-certainty subgroup finding is a selection effect as much as a treatment effect: these interventions only show benefit where baseline fall rates are high. The review's null for vision interventions is about vision improvement as a falls strategy generally and does not overturn the activity-specific VISIBLE result carded at shelf #2856.

shelves.title: HALT: a person-centred deprescribing programme cut regular antipsychotic use by 81.7% over 12 months with no rise in behavioural symptoms — in a single-arm study with no control group
shelves.question: In long-term aged-care residents prescribed antipsychotics, does a person-centred deprescribing intervention (HALT) achieve sustained antipsychotic reduction without worsening behavioural symptoms?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/statistics & numerical data · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antipsychotic Agents/administration & dosage · Australia · Dementia/drug therapy, psychology · Deprescriptions* · Drug Utilization/statistics & numerical data · Female · Health Personnel/education · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Longitudinal Studies · Male · Middle Aged · Neuropsychological Tests · Nursing Homes*
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — HALT is a single-arm longitudinal programme, and everything on this shelf must be read with that limit in front. In the main outcome report (Brodaty H et al., PMID: 29941156), 139 residents of 23 nursing homes who had taken a regular antipsychotic for at least 3 months, without a primary psychotic illness or severe behavioural symptoms, went through a deprescribing protocol with education of general practitioners, pharmacists and nurses in non-pharmacological management: the number on regular antipsychotics fell by 81.7% (95% CI 72.4 to 89.0) over 12 months, without drug substitution and without a significant increase in as-needed antipsychotic or benzodiazepine use, and with no change in behavioural symptoms or in adverse outcomes including falls and hospitalisations. The companion analyses show both the mechanism and the leak: person-centred care training was what champions credited for the change (Chenoweth L et al., PMID: 30069476, the protocol and context paper for the programme; Jessop T et al., PMID: 28266282), and in Aerts L et al. (PMID: 31276255) 39 of 133 participants never ceased or were represcribed, most often at nurses' request (63.2%) for perceived — but not objectively measured — worsening agitation. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): sustained antipsychotic reduction of this size is clearly feasible in selected residents, but a single-arm study cannot show the programme caused it, nor exclude harm in the residents who were excluded or represcribed. The placebo-controlled withdrawal evidence is shelved separately at DART-AD #934.

cards.headline: Brodaty 2018 (HALT): regular antipsychotic use fell by 81.7% over 12 months, with no change in behavioural symptoms, falls or hospitalisations — and no control group
cards.summary: Brodaty 2018 (HALT): regular antipsychotic use fell by 81.7% over 12 months, with no change in behavioural symptoms, falls or hospitalisations — and no control group
cards.type: Single-arm longitudinal study — main HALT outcome report (Brodaty 2018)
cards.people: 139 residents taking regular antipsychotic medication for at least 3 months, recruited by nursing staff from 23 nursing homes in long-term residential care; residents with a primary psychotic illness (such as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder) or severe behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia were excluded. The intervention was an antipsychotic deprescribing protocol plus education of general practitioners, pharmacists and residential care nurses in non-pharmacological prevention and management of behavioural symptoms.
cards.result: The number of older adults on regular antipsychotics over 12 months reduced by 81.7% (95% CI 72.4 to 89.0). Withdrawal was not accompanied by drug substitution or a significant increase in pro re nata (as-needed) antipsychotic or benzodiazepine administration. There was no change in behavioural and psychological symptoms (Neuropsychiatric Inventory, Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory, and social withdrawal) or in adverse outcomes (falls, hospitalizations, and cognitive decline). The authors conclude that in this selected sample, sustained reduction in regular antipsychotic use is feasible without an increase in behavioural symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm, repeated-measures design: there is no comparison group, so the 81.7% figure mixes the programme's effect with selection (residents judged suitable, without severe symptoms), regression to the mean, and any background trend toward less antipsychotic prescribing. Denominators also shift between HALT papers (139 recruited here; 146 in the baseline snapshot; 133 in the represcribing analysis), so percentages should be quoted from this report only.
cards.source: Brodaty H et al. Antipsychotic Deprescription for Older Adults in Long-term Care: The HALT Study. Journal of the American Medical Directors Association. 2018. PMID: 29941156. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Aerts 2019: 39 of 133 HALT participants never ceased or were represcribed — nurses were the commonest drivers (63.2%), usually for perceived agitation that objective measures did not confirm
cards.summary: Aerts 2019: 39 of 133 HALT participants never ceased or were represcribed — nurses were the commonest drivers (63.2%), usually for perceived agitation that objective measures did not confirm
cards.people: The 39 of 133 HALT participants who never ceased their antipsychotic medication or were represcribed a regular or as-needed antipsychotic after initial deprescribing (19% of participants in the study's framing); circumstances were reconstructed by a consensus panel from questionnaires to nursing staff, general practitioners and family, triangulated with file audit of progress notes, medication charts, incident reports and discharge summaries.
cards.result: Nurses were the most common drivers of represcribing (63.2%), followed by family members (39.5%), general practitioners (23.7%), specialists (13.2%), and hospital staff (10.5%); multiple drivers were present in 46.2% of participants. Increased agitated and aggressive behaviours were the most commonly reported reasons for represcribing, even though these changes were not identified over time on objective measures. Consent and dosage practices remained poor despite education.
cards.watchOut: This is a study of the failures only, with no denominator-based comparison against successful deprescriptions beyond the 39/133 count, and the driver percentages overlap (multiple drivers per resident). It explains where a HALT-style programme leaks; it does not estimate how often deprescribing causes real behavioural deterioration — on the objective measures reported in the main study, it did not.
cards.source: Aerts L et al. Why deprescribing antipsychotics in older people with dementia in long-term care is not always successful: Insights from the HALT study. International Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry. 2019. PMID: 31276255. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a large, sustained reduction in a selected single-arm cohort — feasibility shown, causation and generalisability not
cards.summary: Synthesis: a large, sustained reduction in a selected single-arm cohort — feasibility shown, causation and generalisability not
cards.people: One single-arm longitudinal programme (139 residents, 23 nursing homes) with a represcribing analysis of its 133-participant follow-up set; the programme's protocol and person-centred context are described by Jessop T et al. (PMID: 28266282) and Chenoweth L et al. (PMID: 30069476).
cards.result: Antipsychotic use: down 81.7% (95% CI 72.4 to 89.0) at 12 months, without substitution or increased as-needed psychotropic use. Behavioural symptoms, falls, hospitalisations, cognitive decline: no change. Failure mode: 39/133 never ceased or were represcribed, driven mainly by staff perception of agitation. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: The absence of a control group is the whole caveat: motivated homes, selected residents and a national climate of antipsychotic reduction could each produce part of this result. HALT should be cited as proof that a person-centred deprescribing programme can be run and sustained, not as an effect size to expect elsewhere — and never as a substitute for the controlled withdrawal trials (DART-AD, shelf #934). Tier C is set because the evidence is a single-arm programme.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brodaty H et al. Journal of the American Medical Directors Association. 2018 (PMID: 29941156); Aerts L et al. International Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry. 2019 (PMID: 31276255).

shelves.title: Percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation for overactive bladder: 54.5% reported moderate or marked improvement versus 20.9% on sham in the SUmiT trial
shelves.question: In adults with overactive bladder, does percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation improve symptoms versus sham stimulation?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Syndrome · Tibial Nerve · Transcutaneous Electric Nerve Stimulation* · Urinary Bladder, Overactive/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the anchor is a properly sham-controlled trial (Peters KM et al., PMID: 20171677): 220 adults with overactive bladder symptoms randomised 1:1 to 12 weekly percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation sessions or sham, with 54.5% of the stimulation group reporting moderately or markedly improved overall bladder symptoms at week 13 versus 20.9% on sham (p<0.001), statistically significant improvements in voiding-diary frequency, nighttime voids, moderate-to-severe urgency voids and urge incontinence episodes, and no serious device-related adverse events. The wider stimulation literature is supportive but less decisive: a systematic review and meta-analysis of electrical nerve stimulation protocols (Zomkowski K et al., PMID: 35119495) found tibial neurostimulation better than sacral neurostimulation for urge incontinence (mean difference 1.25 episodes, 95% CI 0.12 to 2.38, in 73 participants) but no superiority of any one stimulation protocol over others on frequency, nocturia, urgency or quality of life, with low-to-moderate effect sizes overall. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): twelve weeks of tibial nerve stimulation beats sham on symptoms in the short term; durability, maintenance schedules and standing against drug therapy are not settled by this record. Sacral neuromodulation is shelved separately at #912 and mirabegron at #149.

cards.headline: Peters 2010 (SUmiT): 54.5% on tibial nerve stimulation reported moderate or marked improvement versus 20.9% on sham (p<0.001), with diary improvements and no serious device events
cards.summary: Peters 2010 (SUmiT): 54.5% on tibial nerve stimulation reported moderate or marked improvement versus 20.9% on sham (p<0.001), with diary improvements and no serious device events
cards.people: 220 adults with overactive bladder symptoms in a multicentre, double-blind, randomised controlled trial, allocated 1:1 to 12 weeks of weekly percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation or sham therapy; outcomes were the subject global response assessment at week 13, 3-day voiding diaries, and overactive bladder and quality-of-life questionnaires at baseline and week 13.
cards.result: On the global response assessment for overall bladder symptoms, 54.5% of the stimulation group reported moderately or markedly improved responses compared with 20.9% of sham subjects (p<0.001), and every individual global-response subset symptom component improved significantly versus sham. Voiding-diary parameters after 12 weeks showed statistically significant improvements versus sham in frequency, nighttime voids, voids with moderate to severe urgency, and urinary urge incontinence episodes. No serious device-related adverse events or malfunctions were reported. The authors describe the trial as level I evidence that the therapy is safe and effective for overactive bladder symptoms.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen weeks is the whole horizon: the trial says nothing about how long benefit lasts after the 12 sessions end or what maintenance schedule preserves it. The headline outcome is a subjective global assessment — the outcome most vulnerable to any unblinding of a needle-based intervention — although the diary measures moved the same way. Absolute diary effect sizes are not given in the record, so the size of the day-to-day symptom change cannot be quoted from this card.
cards.source: Peters KM et al. Randomized trial of percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation versus Sham efficacy in the treatment of overactive bladder syndrome: results from the SUmiT trial. cards.headline: Zomkowski 2022: tibial stimulation beat sacral stimulation for urge incontinence (mean difference 1.25 episodes), but no stimulation protocol beat the others on frequency, nocturia, urgency or quality of life
cards.summary: Zomkowski 2022: tibial stimulation beat sacral stimulation for urge incontinence (mean difference 1.25 episodes), but no stimulation protocol beat the others on frequency, nocturia, urgency or quality of life
cards.people: Nine randomised controlled trials of electrical nerve stimulation protocols (intravaginal, percutaneous tibial and transcutaneous tibial) in adults with non-neurogenic overactive bladder, pooled for urinary symptoms (frequency, nocturia, urgency) and quality of life.
cards.result: Tibial neurostimulation showed better results than sacral neurostimulation for urge incontinence (mean difference 1.25 episodes, 95% CI 0.12 to 2.38, n=73). On pooled analysis the different neurostimulation protocols demonstrated similar results for urinary frequency, nocturia and urgency, and for quality of life; effect sizes were generally low to moderate. The best reported parameters for percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation were 20-Hz frequency and 200-microsecond pulse width, once a week.
cards.watchOut: Nine small trials across several different protocols means each comparison rests on very few participants (the tibial-versus-sacral incontinence result on 73). This review compares stimulation methods with each other more than with sham, so it cannot add much certainty to the SUmiT efficacy question — its value is in showing no rival protocol has outrun the percutaneous tibial approach.
cards.source: Zomkowski K et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: one good sham-controlled trial with a clear short-term win, inside a small and fragmented stimulation literature
cards.summary: Synthesis: one good sham-controlled trial with a clear short-term win, inside a small and fragmented stimulation literature
cards.people: One multicentre sham-controlled trial (220 adults, 13 weeks) plus a 9-trial systematic review of electrical nerve stimulation protocols in non-neurogenic overactive bladder.
cards.result: Global improvement: 54.5% versus 20.9% (p<0.001) favouring stimulation; diary frequency, nocturia, urgency voids and urge incontinence episodes all significantly improved versus sham; no serious device-related adverse events. Cross-protocol evidence: no stimulation method superior overall; effect sizes low to moderate. Durability beyond 13 weeks: untested in this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The population skews older but is not an older-adults-only trial, and people with neurogenic bladder are outside this evidence. Weekly clinic visits for 12 weeks are themselves part of the intervention's cost. Tier C is set because the efficacy claim rests essentially on one sham-controlled trial with a short horizon.
cards.source: Synthesis of Peters KM et al. The Journal of Urology. 2010 (PMID: 20171677); Zomkowski K et al. International Urogynecology Journal. 2022 (PMID: 35119495).

shelves.title: Functional incidental training in VA nursing homes: prompted voiding plus exercise improved incontinence, endurance and strength in a crossover trial — delivered by research staff, four times a day
shelves.question: In nursing-home residents with urinary incontinence, does functional incidental training (prompted voiding combined with exercise) reduce wet episodes versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cross-Over Studies · Exercise Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Male · Nursing Homes · Physical Endurance* · Treatment Outcome · Urinary Incontinence/rehabilitation · Walking*
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — functional incidental training (FIT) was tested in one randomised crossover trial in four Veterans Affairs nursing homes (Ouslander JG et al., PMID: 16108924): prompted voiding combined with individualised endurance and strength exercises, offered four times a day, five days a week, for eight weeks, delivered by trained research staff. Of 528 residents screened, 178 were eligible and 107 randomised (52 immediate, 55 delayed intervention); only 64 completed the intervention phase. The record reports a significant effect of FIT on virtually all measures of endurance, strength and urinary incontinence — but not on Functional Independence Measure scores for locomotion or toileting — with effects seen both against the control period and when the delayed group crossed over, deterioration when the first group crossed back to no intervention, and 43 of 64 completers (67%) classified as responders on at least one measure across endurance, strength and incontinence; no FIT-related adverse events occurred. Because the record gives no numeric effect size for wet episodes, and because delivery depended on research staff at an intensity ordinary nursing-home staffing rarely matches, the honest grade is feasibility-plus-signal rather than proven benefit. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence). Community pelvic-floor training is shelved separately at #486.

cards.headline: Ouslander 2005: FIT significantly improved urinary incontinence, endurance and strength in both crossover phases — but only 64 of 107 randomised residents completed, and no wet-episode effect size is reported
cards.summary: Ouslander 2005: FIT significantly improved urinary incontinence, endurance and strength in both crossover phases — but only 64 of 107 randomised residents completed, and no wet-episode effect size is reported
cards.people: Residents of four Department of Veterans Affairs nursing homes: 528 patients screened, 178 eligible, 107 randomised to immediate intervention (n=52) or delayed intervention (n=55). Trained research staff delivered FIT — prompted voiding combined with individualised, functionally oriented endurance and strength-training exercises — four times per day, 5 days per week, for 8 weeks; groups then crossed over. Outcomes included timed walking/wheeling, sit-to-stand, Functional Independence Measure (FIM) locomotion and toileting, one-repetition maximum strength, frequency of urine and stool incontinence, and appropriate toileting ratios; 64 subjects completed the intervention phase.
cards.result: There was a significant effect of the FIT intervention on virtually all measures of endurance, strength, and urinary incontinence, but not on the FIM for locomotion or toileting. Effects appeared when Group 1 received the intervention versus control and again when Group 2 crossed over to it; Group 1 deteriorated in all measures during its 8-week no-intervention crossover period. In within-person comparisons in the 64 completers, 43 (67%) were 'responders' — maintenance or improvement in at least one measure of endurance, strength, and urinary incontinence. No adverse events related to FIT occurred.
cards.watchOut: The abstract reports significance, not magnitude: no wet-check rates or episode counts are given, so nobody can say from this record how much drier a resident becomes. Attrition was heavy (107 randomised, 64 completing the intervention phase), delivery was by research staff four times daily — the authors themselves flag staff workload and cost as the barrier to practice — and VA nursing-home residents are not typical of all long-term care populations.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a single crossover trial showing the combined programme moves incontinence and fitness together, with the size of the continence gain unquantified
cards.summary: Synthesis: a single crossover trial showing the combined programme moves incontinence and fitness together, with the size of the continence gain unquantified
cards.people: One randomised controlled crossover trial (107 randomised, 64 completers) in four VA nursing homes; no second trial or meta-analysis of FIT itself was found to card.
cards.result: Urinary incontinence, endurance and strength: significant improvement in both crossover directions, with deterioration on withdrawal. Independence in locomotion/toileting (FIM): no effect. Responders: 43/64 (67%) on at least one domain. Adverse events: none related to FIT. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: FIT bundles two interventions — prompted voiding and exercise — so this shelf cannot say which component carried the continence effect, and prompted voiding alone has its own separate literature. The result is best read as: an intensive, staff-delivered combined programme can improve continence measures in selected nursing-home residents while it runs. Tier C is set because the evidence is one trial with research-staff delivery and 40% non-completion.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ouslander JG et al. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2005 (PMID: 16108924).

shelves.title: Atomoxetine for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: acute single-dose studies raised standing pressure, but the 4-week placebo-controlled trial found no symptom benefit
shelves.question: In adults with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, does atomoxetine raise standing blood pressure and improve symptoms versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Atomoxetine Hydrochloride*/therapeutic use, administration & dosage · Hypotension, Orthostatic*/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Cross-Over Studies* · Male · Female · Middle Aged · Adrenergic Uptake Inhibitors*/therapeutic use, administration & dosage · Aged · Adult · Treatment Outcome · Blood Pressure/drug effects
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the evidence divides by treatment duration. The one trial of sustained treatment (Mwesigwa N et al., PMID: 39294522), a randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover study of 4-week atomoxetine periods in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, found no difference on its primary symptom endpoint: orthostatic hypotension questionnaire composite scores of −0.3 ± 1.7 on atomoxetine versus −0.4 ± 1.5 on placebo at 2 weeks (P=0.806) and −0.6 ± 2.4 versus −0.5 ± 1.6 at 4 weeks (P=0.251), with no significant differences on the symptom or daily-activity subscales either; the drug was well tolerated. Set against that, a systematic review of the randomised literature (Jung YJ et al., PMID: 36647224) found only four randomised trials, mostly acute-dose, in which atomoxetine effectively increased systolic blood pressure and improved orthostatic symptoms, with effects most pronounced in central autonomic failure such as multiple system atrophy. PROPOSED SPLIT: a single dose can raise standing pressure in the laboratory; four weeks of treatment did not improve symptoms more than placebo in the trial designed to test exactly that. Droxidopa is shelved at #931/#1558 and pyridostigmine at #2691.

cards.headline: Mwesigwa 2024: over 4 weeks, atomoxetine was no better than placebo on orthostatic symptoms (questionnaire composite −0.3 versus −0.4 at 2 weeks, P=0.806)
cards.summary: Mwesigwa 2024: over 4 weeks, atomoxetine was no better than placebo on orthostatic symptoms (questionnaire composite −0.3 versus −0.4 at 2 weeks, P=0.806)
cards.people: Adults with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: 68 patients screened, 40 randomised, 37 completed. After an initial open-label single-dose phase (10 or 18 mg atomoxetine) and a 1-week washout, participants received double-blind 4-week treatment sequences of atomoxetine then placebo or the reverse, separated by a 2-week washout. The primary endpoint was orthostatic symptoms on the Orthostatic Hypotension Questionnaire at 2 weeks.
cards.result: There were no differences in the questionnaire composite score between atomoxetine and placebo at 2 weeks (−0.3 ± 1.7 versus −0.4 ± 1.5; P=0.806) or at 4 weeks (−0.6 ± 2.4 versus −0.5 ± 1.6; P=0.251). The symptom subscale (OHSA) did not differ at 2 weeks (3 ± 1.9 versus 4 ± 2.1; P=0.062) or 4 weeks (3 ± 2.2 versus 3 ± 2.0; P=1.000), nor did the daily-activity subscale (OHDAS) at 2 weeks (4 ± 3.0 versus 5 ± 3.1; P=0.102) or 4 weeks (4 ± 3.0 versus 4 ± 2.7; P=0.095). Atomoxetine was well tolerated. The authors conclude it was not superior to placebo for ameliorating symptoms of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-seven completers is small for a symptom endpoint with wide variability, and a crossover design in a fluctuating condition can dilute real effects; the near-significant 2-week symptom-subscale trend (P=0.062) is the kind of signal a larger trial might resolve either way. But this remains the only sustained-dosing placebo-controlled test, and its point estimates are essentially identical between arms.
cards.source: Mwesigwa N et al. Atomoxetine on neurogenic orthostatic hypotension: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial. Clinical Autonomic Research. 2024. PMID: 39294522. Registry ID: NCT02316821. cards.headline: Jung 2023: across only four randomised trials, atomoxetine raised systolic pressure and improved symptoms — effects most pronounced in multiple system atrophy
cards.summary: Jung 2023: across only four randomised trials, atomoxetine raised systolic pressure and improved symptoms — effects most pronounced in multiple system atrophy
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials, 4 RCTs (Jung 2023)
cards.people: A systematic review (with an expert focus group) of atomoxetine for neurogenic orthostatic hypotension in patients with alpha-synucleinopathies, searching MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, PsycInfo and KoreaMed; only four randomised controlled trials met the inclusion criteria.
cards.result: The reviewers report that atomoxetine effectively increased systolic blood pressure and improved orthostatic-hypotension-related symptoms as monotherapy or in combination with other drugs, that its effects were pronounced in cases with central autonomic failure including multiple system atrophy, and that it might be a safe monotherapy regarding the risk of supine hypertension. They conclude atomoxetine is an effective and safe option for short-term management of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension — while stressing the paucity of evidence and the need for further investigation.
cards.watchOut: The four trials behind this review are largely single-dose or short-term studies, several from the same research tradition that produced the positive acute data; a qualitative synthesis of four small trials cannot outweigh a negative placebo-controlled trial of actual sustained treatment on the symptom outcome patients care about. The subgroup claim (central autonomic failure) is plausible pharmacology, not a demonstrated interaction in a large trial.
cards.source: Jung YJ et al. cards.summary: Synthesis: the split is duration — acute pressor effect, yes; sustained symptom relief, not shown
cards.people: One 4-week double-blind crossover trial (37 completers) plus a systematic review of four mostly acute-dose randomised trials in alpha-synucleinopathy-related neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
cards.result: Symptoms at 2–4 weeks: no difference versus placebo (composite P=0.806 and P=0.251). Acute blood pressure and symptoms: improved in the small short-term trials, most clearly in multiple system atrophy. Tolerability: good in the crossover trial; supine hypertension risk possibly favourable. PROPOSED SPLIT — acute benefit, sustained benefit unproven.
cards.watchOut: Anyone citing the review's 'effective and safe' conclusion should be asked 'for how long, in whom' — the review's own trials do not answer the chronic-dosing question, and the one trial that does is negative. Tier C is set because the whole literature is four small randomised trials plus one crossover study.

shelves.title: Abdominal compression for orthostatic hypotension: a mild 10 mmHg binder applied before rising blunted the standing pressure drop in 13 patients — more compression added nothing
shelves.question: In adults with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, does patient-controlled abdominal compression improve standing blood pressure versus sham compression?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen/physiology · Aged · Blood Pressure/physiology · Blood Pressure Monitoring, Ambulatory · Cross-Over Studies · Equipment Design · Female · Gravity Suits* · Humans · Hypotension, Orthostatic/physiopathology, rehabilitation · Male · Middle Aged · Minnesota · Posture/physiology · Pressure · Severity of Illness Index · Systole/physiology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the entire record for patient-controlled abdominal compression is one randomised crossover laboratory study of 13 adults with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (Figueroa JJ et al., PMID: 25448247). Standing without a binder dropped systolic pressure by a median 57 mmHg; applying a mild 10 mmHg compression before rising blunted that drop to 50 mmHg with a conventional binder (P=.03) and 46 mmHg with an adjustable binder (P=.01). But squeezing harder did not help: subject-selected maximal tolerable compression while standing was associated with drops of 53 and 59 mmHg (both non-significant versus no binder), and easing back to a 'tolerable for prolonged use' level tended to worsen the drop (61 and 67 mmHg). Participants reported no difference between binders in preference or ease of use. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): a mild binder put on before standing probably takes a small edge off the postural drop — roughly 7 to 11 mmHg of a 57 mmHg fall — but this is 13 people, one laboratory, and surrogate blood-pressure readings rather than symptoms, falls or syncope. Atomoxetine in the same condition is shelved at #2870 and the fludrocortisone-versus-midodrine comparison at #2761.

cards.headline: Figueroa 2015: in 13 adults, mild abdominal compression before rising blunted the standing systolic drop from −57 mmHg to −50 (conventional binder) and −46 mmHg (adjustable); maximal compression added nothing
cards.summary: Figueroa 2015: in 13 adults, mild abdominal compression before rising blunted the standing systolic drop from −57 mmHg to −50 (conventional binder) and −46 mmHg (adjustable); maximal compression added nothing
cards.people: 13 adults with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension in a clinical research laboratory, each performing four manoeuvres in randomised crossover fashion: rising from supine to standing without compression; rising with a conventional or an adjustable abdominal binder in place; applying subject-determined maximal tolerable compression while standing; then reducing compression to a level judged tolerable for prolonged use. The primary outcome was the postural change in systolic blood pressure; secondary outcomes were binder preference and ease of use.
cards.result: Supine systolic pressure was unaffected by mild (10 mmHg) compression (median 146 mmHg without a binder, 145 with the conventional binder, 153 with the adjustable binder; P=.85). Standing without a binder produced a median drop of −57 mmHg (interquartile range −40 to −76). Compression of 10 mmHg applied before rising blunted the drop to −50 mmHg (IQR −33 to −70; P=.03) with the conventional binder and −46 mmHg (IQR −34 to −75; P=.01) with the adjustable binder. Increasing compression to maximal tolerance while standing gave drops of −53 mmHg (P=.64) and −59 mmHg (P=.52) — no additional benefit — and reducing to prolonged-tolerable levels tended to worsen the drop (−61 and −67 mmHg). Subjects reported no differences in preference or ease of use between binders.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen participants, medians with very wide interquartile ranges, and a blood-pressure surrogate measured minutes after standing — no symptoms, no falls, no syncope, no follow-up. The 'significant' results are two of many comparisons in a tiny sample, and the dose-response runs the wrong way (more compression, no more benefit), which should temper any mechanistic confidence.
cards.source: Figueroa JJ et al. Effects of patient-controlled abdominal compression on standing systolic blood pressure in adults with orthostatic hypotension. Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation. 2015. PMID: 25448247. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a small, real, but laboratory-bound effect — mild compression before rising, nothing more
cards.summary: Synthesis: a small, real, but laboratory-bound effect — mild compression before rising, nothing more
cards.people: One randomised crossover study of 13 adults with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension; no larger trial or meta-analysis of patient-controlled abdominal compression was found to card.
cards.result: Standing systolic drop: −57 mmHg uncompressed versus −50 mmHg (P=.03) and −46 mmHg (P=.01) with 10 mmHg compression applied before rising. Maximal or reduced compression while standing: no benefit. Symptoms, falls, syncope: unmeasured. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: The practical reading is narrow: if a binder is used, put it on before getting up and keep it mild. The study cannot support claims about dizziness or falls, and its population — neurogenic orthostatic hypotension severe enough to drop 57 mmHg — is not the common age-related postural drop. shelves.title: ACTIVE: cognitive training durably improved the trained ability in 2,832 older adults — speed and reasoning most, memory least — but everyday functioning did not improve at 2 years
shelves.question: In cognitively intact older adults, does cognitive training (memory, reasoning or speed of processing) improve trained cognitive abilities and everyday function versus control?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living* · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cognition* · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy* · Humans · Memory · Mental Processes · Psychological Tests · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — ACTIVE (Ball K et al., PMID: 12425704) randomised 2,832 volunteers aged 65 to 94 to 10 sessions of memory, reasoning or speed-of-processing training or a no-contact control, and the answer depends entirely on which outcome you ask about. On the trained abilities, training worked and lasted: each intervention improved its targeted ability versus baseline, durable to 2 years (P<.001 for all), with reliable improvement immediately after training in 87% of speed-trained, 74% of reasoning-trained and only 26% of memory-trained participants; booster sessions in a 60% subsample enhanced and maintained speed and reasoning gains (speed booster 92% versus 68% without; reasoning 72% versus 49%). The gains were of a magnitude equivalent to the decline expected over 7 to 14 years without dementia. On everyday functioning — the outcome that would justify the effort clinically — no training effects were detected at 2 years, in a cohort that declined minimally in any arm. PROPOSED SPLIT: cognitive training is a reliable way to get better at the kind of task trained, for at least two years; whether that transfers to daily life was not shown here. The multidomain lifestyle approach (FINGER) is shelved separately at #332.

cards.headline: Ball 2002 (ACTIVE): each training improved its own ability for 2 years (reliable gains in 87% speed, 74% reasoning, 26% memory) — and no training effect on everyday functioning was detected
cards.summary: Ball 2002 (ACTIVE): each training improved its own ability for 2 years (reliable gains in 87% speed, 74% reasoning, 26% memory) — and no training effect on everyday functioning was detected
cards.people: 2,832 volunteers aged 65 to 94 years recruited from senior housing, community centres and hospitals/clinics in six US metropolitan areas, randomly assigned to 10-session group training in memory (verbal episodic memory, n=711), reasoning (serial-pattern problem solving, n=705) or speed of processing (visual search and identification, n=712), or a no-contact control group (n=704); a 60% random subsample of each training arm was offered 4-session booster training at 11 months, with 2-year follow-up. Thirty participants were incorrectly randomised and excluded from the analysis.
cards.result: Each intervention improved the targeted cognitive ability compared with baseline, durable to 2 years (P<.001 for all). Reliable cognitive improvement immediately after the intervention period was shown by 87% of speed-, 74% of reasoning- and 26% of memory-trained participants. Booster training enhanced gains in speed (P<.001) and reasoning (P<.001) — speed booster 92% versus 68% without, reasoning booster 72% versus 49% without — maintained at 2-year follow-up. No training effects on everyday functioning were detected at 2 years. The authors note the training effects were of a magnitude equivalent to the amount of decline expected in elderly persons without dementia over 7- to 14-year intervals, and that minimal functional decline across all groups means longer follow-up is likely required to observe any functional effect.
cards.watchOut: Volunteers healthy enough to join a community trial are not the older adults clinicians worry about, and the no-contact control means attention and social contact are uncontrolled — though that matters less for the null functional result. The memory result deserves emphasis: the ability families most often ask about was the least trainable (26% reliable improvement). Two years is also short for a prevention claim; later ACTIVE follow-ups exist but are not part of this card's record.
cards.source: Ball K et al. Effects of cognitive training interventions with older adults: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2002. PMID: 12425704. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: near-transfer yes, far-transfer unproven — the cleanest demonstration in the cognitive-training literature
cards.summary: Synthesis: near-transfer yes, far-transfer unproven — the cleanest demonstration in the cognitive-training literature
cards.people: One large randomised trial (2,832 cognitively intact older adults, 2-year follow-up) with three single-domain training arms and a no-contact control.
cards.result: Trained abilities: improved in all three arms (P<.001), durable to 2 years, boosted by booster sessions for speed and reasoning. Everyday functioning: no effect detected at 2 years. Memory training: weakest response (26% reliable improvers). PROPOSED SPLIT — benefit for trained abilities, no demonstrated benefit for everyday function.
cards.watchOut: Do not let 'equivalent to 7–14 years of decline' be quoted as 'reverses 14 years of ageing' — it compares a test-score gain with expected test-score decline, in the trained domain only. The honest promise to a healthy older adult is narrower: practice a skill and you will keep that skill longer. Tier C is set because, for all its size, this is one trial with a no-contact control and a 2-year horizon.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ball K et al. JAMA. 2002 (PMID: 12425704).

shelves.title: Community occupational therapy in dementia: ten sessions produced very large gains in patients' daily functioning and caregivers' competence in one 135-person trial, still present at three months
shelves.question: In people with dementia and their caregivers, does community occupational therapy improve daily functioning and caregiver sense of competence versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Aged · Ambulatory Care · Caregivers* · Community Health Services* · Dementia/rehabilitation · Female · Humans · Male · Occupational Therapy/methods · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — one single-blind randomised trial (Graff MJ et al., PMID: 17114212) of 135 community-living patients aged 65 or older with mild-to-moderate dementia and their primary caregivers: ten occupational-therapy sessions over five weeks, training patients to use aids compensating for cognitive decline and caregivers in coping and supervision. At six weeks the intervention group had improved far more than controls on every primary measure — process skills by 1.5 points (95% CI 1.3 to 1.7), daily-activity performance by −11.7 points (95% CI −13.6 to −9.7, lower is better), and caregiver sense of competence by 11.0 points (95% CI 9.2 to 12.8) — with effect sizes of 2.5, 2.3 and 1.2 respectively, a number needed to treat of 1.3 (95% CI 1.2 to 1.4) for clinically relevant improvement in motor and process skills, and benefits still significant at three months (effect sizes 2.7, 2.4 and 0.8). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the effects are implausibly large for a psychosocial intervention, which is exactly why the grade stops at possible — one trial, one Dutch memory-clinic setting, outcomes rated on scales the intervention explicitly trained toward. Cognitive stimulation therapy is shelved separately at #2344.

cards.headline: Graff 2006: community occupational therapy improved patients' process skills (difference 1.5), daily-activity performance (−11.7) and caregiver competence (11.0), with an NNT of 1.3 — effects still present at 3 months
cards.summary: Graff 2006: community occupational therapy improved patients' process skills (difference 1.5), daily-activity performance (−11.7) and caregiver competence (11.0), with an NNT of 1.3 — effects still present at 3 months
cards.people: 135 patients aged 65 or older with mild to moderate dementia living in the community, and their primary caregivers, recruited through a geriatrics department's memory and day clinics in the Netherlands. The intervention was 10 sessions of occupational therapy over five weeks at home, including cognitive and behavioural strategies: training patients in the use of aids to compensate for cognitive decline, and caregivers in coping behaviours and supervision. Outcomes at baseline, six weeks and three months were the Assessment of Motor and Process Skills (AMPS), the performance scale of the Interview of Deterioration in Daily Activities in Dementia (IDDD), and the caregiver Sense of Competence Questionnaire (SCQ); assessors were blinded to allocation.
cards.result: Scores improved significantly relative to baseline in the intervention group compared with controls: differences of 1.5 (95% CI 1.3 to 1.7) for the AMPS process scale, −11.7 (95% CI −13.6 to −9.7) for the IDDD performance scale, and 11.0 (95% CI 9.2 to 12.8) for the SCQ competence scale. Improvement remained significant at three months. The number needed to treat for a clinically relevant improvement in motor and process skills was 1.3 (95% CI 1.2 to 1.4) at six weeks. Effect sizes were 2.5, 2.3 and 1.2 at six weeks and 2.7, 2.4 and 0.8 at 12 weeks. Registry ID: NCT00295152.
cards.watchOut: Effect sizes above 2 are almost unheard of for non-drug dementia interventions and should invite replication, not celebration: the therapy trained the very task-performance the AMPS and IDDD measure, participants and caregivers could not be blinded, and caregiver competence is self-reported by people who received five weeks of supportive attention. One trial, one country, mild-to-moderate dementia only, three months of follow-up.
cards.source: Graff MJ et al. Community based occupational therapy for patients with dementia and their care givers: randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2006. PMID: 17114212. Registry ID: NCT00295152. cards.headline: Synthesis: one small trial with exceptionally large effects on function and caregiver competence — promising, and precisely the profile that needs a second trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: one small trial with exceptionally large effects on function and caregiver competence — promising, and precisely the profile that needs a second trial
cards.people: One single-blind randomised trial (135 patient–caregiver dyads, 10 sessions over 5 weeks, 3-month follow-up); no second cardable trial or meta-analysis of this exact community occupational-therapy programme was added.
cards.result: Patient daily functioning: large improvements on both performance measures (effect sizes 2.3–2.5 at 6 weeks, 2.4–2.7 at 12 weeks). Caregiver sense of competence: effect size 1.2 at 6 weeks, 0.8 at 12 weeks. NNT for clinically relevant functional improvement: 1.3. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The gap between these effect sizes and the rest of the non-drug dementia literature is the central fact about this shelf: either this programme is uniquely powerful, or single-trial optimism and outcome-training overlap are inflating it. Either way it is a low-harm, plausible intervention — the stamp grades the certainty, not the wisdom of offering it. Tier C is set because the evidence is one trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Graff MJ et al. BMJ. 2006 (PMID: 17114212).

shelves.title: FINALEX: a year of twice-weekly exercise — at home or in groups — slowed functional decline in Alzheimer's disease, with fewer falls and no increase in total care costs
shelves.question: In people with Alzheimer's disease living at home, does a structured home exercise programme slow functional decline versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living* · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alzheimer Disease/economics, therapy · Caregivers · Day Care, Medical*/economics, organization & administration · Exercise Therapy*/economics, methods, organization & administration · Female · Finland/epidemiology · Follow-Up Studies · House Calls*/economics · Humans · Independent Living · Male · Physical Therapists* · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — FINALEX (Pitkälä KH et al., PMID: 23589097) randomised 210 home-dwelling patients with Alzheimer's disease, each living with a spousal caregiver, to group-based exercise, tailored home-based exercise, or usual community care, with both exercise arms training twice weekly for a full year. Everyone deteriorated, but deterioration on the Functional Independence Measure was significantly slower in both exercise groups at 6 months (P=.003) and 12 months (P=.015): 12-month FIM changes were −7.1 (95% CI −3.7 to −10.5) for home exercise, −10.3 (95% CI −6.7 to −13.9) for group exercise and −14.4 (95% CI −10.9 to −18.0) for controls. The exercise groups also had significantly fewer falls during the follow-up year, and total health and social service costs per dyad were not increased — $25,112 for home exercise (P=.13 versus control), $22,066 for group exercise (P=.03 versus control) and $34,121 for controls. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a sustained, intensive exercise programme slows — it does not stop — functional decline in home-dwelling Alzheimer's disease, from one Finnish trial of spousal-caregiver households. Exercise in dementia more broadly was dropped from this mining round where trials were already carded (DAPA); this shelf is the FINALEX question only.

cards.headline: Pitkälä 2013 (FINALEX): after 12 months, FIM scores had fallen by 7.1 points with home exercise and 10.3 with group exercise versus 14.4 on usual care — with significantly fewer falls in both exercise groups
cards.summary: Pitkälä 2013 (FINALEX): after 12 months, FIM scores had fallen by 7.1 points with home exercise and 10.3 with group exercise versus 14.4 on usual care — with significantly fewer falls in both exercise groups
cards.people: 210 home-dwelling patients with Alzheimer's disease living with their spousal caregiver in Finland, randomised to (1) group-based exercise — 4-hour sessions with approximately 1 hour of training, (2) tailored home-based exercise — 1-hour training sessions, both twice a week for 1 year — or (3) a control group receiving usual community care. Outcomes were the Functional Independence Measure (FIM), the Short Physical Performance Battery, falls, and the use and costs of health and social services.
cards.result: All groups deteriorated in functioning during the year, but deterioration was significantly faster in the control group than in the home-exercise or group-exercise groups at 6 months (P=.003) and 12 months (P=.015). FIM changes at 12 months were −7.1 (95% CI −3.7 to −10.5) in the home-exercise group, −10.3 (95% CI −6.7 to −13.9) in the group-exercise group, and −14.4 (95% CI −10.9 to −18.0) in the control group. The home and group exercise groups had significantly fewer falls than controls during the follow-up year. Total health and social service costs per patient–caregiver dyad per year were $25,112 (95% CI $17,642 to $32,581; P=.13 versus control) for home exercise, $22,066 ($15,931 to $28,199; P=.03 versus control) for group exercise, and $34,121 ($24,559 to $43,681) for controls. The authors report no significant adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: Every participant lived with a spouse — the population most able to sustain a year of twice-weekly sessions — so the result may not travel to people living alone or with paid carers. The benefit is a slower rate of decline (roughly half the FIM loss for home exercise), not improvement, and the fall counts and Short Physical Performance Battery numbers are not given in the record, so neither can be quantified here. One trial, one country.

Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: intensive long-term exercise halves the measured rate of functional decline for a year, in the households best placed to deliver it
cards.summary: Synthesis: intensive long-term exercise halves the measured rate of functional decline for a year, in the households best placed to deliver it
cards.people: One randomised trial (210 patient–spouse dyads, two exercise formats, 12 months) in home-dwelling Alzheimer's disease.
cards.result: Functional decline (FIM at 12 months): −7.1 (home exercise) and −10.3 (group exercise) versus −14.4 (usual care); group differences significant at 6 and 12 months. shelves.title: A five-day multicomponent programme — daylight, out of bed, activity, bedtime routine, quiet nights — strengthened rest/activity rhythms in nursing-home residents; sleep itself was not the measured outcome
shelves.question: In nursing-home residents with disrupted sleep and activity rhythms, does a multicomponent non-pharmacological intervention improve activity rhythms and sleep versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged, 80 and over · Circadian Rhythm/physiology · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Exercise Therapy/methods · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Motor Activity/physiology · Nursing Homes* · Rest/physiology · Retrospective Studies · Sleep/physiology · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/physiopathology, psychology, therapy · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the anchor trial (Martin JL et al., PMID: 17301040) randomised nursing-home residents with disrupted sleep/wake patterns to five days of a multicomponent intervention — increased outdoor bright light, efforts to keep residents out of bed during the day, structured physical activity, a bedtime routine, and reduced nighttime noise and light — or usual care. In the 100 residents with baseline and follow-up wrist actigraphy (mean age 87, 76% women), the intervention increased the duration of the active portion of the 24-hour rest/activity rhythm, primarily by shifting the rhythm's rise to an earlier time, and the findings persisted after adjustment for age, cognitive functioning, medical comorbidities and behavioural disturbances. That is a rhythm result, not a sleep result: the record reports modelled rhythm parameters, not hours slept or sleep quality. The surrounding literature is encouraging but thin — a systematic review of non-pharmacological sleep interventions in nursing homes (Shang B et al., PMID: 30795838) found 28 eligible studies across physical activity, light therapy, mind-body practices, complementary therapies and seven multicomponent programmes, with positive and promising signals but small trial numbers that 'should be interpreted cautiously'. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence). CBT-I basics are shelved elsewhere; this shelf is the institutional, non-CBT-I programme.

cards.headline: Martin 2007: five days of a multicomponent programme lengthened the active portion of the rest/activity rhythm in 100 nursing-home residents — an actigraphy finding, adjusted for cognition and comorbidity
cards.summary: Martin 2007: five days of a multicomponent programme lengthened the active portion of the rest/activity rhythm in 100 nursing-home residents — an actigraphy finding, adjusted for cognition and comorbidity
cards.people: Long-stay nursing-home residents with disrupted sleep/wake patterns; 100 residents had baseline and follow-up wrist actigraphy data (mean age 87 years, 76% women). After a 3-day baseline, participants received 5 days of usual care or the active intervention: increased exposure to outdoor bright light, efforts to keep residents out of bed during the day, structured physical activity, institution of a bedtime routine, and efforts to reduce nighttime noise and light in residents' rooms. Rest/activity rhythms were modelled for acrophase (peak time), nadir, MESOR (midpoint), amplitude, slope and the rest/active period ratio (alpha).
cards.result: The intervention led to an increase in the duration of the 'active' portion of the rhythm, primarily accounted for by a shift in the rest/activity rhythm rise to an earlier time. Findings persisted when analyses were adjusted for age, cognitive functioning, medical comorbidities and behavioural disturbances. The authors conclude the intervention may effectively improve the robustness of rest/activity rhythms in nursing-home residents, and call for research on other circadian measures such as body temperature and melatonin.
cards.watchOut: Five days of intervention and an actigraphic surrogate: the record gives no numeric rhythm values, no sleep duration or quality outcomes, and no follow-up beyond the intervention week — so neither the size nor the persistence of the effect can be stated. A programme requiring staff to keep residents up, out and active all day also competes with the staffing reality of the homes it is meant for.
cards.source: Martin JL et al. A multicomponent nonpharmacological intervention improves activity rhythms among nursing home residents with disrupted sleep/wake patterns. The Journals of Gerontology. cards.headline: Shang 2019: across 28 nursing-home studies, physical activity, mind-body practices, acupressure and chamomile showed promising sleep effects — but trial numbers were small and results need cautious interpretation
cards.summary: Shang 2019: across 28 nursing-home studies, physical activity, mind-body practices, acupressure and chamomile showed promising sleep effects — but trial numbers were small and results need cautious interpretation
cards.people: A systematic review of non-pharmacological interventions to improve sleep quality and nighttime sleep in nursing-home residents, searching English and Chinese databases through December 2018; 28 eligible studies covering physical activity (n=6), light therapy (n=5), mind-body practices (n=2), complementary and alternative therapy (n=8), and multicomponent interventions (n=7).
cards.result: Although the wide variety of interventions in each category limited generalisability, physical activity, mind-body practices, acupressure and chamomile extract intake demonstrated positive and promising impacts on sleep quality and nighttime sleep. The reviewers caution that, due to the small number of included trials, the results should be interpreted cautiously, and call for further higher-quality studies.
cards.watchOut: A narrative systematic review without pooled effect sizes, spanning interventions as different as chamomile extract and exercise; it establishes that this field is active and suggestive, not that any specific programme — including the Martin bundle — improves measured sleep. Publication bias in a literature of small positive trials is a live concern.
cards.source: Shang B et al. Nonpharmacological interventions to improve sleep in nursing home residents: A systematic review. Geriatric Nursing. 2019. PMID: 30795838. cards.people: One randomised trial (100 residents with actigraphy, 5-day intervention) plus a 28-study systematic review of non-pharmacological sleep interventions in nursing homes.
cards.result: Rest/activity rhythm: active portion lengthened, rise shifted earlier, robust to adjustment. Sleep quality/nighttime sleep: promising signals across the review's intervention families, no pooled estimate. Durability, symptoms, hypnotic use: unmeasured in the anchor record. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: This shelf should never be cited as 'the programme improves sleep' — its trial measured wrist movement rhythms. What it supports is a low-risk bundle worth doing for daytime alertness and rhythm regularity while better trials are run. Tier C is set because the anchor is one small short trial with a surrogate outcome.
