shelves.title: Sunbeam: progressive resistance and balance training cut the rate of falls by 55% relative in long-term aged care — one cluster trial of 16 facilities and 221 residents
shelves.question: In residents of long-term aged care, does progressive resistance and balance training (Sunbeam programme) prevent falls versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/prevention & control · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Australia · Cluster Analysis · Combined Modality Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Long-Term Care/methods · Male · Nursing Homes/statistics & numerical data · Postural Balance/physiology · Primary Prevention/organization & administration · Prognosis · Residential Facilities/organization & administration · Resistance Training/methods · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the Sunbeam programme was tested in a cluster randomised trial of 16 residential aged-care facilities and 221 permanent residents (Hewitt J et al., PMID: 29402651): individually prescribed progressive resistance training plus balance exercise in a group setting, 50 hours over 25 weeks followed by a 6-month maintenance period, versus usual care. The rate of falls was reduced by 55% relative in the exercise group (incidence rate ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.74) — the record does not print the absolute fall rates, so no absolute reduction can be quoted — and physical performance on the Short Physical Performance Battery also improved (P=.02), with no serious adverse events. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): this is the setting where falls trials have most often disappointed, and a single cluster trial with a wide confidence interval (the data are compatible with anything from an 83% to a 26% relative reduction) should not be upgraded beyond possible until replicated. The community Otago programme is shelved at #459 and the multifaceted care-home intervention of Becker at the companion falls shelves.

cards.headline: Hewitt 2018 (Sunbeam): falls rate reduced by 55% relative (incidence rate ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.74) and physical performance improved (P=.02), with no serious adverse events
cards.summary: Hewitt 2018 (Sunbeam): falls rate reduced by 55% relative (incidence rate ratio 0.45, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.74) and physical performance improved (P=.02), with no serious adverse events
cards.people: 221 permanent residents of 16 Australian residential aged-care facilities (clusters), randomised by facility to the Sunbeam programme or usual care. Exclusions were terminal illness, no medical clearance, permanent bed- or wheelchair-bound status, advanced Parkinson's disease, or insufficient cognition to participate in group exercise. The programme was individually prescribed progressive resistance training plus balance exercise in a group setting, totalling 50 hours over 25 weeks, followed by a 6-month maintenance period. Assessments at baseline, after intervention and at 12 months covered falls rate (primary), Short Physical Performance Battery, quality of life, functional mobility, fear of falling and cognition.
cards.result: The rate of falls was reduced by 55% relative in the exercise group (incidence rate ratio 0.45, 95% confidence interval 0.17 to 0.74); an improvement was also seen in physical performance (P=.02). There were no serious adverse events. The authors note the finding matters because prior work in this setting has returned inconsistent outcomes, leading best-practice guidelines to be cautious about recommending exercise in long-term care.
cards.watchOut: One cluster trial: 16 facilities is few clusters, the confidence interval is wide, and absolute fall rates are not in the record — so the number of falls actually prevented per resident-year cannot be stated. Residents too ill, too immobile or too cognitively impaired for group exercise were excluded, which removes many of the highest-fall-risk residents from the evidence. Fractures and injurious falls are not reported as outcomes in the record.
cards.source: Hewitt J et al. Progressive Resistance and Balance Training for Falls Prevention in Long-Term Residential Aged Care: A Cluster Randomized Trial of the Sunbeam Program. Journal of the American Medical Directors Association. 2018. PMID: 29402651. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the best single result for exercise in residential care — large, significant, and still one trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: the best single result for exercise in residential care — large, significant, and still one trial
cards.people: One cluster randomised trial (16 facilities, 221 residents, 12-month follow-up) of progressive resistance plus balance training in long-term residential aged care; no second cardable trial of the Sunbeam programme was added.
cards.result: Falls rate: incidence rate ratio 0.45 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.74) — a 55% relative reduction, absolute rates not in the record. Physical performance: improved (P=.02). Serious adverse events: none. Quality of life, mobility, fear of falling, cognition: measured, no significant findings reported in the record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Read alongside the care-home falls literature, which is inconsistent: Sunbeam's individually prescribed, adequately dosed programme (50 hours) may be exactly why it worked where lighter programmes failed — or it may be single-trial optimism. Either way the dose and the exclusions define who this evidence is about. Tier C is set because the evidence is one cluster trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hewitt J et al. Journal of the American Medical Directors Association. 2018 (PMID: 29402651).

shelves.title: Deprescribing and mortality: the pooled randomised result is null (odds ratio 0.82) — but patient-specific deprescribing reduced mortality (0.62) while generalised education programmes did not (1.21)
shelves.question: In older adults, do deprescribing interventions reduce mortality and improve health outcomes versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Deprescriptions* · Humans · Inappropriate Prescribing/adverse effects, mortality · Polypharmacy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — Page AT et al. (PMID: 27077231) pooled 132 papers and 34,143 participants (mean age 73.8 ± 5.4 years) in which older adults had at least one medication deprescribed, and the answer splits cleanly by study design and by intervention type. In non-randomised studies deprescribing was associated with significantly lower mortality (odds ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.60) — the design most exposed to confounding by who gets deprescribed. In randomised studies the pooled result was not significant (odds ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.11). Within the randomised evidence, patient-specific deprescribing interventions significantly reduced mortality (odds ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.88), while generalised educational programmes did not change it (odds ratio 1.21, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.69). PROPOSED SPLIT: 'deprescribing' is not one intervention — tailoring the withdrawal to the individual patient is the version with a randomised mortality signal; mailing education to prescribers is not. This cross-class synthesis complements, and does not duplicate, the drug-specific deprescribing shelves (#132, #500, #2759) and the medication-review shelf #930.

cards.headline: Page 2016: deprescribing cut mortality in non-randomised studies (OR 0.32) but not in the randomised pool (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.11) — except patient-specific interventions (OR 0.62)
cards.summary: Page 2016: deprescribing cut mortality in non-randomised studies (OR 0.32) but not in the randomised pool (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.11) — except patient-specific interventions (OR 0.62)
cards.people: 132 papers meeting inclusion criteria, comprising 34,143 participants aged 73.8 ± 5.4 years, in studies where older adults had at least one medication deprescribed; databases were searched from inception to February 2015, with two researchers independently screening, quality-assessing and extracting data, and pooling in RevMan v5.3. The primary outcome was mortality; secondary outcomes included adverse drug withdrawal events, psychological and physical health outcomes, quality of life, and medication usage.
cards.result: In non-randomized studies, deprescribing polypharmacy significantly decreased mortality (OR 0.32, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.60); in randomized studies it did not (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.61 to 1.11). Subgroup analysis of the randomised studies showed patient-specific deprescribing interventions significantly reduced mortality (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.88), whereas generalized educational programmes did not change mortality (OR 1.21, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.69). The authors conclude that although non-randomized data suggested deprescribing reduces mortality, this was not shown in randomized studies overall — mortality was significantly reduced only when patient-specific interventions were applied in randomized studies.
cards.watchOut: The patient-specific subgroup is a subgroup: it was not the review's primary pooled result, and subgroup findings in a heterogeneous 132-study pool (different drugs, settings, follow-up lengths, and reasons for stopping) are hypothesis-strengthening rather than proof. The non-randomised odds ratio of 0.32 is implausibly large as a causal effect and is best read as a measure of confounding — clinicians deprescribe differently in patients who are recovering. Secondary health and quality-of-life outcomes are not quantified in the record, so this card supports no claim about them.
cards.source: Page AT et al. The feasibility and effect of deprescribing in older adults on mortality and health: a systematic review and meta-analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: one literature, two answers — design and intervention type decide the result
cards.summary: Synthesis: one literature, two answers — design and intervention type decide the result
cards.people: One systematic review and meta-analysis (132 studies, 34,143 older adults) spanning all drug classes and settings, searched to February 2015.
cards.result: Mortality, non-randomised studies: OR 0.32 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.60). Mortality, randomised studies overall: OR 0.82 (95% CI 0.61 to 1.11), not significant. Mortality, randomised patient-specific interventions: OR 0.62 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.88). Mortality, randomised generalised education: OR 1.21 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.69). PROPOSED SPLIT — by intervention type within the randomised evidence.
cards.watchOut: This shelf grades the cross-class question only; it cannot tell anyone whether stopping a particular drug helps — that is what the drug-specific shelves are for. Its durable lesson is about implementation: interventions aimed at a named patient's medication list outperformed interventions aimed at prescribers in general. Tier C is not set: this is a full systematic review and meta-analysis, though its search closes in February 2015.
cards.source: Synthesis of Page AT et al. British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. 2016 (PMID: 27077231).

shelves.title: Pacing for carotid sinus hypersensitivity in older fallers: falls cut from a mean 9.3 to 4.1 per year and injurious events by 70% in SAFE PACE — one 175-patient trial
shelves.question: In older patients with carotid sinus hypersensitivity and unexplained falls or syncope, does dual-chamber pacing reduce falls and syncope compared with no pacing?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/prevention & control/statistics & numerical data · Activities of Daily Living · Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Algorithms · Cardiac Pacing, Artificial/standards · Decision Trees · Emergency Service, Hospital/statistics & numerical data · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Geriatric Assessment · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Mass Screening · Pacemaker, Artificial/standards · Recurrence · Referral and Consultation · Risk Factors · Syncope/complications/prevention & control · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large effect in a single small trial. SAFE PACE (Kenny RA et al., PMID: 11691528) randomised 175 consecutive patients older than 50 (mean age 73; 60% women) attending an emergency facility after a non-accidental fall, all with cardioinhibitory carotid sinus hypersensitivity, to dual-chamber pacemaker implantation or standard treatment. Over one year, falls were reduced by two-thirds: control patients reported 669 falls (mean 9.3; range 0–89) versus 216 (mean 4.1; range 0–29) in paced patients, who were significantly less likely to fall (odds ratio 0.42; 95% CI 0.23–0.75). Syncopal episodes were also fewer (28 in paced patients versus 47 in controls), and injurious events were reduced by 70% (61 versus 202). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pacing a hypersensitive carotid sinus kept older fallers upright in the only randomised trial — an effect size this large, from 175 unblinded patients counting their own falls, invites both belief and a second trial that never came. Tier C: single-trial benefit claim.

cards.headline: Kenny 2001 (SAFE PACE): 216 falls in paced patients versus 669 in controls over one year (means 4.1 versus 9.3); injurious events 61 versus 202; syncope episodes 28 versus 47
cards.summary: Kenny 2001 (SAFE PACE): 216 falls in paced patients versus 669 in controls over one year (means 4.1 versus 9.3); injurious events 61 versus 202; syncope episodes 28 versus 47
cards.people: 175 consecutive patients older than 50 years (mean age 73±10; 60% women) attending an accident and emergency facility because of a non-accidental fall, found to have cardioinhibitory carotid sinus hypersensitivity, randomised to dual-chamber pacemaker implantation (87 patients) or standard treatment (88 patients); primary outcome the number of falls during one year of follow-up.
cards.result: Falls (without loss of consciousness) were reduced by two-thirds: paced patients reported 216 falls (mean 4.1; range 0–29) and controls 669 falls (mean 9.3; range 0–89); paced patients were significantly less likely to fall (odds ratio 0.42; 95% CI 0.23, 0.75). Syncopal events numbered 28 episodes in paced patients versus 47 in controls. Injurious events were reduced by 70%: 61 in paced patients versus 202 in controls.
cards.watchOut: Falls were self-reported by patients who knew whether they had received a pacemaker — the ideal setup for expectation bias in both directions — and a handful of prolific fallers (range to 89 falls in one control patient) drive the totals. The trial selected fallers with a positive carotid-sinus test, a group standard falls assessments of the era never screened; generalising beyond cardioinhibitory hypersensitivity is not licensed by this record. Single trial: Tier C.

shelves.title: Pharmacist-led education aimed at both patient and physician (D-PRESCRIBE): inappropriate prescriptions stopped by 43% versus 12% at 6 months — one cluster trial, four Beers drug classes, one province
shelves.question: In older adults on potentially inappropriate medicines, does a pharmacist-led educational intervention for patients and physicians increase deprescribing versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anti-Inflammatory Agents, Non-Steroidal/therapeutic use · Benzodiazepines/therapeutic use · Female · Glyburide/therapeutic use · Histamine H1 Antagonists/therapeutic use · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives/therapeutic use · Inappropriate Prescribing/prevention & control* · Male · Patient Education as Topic/methods* · Pharmacists* · Quebec
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a pharmacist writing to both the patient and the physician got far more inappropriate prescriptions stopped than usual care did. In D-PRESCRIBE (Martin P et al., PMID: 30422193), a cluster randomised trial in 69 community pharmacies in Quebec, Canada, 489 community-dwelling adults aged 65 years and older (mean age 75 years; 66% women) were prescribed 1 of 4 Beers Criteria medications — sedative-hypnotics, first-generation antihistamines, glyburide, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Pharmacists in the intervention group were encouraged to send patients an educational deprescribing brochure in parallel to sending their physicians an evidence-based pharmaceutical opinion to recommend deprescribing; pharmacists in the control group provided usual care. At 6 months, 106 of 248 patients (43%) in the intervention group no longer filled prescriptions for inappropriate medication, compared with 29 of 241 patients (12%) in the control group (risk difference 31% [95% CI, 23% to 38%]). By drug class, discontinuation in the intervention versus control group was 43.2% versus 9.0% for sedative-hypnotics, 30.6% versus 13.8% for glyburide, and 57.6% versus 21.7% for nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; the first-generation antihistamine class was too small to analyse (n=12). No adverse events requiring hospitalization were reported, although 29 of 77 patients (38%) who attempted to taper sedative-hypnotics reported withdrawal symptoms. The proven gain is discontinuation itself — a prescribing outcome at 6 months — not a fall, fracture, hospitalisation, or mortality outcome, and it rests on this one trial in one province. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a pharmacist-led educational intervention aimed at both patients and physicians increased deprescribing of potentially inappropriate medicines at 6 months in a single cluster randomised trial, with no hospitalisation-level harm reported but with withdrawal symptoms common during sedative-hypnotic tapering.

cards.headline: Martin 2018 (D-PRESCRIBE): inappropriate medication no longer filled at 6 months by 43% (106/248) versus 12% (29/241) — risk difference 31% [95% CI, 23% to 38%]
cards.summary: Martin 2018 (D-PRESCRIBE): inappropriate medication no longer filled at 6 months by 43% (106/248) versus 12% (29/241) — risk difference 31% [95% CI, 23% to 38%]
cards.people: 489 community-dwelling adults aged 65 years and older (mean age 75 years; 66% women) who were prescribed 1 of 4 Beers Criteria medications (sedative-hypnotics, first-generation antihistamines, glyburide, or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), recruited from 69 community pharmacies in Quebec, Canada, from February 2014 to September 2017, with follow-up until February 2018. Randomisation was at the pharmacy level: 34 pharmacies to the intervention group (248 patients) and 35 to the control group (241 patients). Pharmacists in the intervention group were encouraged to send patients an educational deprescribing brochure in parallel to sending their physicians an evidence-based pharmaceutical opinion to recommend deprescribing; pharmacists in the control group provided usual care. Patients, physicians, pharmacists, and evaluators were blinded to outcome assessment. 437 patients (89%) completed the trial (219 [88%] in the intervention group versus 218 [91%] in the control group).
cards.result: The main outcome — discontinuation of prescriptions for inappropriate medication at 6 months, ascertained by pharmacy medication renewal profiles — occurred in 106 of 248 patients (43%) in the intervention group compared with 29 of 241 patients (12%) in the control group (risk difference 31% [95% CI, 23% to 38%]), the absolute rates printed alongside the absolute difference. By drug class, discontinuation in the intervention versus control group was: sedative-hypnotics, 63 of 146 patients (43.2%) versus 14 of 155 (9.0%) (risk difference 34% [95% CI, 25% to 43%]); glyburide, 19 of 62 (30.6%) versus 8 of 58 (13.8%) (risk difference 17% [95% CI, 2% to 31%]); and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, 19 of 33 (57.6%) versus 5 of 23 (21.7%) (risk difference 35% [95% CI, 10% to 55%]) (P for interaction = .09). Analysis of the first-generation antihistamine drug class was not possible because of the small sample size (n=12). No adverse events requiring hospitalization were reported, although 29 of 77 patients (38%) who attempted to taper sedative-hypnotics reported withdrawal symptoms. The authors concluded that, among older adults in Quebec, a pharmacist-led educational intervention compared with usual care resulted in greater discontinuation of prescriptions for inappropriate medication after 6 months, and that the generalizability of these findings to other settings requires further research.
cards.watchOut: The outcome is discontinuation — whether the prescription stopped being filled at 6 months — not a clinical outcome: the trial does not show fewer falls, fractures, hospitalisations, or deaths from stopping, and follow-up ends at 6 months. It is a single cluster randomised trial in one province (Quebec, Canada), randomising pharmacies rather than patients, and the first-generation antihistamine class was too small to analyse (n=12), so the headline result is carried mainly by sedative-hypnotics, with smaller glyburide and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug subgroups. Stopping was not symptom-free: 29 of 77 patients (38%) who attempted to taper sedative-hypnotics reported withdrawal symptoms, even though no adverse events requiring hospitalization were reported.
cards.source: Martin P et al. Effect of a Pharmacist-Led Educational Intervention on Inappropriate Medication Prescriptions in Older Adults: The D-PRESCRIBE Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 30422193. Registry ID: NCT02053194. cards.summary: Synthesis: one cluster trial — a pharmacist educating the patient and advising the physician stopped inappropriate prescriptions in 43% versus 12% — with the re-card declared on the face of the shelf
cards.people: One cluster randomised clinical trial of 489 community-dwelling adults aged 65 years and older in 69 community pharmacies in Quebec, Canada (D-PRESCRIBE), testing a pharmacist-led educational intervention — an educational deprescribing brochure to the patient in parallel with an evidence-based pharmaceutical opinion to the physician — against usual care, with discontinuation assessed at 6 months.
cards.result: Discontinuation of prescriptions for inappropriate medication at 6 months: 106 of 248 patients (43%) in the intervention group versus 29 of 241 (12%) in the control group (risk difference 31% [95% CI, 23% to 38%]). By drug class (intervention versus control): sedative-hypnotics 43.2% versus 9.0%; glyburide 30.6% versus 13.8%; nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs 57.6% versus 21.7%; first-generation antihistamines not analysable (n=12). No adverse events requiring hospitalization were reported; withdrawal symptoms were reported by 29 of 77 patients (38%) who attempted to taper sedative-hypnotics. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Re-card declaration: D-PRESCRIBE (Martin P et al., PMID: 30422193) is also carded as a supporting card on live shelf #500 (Deprescribing benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults: EMPOWER — ask the patient, with a taper in hand), whose question is benzodiazepine-specific — whether direct patient education can get long-term older benzodiazepine users to stop. This shelf asks a genuinely different question: a pharmacist-led intervention aimed at BOTH patients and physicians, across potentially inappropriate medicines generally (sedative-hypnotics, first-generation antihistamines, glyburide, and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), not benzodiazepine-only direct-to-patient education. It is built under the Nov 15 #3104 (RACING) precedent, as applied at #3325 (STRENGTH), #3489 (CAROLINA), #3597 (PROPATRIA), #3628 (survodutide), and #3753 (OPAL): a study carded elsewhere as a supporting card may anchor a new shelf when the new question is genuinely different. Cross-point: for the benzodiazepine-only direct-to-patient education question, see live shelf #500. Tier C is set because a single trial carries the shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Martin P et al. JAMA. 2018 (PMID: 30422193).

shelves.title: Masked taper plus placebo-targeted behavioural therapy got 73.4% off benzodiazepine-receptor agonists at 6 months versus 58.6% with a standard open taper — insomnia no worse
shelves.question: In long-term benzodiazepine-receptor-agonist users, does a masked taper combined with behavioural intervention achieve discontinuation versus an unmasked taper with standard behavioural therapy?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/drug therapy · Middle Aged · Aged · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · GABA-A Receptor Agonists/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Benzodiazepines/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Drug Tapering · Lorazepam/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Hypnotics and Sedatives/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Zolpidem/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Alprazolam/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Clonazepam/therapeutic use/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — in the one randomised trial, hiding the dose during the taper helped more people finish it. Among 188 adults aged 55 or older who had used a benzodiazepine-receptor agonist (lorazepam, alprazolam, clonazepam, temazepam and/or zolpidem) at least 2 nights a week for at least 3 months, discontinuation 6 months after treatment ended was achieved by 73.4% with the masked taper plus augmented cognitive–behavioural therapy for insomnia (MTcap) versus 58.6% with standard CBT-I plus a supervised unmasked gradual taper (odds ratio 1.95; 95% CI 1.03 to 3.70; P=.04). The gap was larger 1 week post-treatment (88.4% vs 67.4%; OR 3.68; 95% CI 1.67 to 8.12). Insomnia Severity Index scores improved in both groups with no significant between-group difference, so the extra discontinuation was not bought with worse sleep. The comparator is an active best-practice taper, not usual care — usual-care discontinuation rates would be far lower. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): masked tapering is a promising upgrade to standard taper-plus-CBT-I, from a single two-centre trial.

cards.headline: Fung 2024: discontinuation at 6 months 73.4% masked vs 58.6% unmasked (OR 1.95; 95% CI 1.03–3.70); at 1 week 88.4% vs 67.4% (OR 3.68)
cards.summary: Fung 2024: discontinuation at 6 months 73.4% masked vs 58.6% unmasked (OR 1.95; 95% CI 1.03–3.70); at 1 week 88.4% vs 67.4% (OR 3.68)
cards.people: 188 adults aged 55 years or older (mean age 69.8 years) at an academic medical centre and a VA medical centre, using lorazepam, alprazolam, clonazepam, temazepam and/or zolpidem for current or prior insomnia at less than 8 mg diazepam-equivalent, at least 2 nights per week for at least 3 months; randomised to masked taper plus augmented CBT-I (MTcap, 92) or standard CBT-I plus supervised unmasked gradual taper (SGT, 96). Discontinuation was measured by 7-day self-reported medication logs, with urine tests in a subset.
cards.result: Benzodiazepine-receptor-agonist discontinuation 6 months after treatment ended: 73.4% in the MTcap group versus 58.6% in the SGT group (OR 1.95; 95% CI 1.03 to 3.70; P=.04). At 1 week post-treatment: 88.4% versus 67.4% (OR 3.68; 95% CI 1.67 to 8.12; P=.001), and MTcap reduced frequency of use at 1 week (−1.31 nights/week; 95% CI −2.05 to −0.57). Insomnia Severity Index improved in both groups with no significant between-group difference at 1 week (P=.16) or 6 months (P=.88).
cards.watchOut: Single trial, two US centres, motivated volunteers with insomnia-predominant use at modest doses — not long-term high-dose users, anxiety indications, or people with dependence complications. The intervention bundles masking with extra behavioural content, so the record cannot separate which ingredient carried the effect; compounding a masked taper is also pharmacy-intensive.
cards.source: Fung CH et al. Masked Taper With Behavioral Intervention for Discontinuation of Benzodiazepine Receptor Agonists: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA internal medicine. 2024. PMID: 39374004. Registry ID: NCT03687086. shelves.title: Admission-avoidance hospital at home: no mortality or readmission difference at 6 months (RR 0.88 and 1.14), but far fewer older patients living in residential care (RR 0.53)
shelves.question: In older adults, does admission-avoidance hospital-at-home care match or beat inpatient hospital care on mortality, readmission and living at home?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Health Facilities · Hospitalization · Hospitals · Inpatients · Patient Discharge · Home Care Services
shelves.balance: SPLIT — hospital-level care at home neither saves lives nor costs them in the pooled trials, but it does keep more older people out of residential care. The 2024 Cochrane review (20 randomised trials, 3,100 participants; in older populations) found admission-avoidance hospital at home probably makes little or no difference to mortality at 6 months (RR 0.88; 95% CI 0.68 to 1.13; 5 trials, 1,502 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) and little or no difference to readmission within 3–12 months (RR 1.14; 95% CI 0.97 to 1.34; 8 trials, 1,757 participants), while probably reducing the likelihood of living in residential care at 6 months (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.69; 4 trials, 1,271 participants). Self-reported health status probably differed little; satisfaction may be improved; initial hospital length of stay was shorter by design. This shelf covers the admission-avoidance model in predominantly older populations; the broader hospital-at-home question for acutely ill adults of all ages sits on its own shelf. PROPOSED SPLIT: equivalent on death and readmission, better on staying out of residential care.

cards.headline: Edgar 2024 Cochrane: mortality RR 0.88 (0.68–1.13), readmission RR 1.14 (0.97–1.34), residential care RR 0.53 (0.41–0.69) — 20 trials, 3,100 participants
cards.summary: Edgar 2024 Cochrane: mortality RR 0.88 (0.68–1.13), readmission RR 1.14 (0.97–1.34), residential care RR 0.53 (0.41–0.69) — 20 trials, 3,100 participants
cards.people: 20 randomised controlled trials with 3,100 participants aged 18 and over comparing admission-avoidance hospital at home with acute inpatient care: 4 trials in COPD, 2 in stroke recovery, 7 in acute medical conditions in mainly older participants, and the remainder in mixed conditions. Older-population estimates are quoted for the primary comparisons.
cards.result: For an older population, admission-avoidance hospital at home probably makes little or no difference to mortality at 6 months (RR 0.88; 95% CI 0.68 to 1.13; P=0.30; I²=0%; 5 trials, 1,502 participants; moderate-certainty evidence) and little or no difference to readmission within 3–12 months (RR 1.14; 95% CI 0.97 to 1.34; P=0.11; 8 trials, 1,757 participants; moderate-certainty). It probably reduces living in residential care at 6 months (RR 0.53; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.69; P<0.001; I²=67%; 4 trials, 1,271 participants; moderate-certainty). Self-reported health status probably showed little to no difference (2,006 participants); satisfaction may be improved (1,812 participants; low-certainty). Hospital length of stay in the inpatient group ranged from 4.1 to 18.5 days versus 1.2 to 5.1 days before hospital-at-home care, whose own duration averaged 3 to 20.7 days.
cards.watchOut: 'Hospital at home' bundles very different services across trials and decades, the residential-care estimate carries substantial heterogeneity (I²=67%), and caregiver effects were rarely reported — the family absorbing care work is the unmeasured cost in most of these trials.
cards.source: Edgar K et al. Admission avoidance hospital at home. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2024. PMID: 38438116. MeSH: Humans · Health Facilities · Hospitalization · Hospitals · Inpatients · Patient Discharge · Home Care Services

shelves.title: After an ED fall visit, multifactorial prevention programmes did not reduce falls in pooled trials (rate ratio 0.78; 95% CI 0.58–1.05) — one older positive trial is the exception, not the rule
shelves.question: In older adults presenting to the emergency department after a fall, do multifactorial falls-prevention programmes reduce further falls versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/prevention & control/statistics & numerical data · Accidents, Home/prevention & control/statistics & numerical data · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Emergency Service, Hospital · Environment Design · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Primary Prevention/methods · Program Development · Program Evaluation · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Risk Assessment · Secondary Prevention/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — as a class, these programmes have not earned their pooled result. The 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis (12 randomised trials, 3,986 community-dwelling older adults presenting to an emergency department with a fall) found no reduction in falls (rate ratio 0.78; 95% CI 0.58 to 1.05), number of fallers (RR 1.02; 95% CI 0.88 to 1.18), fractured neck of femur (RR 0.82; 95% CI 0.53 to 1.25), fall-related ED re-presentations (rate ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.84 to 1.16) or hospitalisations (rate ratio 1.14; 95% CI 0.69 to 1.89). One well-known earlier trial points the other way: Davison 2005, in 313 cognitively intact recurrent fallers, found 36% fewer falls with multifactorial assessment and intervention (RR 0.64; 95% CI 0.46 to 0.90) — though the proportion still falling was unchanged (65% vs 68%) and admissions did not fall. The reviewers' conclusion stands: insufficient evidence to support these programmes for this population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): pooled across programmes and settings, no outcome improved significantly.

cards.headline: Morello 2019 meta-analysis: falls rate ratio 0.78 (0.58–1.05), fallers RR 1.02, ED re-presentations 0.99, hospitalisations 1.14 — nothing significant across 12 trials
cards.summary: Morello 2019 meta-analysis: falls rate ratio 0.78 (0.58–1.05), fallers RR 1.02, ED re-presentations 0.99, hospitalisations 1.14 — nothing significant across 12 trials
cards.people: 12 randomised controlled trials involving 3,986 community-dwelling older adults (aged 60+) from six countries who presented to an emergency department with a fall; multifactorial interventions typically combined education, referral to healthcare services, home modifications, exercise and medication changes, and were of variable methodological quality.
cards.result: Multifactorial programmes did not significantly reduce: falls (rate ratio 0.78; 95% CI 0.58 to 1.05), number of fallers (risk ratio 1.02; 95% CI 0.88 to 1.18), fractured neck of femur (risk ratio 0.82; 95% CI 0.53 to 1.25), fall-related ED presentations (rate ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.84 to 1.16), or hospitalisations (rate ratio 1.14; 95% CI 0.69 to 1.89). The authors conclude there is insufficient evidence to support multifactorial interventions to prevent falls or hospital utilisation in older people presenting to ED after a fall.
cards.watchOut: The falls point estimate (0.78) leans favourable but its interval crosses 1 and the programmes pooled are heterogeneous bundles — a specific well-delivered programme could still work where the average does not; the review cannot identify which components, if any, matter.
cards.source: Morello RT et al. Multifactorial falls prevention programmes for older adults presenting to the emergency department with a fall: systematic review and meta-analysis. Injury prevention : journal of the International Society for Child and Adolescent Injury Prevention. 2019. PMID: 31289112. cards.headline: Davison 2005: 36% fewer falls (RR 0.64; 95% CI 0.46–0.90) in recurrent fallers — but the same proportion kept falling (65% vs 68%) and admissions were unchanged
cards.summary: Davison 2005: 36% fewer falls (RR 0.64; 95% CI 0.46–0.90) in recurrent fallers — but the same proportion kept falling (65% vs 68%) and admissions were unchanged
cards.people: 313 cognitively intact men and women aged over 65 presenting to Accident & Emergency with a fall or fall-related injury plus at least one additional fall in the preceding year, randomised to multifactorial (medical, physiotherapy and occupational therapy) post-fall assessment and intervention (159) or conventional care (154), followed for 1 year.
cards.result: The intervention group had 36% fewer falls (relative risk 0.64; 95% CI 0.46 to 0.90). The proportion of participants continuing to fall was not different (65% (94/144) versus 68% (102/149); RR 0.95; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.12), nor were fall-related attendances or hospital admissions; duration of hospital admission was reduced (mean difference 3.6 days; 95% CI 0.1 to 7.6) and balance confidence was better (mean difference 7.5 points; 95% CI 0.72 to 14.2).
cards.watchOut: A selected population — cognitively intact recurrent fallers at two UK hospitals — is precisely the subgroup most likely to respond, and even here the benefit was fewer falls per person among those still falling, not fewer fallers. Later, broader trials pooled by Morello did not reproduce the headline effect.
cards.source: Davison J et al. Patients with recurrent falls attending Accident & Emergency benefit from multifactorial intervention--a randomised controlled trial. Age and ageing. 2005. PMID: 15716246. cards.headline: Synthesis: the average programme does nothing measurable after an ED fall; one targeted trial in recurrent fallers is the standing exception

cards.people: A 12-trial meta-analysis (3,986 ED fall presenters) plus the 313-patient Davison trial of multifactorial intervention in cognitively intact recurrent fallers.
cards.result: Pooled: falls rate ratio 0.78 (95% CI 0.58 to 1.05), fallers RR 1.02, fractures RR 0.82, re-presentations 0.99, hospitalisations 1.14 — none significant. cards.watchOut: A null pooled result for heterogeneous bundles is not proof that every component is useless — exercise and medication review have their own shelves and their own evidence; this shelf judges the ED-triggered multifactorial package as a whole.

shelves.title: Comprehensive geriatric assessment outside hospital: most reviews find no effect on admissions, function or quality of life — frailty may improve, mortality signals appear in only 2 of 10 reviews
shelves.question: In community-dwelling frail older adults at risk of decline, does home-based comprehensive geriatric assessment improve function and reduce hospital use versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Geriatric Assessment/methods · Aged · Systematic Reviews as Topic · Aged, 80 and over · Home Care Services
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — for the headline outcomes, the accumulated review literature is mostly a null. The 2025 overview of systematic reviews (22 reviews, 478 primary studies, more than 136,336 participants, mostly community and home settings) found most reviews reported no effect of comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) on hospital or long-term-care admissions, quality of life or function; of 10 reviews reporting mortality, only 2 found reductions (13% and 14% relative reductions at longest follow-up), and of 3 reviews reporting frailty, 2 found benefit (one meta-analysis: frailty RR 0.77; 95% CI 0.64 to 0.93). A 2026 meta-analysis of home-based interventions in frail or pre-frail older adults (24 studies, 3,826 participants) — broader than CGA alone — found small improvements in frailty scores (standardised mean difference −0.27) and grip strength, but no significant change in overall or physical quality of life, and physical-function gains only in professionally supervised programmes. CGA models vary so much in content, dose and duration (6–36 months) that 'CGA' barely names one intervention. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): no consistent benefit on admissions or function; a possible frailty effect is the live lead.

cards.headline: Kshatri 2025 overview: 22 reviews, >136,000 participants — most found no effect on admissions, function or QoL; mortality reduced in only 2 of 10 reviews that reported it
cards.summary: Kshatri 2025 overview: 22 reviews, >136,000 participants — most found no effect on admissions, function or QoL; mortality reduced in only 2 of 10 reviews that reported it
cards.people: 22 systematic reviews (478 primary studies, more than 136,336 participants aged 50+) of comprehensive geriatric assessment in non-hospital settings — primary care, outpatient, community, long-term care and home-based care — searched to August 2023; 73% of reviews were based in community or home settings and most reviews were of moderate to good quality.
cards.result: Most reviews found no effect of CGA on rates of admission to hospital or long-term care, quality of life, or function. Of the 10 reviews reporting mortality, only two found a reduction in mortality risk (13% and 14% relative reductions at longest follow-up). Of three reviews reporting frailty, two showed benefit, one meta-analysis finding a significant reduction in frailty (relative risk 0.77; 95% CI 0.64 to 0.93). CGA models were highly heterogeneous in domains, delivery (mostly nurses and multidisciplinary teams), and duration (6–36 months), with poor reporting of assessment frequency. All evidence came from high-income countries.
cards.watchOut: An overview of reviews inherits every inconsistency of the reviews beneath it, and 'CGA' here spans very different programmes; the two positive mortality reviews may reflect the most targeted (highest-risk) populations rather than CGA in general — the authors themselves suggest identifying high-risk individuals first.
cards.source: Kshatri JS et al. Comprehensive geriatric assessment in nonhospitalized settings: An overview of systematic reviews. Geriatrics & gerontology international. 2025. PMID: 39979072. cards.headline: Yao 2026 meta-analysis of home-based interventions in frailty: frailty scores improved (SMD −0.27) and grip strength rose, but overall quality of life did not change
cards.summary: Yao 2026 meta-analysis of home-based interventions in frailty: frailty scores improved (SMD −0.27) and grip strength rose, but overall quality of life did not change
cards.people: 24 studies (20 randomised trials; 3,826 participants) of home-based interventions for older adults with frailty or pre-frailty, searched to October 2024 — a broader set than CGA alone, including exercise, nutrition and multicomponent programmes delivered at home.
cards.result: Home-based interventions significantly reduced frailty phenotype scores (standardised mean difference −0.27; 95% CI −0.39 to −0.15) and depressive symptoms (SMD −0.11; 95% CI −0.20 to −0.01), and increased grip strength (mean difference 0.84; 95% CI 0.26 to 1.42) and mental health-related quality of life (SMD 0.17; 95% CI 0.04 to 0.30). No significant changes were seen in overall quality of life or physical health-related quality of life, and significant physical-function improvements appeared only in the professionally supervised subgroup; the authors caution unsupervised programmes may pose iatrogenic harm risk.
cards.watchOut: This is home-based intervention broadly, not CGA specifically — it supports the frailty signal in the overview rather than the assessment model itself, and effect sizes are small (SMDs of 0.1–0.3).
cards.source: Yao G et al. Effectiveness of Home-Based interventions for older adults with frailty or pre-frailty: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Archives of gerontology and geriatrics. 2026. cards.headline: Synthesis: assessment alone changes little; the frailty signal lives in supervised, intervention-carrying programmes
cards.summary: Synthesis: assessment alone changes little; the frailty signal lives in supervised, intervention-carrying programmes
cards.people: An overview of 22 systematic reviews of non-hospital CGA (>136,336 participants) and a meta-analysis of 24 home-based frailty intervention studies (3,826 participants).
cards.result: CGA outside hospital: no consistent effect on admissions, long-term care, function or quality of life; mortality benefit in 2 of 10 reporting reviews; frailty RR 0.77 (95% CI 0.64 to 0.93) in one meta-analysis. Home-based frailty interventions: frailty SMD −0.27, grip +0.84, overall quality of life unchanged. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) for CGA as named; Tier C flagged.
cards.watchOut: Hospital-based CGA has its own, stronger shelf and is not judged here; this shelf covers community and home delivery, where the intervention's active ingredients are least standardised.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kshatri JS et al. Geriatrics & gerontology international. 2025 (PMID: 39979072); Yao G et al. Archives of gerontology and geriatrics. 2026 (PMID: 41242035).

shelves.question: In older adults with Alzheimer's disease in primary care, does collaborative care management with a nurse care manager improve behavioural symptoms and caregiver burden versus usual care?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for behaviour and caregivers, from one well-run trial. Callahan 2006 randomised 153 older adults with Alzheimer disease and their caregivers (by physician) to 1 year of collaborative care management led by an advanced-practice nurse working with the family caregiver inside primary care, or augmented usual care. Behavioural and psychological symptoms (Neuropsychiatric Inventory total) were significantly lower in the intervention group at 12 months (mean difference −5.6; P=.01) and 18 months (−5.4; P=.01); caregivers reported significantly less distress at 12 months and less depression (PHQ-9) at 18 months. Intervention patients were more likely to receive cholinesterase inhibitors (79.8% vs 55.1%; P=.002) and antidepressants (45.2% vs 27.5%; P=.03), without significantly more antipsychotics or sedative-hypnotics. There were no group differences in depression-in-dementia scores, cognition, activities of daily living, hospitalisation, nursing-home placement or death. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a nurse-led collaborative model improves the symptoms families struggle with most; it does not slow the disease.

cards.headline: Callahan 2006: NPI total −5.6 points at 12 months (P=.01) and −5.4 at 18 months; caregiver distress improved; cognition, ADL, hospitalisation and death unchanged
cards.summary: Callahan 2006: NPI total −5.6 points at 12 months (P=.01) and −5.4 at 18 months; caregiver distress improved; cognition, ADL, hospitalisation and death unchanged
cards.people: 153 older adults with Alzheimer disease and their self-identified caregivers in primary-care practices of two US university-affiliated systems (2002–2004), randomised by physician to collaborative care management (84) or augmented usual care (69). The intervention was 1 year of care management by an interdisciplinary team led by an advanced-practice nurse, integrated in primary care, using protocols for behavioural and psychological symptoms that stressed non-pharmacological management; 89% of intervention patients triggered at least one of 8 protocols (mean 4 per patient).
cards.result: Total Neuropsychiatric Inventory score was significantly lower (better) in the intervention group at 12 months (mean difference −5.6; P=.01) and 18 months (mean difference −5.4; P=.01). Caregivers reported significant improvement in distress (caregiver NPI) at 12 months and in depression (PHQ-9) at 18 months. Intervention patients were more likely to receive cholinesterase inhibitors (79.8% vs 55.1%; P=.002) and antidepressants (45.2% vs 27.5%; P=.03), achieved without significantly increased antipsychotic or sedative-hypnotic use. No group differences were found on the Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia, cognition, activities of daily living, or rates of hospitalisation, nursing-home placement or death.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 153 patients, two academic systems, conducted two decades ago when cholinesterase-inhibitor use was still diffusing — part of the effect may be better standard prescribing that modern usual care already delivers. Randomisation by physician with few clusters also widens true uncertainty beyond the printed P values.
cards.source: Callahan CM et al. Effectiveness of collaborative care for older adults with Alzheimer disease in primary care: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2006. PMID: 16684985. Registry ID: NCT00246896. shelves.title: Advance-care-planning videos in nursing homes changed nothing measured: hospital transfers 3.7 vs 3.9 per 1,000 days in long-stay residents — and only 21.9% of residents ever saw a video
shelves.question: In long-stay nursing-home residents with dementia, does an advance-care-planning video intervention increase goal-concordant care and reduce burdensome hospital transfers versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Advance Care Planning · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Homes for the Aged · Hospice Care · Humans · Male · Nursing Homes · Social Workers · Video Recording
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — the PROVEN pragmatic trial is a large, honest null. Across 360 nursing homes (119 intervention, 241 control), offering five 6–10-minute advance-care-planning videos to long-stay residents with advanced illness (4,171 intervention; 8,308 control) did not significantly reduce the primary outcome, hospital transfers per 1,000 person-days alive (3.7 vs 3.9; rate difference −0.2; 95% CI −0.5 to 0.2), and secondary outcomes — burdensome treatments and hospice enrolment — did not differ in residents with or without advanced illness. The companion short-stay analysis was likewise null (12.3 vs 13.2 transfers per 1,000 days; rate difference −0.8; 95% CI −1.8 to 0.2). The caveat is delivery: champions reported only 21.9% of long-stay residents with advanced illness actually viewed a video (14–15% of short-stay patients), and 11.8% of intervention facilities showed videos to no one. Goal-concordant care itself was not directly measured. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): as implemented at scale, the video programme did not move transfers, burdensome treatment or hospice use.

cards.headline: Mitchell 2020 (PROVEN, long-stay): transfers 3.7 vs 3.9 per 1,000 person-days (difference −0.2; 95% CI −0.5 to 0.2); no secondary-outcome differences; 21.9% viewed a video
cards.summary: Mitchell 2020 (PROVEN, long-stay): transfers 3.7 vs 3.9 per 1,000 person-days (difference −0.2; 95% CI −0.5 to 0.2); no secondary-outcome differences; 21.9% viewed a video
cards.people: 360 nursing homes in 32 US states owned by two for-profit corporations (119 intervention, 241 control), February 2016 to May 2019. Long-stay residents with advanced dementia or cardiopulmonary disease: 4,171 in intervention homes and 8,308 in control homes; residents without advanced illness: 5,764 and 11,773. Intervention homes' champions (mostly social workers) were to offer five 6–10-minute ACP videos on tablets or online at admission and every 6 months; control homes used usual ACP practice. Outcomes were measured over 12 months per resident.
cards.result: Hospital transfers per 1,000 person-days alive in the advanced-illness cohort: 3.7 (95% CI 3.4 to 4.0) in the intervention group versus 3.9 (95% CI 3.6 to 4.1) in the control group (rate difference −0.2; 95% CI −0.5 to 0.2) — not significant. The proportions experiencing one or more hospital transfer, one or more burdensome treatment, and hospice enrolment did not significantly differ between groups among residents with or without advanced illness. By champion reports, 912 of 4,171 residents with advanced illness (21.9%) viewed an ACP video; facility-level showing rates ranged from 0% (14 of 119 facilities) to over 40% (22 facilities).
cards.watchOut: A null with 78% non-viewing is a verdict on the programme as delivered, not proof that a watched video cannot change a conversation; equally, a programme that cannot get itself watched at scale has failed its own test. Goal-concordant care — the candidate question's first outcome — was not directly measured in either report.
cards.source: Mitchell SL et al. Advance Care Planning Video Intervention Among Long-Stay Nursing Home Residents: A Pragmatic Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA internal medicine. 2020. PMID: 32628258. Registry ID: NCT02612688. cards.headline: Loomer 2021 (PROVEN, short-stay): transfers 12.3 vs 13.2 per 1,000 days (difference −0.8; 95% CI −1.8 to 0.2); only ~15% of eligible patients were shown a video
cards.summary: Loomer 2021 (PROVEN, short-stay): transfers 12.3 vs 13.2 per 1,000 days (difference −0.8; 95% CI −1.8 to 0.2); only ~15% of eligible patients were shown a video
cards.type: Pragmatic cluster randomised trial companion report (Loomer 2021, PROVEN)
cards.people: The same 360 nursing homes (119 intervention, 241 control), analysing short-stay patients: 2,538 (intervention) and 5,290 (control) with advanced dementia or cardiopulmonary disease, and 23,302 and 50,815 without advanced illness; follow-up at most 100 days per patient. Champions were to offer a video on admission.
cards.result: Hospital transfers per 1,000 person-days alive in the advanced-illness cohort: 12.3 (95% CI 11.6 to 13.1) intervention versus 13.2 (95% CI 12.5 to 13.7) control (rate difference −0.8; 95% CI −1.8 to 0.2) — not significant. There was a non-significant reduction among short-stay patients without advanced illness, and secondary outcomes (repeat transfers, burdensome treatments including tube-feeding and ICU admission, hospice enrolment) did not differ in either cohort. Champions reported showing videos to 14.2% of eligible patients with advanced illness and 15.3% without.
cards.watchOut: Same trial, second population — this is corroboration of the null across the nursing-home census, not an independent replication; the short-stay transfer rate is roughly triple the long-stay rate, so the absolute stakes differ even though the verdict does not.
cards.source: Loomer L et al. Impact of an Advance Care Planning Video Intervention on Care of Short-Stay Nursing Home Patients. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2021. PMID: 33159697. cards.headline: Synthesis: at 360-home scale the video programme is a null — whether from weak medicine or weak delivery, the transfers did not move
cards.summary: Synthesis: at 360-home scale the video programme is a null — whether from weak medicine or weak delivery, the transfers did not move
cards.people: One pragmatic cluster randomised programme (PROVEN) reported for long-stay residents (12,479 with advanced illness) and short-stay patients (7,828 with advanced illness) across 360 nursing homes.
cards.result: Long-stay transfers: 3.7 versus 3.9 per 1,000 person-days (difference −0.2; 95% CI −0.5 to 0.2). Short-stay: 12.3 versus 13.2 (difference −0.8; 95% CI −1.8 to 0.2). Burdensome treatments and hospice enrolment: no significant differences anywhere. Viewing fidelity: 21.9% (long-stay) and about 15% (short-stay). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: one programme, however large.
cards.watchOut: Facilitated, documented, clinician-led advance care planning is a different intervention from posting videos on a tablet; this null should not be read onto it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Mitchell SL et al. JAMA internal medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32628258); Loomer L et al. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2021 (PMID: 33159697).

shelves.title: Group pelvic-floor training matched individual training in older women: leakage episodes fell 74% in groups versus 70% individually at 1 year — noninferiority confirmed
shelves.question: In older women with urinary incontinence, does group-based pelvic floor muscle training match individual training on leakage episodes?
shelves.mesh: Canada · Exercise Therapy/methods · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Muscle Contraction/physiology · Pelvic Floor · Psychotherapy, Group/methods · Quality of Life · Resistance Training/methods · Treatment Outcome · Urinary Incontinence/rehabilitation · Urinary Incontinence, Stress/rehabilitation
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — group delivery is not a diluted version of the real thing. In the GROUP randomised noninferiority trial (362 community-dwelling women aged 60 or older with stress or mixed urinary incontinence, in two Canadian centres), women learned pelvic-floor contraction in one individual session, then trained for 12 weeks either in groups of 8 (178 women) or individually (184). At 1 year, the median percentage reduction in incontinence episodes was 74% (95% CI 46% to 86%) in the group arm versus 70% (95% CI 44% to 89%) individually; the difference was 4% (95% CI −10% to 7%), with the upper confidence bound below the pre-specified 10% noninferiority margin — noninferiority confirmed. All secondary outcomes (lower urinary tract symptoms, quality of life) were similar at 1 year, and adverse events were minor and uncommon. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): group-based training delivers individual-level results at group-level cost, on one trial's evidence.

cards.headline: Dumoulin 2020 (GROUP): median leakage reduction 74% group vs 70% individual at 1 year; difference 4% (95% CI −10% to 7%), inside the 10% noninferiority margin
cards.summary: Dumoulin 2020 (GROUP): median leakage reduction 74% group vs 70% individual at 1 year; difference 4% (95% CI −10% to 7%), inside the 10% noninferiority margin
cards.people: 362 community-dwelling women aged 60 years or older (mean age 67.9 years) with stress or mixed urinary incontinence at two Canadian research centres, 2012–2018. After one individual session to learn correct pelvic-floor contraction, participants completed 12 weeks of pelvic floor muscle training in groups of 8 women (178) or in individual sessions (184). The primary outcome was percentage reduction in incontinence episodes on a 7-day bladder diary at 1 year; 319 women (88%) completed follow-up and entered the per-protocol analysis.
cards.result: Median percentage reduction in urinary incontinence episodes at 1 year: 70% (95% CI 44% to 89%) with individual training versus 74% (95% CI 46% to 86%) with group-based training. The upper boundary of the 95% CI for the between-group difference (4%; 95% CI −10% to 7%) was lower than the pre-specified noninferiority margin of 10% (P=.58 for the difference), confirming noninferiority. Individual and group training had similar effectiveness for all secondary outcomes at 1 year; adverse events were minor and uncommon.
cards.watchOut: Per-protocol analysis (appropriate for noninferiority, but it drops the 12% who did not complete), single-blind, one country's centres, and both arms received the same expert-designed programme — the result endorses group delivery of good training, not any group class. Women with predominantly urge incontinence or pelvic organ prolapse were not the study population.
cards.source: Dumoulin C et al. Group-Based vs Individual Pelvic Floor Muscle Training to Treat Urinary Incontinence in Older Women: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA internal medicine. 2020. PMID: 32744599. Registry ID: NCT02039830. cards.headline: Synthesis: the group is a delivery vehicle, not a compromise — equal leakage reduction, wider reach
cards.summary: Synthesis: the group is a delivery vehicle, not a compromise — equal leakage reduction, wider reach
cards.people: One randomised noninferiority trial, 362 older women with stress or mixed incontinence, 12 weeks of group (n=8 per group) versus individual pelvic floor muscle training, 1-year follow-up.
cards.result: Median leakage-episode reduction: 74% (group) versus 70% (individual); difference 4% (95% CI −10% to 7%), within the 10% noninferiority margin. Secondary outcomes similar; adverse events minor. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: single trial.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority to an effective treatment is a benefit claim about access and cost as much as efficacy; if individual training is unavailable locally, the relevant comparison — group training versus nothing — is not what this trial tested.
cards.source: Synthesis of Dumoulin C et al. JAMA internal medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32744599).

shelves.title: Fludrocortisone for orthostatic hypotension rests on 28 randomised patients: 3 tiny crossover trials, very low-certainty evidence on blood pressure, symptoms and harms alike
shelves.question: In orthostatic hypotension, does fludrocortisone raise standing blood pressure and improve symptoms versus placebo — and on how much randomised evidence?
shelves.mesh: Bias · Diabetes Mellitus · Domperidone/therapeutic use · Dysautonomia, Familial/complications · Fludrocortisone/therapeutic use · Humans · Hypotension, Orthostatic/drug therapy · Observational Studies as Topic · Parkinson Disease/complications · Pyridostigmine Bromide/therapeutic use · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — 'no difference shown' is the honest reading, because almost nothing has been shown at all. The 2021 Cochrane review found 13 studies (513 participants) but only 3 crossover randomised trials totalling 28 participants, each 2–3 weeks long, in just two conditions (diabetes and Parkinson disease). Against placebo, the entire randomised dataset is one 6-person crossover study in diabetes: standing blood-pressure drop was −26 mmHg systolic on fludrocortisone versus −39 mmHg on placebo (−7 vs −11 mmHg diastolic), and 4 of 5 analysed participants reported improved orthostatic symptoms — all graded very low-certainty evidence. In Parkinson disease, fludrocortisone was compared with pyridostigmine and domperidone, not placebo, with mixed findings. Observational studies fill gaps without resolving them, and adverse-event evidence is likewise very low certainty (reported side effects minimal in these tiny samples). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): a first-line drug by custom, resting on 28 randomised patients — the shelf's real content is the size of the evidence hole.

cards.headline: Veazie 2021 Cochrane: 13 studies, 513 people — but just 28 in randomised trials; the sole placebo comparison is 6 people with diabetes (drop −26 vs −39 mmHg systolic)
cards.summary: Veazie 2021 Cochrane: 13 studies, 513 people — but just 28 in randomised trials; the sole placebo comparison is 6 people with diabetes (drop −26 vs −39 mmHg systolic)
cards.people: 13 studies of 513 participants with orthostatic hypotension from chronic peripheral or central autonomic neuropathy or autonomic failure (excluding drug-induced and acute volume-loss causes): 3 crossover randomised trials (28 participants total, 2–3 weeks each, in diabetes and Parkinson disease only) and 10 observational studies (3 cohort, 6 case series, 1 case-control). Searches to November 2019.
cards.result: Randomised evidence versus placebo exists only in diabetes (1 crossover study, 6 participants): very low-certainty evidence that the standing blood-pressure drop was −26 mmHg systolic on fludrocortisone versus −39 mmHg on placebo, and −7 versus −11 mmHg diastolic; 4 of 5 analysed participants had improvement in orthostatic symptoms on fludrocortisone. In Parkinson disease (very low-certainty): versus pyridostigmine, diastolic drop −14 versus −22.1 mmHg (P=0.036; 9 participants); versus domperidone, no change in blood-pressure drop in either group (13 participants) and orthostatic symptom scores improved to 6 on both treatments. Adverse-event evidence was very low certainty, with side effects reported as minimal. Heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis of the trials. One retrospective cohort of 341 people with familial dysautonomia suggested fludrocortisone may not be harmful long-term, without establishing benefit.
cards.watchOut: This shelf's neighbour shelves cover fludrocortisone in vasovagal syncope and the fludrocortisone-versus-midodrine question in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension; this card is the placebo-evidence audit for orthostatic hypotension itself. Two-to-three-week crossover trials in 28 people cannot detect the harms (supine hypertension, oedema, heart failure, hypokalaemia) that govern real long-term use.
cards.source: Veazie S et al. Fludrocortisone for orthostatic hypotension. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. PMID: 34000076. cards.people: Cochrane review of 13 studies (513 participants), of which 3 crossover randomised trials contribute 28 participants; placebo-controlled randomised data exist for 6 people with diabetes.
cards.result: Versus placebo: standing systolic drop −26 versus −39 mmHg and symptoms improved in 4 of 5 analysed participants — very low-certainty. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — no effect is established in either direction; Tier C flagged.
cards.watchOut: Absence of evidence here is not evidence of absence: the point estimates lean favourable. The stamp records that, at SourceMed's bar, custom and physiology are doing the work that trials have not.

shelves.title: HMB in sarcopenia: grip strength rose 4.6 kg more than placebo over 12 weeks in one 34-person trial — muscle mass itself did not change; a bed-rest trial shows HMB can preserve lean mass under catabolic stress
shelves.question: In older adults with sarcopenia, does beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate (HMB) improve muscle mass and function versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Aged · Sarcopenia/drug therapy · Hand Strength/physiology · Muscle Strength/physiology · Muscle, Skeletal/physiology · Double-Blind Method · Dietary Supplements · Valerates
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for strength and performance, not for mass, and the sarcopenia trial is very small. Yang 2023 randomised 34 older adults with sarcopenia to HMB or placebo twice daily for 12 weeks, both groups doing resistance exercise twice weekly: handgrip strength improved 4.61 kg more with HMB (95% CI 2.93 to 6.28; P<0.001), gait speed 0.11 m/s more (95% CI 0.02 to 0.20), five-times chair-stand time 3.65 seconds faster (95% CI −5.72 to −1.58), and muscle quality rose — but skeletal muscle mass and muscle index did not differ significantly between groups. The mechanistic support comes from Deutz 2013: in healthy older adults confined to 10 days of bed rest, HMB (3 g/day) prevented the lean-body-mass loss seen on placebo (−0.17 kg vs −2.05 kg change; P=0.02), though functional differences could not be detected at that sample size. The publication record for the sarcopenia trial does not name a branded HMB product or its manufacturer, so no product can be endorsed from it — current products may differ in formulation and effect. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): HMB added to resistance training improved strength and performance in one small trial; the mass claim it is usually sold on was not shown in sarcopenic patients.

cards.headline: Yang 2023: grip +4.61 kg (95% CI 2.93–6.28), gait speed +0.11 m/s, chair stand −3.65 s versus placebo — skeletal muscle mass and index not significantly different
cards.summary: Yang 2023: grip +4.61 kg (95% CI 2.93–6.28), gait speed +0.11 m/s, chair stand −3.65 s versus placebo — skeletal muscle mass and index not significantly different
cards.people: 34 older adults (aged 60+) with sarcopenia, assigned to HMB twice daily (18) or placebo (16) for 12 weeks, with both groups receiving resistance exercise training twice weekly. Primary outcome handgrip strength; secondary outcomes gait speed, five-time chair stand, body composition and inflammatory markers. The record does not name a branded HMB product or manufacturer.
cards.result: After 12 weeks the HMB group showed significantly greater improvements than placebo in handgrip strength (4.61 kg; 95% CI 2.93 to 6.28; P<0.001), gait speed (0.11 m/s; 95% CI 0.02 to 0.20; P=0.014), five-time chair stand test (−3.65 s; 95% CI −5.72 to −1.58; P=0.001), muscle quality (2.47; 95% CI 1.15 to 3.80; P=0.001) and the inflammatory marker TWEAK (−15.23 pmol/mL; 95% CI −29.80 to −0.66; P=0.041). No significant between-group differences were found in skeletal muscle mass, skeletal muscle index, or other body-composition parameters.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-four participants, one centre, 12 weeks, and HMB was always paired with resistance training — the trial tests HMB as an exercise adjunct, not a stand-alone treatment, and its strength gains without mass gains rest on small-sample ANCOVA estimates with wide intervals.
cards.source: Yang C et al. Effects of Beta-Hydroxy-Beta-Methylbutyrate Supplementation on Older Adults with Sarcopenia: A Randomized, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Study. The journal of nutrition, health & aging. 2023. PMID: 37248756. Registry ID: ChiCTR2000028778. cards.headline: Deutz 2013 bed-rest trial: HMB prevented lean-mass loss over 10 days of bed rest (−0.17 kg vs −2.05 kg; P=0.02) in 19 evaluable older adults — function unchanged at this size
cards.summary: Deutz 2013 bed-rest trial: HMB prevented lean-mass loss over 10 days of bed rest (−0.17 kg vs −2.05 kg; P=0.02) in 19 evaluable older adults — function unchanged at this size
cards.people: 24 healthy older adults (aged 60–76; SPPB at least 9) randomised to calcium HMB 1.5 g twice daily (3 g/day) or inactive placebo powder, starting 5 days before 10 days of complete bed rest and continuing through 8 weeks of resistance-training rehabilitation; 19 were evaluable at the end of bed rest (11 HMB, 8 control).
cards.result: Bed rest caused a significant decrease in total lean body mass in the control group (−2.05 ± 0.66 kg; P=0.02), while HMB treatment prevented the decline (−0.17 ± 0.19 kg change; P=0.23 within group), with a statistically significant between-group difference in lean-mass change over bed rest (P=0.02). The female sub-analysis also favoured HMB (P=0.04). Differences in functional parameters could not be observed, which the authors attribute to sample size.
cards.watchOut: Healthy volunteers under experimental bed rest are a model of catabolic stress, not sarcopenic patients; the mass preservation did not come with measured functional benefit, and one HMB participant was excluded from the headline analysis. It supports plausibility for the sarcopenia finding rather than replicating it.
cards.source: Deutz NE et al. Effect of beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate (HMB) on lean body mass during 10 days of bed rest in older adults. Clinical nutrition (Edinburgh, Scotland). 2013. PMID: 23514626. Registry ID: NCT00945581. cards.headline: Synthesis: strength and performance moved in sarcopenia; mass moved only under bed rest — two small trials, two different questions, one cautious yes
cards.summary: Synthesis: strength and performance moved in sarcopenia; mass moved only under bed rest — two small trials, two different questions, one cautious yes
cards.people: Two randomised double-blind trials: HMB versus placebo in 34 sarcopenic older adults with concurrent resistance training (12 weeks), and in 24 healthy older adults during 10 days of bed rest (19 evaluable).
cards.result: Sarcopenia: grip +4.61 kg (95% CI 2.93 to 6.28), gait speed +0.11 m/s, chair stand −3.65 s; muscle mass not significantly different. Bed rest: lean-mass change −0.17 kg on HMB versus −2.05 kg on placebo (P=0.02), function not different. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: small single trials for each claim, and no branded product is named in the sarcopenia record.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial exceeds 12 weeks of treatment-phase observation for its primary claim, and neither was powered for falls, fractures, disability or any outcome beyond the laboratory and the gym.
cards.source: Synthesis of Yang C et al. The journal of nutrition, health & aging. 2023 (PMID: 37248756); Deutz NE et al. Clinical nutrition (Edinburgh, Scotland). 2013 (PMID: 23514626).

shelves.title: DO-HEALTH: three years of vitamin D, omega-3s and home exercise changed none of six primary outcomes in healthy adults over 70 — one borderline falls signal for omega-3s aside
shelves.question: In adults aged 70 and over, does the DO-HEALTH combination — vitamin D, omega-3s and a home exercise programme — improve blood pressure, cognition, fractures and infections versus control?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cholecalciferol/therapeutic use · Cognition Disorders/prevention & control · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Fatty Acids, Omega-3/therapeutic use · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Fractures, Bone/prevention & control · Health Status · Humans · Hypertension/therapy · Immunity · Male · Physical Fitness · Resistance Training · Treatment Outcome · Vitamins/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the factorial DO-HEALTH trial of 2,157 adults aged 70 or older followed for 3 years, none of vitamin D3 2000 IU/day, omega-3s 1 g/day, or a strength-training exercise programme, alone or combined, significantly improved any of the six primary outcomes: systolic blood pressure (difference in change −0.8 mm Hg for both vitamin D and omega-3s, 99% CI −2.1 to 0.5), physical performance (SPPB), cognition (MoCA), nonvertebral fractures, or infections (omega-3 infection-rate difference −0.13, rate ratio 0.89, 99% CI 0.78–1.01, p=0.02 against a p<0.01 threshold). The trial's falls analysis found one borderline signal — omega-3s reduced total falls by 10% in relative terms (incidence rate ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.81–1.00, p=0.04) — while vitamin D and the exercise programme had no falls benefit. The participants were unusually healthy and active, which limits how far the null travels to frailer populations. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in healthy, active adults over 70, this popular trio does not improve blood pressure, cognition, fractures, infections or physical performance over 3 years.

cards.headline: Bischoff-Ferrari 2020 (DO-HEALTH): no significant effect of vitamin D, omega-3s or exercise on any of six primary outcomes at 3 years
cards.summary: Bischoff-Ferrari 2020 (DO-HEALTH): no significant effect of vitamin D, omega-3s or exercise on any of six primary outcomes at 3 years
cards.people: 2,157 adults aged 70 years or older (mean age 74.9 years, 61.7% women) with no major health events in the previous 5 years, sufficient mobility and good cognitive status, recruited in five European countries and randomised in a 2×2×2 factorial design to vitamin D3 2000 IU/day, omega-3s 1 g/day, and/or a strength-training exercise programme, or their controls, for 3 years; 1,900 (88%) completed the study, median follow-up 2.99 years.
cards.result: No intervention, alone or in combination, significantly improved any primary outcome. Differences in mean change in systolic blood pressure were −0.8 mm Hg (99% CI −2.1 to 0.5) for vitamin D versus no vitamin D and −0.8 mm Hg (99% CI −2.1 to 0.5) for omega-3s versus no omega-3s; the omega-3 diastolic difference was −0.5 mm Hg (99% CI −1.2 to 0.2). The infection incidence-rate difference for omega-3s was −0.13 (99% CI −0.23 to −0.03), rate ratio 0.89 (99% CI 0.78–1.01; p=0.02, against the prespecified p<0.01 threshold for six endpoints). No effects were found on SPPB physical performance, MoCA cognition, or nonvertebral fracture incidence. Deaths numbered 25, similar across groups.
cards.watchOut: The cohort was healthy, mobile and cognitively intact at entry — a ceiling effect is plausible, and the null does not answer what these interventions do in frail, deficient, or multimorbid older adults. The infection signal for omega-3s missed the trial's own multiplicity-adjusted threshold.
cards.source: Bischoff-Ferrari HA et al. Effect of Vitamin D Supplementation, Omega-3 Fatty Acid Supplementation, or a Strength-Training Exercise Program on Clinical Outcomes in Older Adults: The DO-HEALTH Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2020. PMID: 33170239. Registry ID: NCT01745263. cards.headline: Bischoff-Ferrari 2022 (DO-HEALTH falls analysis): omega-3s cut total falls by a relative 10% (rate ratio 0.90, CI touching 1.00); vitamin D and exercise did nothing
cards.summary: Bischoff-Ferrari 2022 (DO-HEALTH falls analysis): omega-3s cut total falls by a relative 10% (rate ratio 0.90, CI touching 1.00); vitamin D and exercise did nothing
cards.type: Randomised factorial trial — prespecified falls analysis (Bischoff-Ferrari 2022, DO-HEALTH)
cards.people: The same 2,157 community-dwelling DO-HEALTH participants (mean age 74.9 years, 61.7% women, 40.7% with serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D below 20 ng/mL, 83% at least moderately physically active), with falls recorded prospectively over a median 2.99 years; 3,333 falls occurred.
cards.result: Vitamin D and the simple home exercise programme had no benefit on total falls. Omega-3 supplementation versus no omega-3s reduced total falls by 10% in relative terms (incidence rate ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.81–1.00; p=0.04). No treatment interactions were found, so main effects are reported.
cards.watchOut: A secondary analysis of the same trial, not an independent replication: the confidence interval touches 1.00 and p=0.04 would not survive the parent trial's multiplicity discipline. It is a hypothesis about omega-3s and falls, not a demonstrated prevention strategy.
cards.source: Bischoff-Ferrari HA et al. Effects of vitamin D, omega-3 fatty acids, and a simple home strength exercise program on fall prevention: the DO-HEALTH randomized clinical trial. The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2022. PMID: 35136915. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large, well-run factorial trial, six null primary outcomes, and a single borderline secondary falls signal
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large, well-run factorial trial, six null primary outcomes, and a single borderline secondary falls signal
cards.people: One 2×2×2 factorial randomised trial (DO-HEALTH, 2,157 adults ≥70, five European countries, 3 years) and its prespecified falls analysis.
cards.result: Primary outcomes (blood pressure, SPPB, MoCA, nonvertebral fractures, infections): no significant benefit from vitamin D3 2000 IU/day, omega-3s 1 g/day, or strength-training exercise, alone or combined. Falls: omega-3 rate ratio 0.90 (95% CI 0.81–1.00) in relative terms; vitamin D and exercise null. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) for the combination as asked, in this healthy population.
cards.watchOut: A single trial carries this shelf, but it is large, double-blind for the supplements, and internally consistent across six endpoints; the stamp is a null, not a benefit claim, so Tier C is not set. Generalisability stops at healthy, active, largely vitamin-D-replete volunteers.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bischoff-Ferrari HA et al. JAMA. 2020 (PMID: 33170239); Bischoff-Ferrari HA et al. The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2022 (PMID: 35136915).
