shelves.title: Deprescribing in nursing homes reliably cuts inappropriate medicines — but the two meta-analyses split on whether falls, admissions or deaths follow
shelves.question: In nursing-home residents, do deprescribing interventions reduce falls, hospitalisations and mortality versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cause of Death · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Inappropriate Prescribing/prevention & control · Male · Middle Aged · Nursing Homes · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Polypharmacy · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the prescribing outcome moves, the clinical outcomes are contested. A 2019 meta-analysis of 41 randomised trials (18,408 residents) found deprescribing cut the number of residents with potentially inappropriate medications by a relative 59% (odds ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.19–0.89), and in its medication-review subgroup, mortality fell by a relative 26% (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65–0.84) and fallers by a relative 24% (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.62–0.93). A larger 2026 meta-analysis (38 studies, 22 of them RCTs) confirmed fewer drugs per patient (−0.89 within 12 months; −1.60 at ≥12 months) and fewer potentially inappropriate medications, but found no significant effect on falls, hospitalisations or mortality, with moderate-to-high risk of bias across most studies. PROPOSED SPLIT: deprescribing in nursing homes — benefit for prescribing appropriateness is consistent; benefit for falls, hospitalisation and mortality appears in one meta-analysis's subgroup and vanishes in the other's full pool.

cards.headline: Kua 2019: deprescribing cut inappropriate-medication exposure (OR 0.41); medication-review subgroup showed mortality OR 0.74 and fallers OR 0.76
cards.summary: Kua 2019: deprescribing cut inappropriate-medication exposure (OR 0.41); medication-review subgroup showed mortality OR 0.74 and fallers OR 0.76
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Kua 2019)
cards.people: 41 randomised trials totalling 18,408 nursing-home residents aged at least 60 years, testing deprescribing interventions (discontinuation, substitution or dose reduction) delivered by health-care professionals, searched to September 2017.
cards.result: Deprescribing significantly reduced the number of residents with potentially inappropriate medications (odds ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.19–0.89 — a relative reduction of 59%). In subgroup analysis, medication review-directed deprescribing reduced all-cause mortality (OR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65–0.84 — a relative reduction of 26%) and the number of fallers (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.62–0.93 — a relative reduction of 24%).
cards.watchOut: The mortality and falls benefits live in a subgroup (medication-review-directed trials), not in the whole pool — subgroup findings in meta-analyses are hypothesis-grade, and the abstract reports no pooled falls or hospitalisation effect across all intervention types.
cards.source: Kua CH et al. Health Outcomes of Deprescribing Interventions Among Older Residents in Nursing Homes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Journal of the American Medical Directors Association. 2019. PMID: 30581126. cards.headline: Carollo 2026: fewer drugs (−0.89 to −1.60 per patient) and fewer inappropriate medicines — but no significant effect on falls, hospitalisations or mortality
cards.summary: Carollo 2026: fewer drugs (−0.89 to −1.60 per patient) and fewer inappropriate medicines — but no significant effect on falls, hospitalisations or mortality
cards.people: 38 experimental studies (22 RCTs, 16 quasi-experimental) of medication review and deprescribing in older long-term-care residents with polypharmacy, searched to 27 August 2024.
cards.result: Interventions reduced the number of drugs per patient (mean difference −0.89, 95% CI −1.46 to −0.32 within 12 months; −1.60, 95% CI −2.68 to −0.52 at ≥12 months) and potentially inappropriate medications (−0.48 at 6 months; −0.26 at ≥12 months). No significant effects were observed on falls, hospitalisations or mortality. Risk of bias was moderate in 23 studies, high in 14, and low in only 1.
cards.watchOut: Mixing quasi-experimental studies with RCTs and wide heterogeneity cuts both ways: it may dilute a real medication-review effect, or it may be the more honest pool. Either way it directly contradicts the earlier subgroup claim at full-pool level.
cards.source: Carollo M et al. Evaluating the impact of medication review and deprescribing on prescribing appropriateness and clinical outcomes in older people residing in long-term care facilities: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Age and Ageing. 2026. PMID: 41967033. cards.headline: Synthesis: both meta-analyses agree the medicine list shrinks; they disagree on whether residents live longer or fall less
cards.summary: Synthesis: both meta-analyses agree the medicine list shrinks; they disagree on whether residents live longer or fall less
cards.people: Two systematic reviews and meta-analyses of deprescribing and medication-review interventions in nursing-home and long-term-care residents (41 RCTs, 18,408 residents in 2019; 38 studies in 2026).
cards.result: Prescribing: potentially inappropriate medications OR 0.41 (2019) and −0.26 to −0.48 fewer per patient (2026); drugs per patient down 0.89–1.60 (2026). Clinical outcomes: mortality OR 0.74 and fallers OR 0.76 in the 2019 medication-review subgroup; no significant falls, hospitalisation or mortality effect in the 2026 full pool. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C set because a mortality claim is in play and the two syntheses conflict.
cards.watchOut: Nursing-home deprescribing is worth doing for prescribing quality alone; selling it to families as a falls- or life-prolonging intervention goes beyond what the pooled evidence currently supports.
cards.source: Synthesis of Kua CH et al. Journal of the American Medical Directors Association. 2019 (PMID: 30581126); Carollo M et al. Age and Ageing. 2026 (PMID: 41967033).

shelves.title: Adding CBT-I to a supervised hypnotic taper roughly doubles benzodiazepine-free rates in older adults — 85% versus 48%, and 70% versus 24% at one year in the second trial
shelves.question: In older adults with insomnia who take hypnotics, does CBT-I delivered alongside a supervised taper get patients off sleeping tablets and sleeping better versus taper alone?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Anxiety Agents/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Benzodiazepines/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Chronic Disease · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Polysomnography · Prospective Studies · Severity of Illness Index · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders/diagnosis/drug therapy/therapy · Substance Withdrawal Syndrome/etiology/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — two small randomised trials from the same research tradition agree that adding cognitive behaviour therapy for insomnia to a supervised benzodiazepine taper gets far more older adults off the drug than tapering alone. In Morin 2004, 85% of the combined-treatment group were benzodiazepine-free after the 10-week intervention versus 48% with taper alone (54% with CBT-I alone), with gains maintained at 12 months. In Baillargeon 2003, complete withdrawal immediately after treatment was 77% (26/34) on combined treatment versus 38% (11/29) on taper alone (odds ratio 5.3, 95% CI 1.8–16.2), and at 12 months 70% (23/33) versus 24% (7/29) (OR 7.2, 95% CI 2.4–23.7). Sleep improvements in the CBT groups were largely subjective at first and became more noticeable over the following months; no significant withdrawal symptoms or adverse events were associated with tapering in Morin. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): CBT-I alongside a supervised taper approximately doubles durable benzodiazepine discontinuation in older adults with chronic insomnia.

cards.headline: Morin 2004: taper plus CBT left 85% benzodiazepine-free versus 48% for taper alone — maintained at 12 months
cards.summary: Morin 2004: taper plus CBT left 85% benzodiazepine-free versus 48% for taper alone — maintained at 12 months
cards.people: 76 older adult outpatients (mean age 62.5 years) with chronic insomnia and prolonged benzodiazepine use for sleep (mean duration 19.3 years), randomised to a 10-week supervised benzodiazepine withdrawal programme (n=25), CBT-I (n=24), or supervised withdrawal plus CBT-I (n=27), with follow-up at 3 and 12 months.
cards.result: All three interventions cut benzodiazepine quantity by 90% and frequency by 80%, and 63% of patients were drug-free within an average of 7 weeks. After the initial intervention, 85% of the combined group were benzodiazepine-free versus 48% for taper alone and 54% for CBT-I alone. CBT groups perceived greater subjective sleep improvement than taper alone; polysomnography showed more stage 3–4 and REM sleep across all groups. Reductions were maintained to 12 months, and no significant withdrawal symptoms or adverse events accompanied tapering.
cards.watchOut: Small, single-centre, and two decades old; participants were volunteers with a mean age of 62.5 — younger than the frailest hypnotic users — and CBT-I cannot be blinded, so subjective sleep outcomes carry expectation effects.
cards.source: Morin CM et al. Randomized clinical trial of supervised tapering and cognitive behavior therapy to facilitate benzodiazepine discontinuation in older adults with chronic insomnia. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2004. PMID: 14754783. cards.headline: Baillargeon 2003: combined CBT plus taper achieved complete withdrawal in 77% versus 38% post-treatment and 70% versus 24% at 12 months
cards.summary: Baillargeon 2003: combined CBT plus taper achieved complete withdrawal in 77% versus 38% post-treatment and 70% versus 24% at 12 months
cards.people: 65 older adults (mean age 67.4 years) with chronic insomnia who had taken a benzodiazepine every night for more than 3 months, randomised to CBT plus gradual tapering (n=35; 8 weekly small-group CBT sessions with a psychologist, weekly physician-supervised taper over 8 weeks) or gradual tapering only (n=30). Discontinuation was confirmed by blood screening.
cards.result: Immediately after treatment, complete benzodiazepine withdrawal was achieved by 77% (26/34) of the combined group versus 38% (11/29) of the taper-only group (odds ratio 5.3, 95% CI 1.8–16.2; adjusted OR 7.9, 95% CI 2.4–30.9). At 12 months the advantage persisted: 70% (23/33) versus 24% (7/29) (OR 7.2, 95% CI 2.4–23.7; adjusted OR 7.6, 95% CI 2.5–26.6), with similar results at 3 months.
cards.watchOut: Also small (65 randomised, with attrition by follow-up) and from the same Canadian research milieu as Morin 2004, so the two trials are concordant but not fully independent replication; media-recruited volunteers may be more motivated than clinic populations.
cards.source: Baillargeon L et al. Discontinuation of benzodiazepines among older insomniac adults treated with cognitive-behavioural therapy combined with gradual tapering: a randomized trial. CMAJ. 2003. PMID: 14609970. cards.headline: Synthesis: taper alone works for a minority; adding CBT-I roughly doubles success and the effect lasts a year
cards.summary: Synthesis: taper alone works for a minority; adding CBT-I roughly doubles success and the effect lasts a year
cards.people: Two randomised trials (76 and 65 older adults with chronic insomnia and long-term nightly benzodiazepine use) comparing supervised taper alone with taper plus CBT-I, each with 12-month follow-up.
cards.result: Benzodiazepine-free rates: 85% versus 48% post-treatment (Morin 2004) and 77% versus 38% post-treatment, 70% versus 24% at 12 months (Baillargeon 2003, OR 7.2). No significant withdrawal harms from tapering were reported. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the direction and size are consistent across both trials; the stamp stops at POSSIBLE because both trials are small and share one research tradition.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial answers whether group CBT-I delivered at scale in routine primary care reproduces these rates, and neither enrolled the cognitively impaired long-term users in whom discontinuation is hardest.
cards.source: Synthesis of Morin CM et al. The American Journal of Psychiatry. 2004 (PMID: 14754783); Baillargeon L et al. CMAJ. 2003 (PMID: 14609970).

shelves.title: Urinary incontinence in women over 60: across 43 trials, pelvic-floor-based physical therapies top the network for cure — on low- to very-low-certainty evidence
shelves.question: In older women with urinary incontinence, how do conservative, drug and combined interventions compare across the network of randomised trials?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Urinary Incontinence/therapy · Aged · Middle Aged · Bias · Quality of Life · Exercise Therapy · Urinary Incontinence, Stress/therapy · Conservative Treatment/adverse effects
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the 2025 Cochrane network meta-analysis of 43 randomised trials (8,506 women aged 60 and over) found every treatment category might beat its control, with physical therapies — mainly pelvic floor muscle training, with or without complementary therapies or education — performing best for 'cure': physical therapies combined with complementary therapies OR 17.79 (95% CI 2.97–106.46; 1 study, 71 participants), physical therapies alone OR 7.20 (95% CI 2.59–20.03; 4 studies, 310 participants), and physical therapies with education OR 3.25 (95% CI 1.19–8.84; 4 studies, 364 participants). For 'cure or improvement', physical therapies (OR 3.98, 95% CI 2.02–7.82) and physical therapies with education (OR 3.20, 95% CI 1.45–7.02) again led, ahead of β3-adrenergic agonists (OR 2.44, 95% CI 1.28–4.62) and antimuscarinics (OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.19–3.03). But the reviewers rated the evidence low to very low certainty, with sparse data and wide intervals — the ranking is a signal, not a verdict. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): pelvic-floor-based therapy ranks first for cure in older women, on evidence too imprecise to rank the rest with confidence.

cards.headline: Vesentini 2025 (Cochrane NMA): physical therapies best for cure (OR 7.20) and cure-or-improvement (OR 3.98) — certainty low to very low throughout
cards.summary: Vesentini 2025 (Cochrane NMA): physical therapies best for cure (OR 7.20) and cure-or-improvement (OR 3.98) — certainty low to very low throughout
cards.type: Network meta-analysis of randomised trials (Vesentini 2025, Cochrane)
cards.people: 43 RCTs involving 8,506 women aged 60 years and over with urinary incontinence (mean 198 participants per study, range 14–1,438); conservative treatments in 20 trials, pharmacological in 17, surgical in 4, mixed in 2. Searched to 23 March 2025.
cards.result: For 'cure' (conservative and pharmacological network): physical therapies with complementary therapies OR 17.79 (95% CI 2.97–106.46; 1 study, 71 participants); physical therapies OR 7.20 (95% CI 2.59–20.03; 4 studies, 310 participants); physical therapies with education OR 3.25 (95% CI 1.19–8.84; 4 studies, 364 participants) versus control. For 'cure or improvement': physical therapies OR 3.98 (95% CI 2.02–7.82; 3 studies, 197 participants), physical therapies with education OR 3.20 (95% CI 1.45–7.02), β3-adrenergic agonists OR 2.44 (95% CI 1.28–4.62; 1 study, 360 participants), education OR 2.09 (95% CI 1.05–4.17), antimuscarinics OR 1.90 (95% CI 1.19–3.03; 2 studies, 1,469 participants).
cards.watchOut: Certainty was low to very low for essentially every comparison: trials often had 'some concerns' or high risk of bias, networks were sparse (the top-ranked cure estimate rests on one 71-woman study with a confidence interval spanning 2.97 to 106.46), and three studies had to be excluded to connect the networks. Rankings from such networks are fragile.
cards.source: Vesentini G et al. Interventions for treating urinary incontinence in older women: a network meta-analysis. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2025. PMID: 41307301. network meta-analysis of randomised trials (vesentini 2025, cochrane) 43 rcts involving 8,506 women aged 60 years and over with urinary incontinence (mean 198 participants per study, range 14–1,438); conservative treatments in 20 trials, pharmacological in 17, surgical in 4, mixed in 2. searched to 23 march 2025. for 'cure' (conservative and pharmacological network): physical therapies with complementary therapies or 17.79 (95% ci 2.97–106.46; 1 study, 71 participants); physical therapies or 7.20 (95% ci 2.59–20.03; 4 studies, 310 participants); physical therapies with education or 3.25 (95% ci 1.19–8.84; 4 studies, 364 participants) versus control. for 'cure or improvement': physical therapies or 3.98 (95% ci 2.02–7.82; 3 studies, 197 participants), physical therapies with education or 3.20 (95% ci 1.45–7.02), β3-adrenergic agonists or 2.44 (95% ci 1.28–4.62; 1 study, 360 participants), education or 2.09 (95% ci 1.05–4.17), antimuscarinics or 1.90 (95% ci 1.19–3.03; 2 studies, 1,469 participants). certainty was low to very low for essentially every comparison: trials often had 'some concerns' or high risk of bias, networks were sparse (the top-ranked cure estimate rests on one 71-woman study with a confidence interval spanning 2.97 to 106.46), and three studies had to be excluded to connect the networks. rankings from such networks are fragile. vesentini g et al. interventions for treating urinary incontinence in older women: a network meta-analysis. the cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2025. pmid: 41307301. mesh: humans · female · randomized controlled trials as topic · urinary incontinence/therapy · aged · middle aged · bias · quality of life · exercise therapy · urinary incontinence, stress/therapy · conservative treatment/adverse effects

shelves.title: Preventing falls in hospital: tailored education and service-model change probably cut fall rates; exercise and medication optimisation alone remain unproven
shelves.question: In hospitalised older people, do falls-prevention interventions — exercise, medication review, environmental and multifactorial programmes — reduce falls and fall injuries versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Accidental Falls/prevention & control/statistics & numerical data · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Aged · Hospitals/statistics & numerical data · Bias · Aged, 80 and over · Fractures, Bone/epidemiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — what works in hospital depends on the intervention class. The 2026 Cochrane review (55 trials, 104,474 participants, mean age 79) found tailored education (patient, staff or multicomponent) probably reduces the rate of falls (rate ratio 0.73, 95% CI 0.56–0.94; 3 trials, 4,868 participants; moderate-certainty) and the risk of falling (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.40–0.92). Service model change in acute settings probably reduces the fall rate (RaR 0.45, 95% CI 0.27–0.74; 6 trials, 10,825 participants; moderate-certainty). Multifactorial interventions probably reduce the fall rate (RaR 0.87, 95% CI 0.69–1.08; 5 trials, 42,256 participants) and risk of falling (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.63–1.07), but both intervals include no effect. Exercise was uncertain (rate RaR 0.62, 95% CI 0.28–1.36; risk RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.36–1.46), and medication optimisation as a single intervention was likewise uncertain (rate RaR 1.71, 95% CI 0.95–3.07). Pooled across everything, any intervention gave RaR 0.85 (95% CI 0.71–1.02) at very low certainty. Fracture outcomes were poorly reported. PROPOSED SPLIT: education and organisational change carry the hospital falls evidence; exercise and medication review alone do not, yet.

cards.headline: McLennan 2026 (Cochrane): 55 trials, 104,474 patients — education RaR 0.73 and service-model change RaR 0.45 lead; exercise and medication optimisation uncertain
cards.summary: McLennan 2026 (Cochrane): 55 trials, 104,474 patients — education RaR 0.73 and service-model change RaR 0.45 lead; exercise and medication optimisation uncertain
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (McLennan 2026, Cochrane)
cards.people: 55 randomised trials (104,474 participants, mean age 79 years, 45% women) of falls-prevention interventions in hospitals including inpatient rehabilitation, in people aged 65 and over; 32 trials were new in this 2026 update. Most trials were at high risk of bias in at least one domain, mainly lack of blinding.
cards.result: Tailored education probably reduces the rate of falls (RaR 0.73, 95% CI 0.56–0.94; 3 trials, 4,868 participants; moderate-certainty) and risk of falling (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.40–0.92; 5 trials, 5,035 participants). Service model change in acute settings probably reduces fall rate (RaR 0.45, 95% CI 0.27–0.74; 6 trials, 10,825 participants; moderate-certainty) but its effect on risk of falling is uncertain (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.25–3.46). Multifactorial interventions: RaR 0.87 (95% CI 0.69–1.08; 5 trials, 42,256 participants) and RR 0.82 (95% CI 0.63–1.07), moderate-certainty but compatible with no effect. Exercise: rate RaR 0.62 (95% CI 0.28–1.36; very low-certainty), risk RR 0.73 (95% CI 0.36–1.46). Medication optimisation alone: rate RaR 1.71 (95% CI 0.95–3.07; very low-certainty), risk RR 0.94 (95% CI 0.46–1.90). Any intervention pooled: RaR 0.85 (95% CI 0.71–1.02; 27 trials, 72,016 participants; very low-certainty); risk of falling RR 0.83 (95% CI 0.73–0.94; low-certainty). Interventions integrating with the local setting and engaging patients/family may reduce fall rates (RaR 0.68, 95% CI 0.55–0.84).
cards.watchOut: Fracture and economic outcomes were generally poorly reported and very low certainty where reported — the review shows fewer falls, not demonstrably fewer broken bones. One education component (individualised patient education) is also the subject of its own live shelf; this shelf is the whole-hospital comparison, not a re-card of that intervention.
cards.source: McLennan C et al. Interventions for preventing falls in older people in hospitals. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2026. PMID: 42084046. cards.headline: Synthesis: organisational and educational interventions carry the signal; the classic single interventions do not
cards.summary: Synthesis: organisational and educational interventions carry the signal; the classic single interventions do not
cards.people: One Cochrane systematic review of 55 hospital RCTs (104,474 older inpatients) covering exercise, medication optimisation, education, service-model change and multifactorial programmes.
cards.result: Fall rate ratios: education 0.73 (moderate certainty), service model change 0.45 in acute settings (moderate certainty), multifactorial 0.87 (interval includes 1.0), exercise 0.62 (very low certainty, interval 0.28–1.36), medication optimisation 1.71 (very low certainty). shelves.title: HMB during 10 days of bed rest in older adults: lean body mass preserved (−0.17 kg versus −2.05 kg on placebo) in one 19-evaluable-person trial — function unmoved and a larger trial still needed
shelves.question: In older adults confined to bed rest, does HMB preserve lean body mass versus control over 10 days of bed rest?
shelves.mesh: Absorptiometry, Photon · Aged · Aging* · Bed Rest/adverse effects* · Body Composition · Dietary Supplements/adverse effects* · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle Development* · Muscle Proteins/biosynthesis/metabolism · Muscle Strength · Muscle, Skeletal/diagnostic imaging/growth & development/metabolism* · Musculoskeletal Physiological Phenomena · Resistance Training · Sarcopenia/etiology/metabolism/prevention & control/rehabilitation* · Valerates/adverse effects/therapeutic use* · Whole Body Imaging
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for lean body mass over 10 days of bed rest only, on one very small trial. Deutz 2013 randomised 24 healthy older adults (SPPB ≥9; 20 women, 4 men) to calcium HMB 1.5 g twice daily (3 g/day) or inactive placebo powder, starting 5 days before 10 days of complete bed rest and continuing through 8 weeks of resistance-training rehabilitation; 19 were evaluable at the end of bed rest (11 HMB, 8 control). Bed rest caused a significant decrease in total lean body mass in the control group (−2.05 ± 0.66 kg; P=0.02), while HMB treatment prevented the decline (−0.17 ± 0.19 kg change; P=0.23 within group), with a statistically significant between-group difference in lean-mass change over bed rest (P=0.02); the female sub-analysis also favoured HMB (P=0.04). Differences in functional parameters could not be observed, which the authors attribute to sample size, and the authors conclude that HMB supplementation preserves muscle mass during 10 days of bed rest in healthy older adults and that these results need to be confirmed in a larger trial. The fetched record describes the intervention only as calcium HMB (the calcium salt) and names no branded HMB product or company, so no commercial product is named on this shelf and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in one small double-blind trial, HMB preserved lean body mass over 10 days of bed rest in healthy older adults, without a demonstrated functional benefit.

cards.headline: Deutz 2013: lean-mass change over 10 days of bed rest −0.17 kg on HMB versus −2.05 kg on placebo (between-group P=0.02) in 19 evaluable older adults — functional parameters not different
cards.summary: Deutz 2013: lean-mass change over 10 days of bed rest −0.17 kg on HMB versus −2.05 kg on placebo (between-group P=0.02) in 19 evaluable older adults — functional parameters not different
cards.people: 24 healthy older adult subjects (SPPB ≥9; 20 women, 4 men) in a randomised, controlled, double-blinded, parallel-group study, confined to complete bed rest for ten days, followed by resistance training rehabilitation for eight weeks. Subjects in the experimental group were treated with HMB (calcium salt, 1.5 g twice daily — total 3 g/day); control subjects were treated with an inactive placebo powder. Treatments were provided starting 5 days prior to bed rest till the end of the rehabilitation phase, and DXA was used to measure body composition. Nineteen eligible older adults (BMI 21–33; age 60–76 years) were evaluable at the end of the bed rest period (Control n=8; Ca-HMB n=11). The record names no branded HMB product or company.
cards.result: Bed rest caused a significant decrease in total lean body mass (LBM) in the control group (−2.05 ± 0.66 kg; P=0.02, paired t-test). With the exclusion of one subject, treatment with HMB prevented the decline in LBM over bed rest (−0.17 ± 0.19 kg; P=0.23, paired t-test). There was a statistically significant difference between treatment groups for change in LBM over bed rest (P=0.02, ANOVA). Sub-analysis on female subjects (Control=7, HMB=8) also revealed a significant difference in change in LBM over bed rest between treatment groups (P=0.04, ANOVA). However, differences in function parameters could not be observed, probably due to the sample size of the study. The authors concluded that in healthy older adults, HMB supplementation preserves muscle mass during 10 days of bed rest, and that these results need to be confirmed in a larger trial.
cards.watchOut: A single very small trial: 24 randomised and only 19 evaluable at the end of bed rest, in healthy volunteers (SPPB ≥9) under experimental bed rest — a model of catabolic stress, not hospitalised or sarcopenic patients confined to bed by illness. The headline HMB figure rests on the exclusion of one subject, lean body mass by DXA is a surrogate, and no functional benefit was detected at this sample size. The fetched record describes the intervention only as calcium HMB (the calcium salt) and names no branded product or company, so no commercial product is named on this shelf, and current products may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Deutz NE et al. Effect of β-hydroxy-β-methylbutyrate (HMB) on lean body mass during 10 days of bed rest in older adults. Clinical nutrition (Edinburgh, Scotland). 2013. PMID: 23514626. Registry ID: NCT00945581. cards.summary: Synthesis: one small double-blind trial — lean mass preserved over 10 days of bed rest, function not shown — with the re-card declared on the face of the shelf
cards.people: One randomised, controlled, double-blind, parallel-group trial of 24 healthy older adults (19 evaluable at the end of bed rest: 11 HMB, 8 control), testing calcium HMB 1.5 g twice daily (3 g/day) against inactive placebo powder during 10 days of complete bed rest, with treatment starting 5 days before bed rest and continuing through 8 weeks of resistance-training rehabilitation.
cards.result: Total lean body mass change over bed rest: −0.17 ± 0.19 kg on HMB (with the exclusion of one subject; P=0.23 within group) versus −2.05 ± 0.66 kg on placebo (P=0.02 within group), with a statistically significant between-group difference (P=0.02); female sub-analysis P=0.04. Differences in functional parameters could not be observed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Re-card declaration: Deutz NE et al. 2013 (PMID: 23514626) is also carded as a supporting card in programme pack #3824, which asks whether HMB improves muscle mass and function in older adults with sarcopenia, where the bed-rest trial serves as mechanistic support inside that sarcopenia-treatment question. This shelf asks Deutz's exact home question — in older adults confined to bed rest, does HMB preserve lean body mass versus control over 10 days of bed rest — a genuinely different question, built under the #3104 (RACING) / #3325 (STRENGTH) / #3489 (CAROLINA) / #3597 (PROPATRIA) / #3628 / #3753 / #3812 precedent, applied within the programme: a study carded elsewhere as a supporting card may anchor a new shelf when the new question is genuinely different. Pack #3824 keeps its supporting card; both packs are held for the developer's verdicts. Tier C is set because a single small trial carries the shelf. No second supporting study was carded: Deutz 2013 is the trial that asks this exact bed-rest question, and no other study was added speculatively.

shelves.title: MID-FRAIL: a multicomponent programme improved physical performance by 0.85 SPPB points in frail older people with diabetes — and the gains outlasted the training blocks
shelves.question: In frail older adults with type 2 diabetes, does a multicomponent intervention — exercise, nutrition, and education — improve physical function versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Combined Modality Therapy · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2/therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Quality of Life/psychology · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the MID-FRAIL cluster-randomised trial (964 frail and pre-frail adults over 70 with type 2 diabetes, 74 sites in seven European countries) combined a 16-week individualised progressive resistance-exercise programme, a seven-session diabetes and nutrition education programme, and optimised care against usual care. At 12 months the intervention group's Short Physical Performance Battery scores were a mean 0.85 points higher than usual care (95% CI 0.44 to 1.26; p<0.0001) — a clinically relevant margin on a 12-point scale — with an estimated saving of €428.02 per patient per year; no other secondary outcome differed significantly. The trial's two-year follow-up found each 16-week intervention block raised SPPB performance by a mean 36.1% at week 18 and 10.2% at week 68, with values still above baseline at 2 years. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a structured exercise-plus-education programme improves physical function in frail older people with diabetes, at no net cost in the trial's economic analysis.

cards.headline: Rodríguez-Mañas 2019 (MID-FRAIL): SPPB 0.85 points higher than usual care at 12 months (95% CI 0.44–1.26), with €428 saved per patient-year
cards.summary: Rodríguez-Mañas 2019 (MID-FRAIL): SPPB 0.85 points higher than usual care at 12 months (95% CI 0.44–1.26), with €428 saved per patient-year
cards.people: 964 participants aged over 70 (intervention mean age 78.4 years, 49.2% men; usual care 77.6 years, 52.4% men) with type 2 diabetes, frail or pre-frail by Fried's phenotype, at 74 sites in seven European countries. Intervention: individualised progressive resistance exercise for 16 weeks, a structured diabetes and nutritional education programme over seven sessions, and optimised follow-up; comparator was usual care.
cards.result: After 12 months, intervention participants had mean SPPB scores 0.85 points higher than usual care (95% CI 0.44 to 1.26; p<0.0001). Dropouts were higher among frail participants and in the intervention group, but the SPPB difference remained significant in sensitivity analyses. The intervention was associated with an estimated mean saving of €428.02 (2016) per patient per year, and the cost-effectiveness analysis favoured the intervention. No statistically significant differences were detected in any other secondary outcome.
cards.watchOut: Cluster-randomised and unblinded, with differential dropout (more in the intervention arm) — sensitivity analyses held, but performance outcomes in unblinded exercise trials are vulnerable to effort and expectation effects. One trial programme carries the shelf, so Tier C is set.
cards.source: Rodríguez-Mañas L et al. Effectiveness of a multimodal intervention in functionally impaired older people with type 2 diabetes mellitus. cards.headline: Izquierdo 2021 (MID-FRAIL 2-year follow-up): SPPB up a mean 36.1% after the first training block; values remained above baseline at 2 years
cards.summary: Izquierdo 2021 (MID-FRAIL 2-year follow-up): SPPB up a mean 36.1% after the first training block; values remained above baseline at 2 years
cards.type: Two-year follow-up of a randomised intervention cohort (Izquierdo 2021, MID-FRAIL)
cards.people: Frail older patients with type 2 diabetes from the MID-FRAIL programme followed for 2 years, receiving repeated 16-week blocks of resistance training combined with a nutritional programme, with SPPB and maximal power output measured serially.
cards.result: Each 16-week intervention set produced significant SPPB improvements: a mean 36.1% at week 18 (p<0.001) and 10.2% at week 68 (p<0.05). Maximal power output at 30% and 80% of one-repetition maximum improved by 45.2% to 57.2% at week 18 (p<0.01–0.001); no significant changes followed the second intervention period. After 2 years, SPPB and maximal power values remained significantly higher than baseline.
cards.watchOut: A follow-up report of the intervention experience rather than a fresh randomised comparison — the control contrast fades over 2 years, and percentage gains on SPPB are relative to a low frail baseline, so absolute function remained limited.
cards.source: Izquierdo M et al. Two-Year Follow-up of a Multimodal Intervention on Functional Capacity and Muscle Power in Frail Patients With Type 2 Diabetes. shelves.title: CHIPPS: a weekly pharmacist-prescriber service in care homes did not reduce falls (rate ratio 0.91, CI 0.66–1.26) — it did reduce drug burden, safely
shelves.question: In care-home residents, does a pharmacist-led structured medication review reduce falls and hospital admissions versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Aged, 80 and over · Male · Pharmacists · Quality of Life · Northern Ireland · Scotland · Pharmaceutical Services
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — CHIPPS randomised 49 triads (pharmacist independent prescriber, GP practice, care homes) covering 882 residents aged 65 and over across England, Scotland and Northern Ireland to a weekly pharmacist-prescriber service for six months or usual care. The primary outcome did not move: 697 falls (1.55 per resident) in the intervention group versus 538 falls (1.26 per resident) in controls, an adjusted fall rate ratio of 0.91 (95% CI 0.66–1.26). Secondary outcomes — quality of life, Barthel score, hospital admissions and mortality — were not significantly different, except the Drug Burden Index, which significantly favoured the intervention. A third of the pharmacists' 566 interventions (185; 32.7%) involved medicines associated with falls, and no adverse events or safety concerns were identified. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): intensive pharmacist prescribing in care homes is safe and lightens drug burden, but six months of it did not reduce falls or admissions.

cards.headline: Holland 2023 (CHIPPS): fall rate ratio 0.91 (95% CI 0.66–1.26); admissions and mortality unchanged; Drug Burden Index improved
cards.summary: Holland 2023 (CHIPPS): fall rate ratio 0.91 (95% CI 0.66–1.26); admissions and mortality unchanged; Drug Burden Index improved
cards.people: 49 triads and 882 care-home residents (mean age 85 years, 70% women, all aged ≥65 and taking at least one prescribed drug) across England, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Intervention: a pharmacist independent prescriber providing pharmaceutical care to about 20 residents per triad with weekly visits over six months — care plans, medicines review and reconciliation, staff training, deprescribing and prescription authorisation — versus usual GP-led care.
cards.result: At six months, 697 falls (1.55 per resident) were recorded in the intervention group and 538 falls (1.26 per resident) in the control group; the adjusted fall rate risk ratio was 0.91 (95% CI 0.66 to 1.26), not significant. Secondary outcomes (EQ-5D quality of life by proxy, Barthel score, hospital admissions, mortality) were not significantly different, except the Drug Burden Index, which significantly favoured the intervention. Of 566 pharmacist interventions, 185 (32.7%) involved medicines associated with falls. No adverse events or safety concerns were identified.
cards.watchOut: Six months may be too short for deprescribing to convert into fewer falls, and only a third of interventions touched falls-risk medicines at all — the trial tests this service model at this intensity, not pharmacist review in the abstract. Open-label cluster design.
cards.source: Holland R et al. Evaluation of effectiveness and safety of pharmacist independent prescribers in care homes: cluster randomised controlled trial. BMJ. 2023. PMID: 36787910. cards.headline: Synthesis: a large, honest null on falls — with a real prescribing-quality gain and a clean safety record
cards.summary: Synthesis: a large, honest null on falls — with a real prescribing-quality gain and a clean safety record
cards.people: One cluster-RCT of pharmacist independent prescribing in care homes (882 residents, 49 triads, six months).
cards.result: Falls: rate ratio 0.91 (95% CI 0.66–1.26). Hospital admissions and mortality: not significantly different. Drug Burden Index: significantly reduced. Safety: no concerns identified. shelves.title: Geriatric emergency-department interventions: reviews call the evidence weak and inconsistent, while one large nurse-led programme raised discharges (hazard ratio 1.19) without more deaths or returns
shelves.question: In older adults presenting to the emergency department, does a geriatric emergency department intervention — geriatric assessment with dedicated staff and transitional care — reduce hospital admission and return visits versus standard emergency care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Emergency Service, Hospital · Humans
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the evidence is suggestive and structurally weak. A 2021 review of reviews found 15 review articles covering 83 primary studies of ED interventions for older people, with 26 different outcomes reported inconsistently; no individual intervention stood out, though interventions begun in the ED and continued into other settings tended to produce more favourable patient and service outcomes. The largest single evaluation, the nurse-led, physician-championed Geriatric Emergency Department Intervention (GEDI) in Queensland (44,983 presentations by people over 70), found patients seen when the GEDI team was working were more likely to be discharged (hazard ratio 1.19, 95% CI 1.13–1.24) with shorter ED stays (HR 1.42, 95% CI 1.33–1.52), no increase in mortality (HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.23–4.43) and no significant increase in same-cause re-presentation within 28 days (HR 1.21, 95% CI 0.99–1.49), saving an average $35 per presentation and $1,469 per admission. But GEDI was a pre-post pragmatic evaluation, not a randomised trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): geriatric ED teams probably help some older patients go home sooner; randomised proof that they cut admissions or return visits is still missing.

cards.headline: Preston 2021: 15 reviews, 83 primary studies, 26 outcomes — no single ED intervention for older people stands out as proven
cards.summary: Preston 2021: 15 reviews, 83 primary studies, 26 outcomes — no single ED intervention for older people stands out as proven
cards.people: 15 review articles (13 systematic reviews, four with meta-analysis) describing 83 primary studies of interventions for older people initiated or wholly delivered in the emergency department; follow-up durations and outcome choices varied widely within and across reviews.
cards.result: Based on how review authors reported results, evidence clustered into staff-focused, discharge-intervention, population-focused and intervention-component reviews. No individual intervention was found more promising than others, but interventions initiated in the ED and continued into other settings tended to result in more favourable patient and health-service outcomes. Outcomes measured were largely service-focused despite many interventions being holistic and patient-focused.
cards.watchOut: A review of reviews inherits every weakness of its layers: inconsistent reporting and differing emphases by review authors mean the absence of a standout intervention is partly an artefact of how the literature reports itself.
cards.source: Preston L et al. Improving outcomes for older people in the emergency department: a review of reviews. Emergency Medicine Journal. 2021. PMID: 33106287. MeSH: Aged · Emergency Service, Hospital · Humans

cards.headline: Wallis 2018 (GEDI): discharge hazard ratio 1.19 and ED stay hazard ratio 1.42 when the geriatric team was working; mortality and 28-day re-presentation not increased
cards.summary: Wallis 2018 (GEDI): discharge hazard ratio 1.19 and ED stay hazard ratio 1.42 when the geriatric team was working; mortality and 28-day re-presentation not increased
cards.people: All 44,983 presentations by patients aged over 70 to a 385-bed tertiary hospital ED in Queensland, Australia (about 53,000 presentations a year, 20% aged ≥70), comparing periods before, during development of, and after full implementation of the Geriatric Emergency Department Intervention — nurse-led (2.4 full-time-equivalent gerontology nurses, 7 days a week), physician-championed targeted geriatric assessment and care streamlining.
cards.result: Presentations made while the GEDI team was working had an increased likelihood of discharge (hazard ratio 1.19, 95% CI 1.13–1.24) and reduced ED length of stay (HR 1.42, 95% CI 1.33–1.52) versus presentations when the team was not working. There was no increase in in-hospital mortality within 28 days (HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.23–4.43) or same-cause re-presentation to 28 days (HR 1.21, 95% CI 0.99–1.49). Average savings were $35 (95% CI $21–$49) per ED presentation and $1,469 (95% CI $1,105–$1,834) per hospital admission.
cards.watchOut: Pre-post design in a single health service: secular trends, case-mix drift and the team's own learning curve can all masquerade as intervention effect, and the re-presentation interval (HR 1.21) is compatible with a modest increase in returns. Not randomised.
cards.source: Wallis M et al. The Geriatric Emergency Department Intervention model of care: a pragmatic trial. BMC Geriatrics. 2018. PMID: 30509204. Registry ID: ACTRN12615001157561. cards.summary: Synthesis: direction favourable, design weak — discharge more, stay shorter, no safety signal, no randomised confirmation

shelves.title: Preventing depression and anxiety in older people who already have symptoms: stepped care halved new disorders at 12 months (12% vs 24%) in 75-year-olds; problem-solving therapy halved incidence at 2 months in macular degeneration, fading by 6
shelves.question: In older adults with subthreshold depression or anxiety (symptoms but no disorder), do preventive psychological programmes — stepped care or problem-solving therapy — prevent onset of major depression and anxiety disorders?
shelves.mesh: Adaptation, Psychological · Age Factors · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anxiety Disorders/diagnosis/epidemiology/prevention & control · Cognition Disorders/diagnosis/epidemiology · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy/methods · Major Depressive Disorder/diagnosis/epidemiology/prevention & control · Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders · Female · Humans · Male · Neuropsychological Tests · Primary Health Care/statistics & numerical data · Referral and Consultation/statistics & numerical data · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — prevention aimed at people already symptomatic ('indicated' prevention), tested in two randomised trials with the same direction and the same caveat about durability. In 33 Dutch primary care practices, van't Veer-Tazelaar PJ et al. (PMID: 19255379) randomised 170 people aged 75 and older with subthreshold depression or anxiety to a stepped-care programme (watchful waiting, then bibliotherapy, then problem-solving treatment, then medication referral if needed) or usual care: the 12-month cumulative incidence of major depression or anxiety disorder was 0.12 (10/86) versus 0.24 (20/84) — relative risk 0.49 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.98). In age-related macular degeneration, Rovner BW et al. (PMID: 18515689) found problem-solving therapy halved 2-month incidence of depressive disorders (11.6% vs 23.2%; OR 0.43, 0.20 to 0.95), but most benefits had diminished by 6 months. Absolute gains are about 12 prevented disorders per 100 treated in both trials at their best timepoint. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): two concordant trials, one durable to a year, one not — maintenance is the open problem.

cards.headline: van't Veer-Tazelaar 2009: stepped care in over-75s with subthreshold symptoms — disorders by 12 months in 10/86 vs 20/84 (RR 0.49)
cards.summary: van't Veer-Tazelaar 2009: stepped care in over-75s with subthreshold symptoms — disorders by 12 months in 10/86 vs 20/84 (RR 0.49)
cards.people: 170 people aged 75 and older with subthreshold depression or anxiety not meeting diagnostic criteria, recruited in 33 primary care practices in the Netherlands, randomised to an indicated stepped-care prevention programme (n=86) — sequential watchful waiting, CBT-based bibliotherapy, CBT-based problem-solving treatment, and referral for medication if required — or usual care (n=84). Outcome: cumulative incidence of DSM-IV major depressive or anxiety disorder at 12 months (Mini International Neuropsychiatric Interview).
cards.result: The intervention halved 12-month incidence: 0.12 (10 of 86) in the stepped-care group versus 0.24 (20 of 84) in usual care (relative risk 0.49, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.98) — an absolute difference of about 12 disorders prevented per 100 people treated for a year.
cards.watchOut: A single trial of 170 people, with a confidence interval whose upper bound (0.98) only just excludes no effect; the stepped design cannot say which step did the work, and participants had to accept a year-long programme. Screening whole older populations to find the subthreshold group is a cost the trial does not price.
cards.source: van't Veer-Tazelaar PJ et al. Stepped-care prevention of anxiety and depression in late life: a randomized controlled trial. Archives of general psychiatry. 2009. PMID: 19255379. randomised controlled trial (van't veer-tazelaar 2009) 170 people aged 75 and older with subthreshold depression or anxiety not meeting diagnostic criteria, recruited in 33 primary care practices in the netherlands, randomised to an indicated stepped-care prevention programme (n=86) — sequential watchful waiting, cbt-based bibliotherapy, cbt-based problem-solving treatment, and referral for medication if required — or usual care (n=84). outcome: cumulative incidence of dsm-iv major depressive or anxiety disorder at 12 months (mini international neuropsychiatric interview). the intervention halved 12-month incidence: 0.12 (10 of 86) in the stepped-care group versus 0.24 (20 of 84) in usual care (relative risk 0.49, 95% ci 0.24 to 0.98) — an absolute difference of about 12 disorders prevented per 100 people treated for a year. a single trial of 170 people, with a confidence interval whose upper bound (0.98) only just excludes no effect; the stepped design cannot say which step did the work, and participants had to accept a year-long programme. screening whole older populations to find the subthreshold group is a cost the trial does not price. van't veer-tazelaar pj et al. stepped-care prevention of anxiety and depression in late life: a randomized controlled trial. archives of general psychiatry. 2009. pmid: 19255379. registry id: isrctn26474556. mesh: adaptation, psychological · age factors · aged · aged, 80 and over · anxiety disorders/diagnosis/epidemiology/prevention & control · cognition disorders/diagnosis/epidemiology · cognitive behavioral therapy/methods · major depressive disorder/diagnosis/epidemiology/prevention & control · diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders · female · humans · male · neuropsychological tests · primary health care/statistics & numerical data · referral and consultation/statistics & numerical data · surveys and questionnaires

cards.headline: Rovner 2008: problem-solving therapy in macular degeneration — depressive disorders at 2 months 11.6% vs 23.2% (OR 0.43), benefit largely gone by 6 months
cards.summary: Rovner 2008: problem-solving therapy in macular degeneration — depressive disorders at 2 months 11.6% vs 23.2% (OR 0.43), benefit largely gone by 6 months
cards.people: 206 patients with age-related macular degeneration randomised to six sessions of problem-solving treatment delivered at home over 8 weeks (n=105) or usual care (n=101); diagnoses of depressive disorders, depression scores and relinquishing of valued activities assessed at 2 and 6 months.
cards.result: At 2 months, incident depressive disorders were significantly fewer with problem-solving treatment: 11.6% versus 23.2% (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.95). Treatment also reduced the odds of relinquishing a valued activity (OR 0.48, 0.25 to 0.96), which mediated the depression effect. By 6 months, most earlier benefits had diminished.
cards.watchOut: A disease-specific population (vision loss) whose depression risk has a specific driver — loss of valued activities — so the mechanism may not transfer to subthreshold symptoms generally. The fade by 6 months is the trial's most important finding for programme design: prevention here behaves like a treatment that needs maintenance, not a vaccine.
cards.source: Rovner BW et al. Preventing late-life depression in age-related macular degeneration. The American journal of geriatric psychiatry : official journal of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry. 2008. PMID: 18515689. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: indicated prevention works while it is being delivered — the field's unsolved problem is the year after
cards.summary: Synthesis: indicated prevention works while it is being delivered — the field's unsolved problem is the year after
cards.people: Two randomised trials in older adults at high risk of depression: 170 primary-care patients aged 75+ with subthreshold symptoms (stepped care, 12-month endpoint) and 206 patients with macular degeneration (problem-solving therapy, 2- and 6-month endpoints).
cards.result: Incident disorders: RR 0.49 at 12 months (stepped care); OR 0.43 at 2 months fading by 6 months (problem-solving therapy). Absolute differences at best timepoints: about 12 per 100 in both. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Neither trial addresses universal prevention (unselected older people) or selective prevention by risk factor alone; both treat people already carrying symptoms, which is where the effect lives.
cards.source: Synthesis of van't Veer-Tazelaar PJ et al. Archives of General Psychiatry. 2009 (PMID: 19255379); Rovner BW et al. The American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry. 2008 (PMID: 18515689).

shelves.title: In older adults most intervention types show some success but the evidence is weak: a randomised-trial meta-analysis of 70 studies (8,259 people) found mostly small effects — animal therapy and videoconferencing in long-term care looked largest but with very low-quality, highly heterogeneous evidence
shelves.question: In older adults, which intervention types (group, one-to-one, technology, activity) reduce social isolation and loneliness?
shelves.mesh: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy; Exercise; Loneliness/psychology; Psychotherapy; Social Isolation/psychology
shelves.balance: Three syntheses agree on breadth and agree on weakness, so the stamp is POSSIBLE with the weakness printed. The randomised-trial synthesis (Hoang 2022; 70 studies, 8,259 participants; 44 studies in the loneliness meta-analysis) found most interventions had small effects; animal therapy in long-term care (−1.86, 95% CI −3.14 to −0.59, I² = 86%) and videoconferencing technology in long-term care (−1.40, 95% CI −2.37 to −0.44, I² = 70%) looked largest but with high heterogeneity, and overall quality of evidence was very low (PMID: 36251294). Gardiner 2018 (38 studies) found most interventions reported some success with generally weak evidence, the most effective sharing adaptability, a community-development approach and productive engagement (PMID: 27413007). Poscia 2018 (20 studies, 18 interventions) found significant findings in 6 of 11 group interventions, 1 of 4 mixed and all 3 individual interventions, flagging new technologies and community arts as promising (PMID: 29199121). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Hoang 2022 (JAMA Network Open): across 70 randomised trials (8,259 participants aged 55–100), most loneliness interventions in older adults had small effects; animal therapy in long-term care (−1.86, 95% CI −3.14 to −0.59) and videoconferencing in long-term care (−1.40, 95% CI −2.37 to −0.44) looked largest, but heterogeneity was high (I² 86% and 70%) and overall evidence quality was very low
cards.summary: Hoang 2022 (JAMA Network Open): across 70 randomised trials (8,259 participants aged 55–100), most loneliness interventions in older adults had small effects; animal therapy in long-term care (−1.86, 95% CI −3.14 to −0.59) and videoconferencing in long-term care (−1.40, 95% CI −2.37 to −0.44) looked largest, but heterogeneity was high (I² 86% and 70%) and overall evidence quality was very low
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Hoang 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review of 70 randomised clinical trials (8,259 participants) of interventions measuring loneliness, social isolation or support in adults aged 65 and over (participant ages 55–100; study sizes 8–741); 44 studies entered the loneliness meta-analysis (33 community studies, 3,535 participants; 11 long-term-care studies, 1,057 participants). Interventions included animal therapy, psychotherapy/cognitive behavioural therapy, multicomponent programmes, counselling, exercise, music therapy, occupational therapy, reminiscence, social and technological interventions.
cards.result: Most interventions had a small effect size on loneliness (standardised mean differences). Animal therapy in long-term care, when accounting for studies with no active controls, had the largest effect (−1.86, 95% CI −3.14 to −0.59; I² = 86%), followed by technological interventions (videoconferencing) in long-term care (−1.40, 95% CI −2.37 to −0.44; I² = 70%). The authors cautioned that the magnitude should be interpreted carefully given the heterogeneity, that few studies per intervention limit conclusions, and that overall quality of evidence was very low.
cards.watchOut: The two largest effects come from long-term-care subgroups with no-active-control studies included and I² of 70–86% — treat them as signals to test, not as established rankings. 'Very low' overall quality is the authors' own rating.
cards.source: Hoang P, King JA, Moore S, Moore K, et al.. JAMA Network Open. 2022. PMID: 36251294. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy; Exercise; Loneliness/psychology; Psychotherapy; Social Isolation/psychology

cards.headline: Gardiner 2018: across 38 studies of interventions for social isolation and loneliness in older people, the majority reported some success but evidence quality was generally weak; adaptability, a community-development approach and productive engagement marked the most effective interventions
cards.summary: Gardiner 2018: across 38 studies of interventions for social isolation and loneliness in older people, the majority reported some success but evidence quality was generally weak; adaptability, a community-development approach and productive engagement marked the most effective interventions
cards.people: Integrative review of 38 studies (literature 2003 to January 2016) of interventions with a primary or secondary outcome of reducing or preventing social isolation and/or loneliness among older people, evaluated under Evidence for Policy and Practice Information and Co-ordinating Centre guidelines.
cards.result: A wide range of interventions relying on differing mechanisms was described. The majority reported some success in reducing social isolation and loneliness, but the quality of evidence was generally weak. Factors associated with the most effective interventions included adaptability, a community development approach, and productive engagement. The authors called for more robust effectiveness data and better theory on how interventions mediate isolation and loneliness. No pooled effect size is printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: An integrative (not purely randomised) review: 'majority reported some success' is a vote count over weak studies and is vulnerable to publication bias — carded for its mechanism findings (adaptability, community development, productive engagement), not as an effect estimate.
cards.source: Gardiner C, Geldenhuys G, Gott M. Health & Social Care in the Community. 2018. PMID: 27413007. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Poscia 2018: across 20 studies (18 interventions) in older people, 6 of 11 group interventions (55%), 1 of 4 mixed interventions (25%) and all 3 individual interventions reported at least one significant loneliness/isolation finding; new technologies and community-engaged arts were flagged as promising
cards.summary: Poscia 2018: across 20 studies (18 interventions) in older people, 6 of 11 group interventions (55%), 1 of 4 mixed interventions (25%) and all 3 individual interventions reported at least one significant loneliness/isolation finding; new technologies and community-engaged arts were flagged as promising
cards.people: Updated systematic review of studies published January 2011 to February 2016 implementing loneliness/social-isolation interventions in older generations: 15 quantitative and 5 qualitative studies, reporting 18 interventions across the quantitative studies, with intervention effects required as an outcome.
cards.result: Six of 11 group interventions (55%), one of four mixed interventions (25%) and all three individual interventions reported at least one significant finding related to loneliness or social isolation. The review suggested new technologies and community-engaged arts might be promising tools for tackling isolation and loneliness in older individuals, and called for better methodological quality in future studies. No pooled effect size is printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: 'At least one significant finding' is a lenient success bar across multiple outcomes, and only 20 studies met criteria — the percentages describe a thin, uneven literature, not comparative effectiveness.
cards.source: Poscia A, Stojanovic J, La Milia DI, Duplaga M, Grysztar M, Moscato U, Onder G, Collamati A, Ricciardi W, Magnavita N. Experimental Gerontology. 2018. PMID: 29199121. cards.headline: Synthesis: for older adults, something in every intervention family has worked somewhere — group, individual, technology, animal and activity programmes — but the largest randomised synthesis rates the overall evidence very low and most effects small
cards.summary: Synthesis: for older adults, something in every intervention family has worked somewhere — group, individual, technology, animal and activity programmes — but the largest randomised synthesis rates the overall evidence very low and most effects small
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised-trial meta-analysis (70 trials, 8,259 participants), one integrative review (38 studies) and one updated systematic review (20 studies, 18 interventions), all in older adults.
cards.result: Randomised pooling: mostly small standardised effects; largest signals animal therapy −1.86 and videoconferencing −1.40 in long-term care, both highly heterogeneous, overall quality very low (PMID: 36251294). Success correlates: adaptability, community development, productive engagement (PMID: 27413007); significant findings in 55% of group, 25% of mixed and 3/3 individual interventions (PMID: 29199121). The all-ages psychological-intervention evidence is homed on #5482. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — real but weak and small on average.
cards.watchOut: No synthesis here demonstrates durable benefit after programmes end, or benefit on health outcomes beyond loneliness/isolation scores themselves.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hoang P et al. JAMA Network Open. 2022 (PMID: 36251294); Gardiner C et al. Health & Social Care in the Community. 2018 (PMID: 27413007); Poscia A et al. Experimental Gerontology. 2018 (PMID: 29199121).

shelves.title: Digital help for older adults' loneliness: pooled randomised trials found the interventions made no difference — meta-analysis SMD −0.08 (95% CI −0.33 to 0.17) across 6 trials and 391 people
shelves.question: In older adults, do digital-technology interventions (video contact, internet training, messaging) reduce loneliness?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Digital Technology · Female · Humans · Loneliness · Male · Quality of Life · Time Factors
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — and the pooled direction is null. Shah 2021 (PMID: 34085942) pooled five trials and found no significant loneliness difference at 3, 4 or 6 months. Jin 2021 (PMID: 34955948) pooled six randomised trials (391 participants) and found little to no difference (SMD −0.08). The Cochrane rapid review of video calls (Noone 2020; PMID: 32441330) found very uncertain evidence of little to no difference in 201 nursing-home residents. Three independent syntheses, one answer: as tested so far, digital interventions have not been shown to reduce loneliness in older adults (the treatment made no difference in the pooled trials). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Shah 2021: meta-analysis of 5 digital-technology trials in older adults found no significant loneliness reduction at 3, 4 or 6 months (standardised mean differences 0.02, −1.11 and −0.11, all non-significant)
cards.summary: Shah 2021: meta-analysis of 5 digital-technology trials in older adults found no significant loneliness reduction at 3, 4 or 6 months (standardised mean differences 0.02, −1.11 and −0.11, all non-significant)
cards.people: Six studies (one before-and-after study and five clinical trials: four randomised, one quasi-experimental) of digital technology interventions of at least 3 months in adults, totalling 646 participants (154 men, 427 women, 65 with no gender information recorded), average ages 73–78 years; five trials entered the meta-analysis.
cards.result: Pooled standardised mean differences in loneliness versus usual care or non-digital interventions were 0.02 at 3 months (95% CI −0.36 to 0.40; P = .92), −1.11 at 4 months (95% CI −2.60 to 0.38; P = .14) and −0.11 at 6 months (95% CI −0.54 to 0.32; P = .61) — no statistically significant difference at any point (the treatment made no difference). Trial quality was very low to moderate. The authors call for larger randomised trials with longer intervention and follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Only six studies from 4,939 screened, with wide confidence intervals: the data exclude a large benefit but cannot exclude a small one; the 4-month estimate is especially imprecise.
cards.source: Shah SGS, Nogueras D, van Woerden HC, Kiparoglou V. Evaluation of the Effectiveness of Digital Technology Interventions to Reduce Loneliness in Older Adults: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Journal of Medical Internet Research. 2021. cards.headline: Noone 2020 (Cochrane rapid review): video calls in nursing homes — 3 quasi-randomised trials, 201 residents — may result in little to no difference in loneliness at 3, 6 and 12 months; the evidence is very uncertain
cards.summary: Noone 2020 (Cochrane rapid review): video calls in nursing homes — 3 quasi-randomised trials, 201 residents — may result in little to no difference in loneliness at 3, 6 and 12 months; the evidence is very uncertain
cards.people: Three cluster quasi-randomised trials totalling 201 nursing-home residents (mean age at least 65 years), comparing internet video-call interventions with usual care; loneliness measured on the UCLA Loneliness Scale (20 = least lonely to 80 = most lonely); none conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic.
cards.result: Video calls may result in little to no difference in UCLA loneliness scores versus usual care at 3 months (mean difference −0.44, 95% CI −3.28 to 2.41; 3 studies, 201 participants), 6 months (−0.34, 95% CI −3.41 to 2.72; 2 studies, 152 participants) and 12 months (−2.40, 95% CI −7.20 to 2.40; 1 study, 90 participants). Certainty was downgraded three levels for study limitations, imprecision and indirectness. No study reported social isolation; depression scores likewise showed little to no difference at 3 and 6 months.
cards.watchOut: Quasi-randomised nursing-home trials only, all pre-pandemic: very uncertain evidence in a narrow setting, not a verdict on video contact for community-dwelling older adults.
cards.source: Noone C, McSharry J, Smalle M, Burns A, Dwan K, Devane D. Video calls for reducing social isolation and loneliness in older people: a rapid review. cards.headline: Jin 2021: 6 randomised trials of technology-based interventions in 391 older adults — little to no difference in loneliness versus controls (standardised mean difference −0.08, 95% CI −0.33 to 0.17)
cards.summary: Jin 2021: 6 randomised trials of technology-based interventions in 391 older adults — little to no difference in loneliness versus controls (standardised mean difference −0.08, 95% CI −0.33 to 0.17)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Jin 2021)
cards.people: Six randomised controlled trials totalling 391 participants aged 60 years and older, testing technology-based interventions whose core component used technology to reduce loneliness (smartphone-based video calls, and computer training with internet use), searched to April 2021.
cards.result: The meta-analysis suggested technology-based interventions resulted in little to no difference in loneliness reduction compared with control groups (SMD −0.08, 95% CI −0.33 to 0.17; p = 0.53) — the treatment made no difference. Subgroup estimates for both intervention types were likewise non-significant and low quality; three of the six trials were rated low quality and three moderate quality.
cards.watchOut: Small, short trials with heterogeneous technologies pooled together: a null average could hide benefit from a specific well-delivered technology, but none has been shown.
cards.source: Jin W, Liu Y, Yuan S, Bai R, Li X, Bai Z. The Effectiveness of Technology-Based Interventions for Reducing Loneliness in Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Frontiers in Psychology. 2021. cards.headline: Synthesis: three meta-analyses agree — digital-technology interventions, as trialled, do not measurably reduce loneliness in older adults; the trials are small, so a modest benefit is not excluded, but none is demonstrated
cards.summary: Synthesis: three meta-analyses agree — digital-technology interventions, as trialled, do not measurably reduce loneliness in older adults; the trials are small, so a modest benefit is not excluded, but none is demonstrated
cards.people: The carded evidence: two systematic reviews with meta-analysis (6 studies/646 participants; 6 RCTs/391 participants) and one Cochrane rapid review (3 quasi-randomised trials, 201 participants), all in older adults.
cards.result: Shah 2021 found standardised mean differences of 0.02, −1.11 and −0.11 at 3, 4 and 6 months, all non-significant. Jin 2021 found SMD −0.08 (95% CI −0.33 to 0.17). Noone 2020 found video calls may make little to no difference to UCLA loneliness scores at every time point, on very uncertain evidence. The honest summary is absence of demonstrated effect in small trials — not proof that no digital approach can work. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not over-read the null in either direction: confidence intervals still admit a small benefit, and pandemic-era, better-designed trials postdate most of this evidence. What is established is only that benefit is unproven, not that it is impossible.
cards.source: Synthesis of Shah SGS et al. Journal of Medical Internet Research. 2021 (PMID: 34085942); Noone C et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2020 (PMID: 32441330); Jin W et al. Frontiers in Psychology. 2021 (PMID: 34955948).

shelves.title: Experience Corps: in the pilot randomised trial 53% of older volunteers became more active versus 23% of controls — and over 2 years in the full trial, men's brain volumes rose 0.7–1.6% while controls' shrank
shelves.question: In older adults, does intensive intergenerational school volunteering (Experience Corps) improve the volunteers' health and activity?
shelves.mesh: Black or African American · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Baltimore · Female · Health Promotion/methods · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Motor Activity · Pilot Projects · Urban Population · Volunteers
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). One programme, one city, pilot-scale randomised evidence. In the pilot randomised trial, Tan 2006 (PMID: 16763775; 113 volunteers) found 53% of Experience Corps members more active versus 23% of controls (P < 0.01), driven by those inactive at baseline (+110% vs +12%; P = 0.03). In the full Baltimore trial's brain substudy, Carlson 2015 (PMID: 25835516; NCT00000038; 111 participants) found 2-year brain-volume gains in men (+0.7% to 1.6%) against control declines. Frick 2004 (PMID: 15047789) modelled $205,000 per QALY for volunteer health alone, becoming favourable only when children's graduation benefits are counted. The full dual trial (design: Fried 2013, PMID: 23680986) was built around disability and children's reading outcomes. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), single-programme cap.

cards.headline: Tan 2006 (Experience Corps pilot randomised trial): 53% of volunteers were more active after 4–8 months versus 23% of wait-list controls (P < 0.01); previously inactive volunteers raised activity 110% versus 12% in controls (P = 0.03)
cards.summary: Tan 2006 (Experience Corps pilot randomised trial): 53% of volunteers were more active after 4–8 months versus 23% of wait-list controls (P < 0.01); previously inactive volunteers raised activity 110% versus 12% in controls (P = 0.03)
cards.people: 113 randomised older volunteers analysed in Baltimore public elementary schools: ages 59–86 years, 96% African American, 94% women, 84% with annual incomes under $15,000. Experience Corps members served at least 15 hours per week in school roles; controls were wait-listed. Follow-up at 4–8 months.
cards.result: By self-report, 53% of Experience Corps participants were more active than the previous year versus 23% of controls (P < 0.01). Adjusted kilocalorie-per-week change was +40% in participants versus −16% in controls (P = 0.49, a non-significant trend). Among those with low activity at baseline, participants increased activity by an average of 110% versus 12% in controls (P = 0.03); among those previously active there was no significant difference (P = 0.30).
cards.watchOut: Pilot scale and self-reported activity: the headline contrast is significant, the objective-style kilocalorie contrast is not (P = 0.49), and the clearest gain is confined to people inactive at baseline.
cards.source: Tan EJ, Xue QL, Li T, Carlson MC, Fried LP. Volunteering: a physical activity intervention for older adults — The Experience Corps program in Baltimore. Journal of Urban Health. 2006. PMID: 16763775. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Carlson 2015 (Baltimore Experience Corps Trial, brain-health substudy): over 2 years, men's cortical and hippocampal volumes rose 0.7–1.6% on the programme while control men's shrank; women's gains were 0.3–0.54% against ~1% control declines
cards.summary: Carlson 2015 (Baltimore Experience Corps Trial, brain-health substudy): over 2 years, men's cortical and hippocampal volumes rose 0.7–1.6% on the programme while control men's shrank; women's gains were 0.3–0.54% against ~1% control declines
cards.people: 111 older men and women (58 intervention, 53 controls) simultaneously enrolled and randomised within the Baltimore Experience Corps Trial, with brain MRI at baseline and annual follow-up over the 2-year trial exposure; intention-to-treat analyses of cortical and hippocampal volumes, full and sex-stratified samples.
cards.result: Programme-specific increases in brain volumes reached significance in men only (P ≤ .04): control men showed age-related declines over 2 years while Experience Corps men showed 0.7% to 1.6% increases. Women showed modest intervention-specific gains of 0.3% to 0.54% by the second year, contrasting with declines of about 1% in women controls. The authors interpret the findings as purposeful social activity halting, and in men reversing, volume loss in regions vulnerable to dementia.
cards.watchOut: A 111-person imaging substudy with sex-stratified significance (men only at P ≤ .04): a biomarker result, not a demonstrated reduction in dementia or memory loss, and vulnerable to multiple-comparison concerns.
cards.source: Carlson MC, Kuo JH, Chuang YF et al. Impact of the Baltimore Experience Corps Trial on cortical and hippocampal volumes. Alzheimer's & Dementia. 2015. PMID: 25835516. Registry ID: NCT00000038. cards.headline: Frick 2004: modelled on the pilot randomised trial, Experience Corps cost $205,000 per quality-adjusted life year for the volunteers' own health — but needed only 0.3% of exposed children to graduate who otherwise would not for the programme to reach $49,000 per QALY
cards.summary: Frick 2004: modelled on the pilot randomised trial, Experience Corps cost $205,000 per quality-adjusted life year for the volunteers' own health — but needed only 0.3% of exposed children to graduate who otherwise would not for the programme to reach $49,000 per QALY
cards.type: Modelled cost-effectiveness analysis of a pilot randomised trial (Frick 2004)
cards.people: Modelling study using the Experience Corps Baltimore pilot randomised trial's costs, older adults' health status and quality-of-life data, with cost data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey; children's benefits modelled as increased expected lifetime earnings from improved educational attainment.
cards.result: Each quality-adjusted life year (QALY) gained by older adults cost $205,000 on average (lower bound of the 95% confidence interval $65,000 per QALY; upper bound undefined because 15% of simulations showed no QALY improvement). If 0.3% of exposed students changed from not graduating to graduating, the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio fell to $49,000 per QALY; if an additional 0.1% graduated, the programme would be cost-saving. Estimates used conservative assumptions and excluded benefits to teachers, principals and the community.
cards.watchOut: Modelled, not measured: the favourable ratios depend on assumed graduation effects in children, and on the volunteer-health side alone the programme looks expensive ($205,000 per QALY, with 15% of simulations showing no QALY gain at all).
cards.source: Frick KD, Carlson MC, Glass TA et al. Modeled cost-effectiveness of the Experience Corps Baltimore based on a pilot randomized trial. Journal of Urban Health. 2004. PMID: 15047789. cards.headline: Synthesis: intensive school volunteering made inactive older adults substantially more active and was associated with preserved brain volumes over 2 years — genuine randomised evidence, but from one programme in one city, at pilot and substudy scale
cards.summary: Synthesis: intensive school volunteering made inactive older adults substantially more active and was associated with preserved brain volumes over 2 years — genuine randomised evidence, but from one programme in one city, at pilot and substudy scale
cards.people: The carded evidence: the pilot randomised trial's activity report (113 volunteers), the full Baltimore Experience Corps Trial's brain-imaging substudy (111 participants, NCT00000038), and the pilot-based cost-effectiveness model.
cards.result: Activity rose most where it was lowest (Tan 2006). Brain volumes were preserved or increased against control decline, significantly in men (Carlson 2015). Cost-effectiveness is unfavourable on volunteer health alone ($205,000 per QALY) and favourable only if small graduation gains in children are real (Frick 2004). The programme's dual design — volunteer health and children's achievement in one intervention (Fried 2013, PMID: 23680986, design report, not re-carded as outcome evidence) — is its distinctive claim. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: General volunteering evidence is homed on shelf #5488 and is observational; this shelf's randomised programme evidence should not be generalised to lighter-touch volunteering — Experience Corps demands at least 15 hours a week in a structured school role.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tan EJ et al. Journal of Urban Health. 2006 (PMID: 16763775); Carlson MC et al. Alzheimer's & Dementia. 2015 (PMID: 25835516; NCT00000038); Frick KD et al. Journal of Urban Health. 2004 (PMID: 15047789).
