shelves.title: Community choirs for older adults: the Community of Voices trial (390 people, 12 centres) cut loneliness (effect size 0.34) and raised interest in life (0.39) at 6 months
shelves.question: In diverse older adults, does a community choir programme improve well-being and reduce loneliness?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aging/psychology · Female · Health Care Costs/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Loneliness/psychology · Male · Middle Aged · Music/psychology · Music Therapy · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Patient Acceptance of Health Care/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Two randomised trials of two different choir programmes point the same way. Johnson 2020 (PMID: 30412233; NCT01869179), cluster-randomising 12 senior centres and 390 diverse older adults, found greater improvement in loneliness (effect size 0.34) and interest in life (0.39) at 6 months, with no cognitive, physical or cost differences. Galinha 2022 (PMID: 34378330; NCT03985917; 149 participants) found improved positive affect and social well-being from a 34-session programme, sustained at follow-up, with loneliness gains mediated by identification with the group; the trial's health-outcomes report (Galinha 2023; PMID: 34355628) found slowed decline in perceived physical health but more anxiety and depression symptoms in participants with very low cognitive functioning. Both trials used wait-list controls, so singing is not separated from group belonging and expectation. Singing for COPD breathlessness is a different question, homed at pack #5145 and cross-pointed, not re-carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Johnson 2020 (Community of Voices trial): a senior-centre choir cut loneliness (effect size 0.34, P = .02) and raised interest in life (effect size 0.39, P = .008) at 6 months in 390 diverse older adults — with no difference in cognition, physical outcomes or health-care costs
cards.summary: Johnson 2020 (Community of Voices trial): a senior-centre choir cut loneliness (effect size 0.34, P = .02) and raised interest in life (effect size 0.39, P = .008) at 6 months in 390 diverse older adults — with no difference in cognition, physical outcomes or health-care costs
cards.people: 390 community-dwelling adults aged 60 years and older (mean age 71.3 years, SD 7.2; 65% nonwhite) at 12 Administration-on-Aging-supported senior centres, cluster-randomised to start the Community of Voices choir immediately or after a 6-month wait-list period; 6-month retention 92%; intention-to-treat comparison at 6 months.
cards.result: Compared with controls, choir members had significantly greater improvement in loneliness (P = .02; standardised effect size 0.34) and interest in life (P = .008; effect size 0.39). No significant group differences were observed for cognitive or physical outcomes or for health-care costs.
cards.watchOut: Wait-list control and self-reported wellbeing outcomes: expectation and social-contact effects are not separated from singing itself, and 6 months says nothing about durability.
cards.source: Johnson JK, Stewart AL, Acree M, Nápoles AM, Flatt JD, Max WB. A Community Choir Intervention to Promote Well-Being Among Diverse Older Adults: Results From the Community of Voices Trial. The Journals of Gerontology, Series B. 2020. PMID: 30412233. cards.headline: Galinha 2022 (Sing4Health randomised trial): a 34-session singing group programme improved positive affect and social well-being in 149 older day-care users, with effects sustained at follow-up and loneliness gains mediated by identification with the group
cards.summary: Galinha 2022 (Sing4Health randomised trial): a 34-session singing group programme improved positive affect and social well-being in 149 older day-care users, with effects sustained at follow-up and loneliness gains mediated by identification with the group
cards.people: 149 older adults, mostly day-care centre users (mean age 76.66 years, SD 8.79; low average education and income), randomised to a 34-session singing group programme (n = 89) or an active waiting-list control (n = 60); measures included life satisfaction, positive and negative affect, self-esteem, loneliness, social identification and social well-being, plus participant interviews.
cards.result: The programme produced significant effects on positive affect and social well-being, and a marginal effect on self-esteem, sustained at follow-up; qualitative findings corroborated the quantitative results. Mediation analysis showed indirect effects of social identification with the singing group on loneliness, and of self-esteem on positive and negative affect — suggesting belonging to the group, as much as singing, carries the benefit.
cards.watchOut: Small, single-country trial in day-care users with an active wait-list comparator: the mediation story (group identification) is post hoc reasoning on trial data, and loneliness itself improved only indirectly.

cards.headline: Galinha 2023 (Sing4Health, health-outcomes report of the same trial): singing slowed the decline in perceived physical health, benefits held at 6-month follow-up and ran through increased positive affect — but participants with very low cognitive functioning reported more anxiety and depression after the intervention
cards.summary: Galinha 2023 (Sing4Health, health-outcomes report of the same trial): singing slowed the decline in perceived physical health, benefits held at 6-month follow-up and ran through increased positive affect — but participants with very low cognitive functioning reported more anxiety and depression after the intervention
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, second outcome report (Galinha 2023)
cards.people: The same Sing4Health randomised trial population as the preceding card: 149 participants aged 60 to 95 years allocated to an immediate 34-session group singing programme over 4 months or a wait-list active control; blinded assessments at baseline, post-intervention (4 months) and follow-up (6 months), controlling for cognitive status.
cards.result: The intervention group reported a lower decline in perceived physical health after the intervention than controls, and the benefit was maintained at follow-up. Singing-related changes in physical and mental health outcomes were mediated by an increase in positive affect. In moderation analyses, participants with very low cognitive functioning reported more anxiety and depression symptoms after the intervention — a harm signal in that subgroup.
cards.watchOut: A second report of the same 149-person trial as the previous card (same registration, NCT03985917), not independent replication: it adds outcomes and a mechanism, and it is also where the caution lives — more anxiety and depression symptoms in the very-low-cognition subgroup.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two randomised choir trials in older adults both improved social well-being, and the larger one measurably reduced loneliness — modest effects, wait-list controls, and belonging to the group may be the active ingredient
cards.summary: Synthesis: two randomised choir trials in older adults both improved social well-being, and the larger one measurably reduced loneliness — modest effects, wait-list controls, and belonging to the group may be the active ingredient
cards.people: The carded evidence: one cluster randomised trial (12 senior centres, 390 participants) and one individually randomised trial (149 participants, two outcome reports) of community singing programmes in older adults.
cards.result: Community of Voices reduced loneliness (effect size 0.34) and raised interest in life (0.39) at 6 months without changing cognition, physical outcomes or costs (Johnson 2020). Sing4Health improved positive affect and social well-being, sustained at follow-up, with loneliness benefit running through social identification with the group (Galinha 2022), and slowed decline in perceived physical health via increased positive affect, with a harm signal — more anxiety and depression symptoms — in participants with very low cognitive functioning (Galinha 2023). Neither trial separates singing from the social group around it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Cross-point: singing as a breathing intervention in COPD is homed at pack #5145 (singing for COPD quality of life and breathlessness) — a different question with different comparators, not re-carded here. This shelf covers choir participation for well-being and loneliness in older adults generally.

shelves.title: Socially assistive robots in older people's care: reviews report many positive small studies, but the meta-analysis of randomised trials found no statistically significant effect on agitation, anxiety or quality of life
shelves.question: What does the evidence support for socially assistive robots in elderly care?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Aged · Aging · Humans · Interpersonal Relations · Quality of Health Care · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Robotics
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Three syntheses, no strong pooled effect. The scoping review (PMID: 29440212) mapped 33 studies and 1,574 participants across 11 robots and found 28 of 33 papers reporting positive findings — alongside methodological issues limiting the utility of the results. The systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to randomised trials (PMID: 29897445; 11 randomised trials, 9 in the meta-analysis) found social robots appeared to have positive impacts on agitation, anxiety and quality of life, but no statistical significance was found in the meta-analysis, and risk of bias was relatively high. The depression-focused systematic review (PMID: 30198077; 7 studies, 6 of them randomised) found three studies with promising outcomes and three with decreased but non-significant depression scores, and concluded the evidence is not strong enough for recommendations on clinical effectiveness. Specific robot trials, including PARO, are homed on shelf #5519 and are not re-carded here. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Abdi 2018 (scoping review): 28 of 33 studies reported positive findings for socially assistive robots in elderly care — but methodological issues limit the utility of the results
cards.summary: Abdi 2018 (scoping review): 28 of 33 studies reported positive findings for socially assistive robots in elderly care — but methodological issues limit the utility of the results
cards.people: 61 publications describing 33 studies, including 1,574 participants and 11 robots (humanoid and pet robots), in elderly healthcare facilities; acceptability studies, technical reports and physically/surgically assistive robots were excluded.
cards.result: Five roles for socially assistive robots were identified: affective therapy, cognitive training, social facilitator, companionship and physiological therapy. Twenty-eight of the 33 papers reported positive findings. The authors conclude that the reported value of these robots warrants further investigation, while stating plainly that a large proportion of the studies have methodological issues which limit the utility of the results.
cards.watchOut: A scoping review maps a field; it does not pool effects. A count of positive papers (28 of 33) is vulnerable to publication bias and says nothing about effect size or study quality.
cards.source: Abdi J et al. Scoping review on the use of socially assistive robot technology in elderly care. BMJ Open. 2018. PMID: 29440212. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pu 2019 (meta-analysis of randomised trials): social robots appeared to help agitation, anxiety and quality of life — but no statistical significance was found in the meta-analysis
cards.summary: Pu 2019 (meta-analysis of randomised trials): social robots appeared to help agitation, anxiety and quality of life — but no statistical significance was found in the meta-analysis
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (Pu 2019)
cards.people: 13 articles from 11 randomised controlled trials of social robots in older adults, identified from 2,204 articles; 9 studies were included in the meta-analysis of psychological, physiological, quality-of-life and medication outcomes.
cards.result: Social robots appeared to have positive impacts on agitation, anxiety and quality of life for older adults, but no statistical significance was found in the meta-analysis. The narrative review indicated that social robot interactions could improve engagement, interaction and stress indicators, and reduce loneliness and medication use. Risk of bias was relatively high in allocation concealment and blinding, and the authors conclude that conclusions are limited by the lack of high-quality studies and recommend more randomised trials with larger samples.
cards.watchOut: This is the strongest design on this shelf and it is null on pooling: narrative positives from individual small trials do not override a non-significant meta-analysis, which is why this shelf's stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence), not a benefit stamp.
cards.source: Pu L et al. The Effectiveness of Social Robots for Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Studies. The Gerontologist. 2019. PMID: 29897445. cards.headline: Chen 2018 (depression review): of 7 studies of social robots for depression in older adults, three were promising and three showed non-significant decreases — evidence not strong enough for clinical recommendations
cards.summary: Chen 2018 (depression review): of 7 studies of social robots for depression in older adults, three were promising and three showed non-significant decreases — evidence not strong enough for clinical recommendations
cards.people: Seven studies of social robot interventions for depression in older adults — six randomised controlled trials and one comparison study, all classified as good quality — covering companion, communication and health-monitoring robots.
cards.result: Three studies presented promising outcomes for reducing depressive symptoms after social robot interventions, and three studies showed decreased, but non-significant, trends in depression scores. The authors conclude that social robots used in group activities can help alleviate depressive symptoms, but that the evidence is not strong enough to formulate recommendations on clinical effectiveness.
cards.watchOut: Seven small studies with split results (three promising, three non-significant trends, one not summarised in the fetched record) cannot carry a benefit stamp; group-activity delivery also means the robot is bundled with human facilitation and social contact.
cards.source: Chen SC et al. Social Robots for Depression in Older Adults: A Systematic Review. Journal of Nursing Scholarship. 2018. PMID: 30198077. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the robot literature is broad and mostly positive in small studies, but pooled randomised evidence is not statistically significant — weak evidence, honestly labelled
cards.summary: Synthesis: the robot literature is broad and mostly positive in small studies, but pooled randomised evidence is not statistically significant — weak evidence, honestly labelled
cards.people: The carded evidence: one scoping review (33 studies, 1,574 participants), one meta-analysis of randomised trials (11 trials, 9 pooled), and one depression-focused systematic review (7 studies).
cards.result: Positive findings dominate the mapped literature (28 of 33 papers; Abdi 2018), yet the meta-analysis of randomised trials found no statistically significant effect on agitation, anxiety or quality of life (Pu 2019), and the depression review split three promising against three non-significant studies and declined to recommend clinical use (Chen 2018). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence). Trials of one specific robot, PARO, are homed on shelf #5519 and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Blinding a robot intervention is effectively impossible and allocation concealment was often weak in the pooled trials, so even future positive small trials should be read against this pooled null until a large rigorous trial appears.
cards.source: Synthesis of Abdi J et al. BMJ Open. 2018 (PMID: 29440212); Pu L et al. The Gerontologist. 2019 (PMID: 29897445); Chen SC et al. Journal of Nursing Scholarship. 2018 (PMID: 30198077).

shelves.title: PARO companion robot: loneliness fell versus usual activities in a 40-resident randomised trial, quality of life held up in severe dementia in a cluster trial, and medication use fell in a third — three small trials, all under 65 participants
shelves.question: In older people in residential care, does the PARO companion robot improve psychosocial outcomes in a randomised trial?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Aged · Animals · Depression · Dogs · Female · Geriatric Assessment · Humans · Loneliness · Male · New Zealand · Nursing Homes · Quality of Life · Robotics
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). Three small randomised trials of the PARO companion robot, each positive on a different outcome. Robinson 2013 (PMID: 23545466; 40 residential-care residents, 12 weeks of twice-weekly hour-long sessions) found significant decreases in loneliness versus a control group attending normal activities. Petersen 2017 (PMID: 27716673; 61 patients in five secure dementia units) reported decreased stress and anxiety and reductions in psychoactive and pain medication use with PARO versus standard activity programmes. Jøranson 2016 (PMID: 27434512; NCT01998490; cluster-randomised, 53 participants) found quality of life stayed stable with group PARO activity while it decreased in controls among residents with severe dementia, with significantly less psychotropic medication use after the intervention. No single outcome is replicated across two trials, samples are 40 to 61, and the pooled meta-analysis of social robots on shelf #5518 was non-significant — so the stamp stays POSSIBLE, not higher. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Robinson 2013: residents who interacted with PARO had significant decreases in loneliness over 12 weeks versus a control group attending normal activities
cards.summary: Robinson 2013: residents who interacted with PARO had significant decreases in loneliness over 12 weeks versus a control group attending normal activities
cards.people: 40 residents in hospital and rest-home care in Auckland, New Zealand, randomised to PARO sessions (twice a week for an hour over 12 weeks) or a control group attending normal activities; loneliness, depression and quality of life were measured at baseline and follow-up, and social behaviour was observed during robot sessions and during general activities with and without the resident dog.
cards.result: In comparison with the control group, residents who interacted with the robot had significant decreases in loneliness over the trial period. Residents talked to and touched the robot significantly more than the resident dog, more residents joined discussion about the robot, and conversation about the robot occurred more; both the dog and the robot changed the social environment compared with when neither was present. The fetched record reports the loneliness result as significant without a numeric effect size, so none is printed here.
cards.watchOut: One facility, 40 residents, and an unblinded intervention with a normal-activities control: novelty and extra attention are plausible alternative explanations for a loneliness effect, and depression and quality-of-life results are not reported as significant in the fetched record.
cards.source: Robinson H et al. The psychosocial effects of a companion robot: a randomized controlled trial. Journal of the American Medical Directors Association. 2013. PMID: 23545466. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Aged · Animals · Depression · Dogs · Female · Geriatric Assessment · Humans · Loneliness · Male · New Zealand · Nursing Homes · Quality of Life · Robotics

cards.headline: Petersen 2017: in 61 dementia-unit patients, PARO treatment was reported to decrease stress and anxiety and to reduce psychoactive and pain medication use over 12 weeks
cards.summary: Petersen 2017: in 61 dementia-unit patients, PARO treatment was reported to decrease stress and anxiety and to reduce psychoactive and pain medication use over 12 weeks
cards.people: 61 patients (77% female; average age 83.4 years) in five urban secure dementia units, randomised by block design to interaction with the PARO robotic pet or standard activity programmes, with before-and-after measures including anxiety and depression scales, pulse rate, pulse oximetry and galvanic skin response over a 12-week study.
cards.result: The authors report that, compared with the control group, treatment with the PARO robot decreased stress and anxiety in the treatment group and resulted in reductions in the use of psychoactive medications and pain medications. Physiological differences between groups (pulse oximetry and pulse rate) were consistent throughout the 12 weeks. The fetched record gives no numeric effect sizes for the clinical outcomes, so none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: The abstract's scale-level reporting is internally hard to follow (some anxiety/depression scale scores are described as increased in the treatment group while the conclusion reports decreased stress and anxiety), so this card rests on the authors' stated conclusion and the medication-use reductions, not on reconstructed scale numbers.
cards.source: Petersen S et al. The Utilization of Robotic Pets in Dementia Care. Journal of Alzheimer's Disease. 2017. PMID: 27716673. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jøranson 2016: in severe dementia, quality of life stayed stable with group PARO activity while it fell in controls, and psychotropic medication use was significantly lower after the intervention
cards.summary: Jøranson 2016: in severe dementia, quality of life stayed stable with group PARO activity while it fell in controls, and psychotropic medication use was significantly lower after the intervention
cards.people: 53 nursing-home residents with dementia in 10 randomised nursing-home units (27 in group PARO activity, 26 in treatment-as-usual control); the intervention was 30 minutes of group activity with PARO twice a week over 12 weeks, with quality of life in late-stage dementia assessed at baseline, after the intervention and at 3-month follow-up. Registry NCT01998490.
cards.result: An effect was found among participants with severe dementia from baseline to follow-up, showing stable quality of life in the intervention group compared with a decrease in the control group; the intervention explained most of the variance in change on the total scale and on the Tension and Well-being subscales in the severe-dementia group. The intervention group used significantly less psychotropic medication than the control group after the end of the intervention.
cards.watchOut: The quality-of-life effect is a subgroup finding (severe dementia) in a 53-person cluster trial, and 'stable versus declining' is a prevention-of-worsening result, not an improvement — the same pattern as several dementia non-drug interventions.

cards.headline: Synthesis: PARO shows a benefit in each of three small randomised trials, but on a different outcome each time — loneliness, medication use, and quality-of-life stability in severe dementia
cards.summary: Synthesis: PARO shows a benefit in each of three small randomised trials, but on a different outcome each time — loneliness, medication use, and quality-of-life stability in severe dementia
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised trials of the same named robot, 40, 61 and 53 participants, all in residential or dementia-unit care, over 12 weeks each.
cards.result: Loneliness decreased significantly versus normal activities (Robinson 2013); stress, anxiety and psychoactive/pain medication use were reported reduced versus standard activities (Petersen 2017); and quality of life held stable in severe dementia while controls declined, with less psychotropic use (Jøranson 2016; NCT01998490). Because no outcome is confirmed by a second trial and the pooled social-robot meta-analysis (shelf #5518) was non-significant, the stamp is capped. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit). PARO is named as the specific tested product, for clarification.
cards.watchOut: All three trials are 12 weeks or shorter with no long follow-up carded: whether benefits persist after the novelty of the robot wears off is unknown from this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Robinson H et al. Journal of the American Medical Directors Association. 2013 (PMID: 23545466); Petersen S et al. Journal of Alzheimer's Disease. 2017 (PMID: 27716673); Jøranson N et al. Journal of Advanced Nursing. 2016 (PMID: 27434512; NCT01998490).

shelves.title: Mediterranean diet and frailty: cohorts consistently link highest adherence to about a third less incident frailty (relative risk 0.66), and the NU-AGE randomised diet year shifted frailty-linked gut microbes and inflammation — but no trial has yet proven the diet prevents frailty
shelves.question: In older adults at risk of frailty, does a Mediterranean-style diet intervention slow frailty progression versus usual diet?
shelves.mesh: MeSH: Aged · Diet, Mediterranean · Europe · Female · Frailty · Gastrointestinal Microbiome · Health Status · Humans · Male · Patient Compliance · RNA, Ribosomal, 16S · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational-heavy evidence, printed on the face. The incidence evidence is entirely observational: a 2018 meta-analysis of 4 prospective cohorts (5,789 older people) found the highest Mediterranean-diet adherence carried about half the incident-frailty odds of the lowest (pooled OR 0.44), and a 2023 dose-response meta-analysis of 12 cohorts (89,608 participants) found a relative risk of 0.66 for highest versus lowest adherence. The one randomised intervention, NU-AGE (612 non-frail or pre-frail older people, 1 year of a tailored Mediterranean diet across five European countries), shifted the gut microbiome in directions associated with lower frailty markers and lower inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein, interleukin-17) — but it did not report incident frailty as an outcome in this record, so there is no trial proof that prescribing the diet prevents frailty. Healthy-adherer confounding is the standing alternative explanation for the cohort findings. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Ghosh 2020 (NU-AGE): 1 year of a tailored Mediterranean diet in 612 older Europeans changed the gut microbiome toward taxa linked to lower frailty and lower inflammation — a marker study, not a frailty-outcome trial
cards.summary: Ghosh 2020 (NU-AGE): 1 year of a tailored Mediterranean diet in 612 older Europeans changed the gut microbiome toward taxa linked to lower frailty and lower inflammation — a marker study, not a frailty-outcome trial
cards.type: Randomised dietary intervention with microbiome and frailty-marker outcomes (NU-AGE, Ghosh 2020)
cards.people: 612 non-frail or pre-frail older subjects across five European countries (UK, France, Netherlands, Italy and Poland), randomised within the NU-AGE project to a 12-month Mediterranean diet tailored to elderly subjects (NU-AGE diet) or habitual diet; gut microbiota profiled before and after the intervention.
cards.result: Adherence to the diet was associated with specific microbiome alterations: taxa enriched by adherence were positively associated with several markers of lower frailty and improved cognitive function, and negatively associated with inflammatory markers including C-reactive protein and interleukin-17. The diet-modulated microbiome change was associated with increased short/branch-chained fatty acid production and lower production of secondary bile acids, p-cresols, ethanol and carbon dioxide, and the taxa responding positively to the diet occupied keystone positions in the microbiome network while frailty-associated taxa were peripheral. The record reports no incident-frailty or frailty-progression endpoint.
cards.watchOut: This is the only randomised card on the shelf and its frailty content is associative — diet-linked microbes co-varied with frailty markers. It shows the diet changes biology in a favourable direction; it does not show fewer people becoming frail.
cards.source: Ghosh TS et al. Mediterranean diet intervention alters the gut microbiome in older people reducing frailty and improving health status: the NU-AGE 1-year dietary intervention across five European countries. cards.headline: Kojima 2018: across 4 prospective cohorts, the most Mediterranean-adherent older people had about half the incident-frailty odds of the least adherent (pooled OR 0.44)
cards.summary: Kojima 2018: across 4 prospective cohorts, the most Mediterranean-adherent older people had about half the incident-frailty odds of the least adherent (pooled OR 0.44)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohorts (Kojima 2018)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective cohort studies in community-dwelling older adults (mean age 60 or over): 4 studies, 5,789 older people, mean follow-up 3.9 years; frailty incidence compared across Mediterranean diet score (MDS) groups 0–3, 4–5 and 6–9.
cards.result: Greater adherence to a Mediterranean diet was associated with significantly lower incident frailty risk than poorer adherence (MDS 0–3): pooled odds ratio 0.62 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.82, P = .001) for MDS 4–5 and pooled OR 0.44 (95% CI 0.31 to 0.64, P < .001) for MDS 6–9. There was no significant heterogeneity (I2 = 0–16%, P = .30) and no evidence of publication bias. These are observational odds ratios: people who eat this way differ from those who do not in many other ways.
cards.watchOut: Only four cohorts, all observational, and the dose pattern (better adherence, lower frailty) is exactly what healthy-adherer confounding would also produce. The authors themselves call for studies confirming the finding, including in non-Mediterranean populations.
cards.source: Kojima G et al. Adherence to Mediterranean Diet Reduces Incident Frailty Risk: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2018. PMID: 29322507. cards.headline: Poursalehi 2023: a dose-response meta-analysis of 19 studies found highest Mediterranean adherence carried a relative frailty risk of 0.66 in cohorts — with each 2-point score rise linked to a relative risk of 0.86
cards.summary: Poursalehi 2023: a dose-response meta-analysis of 19 studies found highest Mediterranean adherence carried a relative frailty risk of 0.66 in cohorts — with each 2-point score rise linked to a relative risk of 0.86
cards.people: Systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis (search to January 2023) of epidemiologic studies in elderly adults: 19 studies (12 cohorts and 7 cross-sectional). Cohort analyses covered 89,608 participants with 12,866 frailty cases; cross-sectional analyses 13,581 participants with 1,093 cases; a pre-frailty analysis pooled 4 studies (12,745 participants, 4,363 cases).
cards.result: In cohort studies, highest versus lowest Mediterranean-diet adherence was inversely associated with frailty (relative risk 0.66, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.78; I2 = 52.4%), and each 2-point increase in Mediterranean diet score was related to lower frailty risk (relative risk 0.86, 95% CI 0.80 to 0.93). Cross-sectional studies agreed in direction (OR 0.44, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.70) but were highly heterogeneous (I2 = 81.8%). Highest adherence was also linked to lower pre-frailty risk (pooled OR 0.73, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.86). The authors graded the certainty of evidence as high under GRADE for both cohort and cross-sectional bodies of evidence — a grading of observational data, which still cannot exclude confounding.
cards.watchOut: Nineteen studies sounds substantial, but every one is observational and the cross-sectional half cannot separate cause from effect at all — frail people may simply eat less Mediterranean food. The cohort relative risk of 0.66 is the strongest honest number on this shelf.
cards.source: Poursalehi D et al. Adherence to the Mediterranean diet and risk of frailty and pre-frailty in elderly adults: A systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis with GRADE assessment. cards.headline: Synthesis: Mediterranean-style eating is consistently associated with less incident frailty in older people, and a 1-year randomised diet intervention moves frailty-linked biology the right way — but no trial has yet shown the diet itself preventing frailty
cards.summary: Synthesis: Mediterranean-style eating is consistently associated with less incident frailty in older people, and a 1-year randomised diet intervention moves frailty-linked biology the right way — but no trial has yet shown the diet itself preventing frailty
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised 1-year dietary intervention with microbiome/frailty-marker outcomes (612 participants), one meta-analysis of 4 prospective cohorts (5,789 participants), and one dose-response meta-analysis of 12 cohorts (89,608 participants) plus cross-sectional studies. No randomised trial with an incident-frailty endpoint is carded, because none was found in the fetched records.
cards.result: The observational signal is consistent and graded: pooled OR 0.44 for the highest adherence group (Kojima 2018) and cohort relative risk 0.66 for highest versus lowest adherence, with a dose-response of relative risk 0.86 per 2-point score increase (Poursalehi 2023). The NU-AGE intervention (Ghosh 2020) supplies biological plausibility — diet-responsive gut taxa tracked with lower frailty markers and lower C-reactive protein and interleukin-17. What is missing is the decisive design: a trial powered on frailty itself. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational-only for the clinical outcome, with that limitation on the face.
cards.watchOut: Diet scores were measured, not assigned, in every outcome study: income, activity, smoking and overall health travel with Mediterranean adherence and are only partly adjusted away. Read the effect sizes as an upper bound on what prescribing the diet might achieve.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ghosh TS et al. Gut. 2020 (PMID: 32066625); Kojima G et al. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2018 (PMID: 29322507); Poursalehi D et al. Ageing Research Reviews. 2023 (PMID: 36871780).

shelves.title: Stopping culprit medicines in orthostatic hypotension (observational only): withdrawal was followed by fewer falls (adjusted HR 0.48) and resolution of orthostatic hypotension on retesting — but no randomised trial has ever reported falls for this strategy
shelves.question: Does treating orthostatic hypotension by stopping culprit medications reduce falls and syncope?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cohort Studies · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Humans · Prospective Studies · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face. No randomised trial of stopping culprit medicines in orthostatic hypotension has ever reported falls: the Cochrane review of antihypertensive withdrawal in older people (6 trials, 1,073 participants, updated 2025) states plainly that no studies reported falls. What exists is one prospective geriatric-outpatient cohort programme: withdrawing fall-risk-increasing drugs was followed by about half the fall hazard (adjusted HR 0.48; cardiovascular-drug withdrawal HR 0.35) and by significant normalisation of orthostatic hypotension on repeat tilt-table testing (adjusted OR 0.35 for an abnormal orthostatic result persisting). Withdrawal also raised blood pressure in the randomised literature (systolic +9.75 mmHg in the Cochrane pooling), so it is not cost-free. The randomised deprescribing trial most often cited for feasibility in the very old is carded on its own shelf elsewhere in this library and is cross-pointed, not re-carded, in the synthesis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: stopping culprit medications was followed by fewer falls and by resolution of orthostatic hypotension in cohort data, but no randomised trial has tested the strategy on falls or syncope.

cards.headline: van der Velde 2007: in 139 older fallers, withdrawing a fall-risk-increasing drug was followed by far fewer falls — mean 0.3 vs 3.6 falls, adjusted hazard ratio 0.48; for cardiovascular drugs the hazard ratio was 0.35
cards.summary: van der Velde 2007: in 139 older fallers, withdrawing a fall-risk-increasing drug was followed by far fewer falls — mean 0.3 vs 3.6 falls, adjusted hazard ratio 0.48; for cardiovascular drugs the hazard ratio was 0.35
cards.people: 139 geriatric outpatients presenting with one or more falls in the previous year, in a prospective cohort study. A fall-risk-increasing drug was discontinued in 67 patients and dose-reduced in 8 (75 with withdrawal in total); the rest continued treatment. Falls were counted over 2 months of follow-up after a set 1-month withdrawal period.
cards.result: The total number of fall incidents during follow-up was significantly lower in the 75 patients with withdrawal than in those who continued (mean number of falls 0.3 vs 3.6; P = 0.025). After adjustment for age, gender, use of fall-risk-increasing drugs, baseline falls frequency, comorbidity, Mini-Mental State Examination score and reason for referral, the hazard ratio of a fall was 0.48 (95% CI 0.23 to 0.99) for overall drug withdrawal, 0.35 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.82) for cardiovascular drug withdrawal and 0.56 (95% CI 0.23 to 1.38) for psychotropic drug withdrawal. These are relative hazard reductions from an observational cohort, not a randomised comparison.
cards.watchOut: Withdrawal was offered 'if possible', not randomised: patients whose drugs could be stopped may have been less frail or less ill to begin with, and the adjustment cannot remove that confounding. This is the strongest falls evidence for the strategy — and it is still observational.
cards.source: van der Velde N et al. Risk of falls after withdrawal of fall-risk-increasing drugs: a prospective cohort study. British journal of clinical pharmacology. 2007. PMID: 16939531. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Accidental Falls · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cohort Studies · Drug-Related Side Effects and Adverse Reactions · Humans · Prospective Studies · Risk Factors

cards.headline: van der Velde 2007 (tilt-table): after withdrawal of fall-risk-increasing drugs, orthostatic hypotension on repeat tilt-table testing significantly improved — adjusted odds ratio 0.35 for a persisting abnormal orthostatic result; 0.44 for cardiovascular-drug withdrawal
cards.summary: van der Velde 2007 (tilt-table): after withdrawal of fall-risk-increasing drugs, orthostatic hypotension on repeat tilt-table testing significantly improved — adjusted odds ratio 0.35 for a persisting abnormal orthostatic result; 0.44 for cardiovascular-drug withdrawal
cards.type: Prospective cohort study with repeat tilt-table testing (van der Velde 2007)
cards.people: 211 consecutive new geriatric outpatients who had tilt-table testing at baseline (addressing carotid sinus hypersensitivity, orthostatic hypotension and vasovagal collapse); fall-risk-increasing drugs were then withdrawn in all fallers in whom it was safely possible, and tilt-table testing was repeated in 137 participants at a mean follow-up of 6.7 months.
cards.result: After adjustment for confounders, the odds ratios for normalisation of the tilt-table result with overall drug withdrawal were 0.34 (95% CI 0.06 to 1.86) for carotid sinus hypersensitivity, 0.35 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.99) for orthostatic hypotension and 0.27 (95% CI 0.02 to 3.31) for vasovagal collapse — i.e., withdrawal was associated with significantly lower odds of orthostatic hypotension persisting. For cardiovascular-drug withdrawal the adjusted odds ratio was 0.13 (95% CI 0.03 to 0.59) for carotid sinus hypersensitivity and 0.44 (95% CI 0.18 to 1.0) for orthostatic hypotension. The authors conclude that drug withdrawal can cause substantial improvement in cardiovascular homeostasis.
cards.watchOut: Same cohort programme and same non-randomised design as the falls card: this shows the blood-pressure mechanism moving in the right direction after withdrawal, in the same clinic population — it is not independent randomised confirmation, and syncope events themselves were not the outcome.
cards.source: van der Velde N et al. Withdrawal of fall-risk-increasing drugs in older persons: effect on tilt-table test outcomes. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2007. PMID: 17493193. Registry ID: none in the record. prospective cohort study with repeat tilt-table testing (van der velde 2007) 211 consecutive new geriatric outpatients who had tilt-table testing at baseline (addressing carotid sinus hypersensitivity, orthostatic hypotension and vasovagal collapse); fall-risk-increasing drugs were then withdrawn in all fallers in whom it was safely possible, and tilt-table testing was repeated in 137 participants at a mean follow-up of 6.7 months. after adjustment for confounders, the odds ratios for normalisation of the tilt-table result with overall drug withdrawal were 0.34 (95% ci 0.06 to 1.86) for carotid sinus hypersensitivity, 0.35 (95% ci 0.13 to 0.99) for orthostatic hypotension and 0.27 (95% ci 0.02 to 3.31) for vasovagal collapse — i.e., withdrawal was associated with significantly lower odds of orthostatic hypotension persisting. for cardiovascular-drug withdrawal the adjusted odds ratio was 0.13 (95% ci 0.03 to 0.59) for carotid sinus hypersensitivity and 0.44 (95% ci 0.18 to 1.0) for orthostatic hypotension. the authors conclude that drug withdrawal can cause substantial improvement in cardiovascular homeostasis. same cohort programme and same non-randomised design as the falls card: this shows the blood-pressure mechanism moving in the right direction after withdrawal, in the same clinic population — it is not independent randomised confirmation, and syncope events themselves were not the outcome. van der velde n et al. withdrawal of fall-risk-increasing drugs in older persons: effect on tilt-table test outcomes. journal of the american geriatrics society. 2007. pmid: 17493193. registry id: none in the record. mesh: accidental falls · aged · cardiovascular agents · carotid sinus · female · humans · hypotension · hypotension, orthostatic · male · mobility limitation · psychotropic drugs · risk factors · syncope · syncope, vasovagal · tilt-table test

cards.headline: Gnjidic 2025 (Cochrane update): across 6 randomised withdrawal trials (1,073 older participants), NO study reported falls — while stopping antihypertensives raised systolic pressure by 9.75 mmHg and may result in little to no difference in mortality, hospitalisation or stroke
cards.summary: Gnjidic 2025 (Cochrane update): across 6 randomised withdrawal trials (1,073 older participants), NO study reported falls — while stopping antihypertensives raised systolic pressure by 9.75 mmHg and may result in little to no difference in mortality, hospitalisation or stroke
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Cochrane update, Gnjidic 2025)
cards.people: Six randomised controlled trials of complete withdrawal or dose reduction of antihypertensive medication versus continuation, in adults aged 50 years and over living in the community, residential aged care or hospital settings (1,073 participants; study duration and follow-up 4 to 56 weeks). This 2025 update of the 2020 Cochrane review found no new eligible studies.
cards.result: Discontinuing antihypertensives may result in little to no difference in all-cause mortality (OR 2.08, 95% CI 0.79 to 5.46; 4 studies, 630 participants; low certainty), hospitalisation (OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.33 to 2.10; 1 study, 385 participants) and stroke (OR 1.44, 95% CI 0.25 to 8.35; 3 studies, 524 participants); the evidence is very uncertain for myocardial infarction (OR 1.86, 95% CI 0.19 to 17.98). Blood pressure was higher after discontinuation (systolic mean difference 9.75 mmHg, 95% CI 7.33 to 12.18; diastolic 3.5 mmHg, 95% CI 1.82 to 5.18). The review states plainly: 'No studies reported falls.' Certainty was low to very low, mainly due to small studies and low event rates.
cards.watchOut: These withdrawal trials were not conducted in patients selected for orthostatic hypotension, and none measured the outcome this shelf asks about — the card is evidence about the gap in the randomised literature, and about the blood-pressure cost of withdrawal, not evidence that stopping helps or harms fallers.
cards.source: Gnjidic D et al. Withdrawal of antihypertensive drugs in older people. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2025. PMID: 40162571. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: stopping culprit medicines was followed by fewer falls and by resolution of orthostatic hypotension in one prospective cohort programme — but the randomised literature has never reported falls for this strategy, so the benefit claim rests on observational data only
cards.summary: Synthesis: stopping culprit medicines was followed by fewer falls and by resolution of orthostatic hypotension in one prospective cohort programme — but the randomised literature has never reported falls for this strategy, so the benefit claim rests on observational data only
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prospective cohort of 139 older fallers (falls outcome), the same programme's tilt-table cohort (211 tested at baseline, 137 retested; orthostatic outcome), and the Cochrane randomised-withdrawal literature (6 trials, 1,073 participants; no falls reported). Total carded participants exceed 1,400, so no small-N stamp labelling applies. Cross-point (not re-carded): the large randomised antihypertensive-reduction trial in people aged 80 and over is carded on its own shelf in this library; it tested blood-pressure control, not falls in orthostatic hypotension.
cards.result: Falls after withdrawal: adjusted HR 0.48 overall and 0.35 for cardiovascular drugs (van der Velde 2007, cohort). Orthostatic hypotension persisting on retest: adjusted OR 0.35 with withdrawal (van der Velde 2007, tilt-table cohort). Randomised withdrawal trials: no falls data at all; systolic pressure rose 9.75 mmHg after discontinuation, with little to no difference in mortality, hospitalisation or stroke (Gnjidic 2025). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: The two positive cards come from a single clinic's cohort programme in which clinicians chose whose drugs could be stopped — confounding by that choice is the central weakness, and no card on this shelf randomised anyone or counted syncope as an outcome.
cards.source: Synthesis of van der Velde N et al. British journal of clinical pharmacology. 2007 (PMID: 16939531); van der Velde N et al. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2007 (PMID: 17493193); Gnjidic D et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2025 (PMID: 40162571).

shelves.title: Statins after MI past 80 (observational only for this exact question): continuation is associated with fewer events and lower mortality in the oldest cohorts, and trials prove benefit into the early 80s — continue in patients who tolerate them and are likely to live ~2 years
shelves.question: Should statins be continued in patients over 80 after MI?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Bayes Theorem · Coronary Disease · Female · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Male · Risk · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for the over-80 post-MI continuation question, printed on the face; no randomised trial has tested continuing versus stopping a statin after 80. The randomised foundation is one step removed: a meta-analysis of 9 secondary-prevention trials in 19,569 patients aged 65–82 (Afilalo 2008, PMID: 18174034) found statins cut all-cause mortality (15.6% versus 18.7%; relative risk 0.78) — but its oldest participants were 82 and it tested starting, not continuing. The two large ageing trial syntheses are homed elsewhere in this library (the Cholesterol Treatment Trialists' age meta-analysis on shelf #3986; PROSPER in pack #1564) and are cross-pointed, not re-carded. Directly on the question, the evidence is observational: in 3,900 patients aged 80 or older after a first MI, at least 2 years of statin prescriptions were associated with lower composite cardiovascular risk (adjusted HR 0.81) and mortality (adjusted HR 0.84), with numbers needed to treat of 59 and 36 over a median 4.5 years before correction for early deaths (Lefeber 2020, PMID: 31647578); and in Denmark, discontinuation among long-term users aged 75+ was associated with 13 excess major cardiovascular events per 1,000 person-years in the secondary-prevention cohort (Thompson 2021, PMID: 34854906). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: continue the statin after MI past 80 in patients tolerating it and likely to live long enough (about 2 years) to benefit; deprescribing trials in this exact population are still lacking.

cards.headline: Afilalo 2008: meta-analysis of 9 trials in 19,569 patients aged 65–82 with coronary disease — statins cut all-cause mortality from 18.7% to 15.6% (relative risk 0.78)
cards.summary: Afilalo 2008: meta-analysis of 9 trials in 19,569 patients aged 65–82 with coronary disease — statins cut all-cause mortality from 18.7% to 15.6% (relative risk 0.78)
cards.people: Hierarchical Bayesian meta-analysis of randomised trials of statin versus placebo in elderly patients with documented coronary heart disease (secondary prevention), including unpublished elderly-subgroup data from 4 trials and the PROSPER secondary-prevention subgroup: 9 trials encompassing 19,569 patients, age range 65 to 82 years, follow-up at least 6 months.
cards.result: Pooled all-cause mortality was 15.6% with statins and 18.7% with placebo — a relative risk reduction of 22% over 5 years (relative risk 0.78, 95% credible interval 0.65 to 0.89). Statins also reduced coronary heart disease mortality by 30% relatively (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.53 to 0.83), nonfatal myocardial infarction by 26% (RR 0.74), revascularisation by 30% (RR 0.70) and stroke by 25% (RR 0.75). The posterior median number needed to treat to save one life was 28 (95% CI 15 to 56).
cards.watchOut: The trials enrolled patients up to age 82 and randomised starting a statin, not continuing one past 80 after MI; extrapolating to the frailest over-80s — the group clinicians actually hesitate over — goes beyond this data.
cards.source: Afilalo J et al. Statins for secondary prevention in elderly patients: a hierarchical bayesian meta-analysis. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2008. PMID: 18174034. cards.headline: Lefeber 2020: in 3,900 patients aged 80+ after a first MI, at least 2 years of statin prescriptions were associated with lower cardiovascular events (adjusted HR 0.81) and mortality (HR 0.84)
cards.summary: Lefeber 2020: in 3,900 patients aged 80+ after a first MI, at least 2 years of statin prescriptions were associated with lower cardiovascular events (adjusted HR 0.81) and mortality (HR 0.84)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort in the UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink (1999–2016): 9,020 patients aged 65 or older hospitalised after a first myocardial infarction with no statin prescription in the prior year, including 3,900 patients aged 80 years and older; a time-varying Cox model compared at least 2 years of statin prescription time with untreated or shorter exposure; median follow-up 4.5 years.
cards.result: Among patients aged 80 and older, 2 years of statin prescriptions resulted in a lower risk of the composite of recurrent MI, stroke and cardiovascular mortality (adjusted HR 0.81, 95% CI 0.66–0.99) and of all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.73–0.97). The number needed to treat was 59 to prevent one primary outcome and 36 to prevent one death; correcting for the 36.2% of patients who died during the first 2 years raised these to 93 and 61. The authors support statin initiation after a first MI at 80 or older if continued for at least 2 years, especially when 2-year mortality risk is low.
cards.watchOut: Observational: patients who stay on statins for 2 years are survivors who tolerate treatment (healthy-user and immortal-time effects), and the corrected numbers needed to treat (93 and 61) show how much of the apparent benefit depends on living long enough to receive it.
cards.source: Lefeber GJ et al. Statins After Myocardial Infarction in the Oldest: A Cohort Study in the Clinical Practice Research Datalink Database. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2020. PMID: 31647578. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Thompson 2021: among 39,955 Danish secondary-prevention patients aged 75+, stopping statins was associated with 13 excess major cardiovascular events per 1,000 person-years versus continuing
cards.summary: Thompson 2021: among 39,955 Danish secondary-prevention patients aged 75+, stopping statins was associated with 13 excess major cardiovascular events per 1,000 person-years versus continuing
cards.people: Nationwide Danish cohort of all persons aged 75 or older treated with statins for at least 5 consecutive years as of 1 January 2011, followed to 31 December 2016: 67,418 long-term users — 27,463 in primary prevention (median age 79) and 39,955 in secondary prevention (median age 80 years [IQR 77–84]; 47% female). Confounding was addressed with inverse probability of treatment weighting.
cards.result: In the secondary-prevention cohort, the weighted rate difference for major adverse cardiovascular events was 13 per 1,000 person-years (95% CI 8–17) higher in those who discontinued statins than in those who continued, with an adjusted sub-hazard ratio of 1.28 (95% CI 1.18–1.39) — corresponding to 1 excess event per 77 persons who discontinued per year. The primary-prevention cohort showed the same direction (9 per 1,000 person-years; sub-HR 1.32). The authors call for randomised trials of discontinuation.
cards.watchOut: People stop statins because they are dying, frail or intolerant — reasons that themselves predict events — so discontinuation cohorts overstate the harm of stopping; the study population is 75+ (median 80 in secondary prevention), not exclusively post-MI.
cards.source: Thompson W et al. Statin Discontinuation and Cardiovascular Events Among Older People in Denmark. JAMA network open. 2021. PMID: 34854906. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: trial data prove statins save lives in secondary prevention up to the early 80s, and every large cohort of the oldest post-MI patients points the same way — but continuation past 80 itself has never been randomised
cards.summary: Synthesis: trial data prove statins save lives in secondary prevention up to the early 80s, and every large cohort of the oldest post-MI patients points the same way — but continuation past 80 itself has never been randomised
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of 9 randomised trials (19,569 patients aged 65–82), one post-MI cohort (3,900 patients aged 80+ within 9,020), and one nationwide discontinuation cohort (39,955 secondary-prevention patients aged 75+). Total carded participants exceed 60,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is design, not size.
cards.result: Randomised secondary-prevention data in the elderly show mortality 15.6% versus 18.7% (RR 0.78) (Afilalo 2008). After MI at 80+, at least 2 years of statin use was associated with HR 0.81 for cardiovascular events and 0.84 for mortality (Lefeber 2020). Discontinuation at 75+ was associated with 13 excess events per 1,000 person-years in secondary prevention (Thompson 2021). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only for continuation past 80 after MI.
cards.watchOut: The honest residual question is not efficacy but fit: limited life expectancy, polypharmacy burden, muscle symptoms and patient goals can still justify stopping — the cohorts say an average benefit exists, not that every individual over 80 should continue.
cards.source: Synthesis of Afilalo J et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2008 (PMID: 18174034); Lefeber GJ et al. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2020 (PMID: 31647578); Thompson W et al. JAMA network open. 2021 (PMID: 34854906).

shelves.title: Blood pressure over 85: no trial isolates this age — the best-supported target is systolic below 140, toward 120–130 mm Hg if tolerated, extrapolated from SPRINT at 75+ and HYVET at 80+, with frailty setting the limit
shelves.question: What blood pressure target is best for patients over 85 with hypertension?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antihypertensive Agents · Blood Pressure · Blood Pressure Determination · Cause of Death · Female · Heart Failure · Humans · Hypertension · Male · Myocardial Infarction
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for treating hypertension and aiming lower in fit older adults — with the explicit caveat that no trial isolates patients over 85 or their ideal target, so the answer for 85+ is extrapolated. The nearest randomised evidence: in the SPRINT subgroup aged 75 or older (Williamson 2016, PMID: 27195814; 2,636 participants, mean age 79.9), a systolic target under 120 mm Hg beat under 140 mm Hg on the cardiovascular composite (HR 0.66) and all-cause mortality (HR 0.67), without more injurious falls. A meta-analysis of 16 target trials (Roush 2019, PMID: 30870246) found lower targets benefited older patients (mean age 77; RR 0.77) more than younger ones, with the number needed to treat falling steeply with age. For the over-80s specifically, HYVET proved treating to a target of 150/80 mm Hg saves lives — its main results are homed on live shelf #94 and the intensive-trials shelf #93 and are cross-pointed here, not re-carded — and HYVET's frailty analysis (Warwick 2015, PMID: 25880068) found no evidence that frailty removes the benefit. STEP's 6-year follow-up (Song 2025, PMID: 41105077) supports sustained intensive control in older patients, though STEP enrolled ages 60–80. PROPOSED LIKELY: treat hypertension past 85 and aim systolic roughly 120–139 mm Hg in ambulatory, reasonably fit patients — below 140, toward 130 or lower if tolerated without hypotension, kidney injury or falls — individualising downward ambition for frailty, since the trials excluded the most frail.

cards.headline: Williamson 2016 (SPRINT ≥75): a systolic target under 120 beat under 140 in 2,636 patients aged 75+ — composite events HR 0.66, mortality HR 0.67, no excess injurious falls
cards.summary: Williamson 2016 (SPRINT ≥75): a systolic target under 120 beat under 140 in 2,636 patients aged 75+ — composite events HR 0.66, mortality HR 0.67, no excess injurious falls
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial, prespecified age subgroup of SPRINT (Williamson 2016)
cards.people: Prespecified subgroup of the SPRINT randomised trial: 2,636 ambulatory patients aged 75 years or older with hypertension but without diabetes (mean age 79.9 years; 37.9% women), randomised to a systolic blood pressure target under 120 mm Hg (intensive, n = 1,317) or under 140 mm Hg (standard, n = 1,319); median follow-up 3.14 years; 95.2% provided complete follow-up data.
cards.result: The primary cardiovascular composite occurred in 102 intensive-group versus 148 standard-group patients (hazard ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.51–0.85), and all-cause mortality was 73 versus 107 deaths (HR 0.67, 95% CI 0.49–0.91). Overall serious adverse events did not differ (48.4% versus 48.3%; HR 0.99). Absolute rates were higher with intensive treatment for hypotension (2.4% versus 1.4%), syncope (3.0% versus 2.4%), electrolyte abnormalities (4.0% versus 2.7%) and acute kidney injury (5.5% versus 4.0%), but not for injurious falls (4.9% versus 5.5%; HR 0.91).
cards.watchOut: Mean age was 79.9, not 85+: the over-85 stratum is a minority within this subgroup, participants were ambulatory volunteers without diabetes, and blood pressure was measured by a research protocol (unattended automated readings run lower than routine clinic values).

cards.headline: Roush 2019: across 16 target trials, lower systolic targets benefited older patients (mean age 77; RR 0.77) more than younger ones — and the number needed to treat fell by over 94% with age
cards.summary: Roush 2019: across 16 target trials, lower systolic targets benefited older patients (mean age 77; RR 0.77) more than younger ones — and the number needed to treat fell by over 94% with age
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of trials randomising patients to intensive systolic targets of 120–140 mm Hg versus higher targets: 16 trials met criteria; head-to-head meta-analyses and meta-regression examined whether treatment benefit varies with age. The record does not state the pooled participant total.
cards.result: Relative to higher targets, lower targets reduced cardiovascular events, and benefit differed significantly by age: treatment significantly benefited older patients (mean age 77; relative risk 0.77, 95% CI 0.61–0.97, P = 0.025) but not younger patients (mean age 61; RR 0.90, 95% CI 0.78–1.03). The ratio of relative risks at age 80 versus 55 was 0.68 (95% CI 0.47–0.97), and the number needed to treat over 10 years to prevent one cardiovascular event declined with age by more than 94%, without an age-related increase in the relative risk of adverse effects (0.86, 95% CI 0.33–2.26). The authors caution that all trials excluded the most frail older patients.
cards.watchOut: Age effects are compared across trials (meta-regression), not within a single over-85 trial — differences between trial populations can masquerade as age effects, and the top of the age range here is a mean of about 77–81, still short of 85.
cards.source: Roush GC et al. Does the benefit from treating to lower blood pressure targets vary with age? A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of hypertension. 2019. PMID: 30870246. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Warwick 2015 (HYVET frailty analysis): in the over-80 trial population, frailty did not modify the treatment benefit — frailer and fitter patients alike appeared to gain from antihypertensive treatment
cards.summary: Warwick 2015 (HYVET frailty analysis): in the over-80 trial population, frailty did not modify the treatment benefit — frailer and fitter patients alike appeared to gain from antihypertensive treatment
cards.type: Secondary frailty analysis of a randomised trial (Warwick 2015, HYVET)
cards.people: Secondary analysis of HYVET, the double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of antihypertensive treatment in people with hypertension aged 80 and over: participants were randomised 1:1 to indapamide sustained-release 1.5 mg with or without perindopril 2–4 mg, or matching placebo, treated toward the trial's target; a frailty index based on 60 deficits was calculated at entry (median 0.17, IQR 0.11–0.24). The record does not restate HYVET's total enrolment; the main trial results are homed on live shelf #94 in this library.
cards.result: For stroke, total mortality and cardiovascular events, the point estimates of the treatment-effect hazard ratios decreased as frailty index increased, and there was no evidence of an interaction between the effect of treatment for hypertension and frailty. Both the frailer and the fitter older adults with hypertension appeared to gain from treatment. This record reports the interaction analysis, not the main HYVET effect sizes, which are carded on shelf #94.
cards.watchOut: HYVET compared treatment with placebo toward 150/80 mm Hg — it proves treating the over-80s helps, including the moderately frail, but it does not compare lower targets, and its participants were still trial volunteers healthier than typical 85-year-old clinic patients.
cards.source: Warwick J et al. cards.headline: Song 2025 (STEP 6-year): sustained intensive control (target 110 to under 130) beat delayed intensive control over 6 years (HR 0.82) — earlier and sustained lowering paid off in older patients
cards.summary: Song 2025 (STEP 6-year): sustained intensive control (target 110 to under 130) beat delayed intensive control over 6 years (HR 0.82) — earlier and sustained lowering paid off in older patients
cards.people: Extended follow-up of the STEP randomised trial: 8,511 Chinese patients with hypertension originally randomised to an intensive systolic target of 110 to under 130 mm Hg or a standard target of 130 to under 150 mm Hg; after the trial ended, all survivors received intensive treatment, so the comparison is sustained intensive versus delayed intensive treatment; median follow-up 6.11 years. STEP enrolled patients aged 60–80 years, so its population is younger than this shelf's question.
cards.result: Mean systolic pressure was 127.9 mm Hg in the sustained intensive group and 129.5 mm Hg in the delayed intensive group. The primary cardiovascular composite occurred at 1.12% per year versus 1.33% per year (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.71–0.96). No safety-event differences were observed except hypotension, which was more frequent with sustained intensive treatment. G-formula analyses estimated the greatest benefit when intensive treatment began at randomisation (relative risk 0.83, 95% CI 0.70–0.96), attenuating when initiation was delayed 12 months (RR 0.88).
cards.watchOut: Ages 60–80 at entry and a post-trial design in which everyone eventually received intensive treatment: it supports 'lower, sustained' in older patients generally but contributes no direct evidence at 85+, where the sustained-versus-delayed contrast also dilutes the target comparison.
cards.source: Song Q et al. Intensive Blood Pressure Control in Older Patients With Hypertension: 6-Year Results of the STEP Trial. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2025. PMID: 41105077. Registry ID: NCT03015311. cards.headline: Synthesis: no trial answers 'over 85' directly — the evidence ladder (SPRINT at 75+, HYVET at 80+, age meta-analysis, STEP) supports treating and aiming systolic below 140, toward 120–130 if tolerated, individualised for frailty
cards.summary: Synthesis: no trial answers 'over 85' directly — the evidence ladder (SPRINT at 75+, HYVET at 80+, age meta-analysis, STEP) supports treating and aiming systolic below 140, toward 120–130 if tolerated, individualised for frailty
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised age subgroup (2,636 patients, mean age 79.9), one 16-trial age meta-analysis, one frailty analysis of the over-80 HYVET trial population, and one extended trial follow-up (8,511 patients aged 60–80). Total carded participants exceed 11,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the gap is the absence of an over-85 target trial, printed here rather than hidden.
cards.result: Intensive (under 120) versus standard (under 140) systolic targets at 75+: HR 0.66 for cardiovascular events and 0.67 for mortality, without excess injurious falls (Williamson 2016). Lower targets benefited older trial populations more than younger ones, with numbers needed to treat falling steeply with age (Roush 2019). Frailty did not erase treatment benefit at 80+ (Warwick 2015), and sustained intensive control beat delayed control over 6 years (Song 2025). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for treating toward a lower target in fit older adults, extrapolated — not trialled — past 85.
cards.watchOut: Every rung of this ladder stops short of the frailest 85-year-olds: institutionalised patients, those with dementia, orthostatic symptoms or limited life expectancy were excluded or scarce in all four sources, and for them the right target remains a clinical judgement, not a number from this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Williamson JD et al. JAMA. 2016 (PMID: 27195814); Roush GC et al. Journal of hypertension. 2019 (PMID: 30870246); Warwick J et al. BMC medicine. 2015 (PMID: 25880068); Song Q et al. Journal of the American College of Cardiology. 2025 (PMID: 41105077).

shelves.title: Intensive blood-pressure lowering and falls in frail older adults: no increase in injurious falls detected (4.9% vs 5.5% at age 75+) in the trial frailty and oldest-age analyses or a 21-trial review — in ambulatory volunteers, not care-home residents
shelves.question: Does intensive blood pressure lowering increase falls in frail elderly patients?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Humans · Middle Aged · Antihypertensive Agents · Blood Pressure · Frailty · Hypertension · Myocardial Infarction · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (no increase in falls detected) — the falls question about intensive lowering has been asked inside the one big trial programme that enrolled older, higher-risk patients, and the answer there is reassuring but bounded. In SPRINT participants aged 75 and older, injurious falls were 4.9% on intensive treatment versus 5.5% on standard treatment (hazard ratio 0.91, a relative measure; Williamson 2016); at age 80 and older there was no between-group difference in injurious falls (Pajewski 2020); frailty did not significantly modify serious-adverse-event risk (Wang 2023); and a 21-trial Veterans Affairs review concluded that lower targets do not increase falls or cognitive impairment, on low- to moderate-strength evidence (Weiss 2017). The harms that genuinely rose were hypotension, syncope numerically, electrolyte abnormalities and kidney injury. The bounds matter: these were ambulatory volunteers, the parent trial's cardiovascular question is homed on live shelf #93 and this shelf cards only its age and frailty safety reports, the age-75+ falls interval still permits a modest relative increase, and the review itself says frail-elderly data are limited. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no increase in falls detected): intensive blood-pressure lowering did not increase injurious falls in the trial populations studied, including their frail subgroups — evidence that does not extend to institutionalised or already-falling patients.

cards.headline: Wang 2023: in SPRINT's frailty analysis, intensive control helped frail and non-frail patients similarly and did not significantly increase serious adverse events in either group — but the record reports no falls-specific effect size
cards.summary: Wang 2023: in SPRINT's frailty analysis, intensive control helped frail and non-frail patients similarly and did not significantly increase serious adverse events in either group — but the record reports no falls-specific effect size
cards.type: Post hoc frailty analysis of a randomised trial (Wang 2023)
cards.people: Post hoc analysis of the SPRINT randomised trial: 9,306 patients (mean age 67.9 years), of whom 2,560 (26.7% as printed in the record) had frailty, defined as a frailty index above 0.21. Median follow-up 3.22 years; 561 primary cardiovascular outcomes occurred. SPRINT enrolled ambulatory volunteers, not nursing-home residents.
cards.result: Patients with frailty had a significantly higher risk of the primary cardiovascular outcome in both arms (adjusted hazard ratio 2.10 [95% CI 1.59–2.77] in the intensive arm and 1.85 [95% CI 1.46–2.35] in the standard arm, both relative measures). Intensive treatment effects on primary and secondary outcomes did not differ significantly between frail and non-frail patients on a relative or absolute scale, except for cardiovascular death (hazard ratio 0.91 [95% CI 0.52–1.60] with frailty versus 0.30 [95% CI 0.16–0.59] without; P for interaction = 0.01). There was no significant interaction between frailty and the risks for serious adverse events with intensive treatment. The record reports serious adverse events as a group and gives no falls-specific effect size, which is printed here plainly rather than inferred.
cards.watchOut: Post hoc subgroup analysis of a single trial: 'no significant interaction' is not proof of no difference, the frailty index was constructed from trial data rather than measured clinically, and trial volunteers with frailty are typically less frail than the frail elderly seen in clinics and care homes.
cards.source: Wang Z et al. The Effect of Frailty on the Efficacy and Safety of Intensive Blood Pressure Control: A Post Hoc Analysis of the SPRINT Trial. Circulation. 2023. PMID: 37401465. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Aged · Humans · Middle Aged · Antihypertensive Agents · Blood Pressure · Frailty · Hypertension · Myocardial Infarction · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome

cards.headline: Williamson 2016: at age 75 and older, injurious falls were 4.9% on intensive treatment versus 5.5% on standard treatment (the treatment made no difference to falls), while cardiovascular events and deaths fell
cards.summary: Williamson 2016: at age 75 and older, injurious falls were 4.9% on intensive treatment versus 5.5% on standard treatment (the treatment made no difference to falls), while cardiovascular events and deaths fell
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, older subgroup report (Williamson 2016)
cards.people: The SPRINT participants aged 75 years or older: 2,636 ambulatory adults (mean age 79.9 years; 37.9% women) with hypertension but without diabetes, randomised to a systolic target under 120 mm Hg (n = 1,317) or under 140 mm Hg (n = 1,319); 2,510 (95.2%) provided complete follow-up over a median 3.14 years.
cards.result: The primary cardiovascular composite occurred in 102 intensive-group versus 148 standard-group participants (hazard ratio 0.66 [95% CI 0.51–0.85], a relative measure) and all-cause mortality was 73 versus 107 deaths (hazard ratio 0.67 [95% CI 0.49–0.91], relative). Overall serious adverse events did not differ (48.4% versus 48.3%; hazard ratio 0.99 [95% CI 0.89–1.11]). Injurious falls were 4.9% in the intensive group versus 5.5% in the standard group (hazard ratio 0.91 [95% CI 0.65–1.29], relative) — the treatment made no difference to injurious falls. Hypotension (2.4% versus 1.4%), syncope (3.0% versus 2.4%), electrolyte abnormalities (4.0% versus 2.7%) and acute kidney injury (5.5% versus 4.0%) were each numerically more frequent with intensive treatment, with confidence intervals crossing 1.
cards.watchOut: The falls confidence interval (0.65–1.29, relative) cannot exclude a modest increase in injurious falls, falls that did not cause injury were not the reported outcome, and participants were ambulatory community volunteers — not the institutionalised frail elderly at highest falls risk.

cards.headline: Pajewski 2020: at age 80 and older there was no between-group difference in injurious falls, cardiovascular events and deaths fell, and kidney-function declines increased
cards.summary: Pajewski 2020: at age 80 and older there was no between-group difference in injurious falls, cardiovascular events and deaths fell, and kidney-function declines increased
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised trial (Pajewski 2020)
cards.people: Secondary analysis of SPRINT participants aged 80 years or older with hypertension but without diabetes (N = 1,167), randomised to a systolic target below 120 mm Hg versus below 140 mm Hg. Baseline cognition was measured with the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and gait speed with a 4-metre walk test.
cards.result: Intensive treatment reduced cardiovascular events (hazard ratio 0.66 [95% CI 0.49–0.90], relative), mortality (hazard ratio 0.67 [95% CI 0.48–0.93], relative) and mild cognitive impairment (hazard ratio 0.70 [95% CI 0.51–0.96], relative). There was no between-group difference in the rate of injurious falls — the record gives no falls effect size or event counts, printed here plainly. Rates of acute kidney injury and declines of at least 30% in estimated glomerular filtration rate were increased in the intensive group. Benefit on the cardiovascular/mortality composite was strong in participants with higher baseline MoCA scores (hazard ratio 0.40 [95% CI 0.28–0.57]) and absent in those with lower scores (hazard ratio 1.33 [95% CI 0.87–2.03]; interaction P < .001); gait speed did not modify the effect.
cards.watchOut: A secondary analysis of the oldest trial volunteers: 'no difference in injurious falls' without a printed effect size is weaker reassurance than a measured null, and the cognition interaction warns that the least robust patients may gain least while still carrying the kidney risk.

Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2020. PMID: 31840813. Registry ID: NCT01206062.
