secondary analysis of a randomised trial (pajewski 2020) secondary analysis of sprint participants aged 80 years or older with hypertension but without diabetes (n = 1,167), randomised to a systolic target below 120 mm hg versus below 140 mm hg. baseline cognition was measured with the montreal cognitive assessment (moca) and gait speed with a 4-metre walk test. intensive treatment reduced cardiovascular events (hazard ratio 0.66 [95% ci 0.49–0.90], relative), mortality (hazard ratio 0.67 [95% ci 0.48–0.93], relative) and mild cognitive impairment (hazard ratio 0.70 [95% ci 0.51–0.96], relative). there was no between-group difference in the rate of injurious falls — the record gives no falls effect size or event counts, printed here plainly. rates of acute kidney injury and declines of at least 30% in estimated glomerular filtration rate were increased in the intensive group. benefit on the cardiovascular/mortality composite was strong in participants with higher baseline moca scores (hazard ratio 0.40 [95% ci 0.28–0.57]) and absent in those with lower scores (hazard ratio 1.33 [95% ci 0.87–2.03]; interaction p < .001); gait speed did not modify the effect. a secondary analysis of the oldest trial volunteers: 'no difference in injurious falls' without a printed effect size is weaker reassurance than a measured null, and the cognition interaction warns that the least robust patients may gain least while still carrying the kidney risk. pajewski nm et al. intensive vs standard blood pressure control in adults 80 years or older: a secondary analysis of the systolic blood pressure intervention trial. journal of the american geriatrics society. 2020. pmid: 31840813. registry id: nct01206062. mesh: acute kidney injury · aged, 80 and over · blood pressure · cardiovascular diseases · cognitive dysfunction · female · humans · hypertension · incidence · male · mental status and dementia tests · randomized controlled trials as topic

cards.headline: Weiss 2017: across 21 randomised trials in adults 60 and older, lower blood-pressure targets did not increase falls or cognitive impairment (low- to moderate-strength evidence) — and data in frail elderly adults were explicitly limited
cards.summary: Weiss 2017: across 21 randomised trials in adults 60 and older, lower blood-pressure targets did not increase falls or cognitive impairment (low- to moderate-strength evidence) — and data in frail elderly adults were explicitly limited
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis for the US Department of Veterans Affairs: 21 randomised controlled trials comparing blood-pressure targets or treatment intensity in adults aged 60 years or older, plus 3 observational studies assessing harms.
cards.result: Nine trials gave high-strength evidence that control to under 150/90 mm Hg reduces mortality (relative risk 0.90 [95% CI 0.83–0.98]), cardiac events (relative risk 0.77 [95% CI 0.68–0.89]) and stroke (relative risk 0.74 [95% CI 0.65–0.84]) — all relative measures. Six trials gave low- to moderate-strength evidence that lower targets were associated with marginally significant decreases in cardiac events and stroke. Low- to moderate-strength evidence showed that lower blood-pressure targets do not increase falls or cognitive impairment — the record reports this as a graded conclusion and gives no pooled falls effect size, printed here plainly. Lower targets were associated with hypotension, syncope and greater medication burden, and the authors state that data relevant to frail elderly adults and multimorbidity are limited.
cards.watchOut: The falls reassurance is a graded conclusion over heterogeneous trials, most of which did not enrol frail patients; the review itself flags the frail-elderly evidence gap that this shelf's question asks about.

cards.headline: Synthesis: no increase in falls was detected with intensive lowering in any carded report — injurious falls 4.9% versus 5.5% at age 75+, no difference at age 80+, no frailty interaction for serious adverse events, and no falls increase across 21 trials — in ambulatory trial populations
cards.summary: Synthesis: no increase in falls was detected with intensive lowering in any carded report — injurious falls 4.9% versus 5.5% at age 75+, no difference at age 80+, no frailty interaction for serious adverse events, and no falls increase across 21 trials — in ambulatory trial populations
cards.people: The carded evidence: three reports from one trial programme (SPRINT: 9,306 participants in the frailty analysis, including the 2,636 participants aged 75+ and the 1,167 aged 80+ — overlapping subsets of the same cohort, not additive) and one systematic review of 21 trials in adults 60 and older. Unique-participant totals therefore cannot be summed across cards; the trial cohort alone is 9,306, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: Injurious falls were 4.9% with intensive versus 5.5% with standard treatment at age 75 and older (hazard ratio 0.91, relative; Williamson 2016), with no between-group difference at age 80 and older (Pajewski 2020). Frailty did not significantly modify the risk of serious adverse events with intensive treatment (Wang 2023), and a 21-trial review concluded lower targets do not increase falls (Weiss 2017). The harms that did increase were hypotension, electrolyte abnormalities and kidney-function decline. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (no increase in falls detected) — one trial programme plus a concordant review; the frailest and institutionalised elderly were not represented.
cards.watchOut: Every falls-reassuring number comes from ambulatory volunteers in trials; a patient who is frail, institutionalised, or already falling is outside the population that generated this evidence, and the confidence interval at age 75+ still allows a modest relative increase in injurious falls.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wang Z et al. Circulation. 2023 (PMID: 37401465); Williamson JD et al. JAMA. 2016 (PMID: 27195814); Pajewski NM et al. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2020 (PMID: 31840813); Weiss J et al. Annals of internal medicine. 2017 (PMID: 28114673).

shelves.title: Deprescribing antihypertensives in frail elderly patients: no increase in cardiovascular events has been demonstrated — but the evidence is weak, imprecise, and thinnest in the frail long-term-care setting itself
shelves.question: Does deprescribing antihypertensives in frail elderly increase cardiovascular events?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Humans · Antihypertensive Agents · Bias · Cardiovascular Diseases · Hypertension · Primary Prevention · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Stroke · Withholding Treatment
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no increase in cardiovascular events has been demonstrated after supervised antihypertensive deprescribing, but the evidence is too small and imprecise to exclude one, and it is thinnest exactly where this question points: frail elderly patients. The Cochrane pool (6 trials, 1,073 participants) found little to no difference in mortality, stroke or hospitalisation with very wide intervals and low-to-very-low certainty (Gnjidic 2025). In TONE, cardiovascular event rates were flat before, during/after and after resumption of withdrawn therapy (5.5, 5.5 and 6.8 per 100 person-years; Kostis 1998), while withdrawal raised systolic pressure by about 5 mmHg and symptoms clustered during withdrawal (Juraschek 2022). In long-term care, the frailest setting, three randomised studies (1,548 residents) could not be pooled; mortality hazard ratios were 1.02 and 1.65 in the two reporting trials and cardiovascular events were sparsely measured (Jiang 2026). The large modern deprescribing trial programme in patients aged 80 and older is homed on live shelf #132; this shelf cards the wider withdrawal literature and the long-term-care synthesis that speak to frailty and to cardiovascular events specifically. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): deprescribing under supervision, with monitoring and restart rules, has not been shown to increase cardiovascular events — an absence of demonstrated harm on weak evidence, not proof of safety.

cards.headline: Gnjidic 2025 (Cochrane): discontinuing antihypertensives versus continuing showed little to no difference in mortality, stroke or hospitalisation across 6 small trials (1,073 participants) — but certainty was low to very low and myocardial infarction was very uncertain
cards.summary: Gnjidic 2025 (Cochrane): discontinuing antihypertensives versus continuing showed little to no difference in mortality, stroke or hospitalisation across 6 small trials (1,073 participants) — but certainty was low to very low and myocardial infarction was very uncertain
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials (Gnjidic 2025)
cards.people: 2025 Cochrane update: 6 randomised trials of withdrawal or dose reduction versus continuation of antihypertensive medication in older adults (defined as 50 years and over; community, residential aged care and hospital settings), 1,073 participants in total, with follow-up from 4 to 56 weeks. No new studies were found for this update.
cards.result: Discontinuing antihypertensives may result in little to no difference in all-cause mortality (Peto odds ratio 2.08 [95% CI 0.79 to 5.46], a relative measure; 4 studies, 630 participants; low certainty), hospitalisation (odds ratio 0.83 [95% CI 0.33 to 2.10]; 1 study, 385 participants; low certainty) and stroke (odds ratio 1.44 [95% CI 0.25 to 8.35]; 3 studies, 524 participants; low certainty). The evidence is very uncertain about myocardial infarction (odds ratio 1.86 [95% CI 0.19 to 17.98]; 2 studies, 447 participants; very low certainty). Blood pressure was higher after discontinuation (systolic mean difference 9.75 mmHg [95% CI 7.33 to 12.18]; diastolic 3.5 mmHg [95% CI 1.82 to 5.18]). No studies reported falls. The reviewers conclude that firm conclusions cannot be drawn and that future research should focus on people with frailty, older age and polypharmacy.
cards.watchOut: The point estimates for mortality and infarction sit above 1 with very wide intervals: 'little to no difference' is the reviewers' low-certainty grading, not a measured exclusion of harm, and none of the six trials was a frail-elderly cardiovascular-outcome trial.

cards.headline: Kostis 1998 (TONE): cardiovascular event rates were the same before, during/after and after resumption of withdrawn antihypertensive therapy — 5.5, 5.5 and 6.8 events per 100 person-years in the non-overweight group
cards.summary: Kostis 1998 (TONE): cardiovascular event rates were the same before, during/after and after resumption of withdrawn antihypertensive therapy — 5.5, 5.5 and 6.8 events per 100 person-years in the non-overweight group
cards.people: Cardiovascular-events analysis of the TONE randomised trial: 975 older participants whose blood pressure was under 145/85 mm Hg on a single antihypertensive drug; 886 entered the drug-withdrawal phase and 774 were successfully withdrawn, with blood pressure maintained by weight loss and/or sodium reduction where assigned.
cards.result: Thirty-three cardiovascular events (stroke, transient ischaemic attack, myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, heart failure, angina and others) occurred between randomisation and withdrawal (median 3.6 months), 57 during or after withdrawal (14.0 months) and 36 after resumption of therapy (15.9 months). Event rates per 100 person-years were 5.5, 5.5 and 6.8 across the three periods in the non-overweight group (P = 0.84) and 7.2, 5.2 and 5.6 in the overweight group (P = 0.08) — withdrawal was not followed by a rise in events. The authors conclude medication could be safely withdrawn in older persons without clinical cardiovascular disease whose diastolic pressure at withdrawal was not 150/90 mm Hg or above, provided good control was maintained non-pharmacologically.
cards.watchOut: TONE participants were selected, controlled on one drug, and supported by structured lifestyle intervention — the opposite end of the spectrum from frail patients with multimorbidity, and withdrawal was reversed whenever blood pressure rose, which is what kept event rates flat.
cards.source: Kostis JB et al. Does withdrawal of antihypertensive medication increase the risk of cardiovascular events? Trial of Nonpharmacologic Interventions in the Elderly (TONE) Cooperative Research Group. The American journal of cardiology. 1998. PMID: 9874055. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Jiang 2026: in long-term care — the frailest setting — three randomised deprescribing studies (1,548 residents) could not be pooled; mortality hazard ratios were 1.02 in RETREAT-FRAIL and 1.65 in DANTON, and cardiovascular-event evidence was sparse
cards.summary: Jiang 2026: in long-term care — the frailest setting — three randomised deprescribing studies (1,548 residents) could not be pooled; mortality hazard ratios were 1.02 in RETREAT-FRAIL and 1.65 in DANTON, and cardiovascular-event evidence was sparse
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised evidence in long-term care (Jiang 2026)
cards.people: Systematic review of randomised and cluster-randomised studies of planned antihypertensive deprescribing in institutional long-term care: 3 studies involving 1,548 residents, whose populations, deprescribing strategies, monitoring, restart criteria and follow-up differed substantially, so no outcome was considered comparable enough for meta-analysis.
cards.result: RETREAT-FRAIL reported an adjusted hazard ratio for all-cause mortality of 1.02 (95% CI 0.86–1.21, a relative measure) over a median potential follow-up of 38.4 months, whereas DANTON reported a hazard ratio of 1.65 (95% CI 0.95–2.85) to 32 weeks; the third study had no cluster-adjusted comparative mortality estimate. In DANTON at 16 weeks, deprescribing increased systolic blood pressure by 11.0 mmHg (95% CI 5.6–16.4) and reduced the number of antihypertensive drugs by 1.2 (95% CI 1.0–1.4). Evidence for hospitalisation, falls, cardiovascular events, cognition, function and quality of life remained sparse, outcome-specific or at risk of bias, and the reviewers conclude the evidence does not establish a common effect on mortality, hospitalisation or other resident-important outcomes.
cards.watchOut: This is the only carded synthesis set in genuinely frail, institutionalised residents, and it is also the least reassuring: one of its two mortality estimates (DANTON, hazard ratio 1.65) points toward harm with an interval that includes substantial harm, and cardiovascular events specifically were barely measured.

cards.headline: Juraschek 2022 (TONE): withdrawal itself raised systolic pressure by 4.59 mmHg and adverse events clustered during withdrawal — sodium reduction alone increased adverse-event risk (hazard ratio 1.75, relative)
cards.summary: Juraschek 2022 (TONE): withdrawal itself raised systolic pressure by 4.59 mmHg and adverse events clustered during withdrawal — sodium reduction alone increased adverse-event risk (hazard ratio 1.75, relative)
cards.people: Longer-term adverse-event analysis of the TONE trial: 975 participants aged 60–80 years (mean age 66 years; 48% women) on a single antihypertensive with blood pressure under 145/85 mm Hg, randomised to weight loss, sodium reduction, both or neither, with the antihypertensive withdrawn about 3 months after randomisation and restored only if hypertension became uncontrolled; follow-up to 36 months. Adverse events were adjudicated by two masked physicians as symptomatic (lightheadedness, dizziness, vertigo) or clinical (fall, fracture, syncope).
cards.result: Independent of assignment, drug withdrawal increased systolic blood pressure by 4.59 mmHg (95% CI 3.89–5.28) compared with baseline. There were 113 adverse events (84 symptomatic, 29 clinical), primarily during withdrawal. Combined weight loss and sodium reduction mitigated the blood-pressure rise (β = −4.33 mmHg [95% CI −6.48 to −2.17]) and reduced orthostatic symptoms long term (odds ratio 0.62 [95% CI 0.41–0.92], relative) without affecting adverse events (hazard ratio 1.81 [95% CI 0.90–3.65], relative). Sodium reduction alone increased the risk of adverse events (hazard ratio 1.75 [95% CI 1.04–2.95], relative), mainly during withdrawal. The authors conclude that withdrawal may increase symptomatic adverse events and needs caution.
cards.watchOut: Same TONE cohort as the Kostis card — the two cards are two reports of one trial, not two trials — and its adverse events are mostly symptoms during the withdrawal window rather than cardiovascular events, so it informs how to deprescribe safely, not whether events rise.
cards.source: Juraschek SP et al. Effects of Antihypertensive Deprescribing Strategies on Blood Pressure, Adverse Events, and Orthostatic Symptoms in Older Adults: Results From TONE. cards.headline: Synthesis: no increase in cardiovascular events has been demonstrated after supervised deprescribing — event rates were flat across TONE's withdrawal periods and pooled trial differences were null — but every estimate is imprecise and the frailest-setting data are the thinnest
cards.summary: Synthesis: no increase in cardiovascular events has been demonstrated after supervised deprescribing — event rates were flat across TONE's withdrawal periods and pooled trial differences were null — but every estimate is imprecise and the frailest-setting data are the thinnest
cards.people: The carded evidence: a Cochrane pool of 6 small withdrawal trials (1,073 participants), two reports of the single TONE trial (975 participants, counted once), and a long-term-care review of 3 randomised studies (1,548 residents). Review pools overlap the individual trials, so totals are not summed; each component exceeds 30 participants and no small-N labelling applies — the limitation is imprecision and short follow-up, not tiny samples alone.
cards.result: TONE's cardiovascular event rates did not rise during or after withdrawal (5.5 per 100 person-years before versus 5.5 during/after; Kostis 1998). The Cochrane meta-analysis found little to no difference in mortality, stroke or hospitalisation, with very wide intervals (mortality odds ratio 2.08 [95% CI 0.79–5.46], relative; Gnjidic 2025). In long-term care, mortality hazard ratios were 1.02 (RETREAT-FRAIL) and 1.65 (DANTON), unpooled, with cardiovascular events sparsely reported (Jiang 2026). Withdrawal reliably raises blood pressure (about +5 to +11 mmHg systolic across reports) and symptoms cluster in the withdrawal window (Juraschek 2022). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): no demonstrated increase in cardiovascular events, on evidence too imprecise to exclude one.
cards.watchOut: All of the reassuring trials deprescribed under supervision, in selected patients, with restart rules and short follow-up; none was powered for cardiovascular events in frail elderly patients, so the honest claim is 'no increase demonstrated', never 'proven safe'.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gnjidic D et al. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2025 (PMID: 40162571); Kostis JB et al. The American journal of cardiology. 1998 (PMID: 9874055); Jiang G et al. Drugs & aging. 2026 (PMID: 42888381); Juraschek SP et al. American journal of hypertension. 2022 (PMID: 34718403).

shelves.title: Hip protectors in nursing homes (SPLIT): pooled and cluster-trial evidence suggests fewer hip fractures, but the two individually randomised trials — including HIP PRO's within-person test — found the treatment made no difference
shelves.question: In older adults, does hip protector use reduce hip fractures in nursing home residents versus no hip protectors?
shelves.mesh: Aged, 80 and over · Female · Hip Fractures · Homes for the Aged · Humans · Male · Nursing Homes · Protective Clothing
shelves.balance: SPLIT (cluster/pooled evidence: benefit; individually randomised evidence: the treatment made no difference) — hip protectors in nursing homes are a genuinely divided evidence base, and the divide follows study design. The pooled Bayesian estimate over 4 nursing-home trials is an odds ratio of 0.40 (relative; Sawka 2007) and the Hamburg cluster trial that raised wearing from 15% to 68% of fallers recorded 4.6% versus 8.1% hip fractures (relative risk 0.57, relative; P = 0.072; Meyer 2003). Against that, the two trials that randomised the pad itself found nothing: HIP PRO, comparing each resident's protected hip with their own unprotected hip in 1,042 residents with 73.8% adherence, recorded 3.1% versus 2.5% (the treatment made no difference; Kiel 2007), and Cameron 2001 recorded 8 versus 7 fractures (hazard ratio 1.46, relative). The library's umbrella hip-protector shelf, including the large Finnish cluster trial and the Cochrane review, is homed on live shelf #606; this shelf cards the nursing-home trials and their pooled analysis that frame the split. Adherence is the hinge throughout: no fracture in Cameron's trial happened while a protector was worn as directed, yet high supported adherence in HIP PRO still produced no benefit. PROPOSED SPLIT: whether hip protectors reduce hip fractures in nursing-home residents depends on which design you believe — programme-level provision may help; the pad's own measured effect in individually randomised trials is null.

cards.headline: Kiel 2007 (HIP PRO): hip fractures occurred on 3.1% of protected hips versus 2.5% of unprotected hips in the same residents (the treatment made no difference), despite 73.8% adherence
cards.summary: Kiel 2007 (HIP PRO): hip fractures occurred on 3.1% of protected hips versus 2.5% of unprotected hips in the same residents (the treatment made no difference), despite 73.8% adherence
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, within-person design (Kiel 2007, HIP PRO)
cards.people: Multicentre randomised trial in 37 nursing homes in Boston, St Louis and Baltimore: 1,042 residents (mean age 85 years; 79% women) who consented and adhered during a 2-week run-in were randomised by facility to wear a one-sided hip protector on the left or right hip, so each resident's protected hip was compared with their own unprotected hip. Mean participation 7.8 months; facilities were visited 3 times per week to support adherence.
cards.result: After 20 months of follow-up (676 person-years), the trial was terminated for lack of efficacy. The incidence of hip fracture on protected versus unprotected hips did not differ (3.1% [95% CI 1.8%–4.4%] versus 2.5% [95% CI 1.3%–3.7%]; P = .70) — the treatment made no difference. Among the 334 residents with over 80% adherence, fracture incidence also did not differ (5.3% versus 3.5%; P = .42). Overall adherence was 73.8%, and no participant was withdrawn because of adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: The within-person design removes resident-level confounding and adherence was supported and measured — which is why this null carries weight — but a one-sided protector trial cannot detect any benefit that works by changing staff behaviour or fall patterns across a whole home.
cards.source: Kiel DP et al. Efficacy of a hip protector to prevent hip fracture in nursing home residents: the HIP PRO randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2007. PMID: 17652295. cards.headline: Meyer 2003: an education programme that raised protector use from 15% to 68% of fallers was followed by fewer hip fractures (4.6% versus 8.1%; relative risk 0.57, relative), but the difference was not significant (P = 0.072)
cards.summary: Meyer 2003: an education programme that raised protector use from 15% to 68% of fallers was followed by fewer hip fractures (4.6% versus 8.1%; relative risk 0.57, relative), but the difference was not significant (P = 0.072)
cards.people: Cluster randomised trial in 49 nursing homes in Hamburg (25 intervention clusters, 24 control): 942 residents at high risk of falling (459 intervention, 483 control). The intervention was a single education session for nursing staff, who then educated residents, plus three free hip protectors per resident; control homes received brief information and two demonstration protectors per cluster. Mean follow-up 15 versus 14 months.
cards.result: There were 21 hip fractures in 21 residents (4.6%) in the intervention group and 42 fractures in 39 residents (8.1%) in the control group (relative risk 0.57, a relative measure; absolute risk difference −3.5% [95% CI −7.3% to 0.3%]; P = 0.072). After adjustment for cluster randomisation, the proportions of fallers wearing a protector were 68% versus 15% (mean difference 53% [95% CI 38% to 67%]; P = 0.0001). Other fractures were similar (39 versus 38). The authors conclude the programme increases protector use and may reduce hip fractures.
cards.watchOut: The randomised unit was the home and the intervention was education plus free provision, so any benefit may belong to the programme (staff attention, fall awareness) rather than the pad itself; the fracture difference also misses conventional significance and 167 versus 207 residents died or moved away during follow-up.
cards.source: Meyer G et al. Effect on hip fractures of increased use of hip protectors in nursing homes: cluster randomised controlled trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2003. PMID: 12521969. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cameron 2001: 8 hip fractures with protectors versus 7 without (hazard ratio 1.46, relative) in 174 high-risk women — the treatment made no difference, in a trial too small to exclude a 50% relative reduction; no fracture occurred while a protector was worn as directed
cards.summary: Cameron 2001: 8 hip fractures with protectors versus 7 without (hazard ratio 1.46, relative) in 174 high-risk women — the treatment made no difference, in a trial too small to exclude a 50% relative reduction; no fracture occurred while a protector was worn as directed
cards.people: Individually randomised trial in 32 residential aged-care facilities in urban New South Wales, Australia (two-thirds nursing homes): 174 women aged 75 years or older (mean age 85) who had had two or more falls, or one fall requiring hospital admission, in the previous 3 months; 86 were allocated hip protectors with nurse encouragement and 88 to control. Participants had severe disability and major cognitive impairment on average (mean Barthel index 58).
cards.result: A mean of 4.6 falls per person occurred during follow-up. Eight hip fractures occurred in the intervention group and seven in the control group (hazard ratio 1.46 [95% CI 0.53–4.51], a relative measure) — the treatment made no difference. No hip fractures occurred when hip protectors were being worn as directed; adherence was about 57% overall and protectors were worn at the time of 54% of falls. Mortality was identical (28 deaths in each group). The authors note low statistical power: a reduction in hip-fracture risk of up to 50% (relative) may not have been detected.
cards.watchOut: Fifteen fractures in total cannot settle efficacy either way; the 'no fracture while worn' observation is compatible with the pad working when worn and with chance, and adherence varied markedly between institutions (best about 80%).
cards.source: Cameron ID et al. Hip protectors in aged-care facilities: a randomized trial of use by individual higher-risk residents. Age and ageing. 2001. PMID: 11742776. cards.headline: Sawka 2007: pooling the nursing-home trials the Bayesian way gave an odds ratio of 0.40 (95% credibility interval 0.25–0.61, relative) for hip fracture with protector allocation — a pooled benefit the individually randomised trials do not show
cards.summary: Sawka 2007: pooling the nursing-home trials the Bayesian way gave an odds ratio of 0.40 (95% credibility interval 0.25–0.61, relative) for hip fracture with protector allocation — a pooled benefit the individually randomised trials do not show
cards.people: Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis designed to pool cluster-randomised with individually randomised trials of hip protectors in nursing homes: 4 trials of 1,922 nursing-home residents, including three cluster-randomised trials.
cards.result: The pooled mean odds ratio of an elderly nursing-home resident sustaining one or more hip fractures with hip-protector allocation was 0.40 (95% credibility interval 0.25–0.61), a relative measure. The model was robust in sensitivity analyses assuming alternative intracluster correlation values. The authors themselves caution that methodological limitations of the included trials and a possible herd effect in the cluster trials may have influenced the results.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate leans heavily on cluster trials — including the large Finnish cluster trial homed on live shelf #606 — in which whole homes changed behaviour together; when the pad itself is randomised within or between individuals, the benefit disappears (Kiel 2007; Cameron 2001).
cards.source: Sawka AM et al. Hip protectors decrease hip fracture risk in elderly nursing home residents: a Bayesian meta-analysis. Journal of clinical epidemiology. 2007. PMID: 17346606. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.people: The carded evidence: two individually randomised nursing-home trials (1,042 and 174 residents), one cluster-randomised education-and-provision trial (942 residents), and a Bayesian meta-analysis of 4 trials (1,922 residents) that overlaps the primary trials, so totals are not summed. No small-N labelling applies to the shelf as a whole; the smallest trial's N (174) and its 15 fractures are printed on its card face.
cards.result: Hip fracture incidence was 3.1% on protected versus 2.5% on unprotected hips in HIP PRO (the treatment made no difference; Kiel 2007) and 8 versus 7 fractures in Cameron 2001 (hazard ratio 1.46, relative). The cluster trial that raised wearing from 15% to 68% of fallers recorded 4.6% versus 8.1% fractures (relative risk 0.57, relative; P = 0.072; Meyer 2003), and pooling gave an odds ratio of 0.40 (Sawka 2007). Adherence is the hinge in every report: no fracture in Cameron's trial occurred while a protector was worn as directed, yet even 73.8% supported adherence in HIP PRO produced no benefit. cards.watchOut: A shelf that quoted only the pooled odds ratio would mislead: the split tracks study design, not chance alone, and the most rigorous design for the pad's own effect — randomising hips within the same resident — is the one that found nothing.

shelves.title: Stopping benzodiazepines in older adults (weak evidence): cognition and balance measures improve after withdrawal in small uncontrolled studies, but no carded study has counted falls after benzodiazepine-only discontinuation
shelves.question: Does stopping benzodiazepines improve cognition and reduce falls in older adults?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cognition · Female · Flicker Fusion · Flurazepam · Geriatric Assessment · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives · Male · Neuropsychological Tests · Postural Balance · Sleep · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the cognition half of this question has small, uncontrolled, favourable evidence; the falls half has none in the carded set. After tapering off benzodiazepine hypnotics, nursing-home completers improved in postural sway and in immediate memory, language and attention scores, without subjective sleep worsening (Tsunoda 2010; 30 enrolled, 26 completers). In 89 older outpatients, grip strength improved within 3 weeks of starting withdrawal and balance from the first week (Nurminen 2014). Stopping is achievable — tapering achieved 62% discontinuation versus 21% on usual care, with no change in psychological functioning either way (Voshaar 2003) — and a 2025 review of 16 deprescribing studies confirms cessation is common while reporting no pooled falls or cognition effects, because the studies largely did not measure them (McEvoy 2025). The library's randomised trial of gradual psychotropic-medication withdrawal and falls is homed on live shelf #1490, and the big education-to-stop trials are homed on live shelf #500; this shelf cards the outcome studies for cognition and balance specifically. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): stopping benzodiazepines probably improves daytime cognition and balance measures in older adults; a reduction in falls themselves is plausible but unproven in this evidence.

cards.headline: Tsunoda 2010: after tapering off benzodiazepine hypnotics, 26 nursing-home completers (N = 30 enrolled, printed on the face) improved in postural sway and in immediate memory, language and attention scores — an uncontrolled 8-week study
cards.summary: Tsunoda 2010: after tapering off benzodiazepine hypnotics, 26 nursing-home completers (N = 30 enrolled, printed on the face) improved in postural sway and in immediate memory, language and attention scores — an uncontrolled 8-week study
cards.people: Open-label study in a nursing home: 30 residents aged 60 or older (mean age 79.1 ± 8.9 years) receiving a benzodiazepine as a hypnotic (mean flurazepam-equivalent dose 19.5 ± 10.9 mg/day), tapered off over 3 weeks and assessed at baseline and at 8 weeks. Diagnoses were schizophrenia (n = 12), primary insomnia (n = 9), dementia (n = 7) and bipolar disorder (n = 2); 26 participants completed.
cards.result: In the 26 completers, significant changes were found in total length and range of trunk motion with eyes closed on the stabilometric platform (postural sway), and significant improvements were observed in the Critical Flicker Fusion Test and in the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status immediate memory, language and attention index scores. Subjective worsening of sleep was not reported by completers on the Leeds Sleep Evaluation Questionnaire. The record reports these changes as significant without printing effect sizes or P values, which is stated here plainly rather than filled in. The authors conclude discontinuation is feasible in a majority of elderly persons and leads to improved body stability and recovery in cognitive functions during the daytime.
cards.watchOut: No control group, no randomisation, 26 completers with mixed psychiatric diagnoses: practice effects on repeated cognitive testing and spontaneous change over 8 weeks could produce the same picture, and falls themselves were not counted.
cards.source: Tsunoda K et al. Effects of discontinuing benzodiazepine-derivative hypnotics on postural sway and cognitive functions in the elderly. International journal of geriatric psychiatry. 2010. PMID: 20054834. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nurminen 2014: within 3 weeks of starting withdrawal from long-term hypnotics, handgrip strength improved (P ≤ 0.005) and balance began improving in 89 older outpatients — surrogate measures, not falls
cards.summary: Nurminen 2014: within 3 weeks of starting withdrawal from long-term hypnotics, handgrip strength improved (P ≤ 0.005) and balance began improving in 89 older outpatients — surrogate measures, not falls
cards.people: Withdrawal study in 89 chronic users (59 women, 30 men) aged 55 or older of temazepam, zopiclone or zolpidem as hypnotics, with individual physician-directed gradual withdrawal over 1 month and follow-up to 6 months. Withdrawal status was verified by plasma drug determinations at 4 weeks (69 short-term withdrawers, 20 non-withdrawers) and by interview at 6 months (34 long-term withdrawers, 55 non-withdrawers); most non-withdrawers also markedly reduced their use. Balance was measured with the Short Berg Balance Scale and grip with a handheld dynamometer.
cards.result: Within 3 weeks of initiating withdrawal, handgrip strength improved significantly compared with baseline (P ≤ 0.005). Among women, long-term withdrawers improved grip both against their own baseline (P = 0.001) and against non-withdrawers (P = 0.004); men improved against baseline (P = 0.002) without a significant withdrawer-versus-non-withdrawer difference. Balance improved from the first week after withdrawal initiation, but the difference between long-term withdrawers and non-withdrawers was only borderline (P = 0.054). Non-withdrawers also tended to improve as their use fell. The record reports P values without effect sizes for these outcomes, printed here plainly.
cards.watchOut: Grip and balance are falls-risk surrogates, not falls: nobody counted falls or fractures, withdrawers were self-selected by success, and the comparison group also cut down, which dilutes every contrast.
cards.source: Nurminen J et al. Handgrip strength and balance in older adults following withdrawal from long-term use of temazepam, zopiclone or zolpidem as hypnotics. BMC geriatrics. 2014. cards.headline: Voshaar 2003: tapering beat usual care for actually stopping (62% versus 21% successful discontinuation) in 180 long-term users — and neither stopping nor treatment type changed psychological functioning, for better or worse
cards.summary: Voshaar 2003: tapering beat usual care for actually stopping (62% versus 21% successful discontinuation) in 180 long-term users — and neither stopping nor treatment type changed psychological functioning, for better or worse
cards.people: Three-condition randomised trial in general practice: 180 people attempting to discontinue long-term benzodiazepine use, assigned to tapering off plus group cognitive-behavioural therapy, tapering off alone, or usual care, over 3 months with a 3-month controlled follow-up. Participants were long-term users across adult age groups (the record's indexing covers middle-aged and aged adults), not an elderly-only sample.
cards.result: Tapering off led to a significantly higher proportion of successful discontinuations than usual care (62% versus 21%); adding group cognitive-behavioural therapy did not increase the success rate (58% versus 62%). Neither successful discontinuation nor intervention type affected psychological functioning. Both tapering strategies were feasible in general practice.
cards.watchOut: Carded for what it can and cannot say: it proves stopping is achievable at scale without a psychological-functioning penalty, but it measured neither cognition with neuropsychological testing nor falls, and its population was not restricted to older adults.
cards.source: Voshaar RC et al. Tapering off long-term benzodiazepine use with or without group cognitive-behavioural therapy: three-condition, randomised controlled trial. The British journal of psychiatry : the journal of mental science. 2003. PMID: 12777340. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: McEvoy 2025: across 16 deprescribing studies, patient-directed interventions stopped benzodiazepine-receptor agonists in 9%–100% of participants — while clinical outcomes such as falls and cognition were the outcomes the literature largely did not report
cards.summary: McEvoy 2025: across 16 deprescribing studies, patient-directed interventions stopped benzodiazepine-receptor agonists in 9%–100% of participants — while clinical outcomes such as falls and cognition were the outcomes the literature largely did not report
cards.people: Systematic review (searches to January 2024) of patient-directed, non-pharmacological interventions to support deprescribing of benzodiazepine-receptor agonists used for insomnia in older adults (65 or older) and people with cognitive impairment: 17 reports analysing 16 studies in hospital, community and aged-care settings. Most studies were at high risk of bias.
cards.result: Cessation rates ranged from 23% to 72% for written education (6 studies), 14% to 57% for combined written and verbal education (5 studies) and 9% to 100% for multi-component interventions (6 studies). One report in people with cognitive impairment found comparable effectiveness to participants without impairment. The review's outcomes of interest included sleep and clinical outcomes, but its findings report cessation and reduction — the record does not report pooled effects on falls, fractures or cognition, because the underlying studies largely did not measure them, which is printed here plainly as the state of the evidence.
cards.watchOut: A review of how to stop, not of what stopping buys: its silence on falls and cognition outcomes is itself the finding, and it should never be cited as evidence that deprescribing improves either.
cards.source: McEvoy AM et al. Deprescribing Benzodiazepine Receptor Agonists in Older Adults and People With Cognitive Impairment: A Systematic Review. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2025. PMID: 40342014. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: cognition and balance surrogates improve after stopping in small uncontrolled studies, and stopping is achievable without psychological harm — but no carded study counted falls after benzodiazepine-only discontinuation, so the falls half of the question is untested in this evidence set
cards.summary: Synthesis: cognition and balance surrogates improve after stopping in small uncontrolled studies, and stopping is achievable without psychological harm — but no carded study counted falls after benzodiazepine-only discontinuation, so the falls half of the question is untested in this evidence set
cards.people: The carded evidence: one open-label nursing-home discontinuation study (30 enrolled, 26 completers; N on its face), one prospective withdrawal cohort (89 outpatients), one randomised tapering trial (180 long-term users, not elderly-only), and one systematic review of 16 deprescribing studies. Summed enrolment exceeds 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies to the shelf; the small individual Ns (30, 89) are printed on their card faces, and the binding limitation is design — no controlled falls or cognition outcome trial — rather than total N.
cards.result: After discontinuation, postural sway improved and immediate memory, language and attention scores improved in nursing-home completers (Tsunoda 2010); grip strength improved within 3 weeks of withdrawal and balance from the first week (Nurminen 2014). Tapering achieved discontinuation in 62% versus 21% on usual care without affecting psychological functioning (Voshaar 2003). The 2025 systematic review documents cessation success across 16 studies while reporting no pooled falls or cognition effects (McEvoy 2025). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): stopping benzodiazepines probably improves daytime cognition and balance measures in older adults; whether it reduces falls is unproven in the carded evidence.
cards.watchOut: The one randomised falls trial of psychotropic withdrawal in this library is homed on live shelf #1490 and is cross-pointed in this shelf's balance rather than re-carded; within this shelf, every favourable cognition/balance result comes from uncontrolled before–after measurement, where practice effects and regression to the mean point the same way as the hoped-for benefit.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tsunoda K et al. International journal of geriatric psychiatry. 2010 (PMID: 20054834); Nurminen J et al. BMC geriatrics. 2014 (PMID: 25416480); Voshaar RC et al. shelves.title: Leucine and muscle strength in older adults — SPLIT: leucine alone made no difference to strength in the randomised trials (meta-analysis of 17 trials and two long-term RCTs), while leucine combined with vitamin D improved handgrip strength
shelves.question: In older adults, does leucine-enriched protein supplementation improve muscle strength versus standard protein?
shelves.mesh: not captured from the record this session
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the split is named in the stamp. This is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1493 covers a leucine- and vitamin-D-enriched whey supplement in sarcopenic older adults for muscle mass and chair-stand outcomes; the uncovered slice carded here is muscle strength in older adults generally, across the leucine literature. For leucine on its own, the answer is a concordant null: the meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials (Guo 2022; 1,418 participants) found leucine-isolated supplementation had no effect on handgrip strength (weighted mean difference 1.23 kg, 95% CI −0.58 to 3.03; P = 0.183), leg press (−1.35 kg, 95% CI −7.46 to 4.77), or total lean mass (0.03 kg, 95% CI −0.51 to 0.57) — the treatment made no difference. The two long-term trials agree: 3 months of leucine 7.5 g/day in healthy elderly men (Verhoeven 2009; n = 30) and 6 months in elderly men with type 2 diabetes (Leenders 2011; n = 60) each found no change in muscle strength or mass versus placebo. The other half of the split: in the same meta-analysis, leucine-combined supplementation including vitamin D significantly improved handgrip strength (weighted mean difference 2.17 kg, 95% CI 0.24 to 4.10; P = 0.027) and gait speed (0.03 m/s, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.05) — a subgroup signal from combined formulations, not from leucine alone, and the enriched-whey version of that combination in sarcopenic patients homes on #1493. PROPOSED SPLIT: leucine alone does not improve muscle strength in older adults; leucine combined with vitamin D may.

cards.headline: Guo 2022: leucine alone made no difference to handgrip strength (WMD 1.23 kg, CI crossing zero) or leg press across 17 RCTs — but leucine combined with vitamin D improved handgrip by 2.17 kg
cards.summary: Guo 2022: leucine alone made no difference to handgrip strength (WMD 1.23 kg, CI crossing zero) or leg press across 17 RCTs — but leucine combined with vitamin D improved handgrip by 2.17 kg
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 randomised controlled trials (Guo 2022)
cards.people: 1,418 older adults in 17 randomised controlled trials of leucine supplementation (2009–2022), with sarcopenia-related outcomes including handgrip strength, total lean mass, gait speed, leg press, 6-minute walk, short physical performance battery, timed up-and-go, and 30-second chair-stand.
cards.result: Leucine-isolated supplementation showed no effect on total lean mass (weighted mean difference 0.03 kg, 95% CI −0.51 to 0.57; P = 0.917), handgrip strength (WMD 1.23 kg, 95% CI −0.58 to 3.03; P = 0.183), or leg press (WMD −1.35 kg, 95% CI −7.46 to 4.77; P = 0.666) — the treatment made no difference. However, leucine-combined supplementation including vitamin D showed a significant improvement in handgrip strength (WMD 2.17 kg, 95% CI 0.24 to 4.10; P = 0.027) and gait speed (WMD 0.03 m/s, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.05; P = 0.008). The authors conclude leucine-isolated supplementation did not improve muscle mass or strength, while the vitamin-D-containing combination benefited strength and performance.
cards.watchOut: The positive half of this card is a subgroup of combined-supplement trials (leucine plus vitamin D, often in whey protein), so the benefit cannot be attributed to leucine itself; the leucine-isolated analysis is the cleaner test of this shelf's question and it is null on every strength measure.
cards.source: Guo Y et al. The Effect of Leucine Supplementation on Sarcopenia-Related Measures in Older Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of 17 Randomized Controlled Trials. Frontiers in Nutrition. 2022. PMID: 35845777. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Verhoeven 2009: 3 months of leucine (7.5 g/day) in 30 healthy elderly men produced no change in muscle mass or strength versus placebo — the treatment made no difference
cards.summary: Verhoeven 2009: 3 months of leucine (7.5 g/day) in 30 healthy elderly men produced no change in muscle mass or strength versus placebo — the treatment made no difference
cards.people: 30 healthy elderly men (mean age 71 ± 4 years; body mass index 26.1 ± 0.5 kg/m2) randomised to leucine 2.5 g with each main meal (n = 15) or placebo (n = 15) for 3 months; muscle strength was measured as one-repetition maximum and muscle mass by computed tomography and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry.
cards.result: No changes in skeletal muscle mass or strength were observed over time in either the leucine- or placebo-supplemented group, and there were no improvements in whole-body insulin sensitivity, glycated haemoglobin, or plasma lipids. The authors conclude that long-term leucine supplementation (7.5 g/day) does not augment skeletal muscle mass or strength and does not improve glycaemic control or the blood lipid profile in healthy elderly men.
cards.watchOut: Healthy, adequately nourished men are the population least likely to show a supplement effect, and 30 participants cannot exclude a small benefit — but the result matches the pooled null on the meta-analysis card, and this trial is one of the few testing leucine alone rather than an enriched formula.
cards.source: Verhoeven S et al. Long-term leucine supplementation does not increase muscle mass or strength in healthy elderly men. The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2009. PMID: 19321567. cards.headline: Leenders 2011: 6 months of leucine (7.5 g/day) in 60 elderly men with type 2 diabetes likewise made no difference to muscle mass, strength, or glycaemic control
cards.summary: Leenders 2011: 6 months of leucine (7.5 g/day) in 60 elderly men with type 2 diabetes likewise made no difference to muscle mass, strength, or glycaemic control
cards.people: 60 elderly males with type 2 diabetes (age 71 ± 1 years; body mass index 27.3 ± 0.4 kg/m2) given 2.5 g leucine (n = 30) or placebo (n = 30) with each main meal for 6 months (7.5 g/day); body composition, muscle fibre characteristics, muscle strength, and glucose homeostasis were assessed before, during, and after the intervention.
cards.result: Lean tissue mass did not change or differ between groups (leucine group 61.9, 62.2 and 62.0 kg at 0, 3 and 6 months; placebo group 62.2 kg at all three points), and there were no changes in body fat percentage, muscle strength, or muscle fibre type characteristics. Glycated haemoglobin did not change or differ (7.1% leucine vs 7.2% placebo). The authors conclude prolonged leucine supplementation does not modulate body composition, muscle mass, strength, or glycaemic control in elderly type 2 diabetes patients who habitually consume adequate dietary protein.
cards.watchOut: The authors' own qualifier matters: participants habitually consumed adequate dietary protein, so the trial tests leucine added on top of sufficiency — it does not answer whether leucine-enriched protein helps older adults whose baseline protein intake is low, a population the carded trials barely touch.
cards.source: Leenders M et al. Prolonged leucine supplementation does not augment muscle mass or affect glycemic control in elderly type 2 diabetic men. The Journal of Nutrition. 2011. randomised controlled trial (leenders 2011) 60 elderly males with type 2 diabetes (age 71 ± 1 years; body mass index 27.3 ± 0.4 kg/m2) given 2.5 g leucine (n = 30) or placebo (n = 30) with each main meal for 6 months (7.5 g/day); body composition, muscle fibre characteristics, muscle strength, and glucose homeostasis were assessed before, during, and after the intervention. lean tissue mass did not change or differ between groups (leucine group 61.9, 62.2 and 62.0 kg at 0, 3 and 6 months; placebo group 62.2 kg at all three points), and there were no changes in body fat percentage, muscle strength, or muscle fibre type characteristics. glycated haemoglobin did not change or differ (7.1% leucine vs 7.2% placebo). the authors conclude prolonged leucine supplementation does not modulate body composition, muscle mass, strength, or glycaemic control in elderly type 2 diabetes patients who habitually consume adequate dietary protein. the authors' own qualifier matters: participants habitually consumed adequate dietary protein, so the trial tests leucine added on top of sufficiency — it does not answer whether leucine-enriched protein helps older adults whose baseline protein intake is low, a population the carded trials barely touch. leenders m et al. prolonged leucine supplementation does not augment muscle mass or affect glycemic control in elderly type 2 diabetic men. the journal of nutrition. 2011. pmid: 21525248. registry id: nct00643773. mesh: aged · aging/pathology,physiology · amino acids/blood · blood glucose/metabolism · body composition/drug effects · diabetes mellitus, type 2/blood,diet therapy,pathology,physiopathology · dietary supplements · humans · leucine/administration & dosage · lipids/blood · male · muscle strength/drug effects · muscle, skeletal/drug effects,pathology,physiopathology

cards.headline: Synthesis: leucine alone does not improve muscle strength in older adults (pooled null plus two null long-term trials); the only positive signal belongs to leucine combined with vitamin D
cards.summary: Synthesis: leucine alone does not improve muscle strength in older adults (pooled null plus two null long-term trials); the only positive signal belongs to leucine combined with vitamin D
cards.people: The carded evidence: a meta-analysis of 17 randomised trials (1,418 participants) and two long-term placebo-controlled leucine-alone trials (30 healthy elderly men; 60 elderly men with type 2 diabetes). Total carded participants exceed 1,400, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Leucine-isolated supplementation: handgrip WMD 1.23 kg (95% CI −0.58 to 3.03), leg press WMD −1.35 kg, lean mass WMD 0.03 kg — all null (Guo 2022). Verhoeven 2009 and Leenders 2011 each found no strength or mass change over 3–6 months. Leucine combined with vitamin D: handgrip WMD 2.17 kg (95% CI 0.24 to 4.10) and gait speed WMD 0.03 m/s (Guo 2022 subgroup). PROPOSED SPLIT (leucine alone: no benefit; leucine combined with vitamin D: possible benefit).
cards.watchOut: The enriched-whey, sarcopenia-specific version of the combination question homes on live shelf #1493 (mass and chair-stand outcomes) and is cross-pointed, not re-carded; this shelf's null applies to leucine as the added ingredient in generally older, adequately nourished adults.
cards.source: Synthesis of Guo Y et al. Frontiers in Nutrition. 2022 (PMID: 35845777); Verhoeven S et al. The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2009 (PMID: 19321567); Leenders M et al. The Journal of Nutrition. 2011 (PMID: 21525248).

shelves.title: High-protein diet and muscle preservation in sarcopenic obesity (SPLIT): enriched protein supplements preserved muscle during weight loss, but a high-protein diet alone showed no significant effect in its factorial trial — a partial completion of pack #5126
shelves.question: In adults with sarcopenic obesity, does high-protein hypocaloric diet preserve muscle during weight loss versus standard calorie restriction?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Body Composition · Body Mass Index · Body Weight · Diet, Reducing · Dietary Proteins · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Energy Intake · Female · Hand Strength · Humans · Leucine · Male · Middle Aged · Milk Proteins · Motor Activity · Muscle Strength · Muscle, Skeletal · Obesity · Resistance Training · Sarcopenia · Treatment Outcome · Vitamin D · Weight Loss · Whey Proteins
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of pack #5126, which tested a protein-enriched diet combined with resistance exercise in sarcopenic obesity; this shelf homes the diet question during weight loss itself, and #5126's whey-plus-training trial is cross-pointed, not re-carded. The evidence divides on a distinction the question hides: enriched protein supplements versus simply eating a higher-protein diet. In Verreijen 2015, where both arms followed a hypocaloric diet plus resistance training, a whey protein-, leucine- and vitamin D-enriched supplement preserved appendicular muscle mass (+0.4 kg vs. −0.5 kg; between-group difference 0.95 kg, P = 0.03). Memelink 2020 found the same direction for an enriched protein drink during a combined lifestyle intervention (appendicular muscle mass +0.36 kg vs. control). But the one trial that isolated diet alone — Verreijen 2017's 2×2 factorial of high-protein diet (target 1.3 g/kg) and/or resistance exercise — found the high-protein diet did not significantly affect fat-free mass change (the treatment made no significant difference); only the combined diet-plus-exercise group significantly gained fat-free mass. A further limit is printed on every card: these trials enrolled obese older adults at risk of muscle loss, not patients with formally diagnosed sarcopenic obesity. PROPOSED SPLIT (enriched protein supplements during a weight-loss programme: benefit; higher-protein diet alone: no significant difference) — protein enrichment as a supplement preserved muscle during weight loss in two trials where exercise was present in both arms, but a high-protein diet by itself has not been shown to do so.

cards.headline: Verreijen 2015: during a 13-week hypocaloric diet plus resistance training, a whey protein-, leucine- and vitamin D-enriched supplement preserved appendicular muscle mass (+0.4 kg) while controls lost it (−0.5 kg) — between-group difference 0.95 kg, P = 0.03
cards.summary: Verreijen 2015: during a 13-week hypocaloric diet plus resistance training, a whey protein-, leucine- and vitamin D-enriched supplement preserved appendicular muscle mass (+0.4 kg) while controls lost it (−0.5 kg) — between-group difference 0.95 kg, P = 0.03
cards.people: 80 obese older adults (mean age 63 ± 5.6 years, body mass index 33 ± 4.4) in a double-blind randomised trial; all followed a hypocaloric diet (−600 kcal/day) and resistance training 3 times weekly for 13 weeks, randomised to the enriched supplement (150 kcal, 21 g protein, 10 times weekly; achieved protein intake 1.11 ± 0.28 g/kg/day) or an isocaloric control (0.85 ± 0.24 g/kg/day). Participants were obese older adults at risk of sarcopenia; the record does not state a formal sarcopenic-obesity diagnosis as an entry criterion.
cards.result: Both groups lost weight (−3.4 ± 3.6 kg intervention and −2.8 ± 2.8 kg control; both P < 0.001) and fat mass, with no between-group differences in weight or fat loss. The 13-week change in appendicular muscle mass differed between groups: +0.4 ± 1.2 kg with the supplement versus −0.5 ± 2.1 kg with control (β = 0.95 kg, 95% confidence interval: 0.09–1.81; P = 0.03). Muscle strength and physical performance improved over time in both groups without significant between-group differences. The authors conclude the enriched supplement preserves appendicular muscle mass during a hypocaloric diet and resistance exercise programme and might reduce sarcopenia risk.
cards.watchOut: The supplement was a formulated product (whey, leucine, vitamin D and other nutrients), not simply 'more protein in food', and resistance training was in both arms — so this card shows an enriched supplement adds muscle preservation on top of diet-plus-exercise; it does not show a high-protein diet alone works, which the factorial trial on this shelf tested directly and did not confirm.
cards.source: Verreijen AM et al. A high whey protein-, leucine-, and vitamin D-enriched supplement preserves muscle mass during intentional weight loss in obese older adults: a double-blind randomized controlled trial. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2015. PMID: 25646324. Registry ID: NTR2751. cards.headline: Verreijen 2017: the factorial test of diet alone — a high-protein diet (target 1.3 g/kg) did not significantly affect fat-free mass during weight loss (the treatment made no significant difference); only high protein combined with resistance exercise significantly increased fat-free mass (+0.6 kg)
cards.summary: Verreijen 2017: the factorial test of diet alone — a high-protein diet (target 1.3 g/kg) did not significantly affect fat-free mass during weight loss (the treatment made no significant difference); only high protein combined with resistance exercise significantly increased fat-free mass (+0.6 kg)
cards.people: 100 overweight and obese adults aged 55–80 years (mean body mass index 32 ± 4) in a randomised trial with a 2×2 factorial design; all followed a hypocaloric diet for a 10-week weight-loss programme and were randomised to high-protein (1.3 g/kg body weight) or normal-protein (0.8 g/kg) diet, with or without a resistance exercise programme 3 times weekly. Achieved protein intake was 1.13 ± 0.35 g/kg in the high-protein groups versus 0.98 ± 0.29 in the normal-protein groups. Fat-free mass was assessed by air displacement plethysmography. Formal sarcopenic obesity was not an entry criterion in the record.
cards.result: Neither the high-protein diet nor exercise significantly affected change in body weight, fat-free mass or fat mass, and there was no significant protein-by-exercise interaction for fat-free mass (the high-protein diet made no significant difference on its own). Within-group analysis showed only the combined high-protein-plus-exercise group significantly increased fat-free mass (+0.6 ± 1.3 kg, p = 0.011). The authors note the achieved protein contrast was smaller than targeted (a 16.3 ± 5.2 g/day higher intake in the high-protein groups).
cards.watchOut: The achieved protein difference between diet arms was modest (1.13 vs. 0.98 g/kg/day), so the null may reflect a weak contrast rather than proof that dietary protein cannot help; equally, a within-group gain in the combined arm is not a between-group effect — the card is carded precisely because it is the only direct test of the diet-alone slice, and it is null.
cards.source: Verreijen AM et al. Effect of a high protein diet and/or resistance exercise on the preservation of fat free mass during weight loss in overweight and obese older adults: a randomized controlled trial. Nutrition Journal. 2017. PMID: 28166780. Registry ID: NTR4556 (as printed in the record). cards.headline: Memelink 2020: an enriched protein drink during a 13-week lifestyle intervention preserved muscle in older adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes — appendicular muscle mass +0.36 kg and total lean mass +0.92 kg versus isocaloric control
cards.summary: Memelink 2020: an enriched protein drink during a 13-week lifestyle intervention preserved muscle in older adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes — appendicular muscle mass +0.36 kg and total lean mass +0.92 kg versus isocaloric control
cards.people: 123 older adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes randomised in a double-blind trial to a 13-week lifestyle intervention with dietary advice and exercise, receiving either a whey protein drink enriched with leucine and vitamin D (test) or an isocaloric control drink. Muscle mass was assessed by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry. The population had obesity with diabetes; the record does not state a formal sarcopenic-obesity entry criterion.
cards.result: Leg muscle mass showed a nonsignificant increase with the test drink (+0.28 kg; 95% confidence interval, −0.01 to 0.56), while appendicular muscle mass (+0.36 kg; 95% confidence interval, 0.005 to 0.71) and total lean mass (+0.92 kg; 95% confidence interval, 0.19 to 1.65) increased significantly versus control. Insulin sensitivity (Matsuda index) also increased versus control (+0.52; 95% confidence interval, 0.07 to 0.97). The authors conclude the enriched protein drink shows beneficial effects on muscle mass and glycaemic control during combined lifestyle intervention in this population.
cards.watchOut: Again a formulated enriched drink (whey, leucine, vitamin D) layered on a lifestyle programme that included exercise in both arms, in a diabetes population — it corroborates the supplement finding; it does not test a high-protein diet alone, and its appendicular confidence interval (0.005 to 0.71 kg) only just excludes no effect.
cards.source: Memelink RG et al. Effect of an Enriched Protein Drink on Muscle Mass and Glycemic Control during Combined Lifestyle Intervention in Older Adults with Obesity and Type 2 Diabetes: A Double-Blind RCT. Nutrients. 2020. PMID: 33379181. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: enriched protein supplements preserved muscle during weight loss in two trials, but the only trial of a high-protein diet by itself found no significant effect — the diet-alone slice of the question is unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: enriched protein supplements preserved muscle during weight loss in two trials, but the only trial of a high-protein diet by itself found no significant effect — the diet-alone slice of the question is unproven
cards.people: The carded evidence: three randomised trials in obese older adults during intentional weight loss (80, 100 and 123 participants; total 303), two testing enriched whey/leucine/vitamin D supplements on top of diet-plus-exercise programmes and one factorial trial isolating dietary protein level. None required a formal sarcopenic-obesity diagnosis at entry — the population limit is printed here and on every card. Pack #5126's protein-plus-resistance-exercise trial is cross-pointed, not re-carded.
cards.result: Appendicular muscle mass: +0.95 kg between-group difference favouring the enriched supplement (Verreijen 2015) and +0.36 kg favouring the enriched drink (Memelink 2020). Fat-free mass with high-protein diet alone: no significant effect in the factorial trial; only diet plus exercise gained fat-free mass within-group (+0.6 kg) (Verreijen 2017). PROPOSED SPLIT (enriched protein supplements during a weight-loss programme: benefit; higher-protein diet alone: no significant difference).
cards.watchOut: Two of the three trials come from the same research group and test that group's style of enriched supplement; independent replication of the supplement effect, and any trial in formally diagnosed sarcopenic obesity, are both still missing — the shelf's SPLIT is between formulations and designs, not between research groups.
cards.source: Synthesis of Verreijen AM et al. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2015 (PMID: 25646324); Verreijen AM et al. Nutrition Journal. 2017 (PMID: 28166780); Memelink RG et al. Nutrients. 2020 (PMID: 33379181).

shelves.title: Computerised cognitive training in mild cognitive impairment (partial completion of #2872, cognitively intact adults): test cognition improves, everyday function does not demonstrably follow — MAYBE (weak evidence) for function
shelves.question: Does computerized cognitive training improve everyday function in mild cognitive impairment?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Alzheimer Disease · Cognitive Dysfunction · Computer-Assisted Instruction · Humans · Middle Aged · Neuropsychological Tests · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2872, which covers cognitive training in cognitively intact older adults (the ACTIVE trial, Ball 2002, carded there and not re-carded here). The uncovered slice is mild cognitive impairment, and within it the outcome that matters most: everyday function. The cognition half of the story is positive — a meta-analysis of 17 MCI trials (Hill 2017, PMID: 27838936) found a moderate effect on overall cognition (Hedges' g = 0.35) — but the function half is not demonstrated. The Cochrane review of at least 12 weeks of computerised training in MCI (Gates 2019, PMID: 30864747; 8 trials, 660 participants) could not determine any effect on functional performance because the evidence was very low quality. The one randomised trial that measured everyday function directly over two years (Wadley 2025, PMID: 40567104) found processing speed training made no difference to instrumental activities of daily living, driving or community mobility versus a control training protocol. A small virtual-reality training meta-analysis (Son 2022, PMID: 36497946) reports significant ADL/IADL effects but prints no effect sizes in its record and mixes MCI with Alzheimer's disease. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — computerised training improves test cognition in MCI, but an everyday-function benefit is unproven, and the only direct trial found the treatment made no difference.

cards.headline: Hill 2017: computerised cognitive training improved overall cognition in MCI (Hedges' g = 0.35 across 17 trials) — but the record reports no pooled effect on activities of daily living
cards.summary: Hill 2017: computerised cognitive training improved overall cognition in MCI (Hedges' g = 0.35 across 17 trials) — but the record reports no pooled effect on activities of daily living
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of computerised cognitive training in older adults with mild cognitive impairment or dementia, searching to July 1, 2016; the MCI analysis pooled 17 trials, with overall cognition, individual cognitive domains, psychosocial function and activities of daily living pooled separately for MCI and dementia trials.
cards.result: The overall effect on cognition in mild cognitive impairment was moderate (Hedges' g = 0.35, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.51), with small to moderate effects for global cognition, attention, working memory, learning and memory (except nonverbal memory) and for psychosocial functioning including depressive symptoms. Although activities of daily living were among the outcomes pooled, the record reports no pooled ADL effect size for MCI — that absence is printed here plainly rather than filled in. The authors conclude the intervention warrants longer-term and larger-scale trials to examine effects on conversion to dementia.
cards.watchOut: This card establishes the cognition effect, not the function effect: a moderate gain on cognitive tests is exactly what this shelf's question does not ask about, and the everyday-function outcome is simply not quantified in the record.
cards.source: Hill NT et al. Computerized Cognitive Training in Older Adults With Mild Cognitive Impairment or Dementia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. The American journal of psychiatry. 2017. PMID: 27838936. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gates 2019 (Cochrane): with 8 trials and 660 participants, the effect of computerised training on functional performance in MCI could not be determined — evidence very low quality, and no trial reported incident dementia
cards.summary: Gates 2019 (Cochrane): with 8 trials and 660 participants, the effect of computerised training on functional performance in MCI could not be determined — evidence very low quality, and no trial reported incident dementia
cards.people: Cochrane review of randomised and quasi-randomised trials of at least 12 weeks of computerised cognitive training versus active or inactive control in adults with mild cognitive impairment or mild neurocognitive disorder: eight trials with a total of 660 participants, with trial durations from 12 weeks to 18 months; only one trial used an inactive control.
cards.result: No trial provided data on incident dementia. For global cognitive function and for secondary outcomes including functional performance, the evidence was very low quality and the reviewers were unable to determine whether there was any effect, citing risk of bias, inconsistency between trials and highly imprecise results. Low-quality evidence suggested probably no effect on speed of processing (SMD 0.20, 95% CI −0.16 to 0.56; 2 studies; 119 participants), verbal fluency or quality of life. The reviewers concluded the available evidence does not allow a determination of whether computerised training improves or maintains cognitive function in MCI, let alone everyday function.
cards.watchOut: 'Unable to determine' is not proof of no effect — it is a statement about trial quality and size; but it means no everyday-function claim can rest on this literature, which is the point of this shelf.
cards.source: Gates NJ et al. Computerised cognitive training for preventing dementia in people with mild cognitive impairment. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2019. PMID: 30864747. cards.headline: Wadley 2025: over two years, processing speed training made no difference to IADL function, driving or community mobility versus control training in MCI due to Alzheimer's disease (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Wadley 2025: over two years, processing speed training made no difference to IADL function, driving or community mobility versus control training in MCI due to Alzheimer's disease (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 103 persons with mild cognitive impairment (n = 90) or very mild dementia (n = 13) due to Alzheimer's disease, randomised to a processing speed training protocol or a control training protocol (serial assessments, laboratory training and home training over a two-year period), with performance-based instrumental activities of daily living, community mobility and on-road driving as outcomes.
cards.result: Changes in IADL function, driving and community mobility did not differ by training assignment (the treatment made no difference). Greater baseline neurodegeneration on MRI predicted larger declines in all functional outcomes (p values < 0.001). The authors conclude that in persons with MCI or very mild dementia, processing speed training was no more effective for maintaining everyday functions than training involving common computer activities and games that do not target processing speed.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was an active computer-training control, not no treatment, and 13 of the 103 participants had very mild dementia rather than MCI; against an inactive control the result might differ — but against a plausible alternative use of the same computer time, targeted training bought no function.
cards.source: Wadley VG et al. Daily function outcomes in adults with mild cognitive impairment due to Alzheimer's disease after two years of processing speed training versus a control training protocol. cards.headline: Son 2022: virtual-reality cognitive training showed significant ADL and IADL effects in a 5-study meta-analysis — but the record prints no effect sizes and the population mixes MCI with Alzheimer's disease
cards.summary: Son 2022: virtual-reality cognitive training showed significant ADL and IADL effects in a 5-study meta-analysis — but the record prints no effect sizes and the population mixes MCI with Alzheimer's disease
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of virtual reality-based cognitive training studies in patients with mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease published between February 2012 and February 2022: five studies met the inclusion criteria, with activities of daily living (ADL) and instrumental activities of daily living (IADL) as the ecological outcomes.
cards.result: The VR-based cognitive training showed significant effects on ADL and IADL in both MCI and AD patients; when the groups were compared, both showed significant effects, but MCI patients showed lower effects on ADL and IADL than AD patients. The record reports these effects as significant without printing any effect size, confidence interval or participant total — that absence is printed here plainly. The authors suggest VR-based training is ecologically valid because its content resembles real life.
cards.watchOut: Five studies, mixed MCI/Alzheimer's populations, immersive VR rather than standard computerised training, and no effect sizes in the record: this is a signal worth a proper trial, not a demonstrated everyday-function benefit.
cards.source: Son C et al. Ecological Effects of VR-Based Cognitive Training on ADL and IADL in MCI and AD patients: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. cards.headline: Synthesis: in MCI, computerised training improves cognitive test scores but has not been shown to improve everyday function — the direct two-year trial was null and the Cochrane review could not determine any functional effect
cards.summary: Synthesis: in MCI, computerised training improves cognitive test scores but has not been shown to improve everyday function — the direct two-year trial was null and the Cochrane review could not determine any functional effect
cards.people: The carded evidence: a meta-analysis of 17 MCI trials for cognition (Hill 2017), a Cochrane review of 8 trials with 660 participants (Gates 2019), one two-year randomised trial measuring everyday function directly (103 participants; Wadley 2025) and a 5-study virtual-reality meta-analysis (Son 2022). Participant totals exceed 30 on every card, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Cognition improved moderately (g = 0.35; Hill 2017). For everyday function, the Cochrane review could not determine an effect on functional performance (Gates 2019), the one direct trial found no difference in IADL, driving or mobility over two years (Wadley 2025), and the only positive functional pooling is a 5-study VR meta-analysis whose record prints no effect sizes (Son 2022). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — everyday-function benefit unproven.
cards.watchOut: Home shelf #2872 shows the same near-transfer pattern in cognitively intact older adults (ACTIVE); this shelf shows that moving the population to MCI does not rescue the everyday-function claim.
