shelves.title: Repositioning plus mattress versus standard care (PARTIAL completion of #796): 4-hourly turning on viscoelastic foam cut grade II+ ulcers to 3.0% in nursing-home patients — one trial, reviews unsettled
shelves.question: Do regular repositioning and pressure-redistributing mattresses prevent pressure injuries in immobile older adults?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Beds · Equipment Design · Europe/epidemiology · Female · Homes for the Aged · Humans · Incidence · Logistic Models · Male · Multivariate Analysis · Nursing Homes · Posture · Pressure Ulcer/epidemiology/prevention & control · Statistics, Nonparametric
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #796, which covers the slices of frequency (2- versus 4-hourly turning, TURN) and of mattress-versus-mattress comparison (PRESSURE 2); this shelf covers the slice #796 does not: whether repositioning plus a pressure-redistributing mattress prevents pressure injuries at all, against standard care, in immobile older adults. Only one trial answers that directly (Defloor 2005, PMID: 15582638): in 838 nursing-home patients, turning every 4 hours on a viscoelastic foam mattress produced grade II-or-worse ulcers in 3.0%, versus 14.3–24.1% across the other regimens including standard preventive care — while early skin redness (non-blanchable erythema) did not differ (34.8–38.1%). The Cochrane repositioning review (Gillespie 2020, PMID: 32484259) found the frequency evidence very low certainty (2- versus 4-hourly relative risk 1.06), and the Cochrane foam review (Shi 2021, PMID: 34097765) found foam may be worse than air surfaces — neither review contains a trial of the combined package versus no prevention. So the package is supported by one large trial against standard care; the optimal frequency and surface remain unsettled. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): regular repositioning combined with a pressure-redistributing mattress prevents grade II-or-worse pressure injuries in immobile older adults, on single-trial evidence against standard care.

cards.headline: Defloor 2005: turning every 4 hours on a viscoelastic foam mattress gave grade II+ pressure ulcers in 3.0% versus 14.3–24.1% in the other regimens (including standard care) — 838 nursing-home patients
cards.summary: Defloor 2005: turning every 4 hours on a viscoelastic foam mattress gave grade II+ pressure ulcers in 3.0% versus 14.3–24.1% in the other regimens (including standard care) — 838 nursing-home patients
cards.people: 838 geriatric nursing-home patients in a multicentre randomised trial of four preventive regimens over 28 days: turning every 2 hours on a standard institutional mattress (n = 65), every 3 hours on a standard mattress (n = 65), every 4 hours on a viscoelastic foam mattress (n = 67), or every 6 hours on a viscoelastic foam mattress (n = 65); the remaining 576 patients received standard preventive care.
cards.result: The incidence of grade II and higher pressure ulcers in the 4-hourly turning on viscoelastic foam group was 3.0%, compared with incidence figures in the other groups varying between 14.3% and 24.1%. The incidence of non-blanchable erythema (grade I) was 34.8–38.1% and did not differ between groups (the treatment made no difference to early redness). The authors conclude that turning every 4 hours on a viscoelastic mattress significantly reduced pressure ulcer lesions and makes turning feasible in effort and cost.
cards.watchOut: The experimental turning groups were small (65–67 patients each) against a much larger standard-care group, allocation and blinding are limited in a turning trial, and the winning regimen combines two changes at once (mattress plus schedule) — the trial cannot say which component, or whether either alone, did the work.
cards.source: Defloor T et al. The effect of various combinations of turning and pressure reducing devices on the incidence of pressure ulcers.. International journal of nursing studies. 2005. PMID: 15582638. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gillespie 2020 (Cochrane repositioning): 2-hourly versus 4-hourly repositioning relative risk 1.06 — it is uncertain whether frequency changes incidence at all; all eight trials at high risk of bias
cards.summary: Gillespie 2020 (Cochrane repositioning): 2-hourly versus 4-hourly repositioning relative risk 1.06 — it is uncertain whether frequency changes incidence at all; all eight trials at high risk of bias
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cochrane; Gillespie 2020)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of repositioning regimens for pressure injury prevention in adults in any setting: eight trials with 3,941 participants from acute and long-term care, with short follow-up (24 hours to 21 days). Six studies reported the proportion developing a pressure injury of any stage.
cards.result: Pooling three trials (1,074 participants) comparing 2-hourly with 4-hourly repositioning (used with various support surfaces) gave a relative risk of 1.06 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.41) — the reviewers conclude it is uncertain whether 2-hourly repositioning increases or decreases pressure injury incidence compared with 4-hourly, rating the certainty of evidence very low (downgraded twice for risk of bias and once for imprecision). All included studies were at high risk of bias. The record reports no pooled comparison of any repositioning versus no repositioning.
cards.watchOut: This review compares schedules against each other, never against no repositioning — it cannot answer this shelf's prevention-versus-none question, and its very-low-certainty verdict is about frequency, not about whether repositioning works at all.
cards.source: Gillespie BM et al. Repositioning for pressure injury prevention in adults.. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2020. PMID: 32484259. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Shi 2021 (Cochrane foam surfaces): foam may increase ulcer risk compared with air surfaces (relative risk 1.59 versus alternating-pressure air; 2.40 versus reactive air) — foam is the floor, not the ceiling, of mattress prevention
cards.summary: Shi 2021 (Cochrane foam surfaces): foam may increase ulcer risk compared with air surfaces (relative risk 1.59 versus alternating-pressure air; 2.40 versus reactive air) — foam is the floor, not the ceiling, of mattress prevention
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cochrane; Shi 2021)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of foam beds, mattresses and overlays for pressure ulcer prevention: 29 studies with 9,566 participants, mainly from acute care settings, median study size 101 participants and participant ages averaging 47.0 to 85.3 years (median 76.0). Seventeen of 29 studies (58.6%) were at high overall risk of bias.
cards.result: Low-certainty evidence suggests foam surfaces may increase the risk of developing new pressure ulcers compared with alternating pressure (active) air surfaces (relative risk 1.59, 95% CI 0.86 to 2.95; 4 studies, 2,247 participants) and compared with reactive air surfaces (relative risk 2.40, 95% CI 1.04 to 5.54; 4 studies, 229 participants). Comparisons against unspecified surfaces were recorded but not analysed, so the review gives no pooled estimate for foam versus a standard institutional mattress.
cards.watchOut: Mostly acute-care, mostly small and bias-prone trials: the finding that air surfaces beat foam does not contradict Defloor (whose foam mattress was compared with standard care and less-redistributing regimens), but it warns against reading 'pressure-redistributing mattress' as a single uniform intervention.
cards.source: Shi C et al. Foam surfaces for preventing pressure ulcers.. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2021. PMID: 34097765. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large nursing-home trial supports the combined package against standard care (3.0% versus 14.3–24.1% grade II+ ulcers); the reviews settle neither frequency nor surface — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large nursing-home trial supports the combined package against standard care (3.0% versus 14.3–24.1% grade II+ ulcers); the reviews settle neither frequency nor surface — POSSIBLE
cards.people: The carded evidence: one multicentre randomised trial in 838 nursing-home patients (the only card comparing a repositioning-plus-mattress package with standard preventive care) and two Cochrane reviews totalling 3,941 (repositioning) and 9,566 (foam surfaces) participants across schedule- and surface-comparison trials. Total carded participants exceed 30, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Grade II+ ulcers: 3.0% with 4-hourly turning on viscoelastic foam versus 14.3–24.1% in other regimens including standard care (Defloor 2005); grade I redness did not differ. Repositioning frequency: relative risk 1.06 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.41) for 2- versus 4-hourly, very low certainty (Gillespie 2020). Surface: foam worse than air surfaces on low-certainty evidence (Shi 2021). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for the combined package versus standard care.
cards.watchOut: No trial has randomised immobile older adults to repositioning-plus-mattress versus truly no prevention, for ethical reasons; 'standard preventive care' in Defloor is the honest comparator, and the effect rests on that one trial.

shelves.title: Nutrition to prevent pressure injuries (PARTIAL completion of #1223): SPLIT — a 2005 meta-analysis found prevention, the larger 2024 Cochrane review finds little to no difference
shelves.question: Does nutritional supplementation with protein and energy prevent pressure injuries in malnourished older adults?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Dietary Proteins/administration & dosage · Dietary Supplements · Pressure Ulcer/diet therapy/prevention & control · Quality of Life · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Wound Healing
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1223, which covers a nutrition formula for HEALING established pressure ulcers; this shelf covers the different slice #1223 does not: PREVENTION in malnourished older adults. Here the evidence genuinely divides. The older meta-analysis (Stratton 2005, PMID: 16081325) found oral nutritional supplements associated with a significantly lower incidence of pressure ulcer development (odds ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.89; 4 trials, 1,224 at-risk patients). The current Cochrane review (Langer 2024, PMID: 38345088), pooling more and later trials, found energy, protein and micronutrient supplements may result in little to no difference versus standard diet (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.19; 248 versus 269 per 1,000) and protein supplements likewise (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.14) — both low-certainty. The one double-blind trial in a defined malnourished-risk group (Houwing 2003, PMID: 12880608, hip-fracture patients) found overall incidence did not differ (55% versus 59%) though stage II ulcers were less frequent (18% versus 28%). PROPOSED SPLIT: an older meta-analysis found a significant preventive effect of supplementation, while the 2024 Cochrane review of the larger trial base finds little to no difference — prevention by protein-and-energy supplementation is unproven on current evidence.

cards.headline: Langer 2024 (Cochrane): protein-and-energy supplements may result in little to no difference in pressure ulcer incidence versus standard diet (relative risk 0.92; protein alone 0.75, interval crossing 1) — low-certainty evidence
cards.summary: Langer 2024 (Cochrane): protein-and-energy supplements may result in little to no difference in pressure ulcer incidence versus standard diet (relative risk 0.92; protein alone 0.75, interval crossing 1) — low-certainty evidence
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cochrane; Langer 2024)
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of nutritional interventions for preventing and treating pressure ulcers: 33 randomised trials with 7,920 participants overall. For prevention, 11 studies compared six types of nutritional intervention; the energy, protein and micronutrient comparison pooled 3 studies with 1,634 participants, and the protein-supplement comparison 4 studies with 4,264 participants.
cards.result: Compared with standard diet, energy, protein and micronutrient supplements: 248 per 1,000 developed a pressure ulcer versus 269 per 1,000 on standard diet (relative risk 0.92, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.19; low-certainty evidence) — the reviewers' conclusion is that supplements may result in little to no difference. Protein supplements alone: 21 per 1,000 versus 28 per 1,000 (relative risk 0.75, 95% CI 0.49 to 1.14; low-certainty). The evidence is very uncertain about gastrointestinal side effects.
cards.watchOut: Low-certainty throughout, and the pooled populations are people at risk of pressure ulcers generally — not restricted to malnourished older adults, the subgroup in which a benefit is most plausible and least separately reported.

cards.headline: Stratton 2005: oral nutritional supplements were associated with a significantly lower incidence of pressure ulcer development (odds ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.89) in 1,224 at-risk patients
cards.summary: Stratton 2005: oral nutritional supplements were associated with a significantly lower incidence of pressure ulcer development (odds ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.89) in 1,224 at-risk patients
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of enteral nutritional support in patients with, or at risk of, pressure ulcers: 15 studies (8 randomised trials) in the review; the incidence meta-analysis pooled 4 randomised trials of oral nutritional supplements (250–500 kcal, given for 2–26 weeks) versus routine care in 1,224 elderly, post-surgical and chronically hospitalised patients, plus one enteral tube feeding trial (combined n = 1,325).
cards.result: Oral nutritional supplements were associated with a significantly lower incidence of pressure ulcer development than routine care (odds ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.89 — a relative odds measure; the review summarises it as a 25% relative reduction in risk). The combined supplements-plus-tube-feeding analysis gave a similar result (odds ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.88). Individual studies suggested a trend towards improved healing of existing ulcers with high-protein formulas, which the authors say requires robust trials to confirm.
cards.watchOut: A 2005 analysis of an earlier, smaller trial base, with industry-era supplement trials prone to bias; its significant pooled result is exactly what the larger 2024 Cochrane pooling failed to reproduce — the split between these two cards is the shelf's central fact.
cards.source: Stratton RJ et al. Enteral nutritional support in prevention and treatment of pressure ulcers: a systematic review and meta-analysis.. Ageing research reviews. 2005. PMID: 16081325. cards.headline: Houwing 2003: in hip-fracture patients, an enriched supplement did not change overall pressure ulcer incidence (55% versus 59%) but stage II ulcers were less frequent (18% versus 28%) — 103 patients
cards.summary: Houwing 2003: in hip-fracture patients, an enriched supplement did not change overall pressure ulcer incidence (55% versus 59%) but stage II ulcers were less frequent (18% versus 28%) — 103 patients
cards.people: 103 hip-fracture patients at risk of developing pressure ulcers, in a double-blind, randomised, placebo-controlled trial: 400 mL daily of a supplement enriched with protein, arginine, zinc and antioxidants (n = 51) versus a non-caloric water-based placebo (n = 52), with daily ulcer assessment for 28 days or until discharge (median supplementation 10 days).
cards.result: Incidence of pressure ulcers overall was not different between supplement (55%) and placebo (59%) — the treatment made no difference to overall incidence. Incidence of stage II ulcers showed a 9% difference between supplement (18%) and placebo (28%) (difference 0.091; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.25, as printed in the record). Time to onset showed a trend towards later onset with supplement (3.6 versus 1.6 days; P = 0.090); 57% of patients who developed ulcers did so by the second day. The authors conclude supplementation may not prevent ulcers at this stage but may delay onset and progression.
cards.watchOut: A small, short trial (median 10 days of supplementation) in hip-fracture patients whose ulcers mostly appeared by day 2 — arguably before nutrition could act; its stage II signal is a secondary cut of a null primary result and should be read as hypothesis-generating.
cards.source: Houwing RH et al. A randomised, double-blind assessment of the effect of nutritional supplementation on the prevention of pressure ulcers in hip-fracture patients.. cards.people: The carded evidence: the 2024 Cochrane prevention analyses (1,634 and 4,264 participants in the two main comparisons), the 2005 meta-analysis (1,224 patients in its incidence pooling), and one 103-patient double-blind trial in hip-fracture patients. cards.result: Supplements versus standard/routine care: odds ratio 0.75 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.89) for incidence in 2005; relative risk 0.92 (95% CI 0.71 to 1.19) for energy/protein/micronutrient and 0.75 (95% CI 0.49 to 1.14) for protein in 2024, both 'little to no difference', low certainty. cards.watchOut: Neither synthesis isolates malnourished older adults as a separate pooled subgroup, so this shelf cannot exclude a benefit confined to the frankly malnourished — it can only report that prevention is unproven in the at-risk populations actually trialled.

shelves.title: Vitamin D alone and falls in nursing homes (PARTIAL, split by regimen): daily 800–1,000 IU cut fall rates in two trials; a quarterly bolus in the largest trial did nothing
shelves.question: In older adults in nursing homes, does vitamin D supplementation reduce falls versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/prevention & control · Accidental Falls/statistics & numerical data · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Female · Homes for the Aged · Humans · Incidence · Male · Nursing Homes · Proportional Hazards Models · Treatment Outcome · Vitamin D/administration & dosage · Vitamins/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: SPLIT — PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1498. That shelf covers calcium plus vitamin D for fractures in nursing-home women; it does not cover vitamin D alone for falls. This shelf covers the uncovered slice: vitamin D supplementation and falls in nursing-home and residential-care residents. The evidence splits by dose and regimen. In a small multiple-dose trial, only 800 IU daily reduced falls (20% of residents fell vs 44% on placebo; adjusted fall rate ratio 0.28), while 200, 400 and 600 IU did not differ from placebo (Broe 2007). In a 2-year placebo-controlled trial of 625 residents (all on background calcium), about 1,000 IU daily reduced the fall rate (incidence rate ratio 0.73; 95% CI 0.57 to 0.95), though ever-falling was not significantly reduced (Flicker 2005). In the largest trial — 3,717 residents given ergocalciferol as a quarterly bolus equivalent to about 1,100 IU/day — falls were 44% on treatment vs 43% on control and fractures did not differ (Law 2006). PROPOSED SPLIT (daily vitamin D at 800 IU or more: fewer falls in two trials; quarterly bolus in the largest trial: the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: Broe 2007: in 124 nursing-home residents, only the 800 IU dose of vitamin D reduced falls — 20% of residents fell vs 44% on placebo (adjusted fall rate ratio 0.28); the 200, 400 and 600 IU doses did not differ from placebo
cards.summary: Broe 2007: in 124 nursing-home residents, only the 800 IU dose of vitamin D reduced falls — 20% of residents fell vs 44% on placebo (adjusted fall rate ratio 0.28); the 200, 400 and 600 IU doses did not differ from placebo
cards.people: 124 nursing-home residents (average age 89) in a 725-bed long-term care facility, randomly assigned to one of four vitamin D supplement doses (200 IU, 400 IU, 600 IU or 800 IU) or placebo daily for 5 months; fallers and falls were assessed using the facility incident-tracking database. This is a secondary analysis of a previously conducted randomised trial. N = 124 printed on the face.
cards.result: Over 5 months, the proportion of participants with falls was 44% on placebo (11/25), 58% on 200 IU (15/26), 60% on 400 IU (15/25), 60% on 600 IU (15/25) and 20% on 800 IU (5/23). Participants in the 800 IU group had a 72% lower adjusted incidence rate ratio of falls than those taking placebo (rate ratio 0.28; 95% CI 0.11 to 0.75 — a relative measure, with the absolute faller proportions printed above). No significant differences were observed for the adjusted fall rates compared with placebo in any of the other dose groups (the lower doses made no difference).
cards.watchOut: A small dose-ranging study (about 25 residents per arm) with a 5-month horizon: the entire benefit sits in one 23-person arm, and the three lower doses numerically had more fallers than placebo — dose, not vitamin D in the abstract, is what this trial supports.
cards.source: Broe KE et al. A higher dose of vitamin d reduces the risk of falls in nursing home residents: a randomized, multiple-dose study. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2007. cards.headline: Flicker 2005: in 625 residential-care residents over 2 years, vitamin D reduced the rate of falling (incidence rate ratio 0.73; 95% CI 0.57 to 0.95) — though the odds of ever falling did not reach significance (OR 0.82)
cards.summary: Flicker 2005: in 625 residential-care residents over 2 years, vitamin D reduced the rate of falling (incidence rate ratio 0.73; 95% CI 0.57 to 0.95) — though the odds of ever falling did not reach significance (OR 0.82)
cards.people: 625 residents (mean age 83.4 years) of 60 hostels (assisted living facilities) and 89 nursing homes across Australia, with serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels between 25 and 90 nmol/L (about 10 to 36 ng/mL), randomised to vitamin D supplementation (ergocalciferol, initially 10,000 IU once weekly and then 1,000 IU daily) or placebo for 2 years; all subjects received 600 mg elemental calcium daily. Falls and fractures were recorded prospectively in study diaries by care staff.
cards.result: In intention-to-treat analysis, the incident rate ratio for falling was 0.73 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.95 — a relative measure; the record prints no absolute fall rates). The odds ratio for ever falling was 0.82 (95% CI 0.59 to 1.12) and for ever fracturing 0.69 (95% CI 0.40 to 1.18), neither statistically significant. In a subgroup of subjects who took at least half the prescribed capsules (n = 540), the incidence rate ratio for falls was 0.63 (95% CI 0.48 to 0.82), the odds ratio for ever falling 0.70 (95% CI 0.50 to 0.99) and for ever fracturing 0.68 (95% CI 0.38 to 1.22). The authors conclude older people in residential care can reduce their incidence of falls with a vitamin D supplement even if not classically vitamin D deficient.
cards.watchOut: Both arms received 600 mg of calcium daily, so this is a trial of adding vitamin D to background calcium, not of vitamin D in isolation; and the significant result is the fall rate — the proportion of residents who ever fell did not differ significantly in the primary analysis.
cards.source: Flicker L et al. Should older people in residential care receive vitamin D to prevent falls? Results of a randomized trial. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2005. PMID: 16274368. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Law 2006: in 3,717 care-home residents, quarterly ergocalciferol (equivalent to about 1,100 IU/day) did not reduce falls — 44% of treated residents and 43% of controls reported at least one fall (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Law 2006: in 3,717 care-home residents, quarterly ergocalciferol (equivalent to about 1,100 IU/day) did not reduce falls — 44% of treated residents and 43% of controls reported at least one fall (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 3,717 residents (76% women, average age 85) of 223 residential units within 118 homes for elderly people throughout Britain (35% residential care, 42% nursing care, 23% care for elderly mentally infirm residents), cluster-randomised by residential unit to ergocalciferol 2.5 mg every 3 months (equivalent to a daily dose of 1,100 IU) or control; median follow-up 10 months. Fractures were confirmed in hospital and routinely collected falls data were obtained.
cards.result: After median follow-up of 10 months, 64 (3.6%) of 1,762 vitamin D-treated residents and 51 (2.6%) of 1,955 controls had one or more non-vertebral fractures, and 24 (1.3%) and 20 (1.0%) respectively had a hip fracture. The proportion reporting at least one fall was 44% in vitamin D-treated and 43% in control residents. None of the differences between the groups was statistically significant (the treatment made no difference to falls or fractures). The authors note the pre-treatment serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration was high (median 47 nmol/L, about 19 ng/mL, in a 1% sample) and fracture incidence in the homes was low.
cards.watchOut: The largest trial here is the null one — but it used a quarterly bolus (a regimen later experience suggests is not equivalent to daily dosing), its residents were comparatively vitamin-D-replete, and the control group received no placebo, so expectation effects on fall reporting cannot be excluded.
cards.source: Law M et al. Vitamin D supplementation and the prevention of fractures and falls: results of a randomised trial in elderly people in residential accommodation. Age and ageing. 2006. PMID: 16641143. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: daily vitamin D at adequate dose reduced fall rates in two nursing-home trials, while a quarterly-bolus regimen in the largest trial did not — the evidence splits by dose and regimen
cards.summary: Synthesis: daily vitamin D at adequate dose reduced fall rates in two nursing-home trials, while a quarterly-bolus regimen in the largest trial did not — the evidence splits by dose and regimen
cards.people: The carded evidence: one small multiple-dose randomised trial (124 residents, 5 months), one 2-year placebo-controlled trial (625 residents, on background calcium), and one large cluster-randomised trial (3,717 residents, median 10 months). Total carded participants are 4,466, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: At 800 IU daily, fallers were 20% vs 44% on placebo with an adjusted fall rate ratio of 0.28, while 200–600 IU did nothing (Broe 2007). At about 1,000 IU daily on background calcium, the fall rate ratio was 0.73 over 2 years, though ever-falling did not reach significance (Flicker 2005). Given as a 2.5 mg bolus every 3 months to 3,717 residents, vitamin D changed neither falls (44% vs 43%) nor fractures (Law 2006). PROPOSED SPLIT (daily dosing at 800 IU or more: fewer falls in two trials; quarterly bolus dosing in the largest trial: the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Regimen is the confounder running through this shelf: the null trial is simultaneously the largest, the only bolus-dosed, and the one in the most vitamin-D-replete residents — the cards cannot separate those three explanations, and the stamp does not pretend otherwise.
cards.source: Synthesis of Broe KE et al. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2007 (PMID: 17302660); Flicker L et al. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2005 (PMID: 16274368); Law M et al. Age and ageing. 2006 (PMID: 16641143).

shelves.title: Deprescribing in older adults with diabetes (PARTIAL completion of live #930's general medication-review question): benefit on adverse drug events is unproven — very-low-certainty review evidence and a results-pending randomised trial (OMED2)
shelves.question: In older adults with diabetes and polypharmacy, does a structured deprescribing review reduce adverse drug events versus usual care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Deprescriptions · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Humans · Hypoglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Retrospective Studies
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — for diabetes specifically, no completed trial has yet shown that a structured deprescribing review reduces adverse drug events. The updated systematic review of deprescribing antihyperglycaemic medicines in older adults with type 2 diabetes found only 4 controlled studies (2 randomised, 2 cohort): 3 reported no clinically significant change in glucose control after deprescribing and 2 reported reductions in adverse events such as hypoglycaemia, but the certainty of the evidence was rated very low for risk of bias, imprecision and indirectness (Deng 2022). A broader review of deprescribing preventive medicines in older people with cardiometabolic conditions in long-term care or at end of life (13 studies) found deprescribing success rates of 27-94.7%, no significant changes in laboratory values or adverse outcomes, mixed hospitalisation results, and a slight increase in mortality in intervention versus control groups — with a lack of good-quality randomised trials (Hickman 2023). The trial designed to answer this shelf's question directly, the Dutch OMED2 cluster-randomised trial of a general-practice deprescribing programme for insulin and sulfonylureas in overtreated older patients (86 practices, target 406 patients, ISRCTN50008265), has published its protocol only; no results were in the record fetched this session (Andriessen 2024). PARTIAL completion: live shelf #930 covers structured medication review in multimorbid older adults generally (the OPERAM and SPPiRE programmes and drug-related admissions, not re-carded here); this shelf covers the diabetes-specific deprescribing question and its adverse-drug-event outcome, where the honest current answer is 'plausibly safe, benefit unproven'. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Deng 2022: updating the evidence on deprescribing antihyperglycaemic medicines in older adults with type 2 diabetes found just 4 controlled studies — adverse events fell in 2, glucose control held in 3, and the certainty was rated very low
cards.summary: Deng 2022: updating the evidence on deprescribing antihyperglycaemic medicines in older adults with type 2 diabetes found just 4 controlled studies — adverse events fell in 2, glucose control held in 3, and the certainty was rated very low
cards.people: Systematic review (searches to January 2021) of controlled studies of deprescribing versus continuing antihyperglycaemic medicines in adults with type 2 diabetes, updating an earlier review: 4 additional investigations — 2 randomised controlled trials and 2 retrospective cohort studies — in older adults with type 2 diabetes.
cards.result: After deprescribing, 3 studies reported no clinically significant changes in glucose management and 2 studies reported reductions in adverse events (hypoglycaemia, all-cause mortality and non-spine fractures are the examples the record gives). On GRADE assessment the certainty of the evidence was very low, for risk of bias (including unmeasured confounding), imprecision and indirectness. The authors conclude deprescribing antihyperglycaemic medicines in older adults with type 2 diabetes is likely feasible and safe and benefits may outweigh harms — on very-low-certainty evidence, which is how this card prints it.
cards.watchOut: Four studies, two of them retrospective cohorts, and the adverse-event reductions come from individual studies rather than a pooled estimate — there is no meta-analytic number for adverse drug events on this card because the record does not report one.
cards.source: Deng Z et al. Benefits and Harms of Deprescribing Antihyperglycemics for Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review. Canadian Journal of Diabetes. 2022. PMID: 35739041. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Aged · Deprescriptions · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Humans · Hypoglycemia · Hypoglycemic Agents · Retrospective Studies

cards.headline: Hickman 2023: across 13 deprescribing studies in older people with cardiometabolic conditions, deprescribing succeeded in 27-94.7% but adverse outcomes did not significantly change, hospitalisations were mixed, and mortality was slightly higher in intervention groups
cards.summary: Hickman 2023: across 13 deprescribing studies in older people with cardiometabolic conditions, deprescribing succeeded in 27-94.7% but adverse outcomes did not significantly change, hospitalisations were mixed, and mortality was slightly higher in intervention groups
cards.people: Systematic review (searches to March 2022) of observational studies and randomised trials of deprescribing preventive medicines — complete withdrawal, dose reduction/tapering, or switching — in older patients with cardiometabolic conditions who had an end-of-life designation or lived in long-term care facilities: 13 studies.
cards.result: Deprescribing success rates ranged from 27% to 94.7%. The studies reported no significant changes in laboratory values or adverse outcomes, mixed outcomes for hospitalisations, and a slight increase in mortality rates comparing intervention and control groups. No meta-analysis was performed because of heterogeneity. The authors conclude deprescribing in this population is feasible when controlled and regularly monitored by an appropriate clinician and that benefits outweigh potential harm — while noting the lack of good-quality randomised trials, which is the limitation this shelf inherits.
cards.watchOut: This population is long-term-care and end-of-life patients, sicker than the community-dwelling older adults with diabetes and polypharmacy in this shelf's question — its slight mortality increase is a signal to monitor in trials, not a finding about deprescribing review in general practice.
cards.source: Hickman E et al. Deprescribing in cardiometabolic conditions in older patients: a systematic review. GeroScience. 2023. PMID: 37402905. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Aged · Deprescriptions · Cardiovascular Diseases

cards.headline: Andriessen 2024 (OMED2): the trial built to answer this question — a cluster-randomised deprescribing programme for insulin and sulfonylureas in 86 Dutch general practices — has a published protocol and no results in the record
cards.summary: Andriessen 2024 (OMED2): the trial built to answer this question — a cluster-randomised deprescribing programme for insulin and sulfonylureas in 86 Dutch general practices — has a published protocol and no results in the record
cards.people: Protocol for a 1:1 cluster-randomised controlled trial in 86 general practices in the Netherlands: a deprescribing programme (clinician education, practice support visits, and a selection tool to find possibly overtreated patients) aimed at reducing blood glucose-lowering medication in older patients (70 and over) with type 2 diabetes, versus usual care. Target enrolment 406 patients; follow-up 2 years; eligibility keyed to Dutch guideline HbA1c targets by age, diabetes duration, frailty and life expectancy.
cards.result: No outcome results are reported — this is a study protocol. Its primary outcome is the cumulative incidence of events related to under- and overtreatment of type 2 diabetes as recorded in practice records; secondary outcomes include quality of life, cognitive functioning, overtreatment/undertreatment events, biomarkers, prescription counts and cost-effectiveness. The protocol states its rationale plainly: guidelines exist for reducing glucose-lowering medication in older patients, but evidence is lacking that medication reduction can be safely pursued.
cards.watchOut: A protocol card is evidence about the state of the science, not about deprescribing: it is carded so the shelf does not pretend the diabetes-specific adverse-event question has been answered, and it must never be cited as a trial result.
cards.source: Andriessen C et al. A deprescribing programme aimed to optimise blood glucose-lowering medication in older people with type 2 diabetes mellitus, the OMED2-study: the study protocol for a randomised controlled trial. Trials. 2024. PMID: 39049109. Registry ID: ISRCTN50008265 (as printed in the record). cards.headline: Synthesis: diabetes-specific deprescribing looks feasible and has not been shown to worsen glucose control — but a reduction in adverse drug events is unproven, and the definitive trial has not reported
cards.summary: Synthesis: diabetes-specific deprescribing looks feasible and has not been shown to worsen glucose control — but a reduction in adverse drug events is unproven, and the definitive trial has not reported
cards.people: The carded evidence: a diabetes-specific systematic review (4 controlled studies), a cardiometabolic deprescribing review in long-term care/end-of-life populations (13 studies), and one cluster-randomised trial protocol with no results (target 406 patients). The reviews do not print a single pooled participant total in their records, so no total-N figure is claimed on this shelf beyond the protocol's target enrolment.
cards.result: Two of four controlled studies in the diabetes review reported fewer adverse events after deprescribing and three reported no clinically significant change in glucose control, on very-low-certainty evidence (Deng 2022); the broader review found no significant adverse-outcome change and mixed hospitalisations (Hickman 2023); OMED2 (ISRCTN50008265) is the pending randomised test. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: The gap on this shelf is the outcome in the question itself: adverse drug events. Hypoglycaemia reductions in two small studies are the closest signal, and they are hypothesis-generating, not an answer.
cards.source: Synthesis of Deng Z et al. Canadian Journal of Diabetes. 2022 (PMID: 35739041); Hickman E et al. GeroScience. 2023 (PMID: 37402905); Andriessen C et al. Trials. 2024 (PMID: 39049109).

shelves.title: How long is safe on benzodiazepine receptor agonists for insomnia? (PARTIAL completion of live #3816's tapering question): no trial defines a threshold — the 4-week ceiling is where the efficacy evidence ends, not a tested safety boundary
shelves.question: How long can adults safely use benzodiazepine receptor agonists for insomnia before tapering?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antidepressive Agents · Antipsychotic Agents · Benzodiazepines · Cognitive Behavioral Therapy · Comorbidity · Complementary Therapies · Europe · Female · Histamine Antagonists · Humans · Male · Melatonin · Phototherapy · Polysomnography · Sleep · Sleep Initiation and Maintenance Disorders
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — stated honestly: no trial defines a safe-use duration threshold for benzodiazepine receptor agonists in insomnia. What exists is a guideline ceiling, not a tested threshold. The European insomnia guideline found benzodiazepines and benzodiazepine receptor agonists effective only for short-term treatment (at most 4 weeks; weak recommendation, moderate-quality evidence), with cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia the recommended first-line treatment (Riemann 2017). A European review of long-term use repeats the same boundary: use is recommended for at most 4 weeks because long-term efficacy is unproven and because of tolerance, dependence and misuse risk — while in practice these drugs are the most widely used insomnia treatments in the five countries surveyed and are commonly used far longer than recommended (Soyka 2023). The harm side of longer use is observational: in a meta-analysis of 14 studies, Z-drugs were associated with more fractures (OR 1.63; 830,877 participants) and more injuries on zolpidem (OR 2.05), with a non-significant trend to more falls (OR 2.40, interval crossing 1) (Treves 2018). So the defensible answer to 'how long is safe?' is: efficacy is established only out to about 4 weeks, no study has randomised patients to different durations to find where harm begins, and beyond the guideline ceiling the user is outside the tested evidence. PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3816 covers tapering and discontinuation strategies in people already using these drugs long-term; this shelf covers the prior question — the duration boundary itself — and its evidence status. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Riemann 2017 (European guideline): benzodiazepines and receptor agonists are effective for insomnia only in the short term — at most 4 weeks (weak recommendation, moderate-quality evidence); CBT-I is first-line
cards.summary: Riemann 2017 (European guideline): benzodiazepines and receptor agonists are effective for insomnia only in the short term — at most 4 weeks (weak recommendation, moderate-quality evidence); CBT-I is first-line
cards.type: Clinical practice guideline (European insomnia guideline, Riemann 2017)
cards.people: European Sleep Research Society guideline for adults with chronic insomnia disorder, based on a systematic review of meta-analyses published to June 2016, with recommendations graded by GRADE. The guideline population is adults with chronic insomnia of any age.
cards.result: Cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia is recommended as first-line treatment for chronic insomnia in adults of any age (strong recommendation, high-quality evidence). A pharmacological intervention can be offered if CBT-I is not sufficiently effective or unavailable. Benzodiazepines, benzodiazepine receptor agonists and some antidepressants are effective in the short-term treatment of insomnia (at most 4 weeks; weak recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Antihistamines, antipsychotics, melatonin and phytotherapeutics are not recommended (strong to weak recommendations, low- to very-low-quality evidence). The record prints no trial-level effect sizes for the 4-week boundary, and none are invented here.
cards.watchOut: A guideline card, labelled as such: the 4-week figure is where the short-term trial evidence ends, not a duration at which a trial showed harm beginning. Treating it as a tested safety threshold would overstate what the guideline's evidence can say.
cards.source: Riemann D et al. European guideline for the diagnosis and treatment of insomnia. Journal of Sleep Research. 2017. PMID: 28875581. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Soyka 2023: long-term benzodiazepine use in chronic insomnia persists across Europe despite the at-most-4-weeks recommendation, which rests on unproven long-term efficacy plus tolerance and dependence risk
cards.summary: Soyka 2023: long-term benzodiazepine use in chronic insomnia persists across Europe despite the at-most-4-weeks recommendation, which rests on unproven long-term efficacy plus tolerance and dependence risk
cards.people: Narrative review with a pilot survey of the pharmacological treatment landscape for chronic insomnia in five European countries (France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the United Kingdom), covering benzodiazepines and Z-drugs (benzodiazepine receptor agonists) and physicians' attitudes to treatment.
cards.result: The review states that use of these agents is only recommended for at most 4 weeks, due to unproven long-term efficacy in chronic insomnia and the risk of tolerance and the potential for dependence and misuse — yet benzodiazepines and Z-drugs are the most widely used treatments for chronic insomnia in the surveyed countries and are being used for longer than their recommended duration, with country variation in prescription rates. Long-term use is associated with multiple consequences including dependence, and previous benzodiazepine use may increase the risk of opioid use disorder. No effect sizes are reported in the record, and none are invented here.
cards.watchOut: A perspective review, not a systematic evidence synthesis: it documents the gap between the recommended duration and real prescribing, and summarises why the limit exists, but it tests no duration threshold itself.
cards.source: Soyka M et al. Long-term use of benzodiazepines in chronic insomnia: a European perspective. Frontiers in Psychiatry. 2023. PMID: 37599882. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Treves 2018: in 14 observational studies, Z-drugs were associated with more fractures (OR 1.63) and more injuries (OR 2.05), with a non-significant trend to more falls — the harm evidence behind duration caution, all observational
cards.summary: Treves 2018: in 14 observational studies, Z-drugs were associated with more fractures (OR 1.63) and more injuries (OR 2.05), with a non-significant trend to more falls — the harm evidence behind duration caution, all observational
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Treves 2018)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies of Z-drugs (zolpidem, zopiclone, eszopiclone, zaleplon) versus non-use for fractures, falls and injuries: 14 eligible studies; the fracture analysis included 830,877 participants, the falls analysis 19,505, and the zolpidem injury analysis 160,502.
cards.result: Z-drugs were associated with a statistically significant increased risk of fractures (OR 1.63, 95% CI 1.42-1.87; I² = 90%). There was a trend to roughly 2-fold odds of falls that was not statistically significant (OR 2.40, 95% CI 0.92-6.27; I² = 95%). Zolpidem exposure was associated with a significant increased risk of injuries (OR 2.05, 95% CI 1.95-2.15; I² = 0%). Results were similar in sensitivity analyses. The authors note the included studies were observational and susceptible to confounding.
cards.watchOut: These studies compare users with non-users, not shorter with longer use: they show harm associated with exposure in older adults, mostly in the early treatment period in the underlying literature, and cannot locate a week at which risk begins — no card on this shelf can, because no duration trial exists.
cards.source: Treves N et al. Z-drugs and risk for falls and fractures in older adults-a systematic review and meta-analysis. Age and Ageing. 2018. PMID: 29077902. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: there is no trial-defined safe duration — efficacy is established only to about 4 weeks, guidelines cap use there, and the harm data are observational exposure comparisons
cards.summary: Synthesis: there is no trial-defined safe duration — efficacy is established only to about 4 weeks, guidelines cap use there, and the harm data are observational exposure comparisons
cards.people: The carded evidence: one European guideline, one European narrative review with a prescribing survey, and one meta-analysis of 14 observational studies (fracture analysis n = 830,877). No randomised duration comparison exists in the carded evidence, and none was found in the searches behind this build.
cards.result: Short-term efficacy at most 4 weeks (Riemann 2017); the same 4-week ceiling restated with its rationale — unproven long-term efficacy, tolerance, dependence (Soyka 2023); observational fracture OR 1.63 and injury OR 2.05 for Z-drug exposure (Treves 2018). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — the honest answer to the duration question is that the threshold is a guideline ceiling at the edge of the trial evidence, not a measured safety boundary.
cards.watchOut: Anyone quoting '4 weeks' from this shelf should quote its status with it: it marks the end of demonstrated efficacy. Dependence and tolerance can begin within that window in susceptible patients, and this shelf does not certify any duration as safe for an individual.
cards.source: Synthesis of Riemann D et al. Journal of Sleep Research. 2017 (PMID: 28875581); Soyka M et al. Frontiers in Psychiatry. 2023 (PMID: 37599882); Treves N et al. Age and Ageing. 2018 (PMID: 29077902).

shelves.title: Regular acetaminophen alone for agitation in dementia (PARTIAL completion of live #2758's stepwise-protocol question): no agitation benefit in either direct trial — Q-PID and Chibnall both null — despite a real paracetamol pain-score effect in the Husebo programme
shelves.question: Does pain treatment with regular acetaminophen reduce agitation in nursing home residents with dementia?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cross-Over Studies · Dementia · Disease Progression · Double-Blind Method · Female · Geriatric Assessment · Humans · Long-Term Care · Male · Netherlands · Nursing Homes · Pain · Pain Management · Patient Comfort · Placebos · Quality of Life · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — unproven for agitation, with the direct trials null. The Q-PID crossover trial randomised 95 residents with advanced dementia to 6 weeks of regular paracetamol (acetaminophen) and 6 weeks of placebo in random order: there was no difference in neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPI-NH change +1.5 on paracetamol versus -2.1 on placebo, intervals overlapping), nor in quality of life, discomfort or pain (van Dam 2020). The earlier Chibnall crossover trial (25 residents, N printed on the face) gave 4 weeks of acetaminophen 3,000 mg/day versus placebo and found no effects on agitation (Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory), emotional well-being or as-needed psychotropic use — though residents were more socially engaged and active on acetaminophen (Chibnall 2005). The Husebo programme's placebo-controlled DEP.PAIN.DEM trial (162 patients) tested analgesia for depression, not agitation; its paracetamol subgroup did show a significant pain reduction versus placebo from week 6 to 13 (-1.11 points), without a depression change — evidence that regular paracetamol can reduce measured pain in dementia even though the agitation trials are null (Erdal 2018). PARTIAL completion: live shelf #2758 covers the stepwise multi-drug pain protocol (paracetamol as first step, escalating to morphine, buprenorphine or pregabalin), which did reduce agitation in the Husebo cluster trial; this shelf isolates step 1 alone — regular acetaminophen by itself — where the treatment made no difference to agitation in either direct trial. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: van Dam 2020 (Q-PID): in a 95-person crossover trial, regular paracetamol showed no difference versus placebo on neuropsychiatric symptoms, quality of life, discomfort or pain in advanced dementia
cards.summary: van Dam 2020 (Q-PID): in a 95-person crossover trial, regular paracetamol showed no difference versus placebo on neuropsychiatric symptoms, quality of life, discomfort or pain in advanced dementia
cards.type: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial (Q-PID, van Dam 2020)
cards.people: Multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial in 17 long-term care facilities in the Netherlands: 95 residents aged 65 and over with (advanced) dementia and moderate-to-low quality of life (mean age 83.9 years; 57.9% women), enrolled irrespective of pain presence. Each participant received paracetamol and placebo for 6 weeks each in random order, separated by a 1-week washout, over 13 weeks.
cards.result: Repeated linear mixed models showed no difference favouring either treatment: quality of life (QUALIDEM change +1.3 on paracetamol [95% CI -1.0 to 3.5] versus +1.5 on placebo [-0.7 to 3.8]), discomfort (DS-DAT -0.1 versus +0.6), pain (MOBID-2 0.0 versus -0.2) and neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPI-NH +1.5 [-2.3 to 5.4] versus -2.1 [-6.0 to 1.7]). The authors conclude paracetamol showed no positive effect on quality of life, discomfort, pain or neuropsychiatric symptoms in persons with advanced dementia with low quality of life — for agitation-type outcomes, the treatment made no difference.
cards.watchOut: Residents were enrolled for low quality of life, not for pain or agitation — a trial of paracetamol in unselected advanced dementia cannot exclude a benefit in the subgroup with demonstrable untreated pain, which is the subgroup the stepwise protocol on the home shelf was treating.
cards.source: van Dam PH et al. Does paracetamol improve quality of life, discomfort, pain and neuropsychiatric symptoms in persons with advanced dementia living in long-term care facilities? A randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover (Q-PID) trial. BMC Medicine. 2020. PMID: 33342434. Registry ID: NTR6766. cards.headline: Chibnall 2005: in 25 residents with moderate-to-severe dementia (small N on the face), 4 weeks of regular acetaminophen 3,000 mg/day had no effect on agitation, well-being or psychotropic use — but residents were more engaged and active
cards.summary: Chibnall 2005: in 25 residents with moderate-to-severe dementia (small N on the face), 4 weeks of regular acetaminophen 3,000 mg/day had no effect on agitation, well-being or psychotropic use — but residents were more engaged and active
cards.people: Randomised double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial in nursing homes: 25 residents with moderate-to-severe dementia (small single-study N = 25, printed here as required), each receiving 4 weeks of regularly scheduled acetaminophen 3,000 mg/day and 4 weeks of placebo. Behaviour and well-being were observed with Dementia Care Mapping; agitation was measured with the Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory; as-needed psychotropic use came from medication logs.
cards.result: There were no effects on agitation, emotional well-being, or as-needed psychotropic medication use — for agitation, the treatment made no difference. Participants did spend more time in social interaction, engaged with media, talking to themselves and in work-like activity on acetaminophen, and less time in their rooms, off the unit, or in personal care activities; time in unattended distress was also higher on acetaminophen in the record's domain list. The authors interpret untreated pain as inhibiting activity in this population, with pain treatment facilitating engagement.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-five participants in a crossover design: the null on agitation is a small trial's null, and the engagement findings come from 26 observational behaviour domains, where some positive domains are expected by chance — the card keeps the trial's own agitation result first for that reason.
cards.source: Chibnall JT et al. Effect of acetaminophen on behavior, well-being, and psychotropic medication use in nursing home residents with moderate-to-severe dementia. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2005. PMID: 16274373. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Erdal 2018 (DEP.PAIN.DEM): analgesia did not improve depression overall, but the paracetamol subgroup did reduce pain versus placebo from week 6 to 13 (-1.11 points) — regular paracetamol moves pain scores even where behaviour outcomes are null
cards.summary: Erdal 2018 (DEP.PAIN.DEM): analgesia did not improve depression overall, but the paracetamol subgroup did reduce pain versus placebo from week 6 to 13 (-1.11 points) — regular paracetamol moves pain scores even where behaviour outcomes are null
cards.people: Multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial in 47 Norwegian nursing homes (the Husebo programme): 162 patients aged 60 and over with dementia (MMSE at most 20) and clinically significant depressive symptoms, randomised for 13 weeks to active analgesic treatment (paracetamol if not already on analgesics, or buprenorphine transdermal system; n = 80) or identical placebo (n = 82).
cards.result: The trial's primary outcome was depression, not agitation: mean depression change was -0.66 on active treatment versus -3.30 on placebo, an estimated treatment effect of 2.64 (95% CI 0.55-4.72; P = 0.013) favouring placebo, driven by buprenorphine's adverse effects (35 withdrawals for adverse reactions, deterioration or death: 25 on active treatment, 23 of them on buprenorphine, versus 10 on placebo). In the paracetamol subgroup, pain was significantly reduced versus placebo from week 6 to 13 (-1.11, 95% CI -2.16 to -0.06; P = 0.037) without a change in depression. Buprenorphine had no significant effect on depression or pain.
cards.watchOut: Carded for its paracetamol-subgroup pain result only: the trial asked about depression, its headline comparison pools paracetamol with buprenorphine, and its placebo-favouring depression result is a buprenorphine-harm story — none of that is evidence about paracetamol and agitation either way.
cards.source: Erdal A et al. Efficacy and Safety of Analgesic Treatment for Depression in People with Advanced Dementia: Randomised, Multicentre, Double-Blind, Placebo-Controlled Trial (DEP.PAIN.DEM). Drugs & Aging. 2018. PMID: 29725986. Registry ID: NCT02267057. cards.headline: Synthesis: regular acetaminophen alone has not reduced agitation in either direct trial — the stepwise protocol's agitation benefit on the home shelf belongs to the full escalating protocol, not to step 1 alone
cards.summary: Synthesis: regular acetaminophen alone has not reduced agitation in either direct trial — the stepwise protocol's agitation benefit on the home shelf belongs to the full escalating protocol, not to step 1 alone
cards.people: The carded evidence: two placebo-controlled crossover trials of regular acetaminophen alone with behaviour outcomes (95 and 25 participants) and one placebo-controlled analgesia trial with a paracetamol subgroup pain analysis (162 participants). Total carded participants are 282, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the smallest trial's N (25) is printed on its card face.
cards.result: Q-PID: no difference in neuropsychiatric symptoms (+1.5 versus -2.1 change, intervals overlapping) (van Dam 2020). Chibnall: no effect on agitation, well-being or psychotropic use (2005). DEP.PAIN.DEM: paracetamol subgroup reduced pain (-1.11 points) without behavioural-outcome evidence (Erdal 2018). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — unproven for agitation, null in the direct trials.
cards.watchOut: Null in unselected residents is not null in residents with identified untreated pain: neither direct trial required pain at entry, and that selection gap is the strongest reason the stepwise result and these results can both be true.
cards.source: Synthesis of van Dam PH et al. BMC Medicine. 2020 (PMID: 33342434); Chibnall JT et al. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2005 (PMID: 16274373); Erdal A et al. Drugs & Aging. 2018 (PMID: 29725986).

shelves.title: Multicomponent exercise in frail community-dwellers (partial completion of #459): strength, balance and mobility improve, but the frail-specific trials that counted falls — LIFE and Fairhall — found no fall reduction
shelves.question: Does a multicomponent exercise program prevent falls in frail older adults living in the community?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Exercise Therapy · Female · Gait · Health Education · Humans · Lower Extremity · Male · Muscle Strength · Postural Balance · Sedentary Behavior · Sex Factors · Single-Blind Method · United States
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #459, which covers exercise — including the Otago home strength-and-balance programme — for fall prevention in community-dwelling older adults generally; this shelf asks the narrower frail-specific question #459 does not separate out. The answer divides. The two randomised trials that enrolled frail or functionally limited community-dwellers and counted falls found no fall reduction: in the LIFE programme's prespecified fall-injury analysis (Gill 2016), serious fall injuries ran 9.2% on structured physical activity versus 10.3% on health education (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.23; the treatment made no difference), and Fairhall 2014's frailty-targeted multifactorial programme improved strength, sway, physical performance and walking speed yet left the fall rate unchanged (incidence rate ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.63; the treatment made no difference to falls). Against that, a systematic review of exercise in physically frail older adults (Cadore 2013) found seven of ten fall-incidence trials reported fewer falls after training and judged multicomponent training the best strategy. The LIFE programme's mobility-disability benefit is homed on live shelves #130 and #343 and is not re-carded here; what this slice adds is that preventing disability and preventing falls are not the same outcome in frail people. PROPOSED SPLIT (function improves, falls unproven in frail-specific trials): multicomponent programmes reliably improve the physical risk factors for falling in frail community-dwellers, smaller and review-level evidence leans toward fewer falls, but the two frail-population randomised trials that counted falls found no reduction in fall rates or serious fall injuries.

cards.headline: Gill 2016 (LIFE): serious fall injuries 9.2% on structured physical activity versus 10.3% on health education — hazard ratio 0.90, not significant (the treatment made no difference to serious fall injuries)
cards.summary: Gill 2016 (LIFE): serious fall injuries 9.2% on structured physical activity versus 10.3% on health education — hazard ratio 0.90, not significant (the treatment made no difference to serious fall injuries)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, prespecified secondary-outcome analysis (Gill 2016, LIFE)
cards.people: 1,635 sedentary adults aged 70–89 years with functional limitations (Short Physical Performance Battery score 9 or below, able to walk 400 m), randomised at eight US centres to a structured, moderate-intensity physical activity programme (n = 818; centre-based twice weekly plus home sessions 3–4 times weekly, including aerobic, strength, flexibility and balance training) or a health education programme (n = 817). Serious fall injury was a prespecified secondary outcome of the LIFE study.
cards.result: Over a median follow-up of 2.6 years, a serious fall injury was experienced by 75 participants (9.2%) in the physical activity group and 84 (10.3%) in the health education group (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% confidence interval 0.66 to 1.23; P = 0.52). The authors note the trial was underpowered to detect small but possibly important reductions. In analyses that were not prespecified, rates of all serious fall injuries, fall-related fractures and fall-related hospital admissions were lower in men on physical activity (rate ratios 0.54, 0.47 and 0.41) but not in women (1.07, 1.12 and 1.10), with significant sex interactions — hypothesis-generating only, as printed in the record.
cards.watchOut: LIFE enrolled sedentary older adults with functional limitations rather than people meeting a formal frailty definition, and its primary outcome was mobility disability (homed on shelves #130 and #343) — this card answers only the falls slice, and the favourable male subgroup findings were not prespecified.
cards.source: Gill TM et al. Effect of structured physical activity on prevention of serious fall injuries in adults aged 70-89: randomized clinical trial (LIFE Study). BMJ. 2016. PMID: 26842425. Registry ID: NCT01072500. cards.headline: Fairhall 2014: a frailty-targeted multifactorial programme improved strength, sway, performance and walking speed in 241 frail community-dwellers — but the fall rate did not fall (incidence rate ratio 1.12; the treatment made no difference to falls)
cards.summary: Fairhall 2014: a frailty-targeted multifactorial programme improved strength, sway, performance and walking speed in 241 frail community-dwellers — but the fall rate did not fall (incidence rate ratio 1.12; the treatment made no difference to falls)
cards.people: 241 community-dwelling people aged 70 years or older without severe cognitive impairment who met the Cardiovascular Health Study frailty definition (mean age 83.3 years, 68% women), randomised to a multifactorial, interdisciplinary intervention targeting frailty characteristics — including an individualised home exercise programme prescribed over 10 physiotherapist home visits plus interdisciplinary management of medical, psychological and social problems — or control; 216 (90%) completed the study. Falls were monitored with calendars over 12 months.
cards.result: After 12 months the intervention group performed significantly better on quadriceps strength (between-group difference 1.84 kg, 95% CI 0.17 to 3.51), body sway (−90.63 mm, 95% CI −168.6 to −12.6), Short Physical Performance Battery (1.58, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.14) and 4-metre walk (0.06 m/s, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.10), with a trend toward a better total Physiological Profile Assessment score (−0.40, 95% CI −0.83 to 0.04; P = 0.07) — but no difference in fall rates (incidence rate ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.63; P = 0.53). The authors conclude the intervention improved performance on risk factors for falls but did not reduce the rate of falls.
cards.watchOut: This was a multifactorial frailty intervention, not exercise alone — medical, psychological and social management rode along with the home exercise programme — and improved risk-factor scores did not translate into fewer falls within 12 months.
cards.source: Fairhall N et al. Effect of a multifactorial, interdisciplinary intervention on risk factors for falls and fall rate in frail older people: a randomised controlled trial. Age Ageing. 2014. PMID: 24381025. Registry ID: ACTRN12608000250336. cards.headline: Cadore 2013: across 20 exercise trials in physically frail older adults, seven of the ten that counted falls found fewer falls after training — and multicomponent training looked the best strategy
cards.summary: Cadore 2013: across 20 exercise trials in physically frail older adults, seven of the ten that counted falls found fewer falls after training — and multicomponent training looked the best strategy
cards.people: Systematic review of 20 studies of exercise training in physically frail older adults (multicomponent exercise training 10, resistance training 6, endurance training 1, balance training 3), searched across Scielo, Science Citation Index, MEDLINE, Scopus, Sport Discus and ScienceDirect from 1990 to 2012; ten trials investigated the effect of exercise on the incidence of falls. Total participant N across the reviewed trials is not documented in the record.
cards.result: Seven of the ten fall-incidence trials found a lower falls incidence after physical training compared with control. Eleven trials investigated gait ability (six showed enhancements), ten investigated balance (seven demonstrated enhanced balance) and thirteen investigated muscle strength (nine showed increases). The reviewers conclude that the multicomponent exercise intervention composed of strength, endurance and balance training seems to be the best strategy to improve the rate of falls, gait ability, balance and strength performance in physically frail older adults. No pooled effect size for falls is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: A narrative count of positive trials (seven of ten) is weaker evidence than a pooled estimate, and the smaller trials in this review predate the two large null frail-population trials carded above — the review cannot outweigh them on the fall-rate question.
cards.source: Cadore EL et al. Effects of different exercise interventions on risk of falls, gait ability, and balance in physically frail older adults: a systematic review. Rejuvenation Research. 2013. PMID: 23327448. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: in frail community-dwellers, multicomponent programmes improve strength, balance and mobility — but the two randomised trials that counted falls in frail or functionally limited people found no fall reduction, against a review-level lean toward benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: in frail community-dwellers, multicomponent programmes improve strength, balance and mobility — but the two randomised trials that counted falls in frail or functionally limited people found no fall reduction, against a review-level lean toward benefit
cards.people: The carded evidence: one prespecified fall-injury analysis of the LIFE randomised programme (N = 1,635), one frailty-targeted multifactorial randomised trial with calendar-counted falls (N = 241), and one systematic review of 20 exercise trials in physically frail older adults (total N not documented in the record). Unique participants across the two trials total 1,876, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Serious fall injuries on the LIFE structured physical activity programme ran 9.2% versus 10.3% on health education (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.23; Gill 2016), and Fairhall 2014's programme left the fall rate unchanged (incidence rate ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.63) despite better strength, sway, performance and gait — while Cadore 2013's review found seven of ten fall-counting trials in frail adults reported fewer falls with training. The general community-dwelling evidence, including Otago, stays on live shelf #459; the LIFE mobility-disability result stays on shelves #130 and #343. PROPOSED SPLIT (function improves, falls unproven in frail-specific trials).
cards.watchOut: Do not let the mobility-disability benefit of these programmes (real, and homed elsewhere) be read as a falls benefit: on the falls outcome itself, the frail-specific randomised record is null, and the positive signal comes from smaller, older trials gathered in a review.
cards.source: Synthesis of Gill TM et al. BMJ. 2016 (PMID: 26842425); Fairhall N et al. Age Ageing. 2014 (PMID: 24381025); Cadore EL et al. Rejuvenation Research. 2013 (PMID: 23327448).

shelves.title: Prompted voiding on its own in care homes (partial completion of #2869): fewer wet episodes while the programme is actively delivered — short-term, small-trial evidence, nothing beyond six months
shelves.question: Does scheduled toileting and prompted voiding reduce incontinence episodes in care home residents?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Behavior Therapy · Humans · Middle Aged · Urinary Incontinence
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #2869, which covers prompted voiding only as one half of functional incidental training (prompted voiding combined with exercise, Ouslander 2005); this shelf asks what prompted voiding and scheduled toileting do on their own. The evidence is old, small and short-term, but it points one way. The Cochrane review (Eustice 2000) gathered five trials in 355 elderly people and found prompted voiding increased self-initiated voiding and decreased incontinent episodes in the short term, with no evidence about long-term effects and insufficient evidence for firm conclusions. A staff-delivered randomised trial (Lai 2017, N = 52) found the benefit could be sustained by ordinary nursing-home staff over six months, with a 9.1% decrease in the incontinence rate in the intervention group. An implementation study (Schnelle 1993) showed wet checks falling from 43% to 21% over six months when supervisory nurses ran a quality-control system for the toileting programme — evidence about keeping the programme delivered, not a randomised comparison. Nothing here separates the effect of the schedule itself from the staff attention and positive reinforcement that prompted voiding, by definition, bundles with it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): prompted voiding/scheduled toileting probably reduces wet episodes in care-home residents while it is actively delivered, on short-term and small-trial evidence; durability beyond six months and any effect independent of staff attention are unproven.

cards.headline: Eustice 2000 (Cochrane): five trials, 355 elderly people — prompted voiding increased self-initiated voiding and decreased incontinent episodes in the short term; evidence insufficient for firm conclusions
cards.summary: Eustice 2000 (Cochrane): five trials, 355 elderly people — prompted voiding increased self-initiated voiding and decreased incontinent episodes in the short term; evidence insufficient for firm conclusions
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of all randomised or quasi-randomised trials of prompted voiding for urinary incontinence in adults; five trials involving 355 elderly people, most of them women, were included (one further trial excluded for reporting no relevant outcome data, one awaiting assessment). Prompted voiding — verbal prompts and positive reinforcement, used mainly in North American nursing homes, in people with or without dementia — was compared with no prompted voiding in four trials.
cards.result: The limited evidence suggested that prompted voiding increased self-initiated voiding and decreased incontinent episodes in the short term. There was no evidence about long-term effects. A single small trial suggested adding the muscle relaxant oxybutynin reduced incontinent episodes in the short term (cross-over design; long-term effects not addressed). The reviewers' conclusion, printed plainly: there was insufficient evidence to reach firm conclusions for practice, with suggestive but inconclusive evidence of short-term benefit. No pooled effect size is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: The review is from 2000 and rests on five small trials; 'suggestive, although inconclusive' is the reviewers' own wording, and no included trial followed residents long enough to say whether the benefit outlasts the programme's novelty.
cards.source: Eustice S et al. Prompted voiding for the management of urinary incontinence in adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2000. PMID: 10796861. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Aged · Behavior Therapy · Humans · Middle Aged · Urinary Incontinence

cards.headline: Lai 2017: staff-delivered prompted voiding for six months beat usual care on wet episodes per day, incontinence rate and continent toileting — incontinence rate down 9.1% in the intervention group (N = 52, printed on the face)
cards.summary: Lai 2017: staff-delivered prompted voiding for six months beat usual care on wet episodes per day, incontinence rate and continent toileting — incontinence rate down 9.1% in the intervention group (N = 52, printed on the face)
cards.people: Randomised controlled trial in five Hong Kong nursing homes: 52 residents admitted for at least six months whose incontinence had been stable over the prior six months. All nursing-home staff were trained to deliver prompted voiding correctly before the study; the intervention group received staff-delivered prompted voiding for six months and the control group received usual care. Outcomes — wet episodes per day, incontinence rate per day, self-initiated toileting per day and total continent toileting per day — were collected at baseline, three months and six months.
cards.result: There were significant differences between the two groups in wet episodes per day, incontinence rate per day and total continent toileting per day at six months, with positive results in the intervention group; a decrease of 9.1% was observed in the incontinence rate of the intervention group. The authors conclude prompted voiding showed positive effects, although not as powerful as those found in overseas (research-staff-delivered) studies, and that the staff-delivered intervention was sustainable for six months. No exact between-group effect size beyond the 9.1% figure is reported in the record.
cards.watchOut: Fifty-two residents in one city's homes, with staff specially trained for the study: the trial shows a trained-staff programme can hold its effect for six months, not that routine staffing levels everywhere will reproduce it.
cards.source: Lai CKY et al. Using Prompted Voiding to Manage Urinary Incontinence in Nursing Homes: Can It Be Sustained?. Journal of the American Medical Directors Association. 2017. PMID: 28236604. cards.headline: Schnelle 1993: when supervisory nurses ran quality control on a prompted-voiding programme, random-hour wet checks fell from 43% to 21% and stayed down for six months — an implementation study, not a randomised trial (participant N not documented in the record)
cards.summary: Schnelle 1993: when supervisory nurses ran quality control on a prompted-voiding programme, random-hour wet checks fell from 43% to 21% and stayed down for six months — an implementation study, not a randomised trial (participant N not documented in the record)
cards.people: Implementation study in seven nursing homes: supervisory nurses were taught a quality-control management system that permitted time-efficient assessment of how well a prompted voiding toileting programme continued to be implemented by nursing aides. Random-hour wet checks were taken during the six-month management period. The number of residents assessed is not documented in the record (N not documented).
cards.result: Random-hour wet checks taken during the six-month management period revealed a reduction in wetness from 43% to 21% (P < .0001), sustained over the full six-month period. The record reports no control group and no randomised comparison: the finding is that continence gains depend on the programme actually being delivered, and that a supervisory quality-control system kept delivery — and the lower wet rate — going.
cards.watchOut: Without a comparison group, the 43%-to-21% fall cannot be credited to prompted voiding alone — regression, attention and the quality-control system itself are all in the mix; the card is evidence about sustaining delivery, and is labelled as such.
cards.source: Schnelle JF et al. Maintaining continence in nursing home residents through the application of industrial quality control. The Gerontologist. 1993. PMID: 8440494. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: prompted voiding alone probably cuts wet episodes while it is actively delivered — short-term trial evidence, one six-month staff-delivered trial, and implementation data all point the same way, none of it large or long
cards.summary: Synthesis: prompted voiding alone probably cuts wet episodes while it is actively delivered — short-term trial evidence, one six-month staff-delivered trial, and implementation data all point the same way, none of it large or long
cards.people: The carded evidence: a Cochrane review of five trials (355 elderly people), one staff-delivered randomised trial (N = 52, six months), and one uncontrolled implementation study in seven nursing homes (resident N not documented in the record). Documented participants total over 400, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is trial age, size and follow-up length, printed here.
cards.result: Prompted voiding increased self-initiated voiding and decreased incontinent episodes in the short term across the Cochrane trials (Eustice 2000); staff-delivered prompted voiding still beat usual care at six months, with a 9.1% decrease in incontinence rate (Lai 2017); and wet checks halved (43% to 21%) when a quality-control system kept a toileting programme delivered (Schnelle 1993). The combination programme with exercise stays on live shelf #2869. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — short-term, small-trial evidence.
cards.watchOut: Every carded report bundles the toileting schedule with staff prompts, attention and reinforcement — no carded study isolates the clock-based schedule alone, and none follows residents beyond six months.
