shelves.title: Pelvic floor exercises in community-dwelling older women (PARTIAL completion of live #3831): real but modest improvement in four randomised trials — and a self-help booklet came close in one
shelves.question: Do pelvic floor exercises improve urinary incontinence in older women living in the community?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Behavior Therapy · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Middle Aged · Psychotherapy, Group · Surveys and Questionnaires · Treatment Outcome · Urinary Incontinence
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — printed on the face. This pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #3831 homes the 43-trial Cochrane network meta-analysis of all conservative, drug and combined treatments in women over 60 (Vesentini 2025, PMID 41307301 — homed there, not re-carded here), which ranks treatments against each other but does not isolate pelvic floor muscle training against no treatment in community-dwelling women. Four free randomised trials fill that slice. The largest, GLADIOLUS (463 women aged 55 and over), found a one-time group behavioural class built around pelvic floor exercises beat no treatment on incontinence scores at every time point, though the 3-month difference (−0.96 points) fell short of the trial's own 3-point target for clinical importance. A Hong Kong programme trial (55 women over 65) found 6.4 fewer leakage episodes per week than pamphlet advice alone. An Australian trial (83 women over 65) found intensive pelvic floor training beat bladder training on measured leakage. Against that, Burgio 2002 (222 women) found coached behavioural training reduced episodes by 63–69%, but a self-help booklet alone achieved 58.6%, with no significant difference between groups. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pelvic floor exercises help older women living in the community, modestly; how much the coaching adds beyond a good booklet is unsettled.

cards.headline: GLADIOLUS 2018: a one-time group class in bladder health and pelvic floor exercises beat no treatment in 463 older women — significantly, but by less than the trial's own 3-point target at 3 months
cards.summary: GLADIOLUS 2018: a one-time group class in bladder health and pelvic floor exercises beat no treatment in 463 older women — significantly, but by less than the trial's own 3-point target at 3 months
cards.people: 463 community-dwelling women aged 55–91 (mean 64) with urinary incontinence of at least 3 months' duration, recruited by mail to three US academic medical centres and randomised to a one-time 2-hour group behavioural treatment class (bladder health education, pelvic floor muscle exercise instruction, written materials and an audio CD; n = 232) or no treatment (n = 231); 398 completed the 12-month study.
cards.result: Incontinence scores (ICIQ-SF) favoured the class at every time point: the between-group difference was −0.96 points at 3 months (95% CI −1.51 to −0.41) — statistically significant but below the 3-point difference the trial was designed around — and −1.36 at 6 months, −2.13 at 9 months and −1.77 at 12 months. All secondary outcomes (severity, quality of life, perceived improvement) favoured the class except pelvic floor muscle strength itself. The incremental cost per treatment success was $723 at 3 months, and by 12 months the class dominated (better outcomes at lower cost).
cards.watchOut: The intervention was a single class plus home materials, not a supervised exercise course, and the mean age was 64 — younger than the frailest community populations; the effect is real but small on the trial's own yardstick.
cards.source: Diokno AC et al. Effect of Group-Administered Behavioral Treatment on Urinary Incontinence in Older Women: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA internal medicine. 2018. PMID: 30193294. cards.headline: Leong 2015: a 12-week continence physiotherapy programme cut leakage by 6.4 episodes a week more than an advice pamphlet in women over 65
cards.summary: Leong 2015: a 12-week continence physiotherapy programme cut leakage by 6.4 episodes a week more than an advice pamphlet in women over 65
cards.people: 55 Chinese women aged over 65 with mild-to-moderate stress, urge or mixed urinary incontinence attending six elderly community health centres in Hong Kong, randomly assigned to eight sessions of a standardised Urinary Continence Physiotherapy Programme over 12 weeks (education, pelvic floor muscle training with manual palpation and verbal feedback, and behavioural therapy; n = 27) or to advice and an educational pamphlet (n = 28).
cards.result: Compared with the pamphlet group, the programme group had significantly fewer incontinence episodes per week (mean difference −6.4, 95% CI −8.9 to −3.9; P<0.001), better quality of life (mean difference −3.93 on the modified Chinese Incontinence Impact Questionnaire short form, 95% CI −5.08 to −2.78; P<0.001) and far higher perceived improvement (8.7 vs 1.4 on an 11-point scale; P<0.001); treatment satisfaction averaged 9.5 of 11.
cards.watchOut: Only 55 women, mild-to-moderate symptoms, and an unblinded programme-versus-pamphlet comparison — expectation and attention effects cannot be separated from the exercise effect here.
cards.source: Leong BS et al. Effectiveness of a new standardised Urinary Continence Physiotherapy Programme for community-dwelling older women in Hong Kong. Hong Kong medical journal = Xianggang yi xue za zhi. 2015. PMID: 25377297. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sherburn 2011: intensive pelvic floor training beat bladder training on measured leakage in women over 65 with stress incontinence (median 0.0 g vs 0.3 g on a cough stress test)
cards.summary: Sherburn 2011: intensive pelvic floor training beat bladder training on measured leakage in women over 65 with stress incontinence (median 0.0 g vs 0.3 g on a cough stress test)
cards.people: 83 community-dwelling women over 65 (mean age 71.8 years) with urodynamic stress incontinence at two Australian metropolitan hospitals, randomised in an assessor-blinded trial to 20 weeks of high-intensity pelvic floor muscle training or bladder training.
cards.result: Both groups improved, but the pelvic floor group leaked significantly less on the cough stress test (median 0.0 g, 95% CI 0.2–0.9, vs 0.3 g, 95% CI 0.2–1.7; P=0.006), reported better symptom and bother scores (ICIQ-UI SF mean 5.9 vs 8.5) and far more often perceived improvement (73.6% vs 36.4%; P=0.002) after 5 months.
cards.watchOut: The comparator was another active therapy (bladder training), not no treatment, and the population was stress incontinence specifically — this card shows pelvic floor training works in older women, not how it compares with doing nothing.
cards.source: Sherburn M et al. Incontinence improves in older women after intensive pelvic floor muscle training: an assessor-blinded randomized controlled trial. Neurourology and urodynamics. 2011. PMID: 21284022. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Burgio 2002: coached behavioural training cut urge-incontinence episodes by 63–69% — but a self-help booklet alone cut them by 58.6%, with no significant difference between groups
cards.summary: Burgio 2002: coached behavioural training cut urge-incontinence episodes by 63–69% — but a self-help booklet alone cut them by 58.6%, with no significant difference between groups
cards.people: 222 ambulatory, community-dwelling women aged 55–92 with urge incontinence, or mixed incontinence with urge predominant, randomised at a US university continence clinic to 8 weeks of biofeedback-assisted behavioural training (n = 73), behavioural training with verbal feedback based on vaginal palpation (n = 74), or a self-administered behavioural programme using a self-help booklet (control condition; n = 75). Behavioural training centred on pelvic floor muscle control.
cards.result: Mean reductions in incontinence episodes were 63.1% with biofeedback-assisted training, 69.4% with verbal-feedback training and 58.6% with the booklet alone — not significantly different from each other (P=.23); coached training made no demonstrated difference over the booklet. Satisfaction did differ: 75.0% of the biofeedback group and 85.5% of the verbal-feedback group were completely satisfied, versus 55.7% of the booklet group (P=.001), and quality of life improved significantly in all three groups.
cards.watchOut: The booklet was itself an active self-treatment, not a no-treatment control — so this trial caps how much credit coaching can claim, without showing that pelvic floor exercises do nothing.
cards.source: Burgio KL et al. Behavioral training with and without biofeedback in the treatment of urge incontinence in older women: a randomized controlled trial. JAMA. 2002. PMID: 12425706. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: pelvic floor programmes improved incontinence in all four trials — the size of the gain depends on the comparison
cards.summary: Synthesis: pelvic floor programmes improved incontinence in all four trials — the size of the gain depends on the comparison
cards.people: The carded evidence: four randomised trials in community-dwelling older women (GLADIOLUS 463, Burgio 222, Sherburn 83, Leong 55 participants; 823 in total), so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Pelvic-floor-based programmes improved incontinence in every trial: against no treatment the gain was statistically solid but modest (GLADIOLUS), against a pamphlet it was large (Leong, −6.4 episodes per week), against bladder training it favoured pelvic floor training on measured leakage (Sherburn), and against a self-help booklet coached training showed no significant advantage (Burgio). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): pelvic floor exercises improve urinary incontinence in older women living in the community; the size of the benefit depends heavily on what they are compared with. The network ranking of all treatments in women over 60 is homed on live shelf #3831.
cards.watchOut: None of these trials enrolled women in residential care, and incontinence type differs across cards (stress, urge, mixed) — read each card's population before generalising.
cards.source: Synthesis of Diokno AC et al. JAMA internal medicine. 2018 (PMID: 30193294); Leong BS et al. Hong Kong medical journal = Xianggang yi xue za zhi. 2015 (PMID: 25377297); Sherburn M et al. Neurourology and urodynamics. 2011 (PMID: 21284022); Burgio KL et al. JAMA. 2002 (PMID: 12425706).

shelves.title: Sarcopenia is both: motor units and fibres are lost (and sarcopenic muscle fails to reinnervate), while the surviving muscle is anabolically resistant to amino acids and exercise
shelves.question: What drives human sarcopenia at the muscle level — motor-unit loss, anabolic resistance to dietary protein, or both — and what do human biopsy and tracer studies show?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aging/pathology · Cell Count · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Muscles/pathology · Muscular Atrophy/pathology · Thigh
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology — motor-unit organisation, muscle fibre types and protein turnover). The question poses an either/or; the human biopsy, autopsy and tracer evidence answers both. On the denervation side: Lexell 1988 counted fibres in whole vastus lateralis from 43 men and found ageing atrophy from about age 25, accelerating, caused mainly by fibre loss with no fibre type spared; Piasecki 2018 measured motor units directly and found numbers reduced in all older men, with non-sarcopenic and pre-sarcopenic men compensating by enlarging surviving units through reinnervation — and sarcopenic men (n = 29) failing to do so. On the anabolic side: Cuthbertson 2005 (44 men, tracer/biopsy, insulin clamped) found basal synthesis normal in old muscle but the response to essential amino acids blunted, with reduced mTOR-pathway signalling; Kumar 2009 (25 young, 25 old) found the same blunting for resistance exercise at every intensity. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED: motor-unit loss removes fibres; anabolic resistance stops the remainder being maintained.

cards.headline: Lexell 1988: whole vastus lateralis muscles from 43 men aged 15–83 showed ageing atrophy beginning around age 25 and accelerating — caused mainly by loss of fibres (no fibre type spared), and to a lesser extent by shrinkage of type 2 fibres
cards.summary: Lexell 1988: whole vastus lateralis muscles from 43 men aged 15–83 showed ageing atrophy beginning around age 25 and accelerating — caused mainly by loss of fibres (no fibre type spared), and to a lesser extent by shrinkage of type 2 fibres
cards.type: Primary human whole-muscle fibre-count study (Lexell 1988) — N = 43
cards.people: Cross-sections of whole vastus lateralis muscle obtained at autopsy from 43 previously physically healthy men between 15 and 83 years of age; total number, size, proportion and distribution of type 1 (slow-twitch) and type 2 (fast-twitch) fibres were analysed by multivariate regression.
cards.result: Ageing atrophy of this muscle begins around 25 years of age and thereafter accelerates. It is caused mainly by a loss of fibres, with no predominant effect on any fibre type, and to a lesser extent by a reduction in fibre size, mostly of type 2 fibres. The authors also describe other age-related adaptive changes in fibre size, number and enzyme histochemistry — fibre loss at autopsy is the anatomical footprint of motor units (and their motor neurons) being lost, since each fibre belongs to one motor unit.
cards.watchOut: Autopsy cross-sections are cross-sectional: 43 different men at different ages, not the same men followed over time, and fibre loss is an indirect readout of motor-unit loss — the electrophysiological card (Piasecki 2018) measures motor units directly. One muscle (vastus lateralis) in men only.
cards.source: Lexell J et al. What is the cause of the ageing atrophy? Total number, size and proportion of different fiber types studied in whole vastus lateralis muscle from 15- to 83-year-old men. Journal of the neurological sciences. 1988. PMID: 3379447. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Piasecki 2018: motor unit numbers were reduced in all older groups versus young men, and sarcopenic men (n = 29) had failed to enlarge their surviving motor units — the failed reinnervation compensation that distinguishes sarcopenic from non-sarcopenic muscle
cards.summary: Piasecki 2018: motor unit numbers were reduced in all older groups versus young men, and sarcopenic men (n = 29) had failed to enlarge their surviving motor units — the failed reinnervation compensation that distinguishes sarcopenic from non-sarcopenic muscle
cards.type: Primary human motor-unit electrophysiology study (Piasecki 2018) — N = 143 men across groups
cards.people: Young men (n = 48) compared with non-sarcopenic old (n = 13), pre-sarcopenic (n = 53) and sarcopenic (n = 29) older men; motor unit potentials were isolated from intramuscular and surface EMG recordings of vastus lateralis.
cards.result: Motor unit numbers were reduced in all groups of old compared with young men (all P < 0.001). Motor unit potentials were higher (larger units) in non-sarcopenic and pre-sarcopenic men than in young men (P = 0.039 and P = 0.001 respectively) — evidence of reinnervation expanding surviving units — but not in the vastus lateralis of sarcopenic men (P = 0.485). The authors conclude extensive motor unit remodelling occurs early in ageing and precedes sarcopenia, and that a failure to expand motor unit size to compensate for declining numbers distinguishes sarcopenic from pre-sarcopenic muscle.
cards.watchOut: Cross-sectional group comparisons in men, one muscle; 'failure to expand' is inferred from unit size at one time point, not observed longitudinally. It identifies a distinguishing feature of sarcopenic muscle, not by itself a proven causal sequence.
cards.source: Piasecki M et al. Failure to expand the motor unit size to compensate for declining motor unit numbers distinguishes sarcopenic from non-sarcopenic older men. The Journal of physiology. 2018. PMID: 29527694. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cuthbertson 2005: in 44 young and old men, basal muscle protein synthesis was the same, but older muscle responded less to essential amino acids — anabolic resistance, with reduced expression/activation of mTOR-pathway signalling and more NFkappaB
cards.summary: Cuthbertson 2005: in 44 young and old men, basal muscle protein synthesis was the same, but older muscle responded less to essential amino acids — anabolic resistance, with reduced expression/activation of mTOR-pathway signalling and more NFkappaB
cards.type: Primary human tracer/biopsy anabolic-resistance study (Cuthbertson 2005) — N = 44 men
cards.people: 44 healthy young and old men of similar body build in whom myofibrillar and sarcoplasmic muscle protein synthesis rates were measured (tracer/biopsy methodology) after ingesting different amounts of essential amino acids, with plasma insulin clamped at basal values; intramuscular anabolic signalling proteins were measured.
cards.result: Basal rates of muscle protein synthesis were indistinguishable between young and old, but the elderly showed less anabolic sensitivity and responsiveness of synthesis to essential amino acids, associated with decreased intramuscular expression and activation (phosphorylation) after amino acids of amino-acid sensing/signalling proteins (mTOR, p70 S6 kinase, eIF4BP-1, eIF2B), independent of insulin signalling, and with marked increases in the inflammation-associated transcription factor NFkappaB. The authors conclude the decreased sensitivity and responsiveness to amino acids are probably major contributors to the failure of muscle maintenance in the elderly.
cards.watchOut: Acute post-ingestion synthesis responses in a laboratory protocol are not the same as long-term muscle gain from dietary protein; the study shows the signalling and synthesis deficit exists, in men, at the doses tested. It does not show the deficit cannot be overcome by dose, timing or exercise — the Kumar card shows exercise responses are also blunted, not absent.
cards.source: Cuthbertson D et al. Anabolic signaling deficits underlie amino acid resistance of wasting, aging muscle. FASEB journal : official publication of the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology. 2005. PMID: 15596483. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kumar 2009: resistance exercise raised muscle protein synthesis in a dose–response up to 60–90% of maximum in both age groups (25 young, 25 old men), but the response was blunted at every intensity in the older men
cards.summary: Kumar 2009: resistance exercise raised muscle protein synthesis in a dose–response up to 60–90% of maximum in both age groups (25 young, 25 old men), but the response was blunted at every intensity in the older men
cards.type: Primary human tracer/biopsy exercise study (Kumar 2009) — N = 50 men (25 young, 25 old)
cards.people: Two groups of 25 post-absorptive healthy men — young (24 ± 6 years) and old (70 ± 5 years), with identical body mass indices — who performed resistance exercise at 20–90% of one-repetition maximum; vastus lateralis was sampled before and up to 4 hours after exercise, with myofibrillar protein synthesis measured by [1,2-13C] leucine incorporation and signalling by phosphorylation of p70S6K and 4EBP1.
cards.result: In each group there was a sigmoidal dose–response relationship between synthesis at 1–2 hours post-exercise and exercise intensity, which was blunted in the older men (P < 0.05); synthesis fell to near-basal values by 2–4 hours in both groups. Phosphorylation of p70S6K and 4EBP1 at 60–90% intensity was blunted in older men, and at 1 hour post-exercise p70S6K phosphorylation predicted synthesis rates in the young but not the old. The authors conclude older men show anabolic resistance of signalling and muscle protein synthesis to resistance exercise.
cards.watchOut: Post-absorptive, single-bout, laboratory responses in healthy men; feeding plus exercise in free-living older adults (including women) may behave differently. Blunted is not absent: older muscle still responded, rising to a plateau at 60–90% of maximum.
cards.source: Kumar V et al. Age-related differences in the dose-response relationship of muscle protein synthesis to resistance exercise in young and old men. The Journal of physiology. 2009. PMID: 19001042. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: both mechanisms are real in human tissue — motor units and their fibres are lost (with failed reinnervation compensation in sarcopenic muscle), and the muscle that remains is anabolically resistant to amino acids and to exercise
cards.summary: Synthesis: both mechanisms are real in human tissue — motor units and their fibres are lost (with failed reinnervation compensation in sarcopenic muscle), and the muscle that remains is anabolically resistant to amino acids and to exercise
cards.people: The carded human evidence: whole-muscle fibre counts at autopsy (Lexell 1988, N = 43), motor-unit electrophysiology across young, pre-sarcopenic and sarcopenic men (Piasecki 2018, N = 143), an amino-acid tracer/biopsy study (Cuthbertson 2005, N = 44), and a resistance-exercise tracer/biopsy study (Kumar 2009, N = 50). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology (motor unit organisation and muscle protein turnover), named as framing, not as an evidence card.
cards.result: The question's either/or framing is answered 'both' by the human data. Anatomically, ageing muscle loses fibres — mainly fibre (hence motor-unit) loss from about age 25, accelerating thereafter (Lexell) — and electrophysiology shows motor unit numbers fall in all older men, with sarcopenic men distinguished by failure of surviving units to expand by reinnervation (Piasecki). Functionally, the remaining muscle synthesises protein normally at baseline but responds less to essential amino acids (Cuthbertson) and less to resistance exercise at every intensity (Kumar), with blunted mTOR-pathway signalling in both settings. PROPOSED PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: All four carded studies are in men, and three study the vastus lateralis; the relative weight of denervation versus anabolic resistance may differ in women, in other muscles, and in sarcopenia driven by disease or immobility rather than ageing alone.
cards.source: Synthesis of Lexell J et al. Journal of the neurological sciences. 1988 (PMID: 3379447); Piasecki M et al. The Journal of physiology. 2018 (PMID: 29527694); Cuthbertson D et al. FASEB journal. 2005 (PMID: 15596483); Kumar V et al. The Journal of physiology. 2009 (PMID: 19001042). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology.

shelves.title: Driving in dementia: dementia severity (Clinical Dementia Rating) and a caregiver's rating of 'marginal or unsafe' are the useful signals; the patient's own rating is not, and no office cognitive test has a validated cut-off
shelves.question: In people with dementia who wish to keep driving, which clinical characteristics and tests (CDR stage, caregiver rating, cognitive tests, on-road assessment) best predict unsafe driving?
shelves.mesh: Automobile Driver Examination/legislation & jurisprudence,psychology · Automobile Driving/psychology,standards · Caregivers · Cognition Disorders/diagnosis,psychology · Dementia/diagnosis,psychology · Disability Evaluation · Humans · Neuropsychological Tests/standards · Personality Disorders/diagnosis,etiology · Psychomotor Performance/physiology · Risk Assessment
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE as an evidence synthesis — this is a prediction question, so the currency is what the American Academy of Neurology's evidence-graded parameter and three systematic reviews agree on. Useful for identifying increased risk: Clinical Dementia Rating stage (AAN Level A — the strongest single item), a caregiver rating the patient's driving as marginal or unsafe (Level B), a history of crashes or citations, reduced mileage or situational avoidance, MMSE scores of 24 or less, and aggressive or impulsive traits (all Level C). Not useful: the patient's own rating of their driving (Level A evidence against), and neuropsychological testing beyond dementia severity (Level U — insufficient evidence). The meta-analytic data quantify the gradient: on-road failure in 13.6% at CDR 0.5 and 33.3% at CDR 1 versus 1.6% in healthy controls, with executive function, attention, visuospatial function and global cognition each moderately predictive (effect sizes ~0.5–0.6) and the Maze test and Trail Making tests the best single cognitive predictors. The uncomfortable gap, shown by two reviews: the office tests guidelines recommend have no validated cut-off scores — fifteen of sixteen studies in one review reported none — so no test score by itself licenses or bans a driver; the on-road assessment remains the reference standard the office measures only approximate.

cards.headline: AAN practice parameter (Iverson 2010): CDR stage is Level A evidence for identifying unsafe drivers, caregiver rating Level B; the patient's self-rating is Level A evidence of NOT being useful
cards.summary: AAN practice parameter (Iverson 2010): CDR stage is Level A evidence for identifying unsafe drivers, caregiver rating Level B; the patient's self-rating is Level A evidence of NOT being useful
cards.type: Practice parameter update (evidence-graded systematic review), Neurology 2010
cards.people: Systematic review conducted to the American Academy of Neurology's evidence-based methods, covering demographic characteristics, driving history and cognitive testing as predictors of driving capability in patients with dementia, and the efficacy of driving-risk-reduction strategies.
cards.result: Characteristics judged useful for identifying patients at increased risk of unsafe driving: Clinical Dementia Rating scale (Level A); a caregiver's rating of the patient's driving ability as marginal or unsafe (Level B); a history of crashes or traffic citations (Level C); reduced driving mileage or self-reported situational avoidance (Level C); Mini-Mental State Examination scores of 24 or less (Level C); and aggressive or impulsive personality characteristics (Level C). Judged not useful: a patient's self-rating of safe driving ability (Level A) and lack of situational avoidance (Level C). Evidence was insufficient to support or refute neuropsychological testing (after controlling for dementia severity) or any interventional strategy (Level U).
cards.watchOut: A practice parameter grades the evidence as it stood in 2010; its Levels are about usefulness for risk identification in groups, not a licensing rule for an individual. Level A for the CDR reflects consistent study quality, not a large effect size.
cards.source: Iverson DJ et al. Practice parameter update: evaluation and management of driving risk in dementia: report of the Quality Standards Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology. Neurology. 2010. PMID: 20385882. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Hird 2016: across 32 studies, on-road failure rose with dementia stage (13.6% at CDR 0.5, 33.3% at CDR 1, vs 1.6% of controls); executive function, attention, visuospatial and global cognition predicted performance (effect sizes 0.50–0.61), Maze and Trail Making tests best of the single tests
cards.summary: Hird 2016: across 32 studies, on-road failure rose with dementia stage (13.6% at CDR 0.5, 33.3% at CDR 1, vs 1.6% of controls); executive function, attention, visuospatial and global cognition predicted performance (effect sizes 0.50–0.61), Maze and Trail Making tests best of the single tests
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, Journal of Alzheimer's Disease 2016
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 32 articles covering 1,293 patients with Alzheimer's disease, 92 with mild cognitive impairment and 2,040 healthy older controls; driving outcomes included on-road test scores and pass/fail, errors, caregiver reports, real-world crash involvement and simulator collisions or risky behaviour.
cards.result: Significant predictors of driving performance were executive function (effect size 0.61; 95% CI 0.41 to 0.81), attention (0.55; 0.33 to 0.77), visuospatial function (0.50; 0.34 to 0.65) and global cognition (0.61; 0.39 to 0.83). The best single tests were the Maze test (0.88; 0.60 to 1.15), Trail Making Test Part A (0.65; 0.08 to 1.21) and Part B (0.61; 0.28 to 0.94). Patients with very mild Alzheimer's disease (CDR 0.5) failed on-road tests in 13.6% of cases and those with mild disease (CDR 1) in 33.3%, versus 1.6% of healthy controls (CDR 0). The authors noted inconsistent cognitive predictors and driving outcomes across studies.
cards.watchOut: Effect sizes around 0.5–0.6 are moderate group-level associations — far too weak to classify an individual driver — and the pooled outcomes mix road tests, simulators and caregiver reports. Even at CDR 1, two-thirds of patients passed the on-road test, which is why stage alone cannot settle fitness.
cards.source: Hird MA et al. A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of On-Road Simulator and Cognitive Driving Assessment in Alzheimer's Disease and Mild Cognitive Impairment. Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD. 2016. PMID: 27176076. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Molnar 2006: of 16 studies of office cognitive tests in dementia, the guideline-recommended tests showed no robust findings and 15 reported no cut-off scores at all — 'impossible to employ tests in a standardized fashion'
cards.summary: Molnar 2006: of 16 studies of office cognitive tests in dementia, the guideline-recommended tests showed no robust findings and 15 reported no cut-off scores at all — 'impossible to employ tests in a standardized fashion'
cards.type: Systematic review, Journal of the American Geriatrics Society 2006
cards.people: Systematic review of prospective and retrospective cohort and case-control studies (1984–2005) of in-office cognitive tests distinguishing safe from unsafe drivers with dementia or Alzheimer's disease, against crash, simulator or on-road outcomes; sixteen articles met the inclusion criteria, each independently quality-rated by two reviewers.
cards.result: Tests recommended by existing guidelines (American and Canadian Medical Association) either did not demonstrate robustly positive findings in the included studies (Mini-Mental State Examination, Trails B) or had never been evaluated in any included study (Clock Drawing). Fifteen of the sixteen studies reported no cutoff scores. The authors concluded that without validated cutoffs it is impossible to use these tests in a standardised fashion in front-line clinical settings, and called for routine cutoff analyses and consensus methods work.
cards.watchOut: An absence-of-validation finding, not a finding that cognitive testing is worthless: the 2016 meta-analysis (previous card) later pooled moderate predictive effects for several domains. What remains true from this card is the cut-off gap — a score without a validated threshold cannot be a pass/fail rule.
cards.source: Molnar FJ et al. Clinical utility of office-based cognitive predictors of fitness to drive in persons with dementia: A systematic review. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2006. PMID: 17198485. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Man-Son-Hing 2007: drivers with dementia performed worse on road tests and simulators in all 23 studies, yet only one objective crash study showed more crashes — and no study tested any compensatory strategy
cards.summary: Man-Son-Hing 2007: drivers with dementia performed worse on road tests and simulators in all 23 studies, yet only one objective crash study showed more crashes — and no study tested any compensatory strategy
cards.type: Systematic review, Journal of the American Geriatrics Society 2007
cards.people: Systematic review of 23 case-control studies of drivers with a diagnosis of dementia, using state- and caregiver-reported crash rates, performance-based road tests and driving simulator evaluations as outcomes.
cards.result: Drivers with dementia universally exhibited poorer performance on road tests and simulator evaluations than cognitively normal drivers. However, only one study using an objective measure of motor vehicle crashes was able to show that drivers with dementia were involved in more crashes than control subjects. No studies were found examining the efficacy of methods to compensate for or accommodate the worse driving performance.
cards.watchOut: Crash rates are diluted by self-restriction — people with dementia drive less and avoid hard situations — so flat crash counts do not mean flat risk per mile. This card is the corrective to reading the on-road failure gradient as a crash gradient.
cards.source: Man-Son-Hing M et al. Systematic review of driving risk and the efficacy of compensatory strategies in persons with dementia. Journal of the American Geriatrics Society. 2007. cards.headline: Synthesis: stage and caregiver judgement carry the signal; self-rating carries none; cognitive tests predict modestly but have no validated cut-offs — POSSIBLE (evidence synthesis)
cards.summary: Synthesis: stage and caregiver judgement carry the signal; self-rating carries none; cognitive tests predict modestly but have no validated cut-offs — POSSIBLE (evidence synthesis)
cards.people: Synthesis of the four cards above.
cards.result: The convergent answer: ask the caregiver, stage the dementia, take the crash and citation history, and discount the patient's own reassurance — that bundle is what the AAN graded as useful. Cognitive testing adds moderate group-level prediction (executive function, attention, visuospatial skills; Maze and Trail Making tests best) but no score in the fetched records has a validated fitness cut-off, and on-road assessment remains the arbiter when the office picture is contested — remembering that even at CDR 1 most patients passed it. The stamp is POSSIBLE because every strand is observational prediction evidence, and the one outcome that matters most, crashes, is the least consistently demonstrated.
cards.watchOut: Nothing in this shelf sets a legal or licensing threshold; reporting duties and formal assessment pathways are jurisdiction-specific and sit outside this evidence question.

shelves.title: Deintensifying diabetes treatment in older adults: only about a quarter of tightly controlled patients are ever deintensified, but observational data show it succeeds in 62–75% with small HbA1c rises — and no trial has tested the hypoglycaemia benefit
shelves.question: In older adults with type 2 diabetes and tight glycaemic control or hypoglycaemia risk, does deintensification/deprescribing of glucose-lowering therapy, compared with continuation, reduce hypoglycaemia and harm without worsening control?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Glucose · Diabetes Mellitus · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glycated Hemoglobin · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Life Expectancy · Male · Retrospective Studies
shelves.balance: This shelf is observational throughout — no completed randomised trial has tested whether deintensifying glucose-lowering therapy reduces hypoglycaemia. What the cohorts show consistently is, first, how rarely it happens: in 179,991 actively treated older veterans, only 27.0% of those with a very low HbA1c (under 6.0%) had treatment deintensified within six months, and under 0.8% of the rest later showed an elevated HbA1c (Sussman 2015). Second, the pattern repeats after harm and in frailty: even after a hypoglycaemia hospital episode or in frail inpatients, deintensification is the exception (19.1% in Melson 2024's 665 frail inpatients, where being overtreated — HbA1c under 7.0% [53 mmol/mol] on glucose-lowering medication — was itself associated with adverse inpatient outcomes). Third, when deintensification is done, the scoping-review evidence (Oktora 2021; 14 studies) finds it succeeds in 62–75% of attempts with only small HbA1c rises, and reminder systems that flag hypoglycaemia produced less overtreatment and fewer hypoglycaemic events. The neighbouring shelves #5629 (sulfonylurea deprescribing at limited life expectancy) and #5983 (structured deprescribing reviews) card different studies and questions; this shelf's studies are not carded there. Bottom line: deintensification is uncommon, feasible, and glycaemically safe in observational data — but the claim that it prevents hypoglycaemia rests on association, not experiment.

cards.headline: VA cohort: only 27.0% of older patients with HbA1c under 6.0% were deintensified — and fewer than 0.8% of the others later ran high (HbA1c cohort N = 179,991)
cards.summary: VA cohort: only 27.0% of older patients with HbA1c under 6.0% were deintensified — and fewer than 0.8% of the others later ran high (HbA1c cohort N = 179,991)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of US Veterans Health Administration patients older than 70 years with diabetes receiving active glucose-lowering treatment (other than metformin alone) in 2012; the HbA1c analysis cohort comprised 179,991 participants, classified by last HbA1c as very low (under 6.0%), moderately low (6.0–6.4%) or not low, with deintensification defined as discontinuation or dose decrease within 6 months.
cards.result: Deintensification occurred in 17.5% of patients whose HbA1c was not low, 20.9% of those with moderately low HbA1c, and 27.0% of the 12,917 patients with very low HbA1c. Among very-low-HbA1c patients whose treatment was not deintensified, fewer than 0.8% had a follow-up HbA1c that was elevated (7.5% or higher) — that is, almost none drifted into poor control, and almost none were rescued by deintensification either; most simply stayed tightly controlled on unchanged therapy. The authors called the low deintensification rate a major opportunity to reduce medication harm.
cards.watchOut: This study measures how often deintensification happens, not whether it improves outcomes; veterans are predominantly men, and claims/EHR data cannot capture hypoglycaemia that never reached medical attention.
cards.source: Sussman JB et al. Rates of Deintensification of Blood Pressure and Glycemic Medication Treatment Based on Levels of Control and Life Expectancy in Older Patients With Diabetes Mellitus. JAMA Intern Med. 2015. PMID: 26502220. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Frail inpatients: deintensification in only 19.1%, and overtreatment (HbA1c under 7.0% [53 mmol/mol] on treatment) tracked with adverse outcomes (N = 665)
cards.summary: Frail inpatients: deintensification in only 19.1%, and overtreatment (HbA1c under 7.0% [53 mmol/mol] on treatment) tracked with adverse outcomes (N = 665)
cards.people: Retrospective review of all 665 people with diabetes and moderate-to-severe frailty (clinical frailty score 6 or more) discharged from a UK tertiary medical unit in 2022.
cards.result: Only 9.0% of patients without an HbA1c in the preceding six months had one assessed during the admission, and the deintensification rate was 19.1%. Factors associated with adverse inpatient outcomes included inpatient hypoglycaemia, non-White ethnicity, and being overtreated — defined as HbA1c under 7.0% (53 mmol/mol) while taking any glucose-lowering medication.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre audit; the overtreatment–harm link is an association from the same admission, not evidence that deintensifying these patients would have prevented the outcomes.

cards.headline: Scoping review: deintensification succeeds in 62–75% of attempts with small HbA1c rises; reminder systems cut overtreatment and hypoglycaemic events (14 studies)
cards.summary: Scoping review: deintensification succeeds in 62–75% of attempts with small HbA1c rises; reminder systems cut overtreatment and hypoglycaemic events (14 studies)
cards.type: Scoping review of observational and implementation studies
cards.people: Scoping review of 14 deprescribing studies in people with type 2 diabetes (literature 2007–2019), covering rates, determinants and success of deprescribing glucose-, blood-pressure- and lipid-lowering medication.
cards.result: Deprescribing rates were 14–27% in older people with low HbA1c and were little affected by age, sex, frailty or life expectancy. Deprescribing glucose-lowering medication was successfully completed in 62–75% of participants with small rises in HbA1c. Where a reminder system identified people with hypoglycaemia, overtreatment fell and fewer hypoglycaemic events occurred. The review judged the bias in success studies to be high and called implementation uncommon overall.
cards.watchOut: A scoping review without pooled effect estimates, over studies the reviewers themselves rated at high risk of bias for the success outcomes; 'small HbA1c rises' is the review's qualitative summary, not a meta-analytic number.
cards.source: Oktora MP et al. Rates, determinants and success of implementing deprescribing in people with type 2 diabetes: A scoping review. Diabet Med. 2021. PMID: 32969063. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Antihypertensive Agents · Deprescriptions · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Humans · Hypoglycemic Agents · Hypolipidemic Agents

cards.headline: Synthesis: deintensification is rare, feasible and glycaemically safe in observational data — its hypoglycaemia benefit is plausible, not proven
cards.summary: Synthesis: deintensification is rare, feasible and glycaemically safe in observational data — its hypoglycaemia benefit is plausible, not proven
cards.people: Over 180,000 older adults across the carded cohorts and 14 studies in the carded scoping review; all evidence observational.
cards.result: Across settings — US veterans with very low HbA1c, UK frail inpatients, and the international deprescribing literature — only about one in five to one in four eligible patients is deintensified; where it is done, 62–75% of attempts succeed with small HbA1c rises, and almost no tightly controlled patient later drifts into poor control. No carded study is a randomised comparison of deintensification versus continuation with hypoglycaemia as the outcome. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — observational only, pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C).
cards.watchOut: Every card is observational: sicker or frailer patients are both more likely to be deintensified and more likely to come to harm, so these data cannot establish that deintensification itself prevents hypoglycaemia — only that tight control usually persists safely when doses are reduced.
cards.source: Synthesis of Sussman JB et al. JAMA Intern Med. 2015 (PMID: 26502220); Melson E et al. Clin Med (Lond). 2024 (PMID: 38387535); Oktora MP et al. Diabet Med. 2021 (PMID: 32969063). Registry IDs: none in the records.

shelves.title: Ibutamoren (MK-677) in healthy older adults: fat-free mass +1.1 kg vs −0.5 kg on placebo over a year — with NO improvement in strength or function, and a glucose cost (fasting glucose +0.3 mmol/L [+5 mg/dL], insulin sensitivity down)
shelves.question: In healthy older adults, does two years of daily ibutamoren, an oral growth-hormone secretagogue, increase fat-free mass and strength and improve function versus placebo — and what does it cost in glucose tolerance and other adverse effects?
shelves.mesh: Adipose Tissue/drug effects · Administration, Oral · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Appetite/drug effects · Blood Glucose/metabolism · Body Composition/drug effects · Double-Blind Method · Female · Human Growth Hormone/drug effects,metabolism · Humans · Indoles/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Insulin/blood · Insulin-Like Growth Factor Binding Protein 1/blood,drug effects · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle, Skeletal/anatomy & histology · Pain/chemically induced · Spiro Compounds/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Thigh
shelves.balance: SPLIT answer, and the split is the point of this shelf. On body composition, ibutamoren (MK-677) does what its mechanism promises: in Nass 2008 (65 healthy adults aged 60–81, 2-year double-blind trial with the primary endpoints at 1 year), growth hormone and IGF-I rose to young-adult levels and fat-free mass increased by +1.1 kg on drug while falling −0.5 kg on placebo (p<0.001) — a 1.6 kg between-group difference — with body weight up 2.7 kg versus 0.8 kg. On the outcomes that matter, it did not deliver: increased fat-free mass did not result in changes in strength or function, in Nass or in the second randomised trial (Bach 2004; 161 older hip-fracture patients, 6 months of MK-0677), where IGF-I rose 84% versus 17% on placebo yet functional performance measures and overall Sickness Impact Profile scores showed no significant differences (the treatment made no difference to function in either trial). The metabolic price is on the face: fasting blood glucose rose by an average of 0.3 mmol/L (5 mg/dL) on MK-677 in Nass (p=0.015) and insulin sensitivity decreased; cortisol rose by 47 nmol/L (1.7 µg/dL). (The fetched abstract record does not print an HbA1c figure, so none is quoted; the glucose and insulin-sensitivity findings are the record's own.) Other frequent effects were increased appetite (subsiding over months) and transient mild lower-extremity oedema and muscle pain; LDL cholesterol fell slightly (−0.14 mmol/L [−5.4 mg/dL]). Mass without function, with a metabolic price.

cards.headline: Nass 2008 (65 healthy older adults, 2 years): fat-free mass +1.1 kg on MK-677 vs −0.5 kg on placebo (p<0.001) — but strength and function did NOT change; fasting glucose +0.3 mmol/L (+5 mg/dL), insulin sensitivity fell
cards.summary: Nass 2008 (65 healthy older adults, 2 years): fat-free mass +1.1 kg on MK-677 vs −0.5 kg on placebo (p<0.001) — but strength and function did NOT change; fasting glucose +0.3 mmol/L (+5 mg/dL), insulin sensitivity fell
cards.people: 65 healthy adults aged 60–81 (men, women on hormone replacement and women not on it) in a 2-year, double-blind, placebo-controlled, modified-crossover trial at a university general clinical research centre, receiving oral MK-677 25 mg or placebo once daily. Primary endpoints after 1 year: fat-free mass and abdominal visceral fat; other endpoints included strength (isokinetic), function, quality of life, insulin sensitivity, lipids, cortisol and bone mineral density, assessed every 6 months.
cards.result: Growth hormone and IGF-I rose to healthy young-adult levels without serious adverse effects. Fat-free mass changed by +1.1 kg (95% CI 0.7 to 1.5) on MK-677 versus −0.5 kg (−1.1 to 0.2) on placebo (p<0.001), and body weight by +2.7 kg versus +0.8 kg (p=0.003); abdominal visceral fat and total fat mass did not differ significantly, while limb fat rose more on drug (1.1 vs 0.24 kg; p=0.001). Crucially, the increased fat-free mass did not result in changes in strength or function (the treatment made no difference on those endpoints). Fasting blood glucose increased by an average of 0.3 mmol/L (5 mg/dL) on MK-677 (p=0.015) and insulin sensitivity decreased; cortisol rose 47 nmol/L (1.7 µg/dL [95% CI 1.0 to 2.6]; p=0.020) and LDL cholesterol fell by 0.14 mmol/L (−5.4 mg/dL; p=0.026). The commonest side effects were increased appetite subsiding over a few months and transient, mild lower-extremity oedema and muscle pain. Two-year exploratory analyses confirmed the 1-year results.
cards.watchOut: The trial itself states its power (duration and participant number) was insufficient to evaluate functional endpoints in healthy elderly people — so the function null here is 'not shown in an underpowered test', which is why this shelf pairs it with the larger hip-fracture trial below before calling the functional answer. The abstract record prints no HbA1c value; the glucose cost is carded as the record states it.

cards.headline: Bach 2004 hip-fracture trial (161 patients aged ≥65): IGF-I up 84% vs 17% on placebo — functional recovery and overall Sickness Impact Profile NOT significantly different (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Bach 2004 hip-fracture trial (161 patients aged ≥65): IGF-I up 84% vs 17% on placebo — functional recovery and overall Sickness Impact Profile NOT significantly different (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (Bach 2004, MK-0677 after hip fracture)
cards.people: 161 previously mobile patients aged 65 and over, recruited 3–14 days after hip-fracture surgery (or within 18 days of fracture) at 13 centres in Europe and North America; patients with diabetes mellitus, cancer, uncontrolled hypertension, heart failure or multiple fractures were excluded. Randomised to 6 months of daily MK-0677 (ibutamoren) or placebo, with 6 further months of follow-up. Primary outcome: change from week 6 to week 26 in a panel of functional performance measures; other outcomes included the Sickness Impact Profile for Nursing Homes and ability to live independently.
cards.result: MK-0677 raised serum IGF-I by 84% (95% CI 63–107) versus 17% (8–28) on placebo. There were no significant differences between MK-0677 and placebo in improvement in functional performance measures or in the overall Sickness Impact Profile score (the treatment made no difference to functional recovery). Greater improvement on drug in three of four lower-extremity measures, the physical domain of the Sickness Impact Profile and independent living did not reach statistical significance.
cards.watchOut: This is the population with the most to gain — older adults recovering from hip fracture — and the functional answer is still null, which converts Nass's underpowered null into a consistent cross-trial pattern. Excluding patients with diabetes also hides the glucose cost where it would bite hardest.

cards.headline: Murphy 1999 pooled bone-turnover analysis (187 older adults across three short RCTs): MK-677 raised bone-formation and resorption markers and IGF-I by 55–94% — biomarker movement, again without a function endpoint
cards.summary: Murphy 1999 pooled bone-turnover analysis (187 older adults across three short RCTs): MK-677 raised bone-formation and resorption markers and IGF-I by 55–94% — biomarker movement, again without a function endpoint
cards.type: Pooled analysis of three randomised trials (Murphy 1999)
cards.people: 187 adults aged 65 and over enrolled in three randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies of oral MK-677 lasting 2–9 weeks, including 50 healthy elderly given 25 mg daily for 2 weeks then 50 mg daily for 2 weeks, and 105 elderly subjects meeting objective criteria for functional impairment given 5–25 mg daily for up to 9 weeks (63 on MK-677 and 28 on placebo completed). Outcomes were biochemical: urinary N-telopeptide (resorption), serum osteocalcin and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase (formation) and IGF-I.
cards.result: MK-677 increased urinary N-telopeptide by 10% (10 mg) and 17% (25 mg) at 2 weeks (p<0.05 vs placebo), serum osteocalcin by 8% in the 4-week study and, in the functionally impaired cohort, osteocalcin by 29.4% and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase by 10.4% (p<0.001) with urinary N-telopeptide up 22.6% (p<0.05); serum IGF-I rose significantly in every study (55–94%). The authors conclude once-daily MK-677 stimulates bone turnover in elderly subjects, based on marker elevations.
cards.watchOut: Two-to-nine-week biomarker studies: both formation AND resorption markers rose (net bone effect unknown), no fracture, strength or function outcome was tested, and these short exposures cannot speak to the glucose cost that the 2-year Nass trial documented.
cards.source: Murphy MG et al. Oral administration of the growth hormone secretagogue MK-677 increases markers of bone turnover in healthy and functionally impaired elderly adults. cards.headline: Synthesis: the honest answer — mass without function, with a metabolic price
cards.summary: Synthesis: the honest answer — mass without function, with a metabolic price
cards.people: Two double-blind randomised trials of daily oral ibutamoren (MK-677) — 65 healthy older adults treated for up to 2 years (Nass 2008) and 161 older hip-fracture patients treated for 6 months (Bach 2004) — plus a pooled bone-turnover analysis of three short trials (187 older adults; Murphy 1999).
cards.result: Fat-free mass rose (+1.1 kg vs −0.5 kg) and the GH/IGF-I axis was restored to young-adult levels, yet neither trial showed improved strength, functional performance or recovery — while fasting glucose rose 0.3 mmol/L (5 mg/dL), insulin sensitivity fell and cortisol rose in the healthy-volunteer trial. A growth-hormone secretagogue can change what an older body is made of without changing what it can do, and it charges glucose tolerance for the difference.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial enrolled frail or sarcopenic patients as such, and neither was powered as a definitive function trial; a larger trial in frankly frail patients could in principle differ — but on the published record, no functional claim for ibutamoren in older adults is supportable.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above. No new data.

shelves.title: Urolithin A in older adults (tested product: Mitopure in the randomised trials): leg and hand muscle endurance improved in a 66-person trial, but the 6-minute walk and maximal ATP production did not significantly separate from placebo
shelves.question: In older adults, does urolithin A (a mitophagy-activating metabolite; name the tested product in each trial) improve muscle endurance/strength and walk distance versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antioxidants/therapeutic use · Coumarins/therapeutic use · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Muscle, Skeletal/metabolism · Vital Capacity/drug effects · Walk Test · Walking
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — small, short, industry-linked trials with mixed functional outcomes. The first-in-human study (Andreux 2019; n=60 sedentary elderly people) showed safety and a muscle mitochondrial gene-expression signature over 4 weeks, with no functional endpoint. In the older-adult randomised trial (Liu 2022; n=66, ages 65–90, tested product Mitopure 1000 mg/day for 4 months), muscle endurance in hand and leg muscles improved versus placebo at 2 months, but the two primary endpoints did not significantly separate: 6-minute walk distance rose 60.8 m on urolithin A versus 42.5 m on placebo (a non-significant difference), and maximal ATP production was essentially unchanged. In middle-aged adults (Singh 2022; n=88, Mitopure), muscle strength rose about 12% in relative terms and aerobic endurance measures improved, but the primary endpoint — peak power output — did not significantly improve. Plasma acylcarnitines and C-reactive protein fell in both randomised trials. No trial is large or long enough to answer falls, disability or independence, so the stamp is capped at POSSIBLE and the Ns are printed: 60, 66 and 88.

cards.headline: Andreux 2019 — first-in-human (n=60): urolithin A was safe over 4 weeks and induced a skeletal-muscle mitochondrial gene-expression signature; no functional endpoint was tested
cards.summary: Andreux 2019 — first-in-human (n=60): urolithin A was safe over 4 weeks and induced a skeletal-muscle mitochondrial gene-expression signature; no functional endpoint was tested
cards.people: 60 healthy, sedentary elderly individuals given urolithin A as a single dose or as multiple doses (500 mg or 1000 mg daily) over a 4-week period; the tested preparation was the Amazentis urolithin A preparation used across this programme (the later randomised trials name it Mitopure).
cards.result: The primary outcome — safety — was favourable, and urolithin A was bioavailable in plasma at all doses tested. After 4 weeks at 500 mg and 1000 mg, plasma acylcarnitines were modulated and skeletal-muscle mitochondrial gene expression changed in a pattern the authors read as a molecular signature of improved mitochondrial and cellular health. No strength, endurance or walking outcome was reported.
cards.watchOut: A safety and biomarker study, not an efficacy trial: a gene-expression signature is not the same as stronger muscles or better walking, and 60 people over 4 weeks cannot detect uncommon harms.
cards.source: Andreux PA et al. The mitophagy activator urolithin A is safe and induces a molecular signature of improved mitochondrial and cellular health in humans. Nature Metabolism. 2019. PMID: 32694802. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Liu 2022 — older adults (n=66, Mitopure 1000 mg/day, 4 months): hand and leg muscle endurance improved versus placebo, but 6-minute walk distance (+60.8 m vs +42.5 m) and maximal ATP production did not significantly separate
cards.summary: Liu 2022 — older adults (n=66, Mitopure 1000 mg/day, 4 months): hand and leg muscle endurance improved versus placebo, but 6-minute walk distance (+60.8 m vs +42.5 m) and maximal ATP production did not significantly separate
cards.people: 66 adults aged 65 to 90 years at centres in Seattle, Washington, randomised to daily oral urolithin A 1000 mg (tested product: Mitopure) (n=33) or placebo (n=33) for 4 months; mean age 71.7 years and 75.8% were women. Primary endpoints were change in 6-minute walk distance and change in maximal ATP production in hand skeletal muscle; secondary endpoints were endurance of the tibialis anterior (leg) and first dorsal interosseus (hand) muscles.
cards.result: Muscle endurance — contractions until fatigue — improved significantly more on urolithin A than placebo at 2 months in both muscles (first dorsal interosseus +95.3 versus +11.6 contractions; tibialis anterior +41.4 versus +5.7, as mean changes with wide standard deviations). The primary endpoints did not significantly improve: mean 6-minute walk distance increased 60.8 m on urolithin A versus 42.5 m on placebo, and maximal ATP production changes were near-identical between groups. Several plasma acylcarnitines, ceramides and C-reactive protein fell on urolithin A. Adverse events did not differ statistically between groups.
cards.watchOut: Both groups walked substantially further at follow-up (a training/placebo effect of about 43 m on placebo), the endurance gains carry very wide variability, and the trial's own primary endpoints were negative — the positive reading rests on secondary endurance measures in 66 people.
cards.source: Liu S et al. Effect of Urolithin A Supplementation on Muscle Endurance and Mitochondrial Health in Older Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Network Open. 2022. PMID: 35050355. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03283462, from the record. cards.headline: Singh 2022 (ATLAS) — middle-aged adults (n=88, Mitopure): muscle strength rose about 12% in relative terms, but the primary endpoint, peak power output, did not significantly improve
cards.summary: Singh 2022 (ATLAS) — middle-aged adults (n=88, Mitopure): muscle strength rose about 12% in relative terms, but the primary endpoint, peak power output, did not significantly improve
cards.people: 88 untrained, overweight middle-aged adults randomised at a single centre to urolithin A (tested product: Mitopure) at 500 mg or 1000 mg daily, or placebo, for 4 months; mean ages were about 51–54 years across groups and mean body mass index was about 29 kg/m2.
cards.result: Muscle strength improved significantly with urolithin A (about 12% in relative terms), and the authors reported clinically meaningful improvements in aerobic endurance (peak oxygen consumption) and physical performance (6-minute walk test), but no significant improvement in peak power output — the trial's primary endpoint. Plasma acylcarnitines and C-reactive protein were significantly lower on urolithin A, and muscle proteins linked to mitophagy and mitochondrial metabolism increased.
cards.watchOut: A middle-aged, overweight population — not the older, frailer population of the shelf question — and a missed primary endpoint behind positive secondary measures; the trial was run with the product's maker (Amazentis authors), as was the whole urolithin A programme.

cards.headline: Synthesis: endurance and biomarker signals in small trials, walk and power primaries missed — a POSSIBLE, not a proven, muscle treatment
cards.summary: Synthesis: endurance and biomarker signals in small trials, walk and power primaries missed — a POSSIBLE, not a proven, muscle treatment
cards.people: Across the programme: 60 sedentary elderly people in a 4-week safety/biomarker study, 66 older adults (65–90 years) in a 4-month randomised trial, and 88 middle-aged adults in a 4-month randomised trial — 214 people in total, all studied with the same maker's urolithin A preparation (Mitopure in the randomised trials).
cards.result: The consistent findings are biological: mitochondrial gene/protein signatures, lower acylcarnitines and lower C-reactive protein. The functional findings are mixed: muscle endurance (Liu 2022) and muscle strength (Singh 2022) improved, while the prespecified primary functional endpoints — 6-minute walk distance and maximal ATP production in older adults, peak power output in middle-aged adults — did not significantly separate from placebo (the treatment made no significant difference on those endpoints).
cards.watchOut: Supplement preparations differ by maker, so these results belong to the tested product and cannot be read across to other urolithin A products; industry sponsorship runs through the programme, follow-up is 4 months at most, and no trial measured falls, fractures, disability or independence.
cards.source: Synthesis of Andreux PA et al. Nature Metabolism. 2019 (PMID: 32694802); Liu S et al. JAMA Network Open. 2022 (PMID: 35050355); Singh A et al. Cell Reports Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 35584623).

shelves.title: Nicotinamide riboside in older adults (total N=182 across three trials; the two older-adult trials are n=30 and n=12): NAD+ rises reliably, but blood pressure, arterial stiffness and physical function are unproven — the only blood-pressure signal is a post-hoc subgroup
shelves.question: In healthy middle-aged and older adults, does nicotinamide riboside raise NAD+ and improve systolic blood pressure, aortic stiffness or physical performance versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Caloric Restriction/methods · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · NAD/analysis/metabolism · Niacinamide/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Pyridinium Compounds · Vascular Stiffness/drug effects
shelves.balance: MAYBE (benefit) — a biomarker answer, not a treatment answer, from very small trials: N=30, N=12 and N=140 (total 182). Nicotinamide riboside (tested product NIAGEN, nicotinamide riboside chloride, in the largest trial) reliably raises NAD+: by about 60% in blood cells over 6 weeks (Martens 2018; n=30 crossover, 24 completers in the blood-pressure analyses) and dose-dependently by 22%, 51% and 142% at 100, 300 and 1000 mg/day over 8 weeks (Conze 2019; n=140 overweight adults). It also raised the muscle NAD+ metabolome in 12 older men over 21 days (Elhassan 2019), without changing muscle mitochondrial bioenergetics. The clinical claims do not hold up at this size: overall systolic blood pressure and aortic pulse-wave velocity changes in Martens 2018 were not statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons; the often-quoted 9 mmHg lower systolic pressure appeared only in a post-hoc subgroup of 13 participants whose baseline pressure was already elevated (subgroup-only signal, labelled as such), with no change in the normal-pressure subgroup. This shelf answers an evidence question about a heavily marketed supplement; it is not a treatment recommendation.

cards.headline: Martens 2018 — n=30 crossover: NAD+ rose about 60%; systolic blood pressure and aortic stiffness changes were not significant overall — the 9 mmHg lower systolic pressure was confined to a post-hoc subgroup of 13 people with elevated baseline pressure
cards.summary: Martens 2018 — n=30 crossover: NAD+ rose about 60%; systolic blood pressure and aortic stiffness changes were not significant overall — the 9 mmHg lower systolic pressure was confined to a post-hoc subgroup of 13 people with elevated baseline pressure
cards.people: 30 healthy middle-aged and older adults (mean age about 65 years) in a 2 × 6-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of nicotinamide riboside; 24 participants completed and contributed to the blood-pressure and arterial-function analyses (12 per sequence group).
cards.result: Nicotinamide riboside elevated NAD+ in peripheral blood mononuclear cells by about 60% versus placebo and was well tolerated, with no serious adverse events. Mean systolic blood pressure tended to be 3.9 mmHg lower and diastolic 2.0 mmHg lower on nicotinamide riboside, and aortic pulse-wave velocity tended to fall, but none of these comparisons was statistically significant after correction for multiple comparisons. In a post-hoc, exploratory subgroup analysis, mean systolic pressure was 9 mmHg lower after nicotinamide riboside versus placebo in the 13 participants with elevated/stage 1 baseline pressure (120–139/80–89 mmHg), with no change in the 11 participants with normal baseline pressure — a subgroup-only signal on which, in the authors' words, no statistical inferences can be made.
cards.watchOut: The headline blood-pressure claim for this supplement comes from 13 people in an analysis the trialists themselves label exploratory; the whole-group result was null after multiplicity correction, and one-tailed tests were used for several comparisons.
cards.source: Martens CR et al. Chronic nicotinamide riboside supplementation is well-tolerated and elevates NAD+ in healthy middle-aged and older adults. Nature Communications. 2018. PMID: 29599478. cards.headline: Elhassan 2019 — n=12 older men: 21 days of nicotinamide riboside raised the muscle NAD+ metabolome and lowered circulating inflammatory cytokines, but did not alter muscle mitochondrial bioenergetics
cards.summary: Elhassan 2019 — n=12 older men: 21 days of nicotinamide riboside raised the muscle NAD+ metabolome and lowered circulating inflammatory cytokines, but did not alter muscle mitochondrial bioenergetics
cards.people: 12 aged men supplemented with nicotinamide riboside 1 g per day for 21 days in a placebo-controlled, randomised, double-blind crossover trial, with muscle biopsies, targeted metabolomics and RNA sequencing.
cards.result: Nicotinamide riboside elevated the skeletal-muscle NAD+ metabolome (increased nicotinic acid adenine dinucleotide and nicotinamide clearance products), downregulated energy-metabolism and mitochondrial pathways on RNA sequencing, and depressed levels of circulating inflammatory cytokines. It did not alter mitochondrial bioenergetics. No physical-function outcome was shown to improve.
cards.watchOut: Twelve men, 21 days, biomarker endpoints only: this establishes that the supplement reaches aged human muscle, not that it improves strength, walking, blood pressure or any clinical outcome.
cards.source: Elhassan YS et al. Nicotinamide Riboside Augments the Aged Human Skeletal Muscle NAD+ Metabolome and Induces Transcriptomic and Anti-inflammatory Signatures. Cell Reports. 2019. cards.headline: Conze 2019 — n=140 overweight adults (NIAGEN): whole-blood NAD+ rose dose-dependently by 22%, 51% and 142% at 100, 300 and 1000 mg/day, with no difference in adverse events versus placebo over 8 weeks
cards.summary: Conze 2019 — n=140 overweight adults (NIAGEN): whole-blood NAD+ rose dose-dependently by 22%, 51% and 142% at 100, 300 and 1000 mg/day, with no difference in adverse events versus placebo over 8 weeks
cards.people: 140 healthy overweight men and women enrolled in an 8-week randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of the tested product NIAGEN (nicotinamide riboside chloride) at 100, 300 or 1000 mg per day versus placebo (35 per group at screening).
cards.result: Blood NAD+ increased dose-dependently and significantly — by 22%, 51% and 142% at 100, 300 and 1000 mg per day — within 2 weeks, and the increases were maintained to 8 weeks. There were no reports of flushing and no significant differences in adverse events between nicotinamide riboside and placebo groups or across doses; low-density lipoprotein cholesterol was not elevated and 1-carbon metabolism was not dysregulated. No blood-pressure, arterial-stiffness or physical-function efficacy outcome was tested.
cards.watchOut: A safety and metabolism trial in overweight (not specifically older) adults, run to support a tolerable upper intake level for a commercial ingredient — it strengthens the 'raises NAD+, appears well tolerated' claim and says nothing about clinical benefit.
cards.source: Conze D et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: NAD+ goes up in every trial; no clinical outcome has been shown to improve — the blood-pressure story rests on a 13-person post-hoc subgroup
cards.summary: Synthesis: NAD+ goes up in every trial; no clinical outcome has been shown to improve — the blood-pressure story rests on a 13-person post-hoc subgroup
cards.people: Three randomised trials totalling 182 people: 30 middle-aged and older adults (crossover), 12 older men (crossover) and 140 overweight adults; treatment lasted 21 days to 8 weeks.
cards.result: The biomarker claim is solid and replicated: oral nicotinamide riboside raises blood and muscle NAD+ measures, dose-dependently, and short-term tolerability looks good. The clinical claims are unproven: overall blood-pressure and aortic-stiffness effects were not significant in the one trial that measured them, the 9 mmHg systolic figure is a post-hoc subgroup result in 13 participants, muscle mitochondrial bioenergetics did not change in the biopsy trial, and no trial measured physical performance as a demonstrated benefit.
cards.watchOut: Marketing for this supplement routinely presents the subgroup blood-pressure figure and the NAD+ rise as established clinical benefit; at N=30 and N=12 in older adults, this shelf can only answer MAYBE, and it is an evidence summary, not a recommendation to take or prescribe the product.
cards.source: Synthesis of Martens CR et al. Nature Communications. 2018 (PMID: 29599478); Elhassan YS et al. Cell Reports. 2019 (PMID: 31412242); Conze D et al. Scientific Reports. 2019 (PMID: 31278280).

shelves.title: Senolytics (dasatinib + quercetin) — first human pilots only, total N=23 in the two single-arm reports (IPF n=14; diabetic kidney disease n=9), plus a 12-person randomised pilot in which function did not differ meaningfully: no efficacy claim beyond pilot size is supportable
shelves.question: In older adults with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis or diabetic kidney disease, does intermittent dasatinib + quercetin reduce senescent-cell burden markers and improve physical function versus baseline/controls?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Biomarkers · Cellular Senescence/drug effects/genetics · Dasatinib/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis/drug therapy/etiology/metabolism/physiopathology · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Compliance · Patient Reported Outcome Measures · Pilot Projects · Quality of Life · Quercetin/administration & dosage/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Respiratory Function Tests · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (benefit) at most — and only as a statement about pilot feasibility and biology, with the small N printed: the two first-in-human reports total N=23, both single-arm and open-label. In idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (Justice 2019; n=14), three weeks of intermittent dasatinib + quercetin was feasible, retention was 100%, and 6-minute walk distance, gait speed and chair-stand time improved versus baseline — with no control group, so placebo, learning and regression effects cannot be separated from drug effect; pulmonary function and frailty measures did not change. In diabetic kidney disease (Hickson 2019; n=9), three days of dosing reduced senescent-cell burden in fat and skin biopsies and lowered circulating SASP factors within 11 days — a biological proof of mechanism in 9 people, with no clinical outcome. The one randomised pilot (Nambiar 2023; n=12, placebo-controlled) found more non-serious adverse events on dasatinib + quercetin and stated that frailty, pulmonary and physical-function measures did not appear to differ meaningfully between groups. No efficacy claim beyond these pilots is supportable.

cards.headline: Justice 2019 — IPF pilot, SINGLE-ARM open-label, n=14: feasibility shown and walk distance, gait speed and chair-stand time improved versus baseline; lung function and frailty did not change
cards.summary: Justice 2019 — IPF pilot, SINGLE-ARM open-label, n=14: feasibility shown and walk distance, gait speed and chair-stand time improved versus baseline; lung function and frailty did not change
cards.people: 14 participants with stable idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis at two centres, given intermittent dasatinib 100 mg/day plus quercetin 1250 mg/day, three days per week over three weeks, with no control group. Primary endpoints were retention and completion of planned assessments; secondary endpoints were safety and change in functional and reported health measures.
cards.result: Retention was 100% with no discontinuations, and planned assessments were completed in 13 of 14 participants. One serious adverse event was reported; non-serious events were mostly mild to moderate (respiratory symptoms, skin irritation/bruising and gastrointestinal discomfort the most frequent). Physical function — 6-minute walk distance, 4-m gait speed and chair-stand time — was significantly and, in the authors' judgement, clinically meaningfully improved (p<0.05 versus baseline). Pulmonary function, clinical chemistries, frailty index and reported health were unchanged, and effects on circulating SASP factors were inconclusive.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm, n=14, unblinded: every functional gain is measured against the participants' own baseline, so practice effects on walk and chair-stand tests, placebo effect and natural fluctuation are fully confounded with any drug effect. This design cannot establish efficacy.
cards.source: Justice JN et al. Senolytics in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: Results from a first-in-human, open-label, pilot study. EBioMedicine. 2019. PMID: 30616998. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02874989, from the record. cards.headline: Hickson 2019 — diabetic kidney disease pilot, SINGLE-ARM open-label, n=9 (below the usual 10-person floor, N printed on the face): 3 days of dasatinib + quercetin reduced senescent-cell burden in fat and skin within 11 days
cards.summary: Hickson 2019 — diabetic kidney disease pilot, SINGLE-ARM open-label, n=9 (below the usual 10-person floor, N printed on the face): 3 days of dasatinib + quercetin reduced senescent-cell burden in fat and skin within 11 days
cards.people: 9 subjects with diabetic kidney disease (mean age 68.7 years; 2 women; mean body mass index 33.9 kg/m2; mean eGFR 27.0 mL/min/1.73 m2) given 3 days of oral dasatinib 100 mg and quercetin 1000 mg, with fat tissue, skin biopsies and blood collected before treatment and 11 days after completing it. No control group. This report is carded with its N printed plainly because the shelf exists to answer the senolytic question honestly at pilot size.
cards.result: Within 11 days, adipose-tissue senescent-cell burden fell — fewer p16INK4A- and p21CIP1-expressing cells, fewer cells with senescence-associated beta-galactosidase activity, and fewer adipocyte progenitors with limited replicative potential — and adipose macrophages and crown-like structures decreased. Skin epidermal p16INK4A+ and p21CIP1+ cells were reduced, as were circulating SASP factors including IL-1alpha, IL-6 and MMP-9 and MMP-12. No kidney-function or other clinical outcome was tested.
cards.watchOut: Nine people, no comparator, biopsy biomarkers only: this is proof that the drugs can reduce senescent-cell markers in human tissue, not evidence that kidney disease, function or survival improves — and dasatinib is a chemotherapy drug with its own serious toxicity profile outside pilot supervision.
cards.source: Hickson LJ et al. Senolytics decrease senescent cells in humans: Preliminary report from a clinical trial of Dasatinib plus Quercetin in individuals with diabetic kidney disease. EBioMedicine. 2019. PMID: 31542391. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02848131, from the record. cards.headline: Nambiar 2023 — the one RANDOMISED pilot, n=12: dasatinib + quercetin was completable, with more non-serious adverse events than placebo, and frailty, lung and physical-function measures did not appear to differ meaningfully between groups (the treatment made no meaningful difference)
cards.summary: Nambiar 2023 — the one RANDOMISED pilot, n=12: dasatinib + quercetin was completable, with more non-serious adverse events than placebo, and frailty, lung and physical-function measures did not appear to differ meaningfully between groups (the treatment made no meaningful difference)
cards.people: 12 participants with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis aged over 50 years, blinded and randomised 1:1 to three weeks of intermittent dasatinib 100 mg/day plus quercetin 1250 mg/day (three consecutive days per week) or matching placebo, in a single-centre phase 1 pilot whose primary objective was adverse events and feasibility.
cards.result: All participants completed the scheduled dosing (108 of 108 doses) and assessments (60 of 60). The placebo arm reported fewer overall non-serious adverse events (the dasatinib + quercetin arm reported more events in total), there were no serious adverse events related to dasatinib + quercetin, and sleep disturbances and anxiety were disproportionately reported on active treatment (4 of 6 versus 0 of 6). Frailty, pulmonary and physical-function measures, though underpowered, did not appear to differ meaningfully between groups.
cards.watchOut: With 6 people per arm this pilot can neither confirm nor refute efficacy — but it is the only controlled evidence on the shelf, and it does not reproduce the open-label pilot's functional gains; the adverse-event burden also ran higher on active treatment.
cards.source: Nambiar A et al. Senolytics dasatinib and quercetin in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: results of a phase I, single-blind, single-center, randomized, placebo-controlled pilot trial on feasibility and tolerability. EBioMedicine. 2023. PMID: 36857968. Registry ID: none in the record (the report carries the same NCT02874989 programme identifier in its text). MeSH: not captured from the record this session
