cards.headline: Synthesis: senescent-cell markers can be lowered in humans (n=9 biopsies) and the regimen is feasible (n=14) — but controlled functional evidence (n=12) shows no meaningful difference, so efficacy is unproven at total pilot N=35
cards.summary: Synthesis: senescent-cell markers can be lowered in humans (n=9 biopsies) and the regimen is feasible (n=14) — but controlled functional evidence (n=12) shows no meaningful difference, so efficacy is unproven at total pilot N=35
cards.people: Three pilot reports totalling 35 people: 14 with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (single-arm), 9 with diabetic kidney disease (single-arm) and 12 with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (randomised, placebo-controlled).
cards.result: What the pilots support: intermittent dasatinib + quercetin can be delivered, is usually completed, and reduces senescent-cell burden markers in fat and skin within days. What they do not support: any claim of improved function, lung or kidney outcomes, or survival — the single-arm functional improvements were uncontrolled, and the randomised pilot found no meaningful between-group functional difference (the treatment made no difference on those measures at this size).
cards.watchOut: Dasatinib + quercetin is widely promoted and sold off-label as an 'anti-ageing' intervention; the human evidence base for that claim is these 35 pilot participants, and unsupervised dasatinib carries risks (bleeding, fluid retention, pulmonary hypertension) that a 3-week supervised pilot cannot characterise.
cards.source: Synthesis of Justice JN et al. EBioMedicine. 2019 (PMID: 30616998); Hickson LJ et al. EBioMedicine. 2019 (PMID: 31542391); Nambiar A et al. EBioMedicine. 2023 (PMID: 36857968).

shelves.title: Spermidine (tested product: spermidine-rich wheat-germ extract) and memory: a 30-person pilot suggested benefit, but the larger 12-month phase 2b smartAGE trial (n=100) was NEGATIVE on its primary memory endpoint — the pair is the complete answer
shelves.question: In older adults with subjective cognitive decline, does daily spermidine supplementation (name the tested product — wheat-germ extract in the trials) improve memory performance versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cognitive Dysfunction/psychology · Dementia/psychology · Dietary Supplements · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Memory/drug effects · Middle Aged · Neuropsychological Tests · Risk Factors · Spermidine/pharmacology
shelves.balance: UNLIKELY (benefit) at the tested dose — the complete record is a small positive pilot followed by a larger negative trial, and the larger trial governs. In the phase 2a pilot (Wirth 2018; n=30, 3 months), the tested product — a spermidine-rich wheat-germ plant extract — was associated with moderately better memory performance than placebo, reported as effect sizes (Cohen's d about 0.77) with confidence intervals that reached zero on the main contrast. In the 12-month phase 2b smartAGE trial (Schwarz 2022; n=100 randomised, 89 completers, 0.9 mg spermidine/day from wheat-germ extract), the primary endpoint — change in mnemonic discrimination performance — did not differ between groups (between-group difference -0.03, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.05; p=0.47; the treatment made no difference), and secondary outcomes were likewise unchanged; exploratory signals on verbal memory and inflammation were hypothesis-generating only. Adverse events were balanced. A benefit at higher doses remains untested, not established.

cards.headline: Wirth 2018 — phase 2a pilot (n=30, 3 months): memory performance was moderately better on the spermidine-rich wheat-germ extract than placebo, reported as effect sizes whose main confidence interval reached zero
cards.summary: Wirth 2018 — phase 2a pilot (n=30, 3 months): memory performance was moderately better on the spermidine-rich wheat-germ extract than placebo, reported as effect sizes whose main confidence interval reached zero
cards.people: 30 cognitively intact adults aged 60–80 years with subjective cognitive decline, randomised to a spermidine-rich plant extract supplement (tested product: spermidine-rich wheat-germ extract) or placebo for 3 months in a double-blind phase 2a pilot, with memory assessed by a mnemonic similarity task at baseline and post-intervention.
cards.result: Memory performance was moderately enhanced in the spermidine group compared with placebo at the end of the intervention (contrast mean 0.17, 95% CI -0.01 to 0.35; Cohen's d 0.77, 95% CI 0 to 1.53). Mnemonic discrimination improved within the spermidine group (mean difference -0.11, 95% CI -0.19 to -0.03; d 0.79) and did not improve in the placebo group. The authors framed the result as a positive pilot signal requiring a phase 2b trial to validate it.
cards.watchOut: Thirty people, 3 months, and effect-size reporting: the headline between-group confidence interval includes essentially no effect (-0.01), so even the pilot was compatible with a very small benefit — it was a reason to run the bigger trial, not a result to act on.
cards.source: Wirth M et al. The effect of spermidine on memory performance in older adults at risk for dementia: A randomized controlled trial. Cortex. 2018. PMID: 30388439. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02755246, from the record. cards.headline: Schwarz 2022 (smartAGE) — phase 2b (n=100, 12 months): primary memory endpoint NEGATIVE — mnemonic discrimination difference -0.03 (95% CI -0.11 to 0.05; p=0.47) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Schwarz 2022 (smartAGE) — phase 2b (n=100, 12 months): primary memory endpoint NEGATIVE — mnemonic discrimination difference -0.03 (95% CI -0.11 to 0.05; p=0.47) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 100 adults aged 60 to 90 years with subjective cognitive decline at a German academic centre, randomly assigned to 12 months of a spermidine-rich dietary supplement extracted from wheat germ (tested product: wheat-germ extract providing 0.9 mg spermidine/day) (n=51) or placebo (microcrystalline cellulose) (n=49); 89 participants (89%) completed the intervention. The primary outcome was change in memory performance (mnemonic discrimination on the Mnemonic Similarity Task) from baseline to 12 months, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Over 12 months, no significant change was observed in mnemonic discrimination performance (between-group difference -0.03, 95% CI -0.11 to 0.05; P=0.47), and secondary neuropsychological, behavioural and physiological outcomes were likewise unchanged. Exploratory analyses indicated possible beneficial effects on inflammation and verbal memory. Adverse events were balanced between groups. The authors concluded that longer-term spermidine supplementation did not modify memory or biomarkers compared with placebo at this dose.
cards.watchOut: The tested dose was low (0.9 mg/day) and the population had subjective (not objective) cognitive decline, so the null answers this product, dose and population — it does not test higher-dose spermidine or treatment of established dementia, neither of which has positive randomised evidence either.
cards.source: Schwarz C et al. Effects of Spermidine Supplementation on Cognition and Biomarkers in Older Adults With Subjective Cognitive Decline: A Randomized Clinical Trial. cards.headline: Pekar 2021 — nursing-home preliminary study in dementia (n=85, 3 months): the higher-spermidine-intake group with mild dementia gained 2.23 MMSE points (p=0.026), while the lower-intake group was flat or declining; a second test did not separate (p=0.47)
cards.summary: Pekar 2021 — nursing-home preliminary study in dementia (n=85, 3 months): the higher-spermidine-intake group with mild dementia gained 2.23 MMSE points (p=0.026), while the lower-intake group was flat or declining; a second test did not separate (p=0.47)
cards.people: 85 subjects aged 60 to 96 years in 6 nursing homes in Styria, Austria, with dementia of varying severity, given oral spermidine supplementation at higher or lower intake levels for 3 months, with memory testing (including the Mini Mental State Examination) and blood spermidine and metabolic measurements.
cards.result: The authors reported a clear correlation between spermidine intake and improved cognitive performance in subjects with mild and moderate dementia in the higher-dosage group: in mild dementia, MMSE rose by 2.23 points (p=0.026), while phonematic fluency rose 1.99 points without significance (p=0.47). The lower-intake group showed consistent or declining cognitive performance.
cards.watchOut: A preliminary, short report in a different population (established dementia in nursing homes, not subjective cognitive decline), analysed by intake group and severity subgroup, with the significant result on one test in one subgroup and a non-significant result on the other test; it does not overturn the larger, placebo-controlled smartAGE null in the shelf's own population, and the tested preparation and doses are not fully specified in the record.
cards.source: Pekar T et al. The positive effect of spermidine in older adults suffering from dementia: First results of a 3-month trial. Wiener klinische Wochenschrift. 2021. PMID: 33211152. cards.headline: Synthesis: pilot positive, definitive-sized trial negative — at 0.9 mg/day from wheat-germ extract, spermidine does not improve memory in subjective cognitive decline
cards.summary: Synthesis: pilot positive, definitive-sized trial negative — at 0.9 mg/day from wheat-germ extract, spermidine does not improve memory in subjective cognitive decline
cards.people: Two randomised trials of the same wheat-germ-extract product family in older adults with subjective cognitive decline — a 3-month pilot (n=30) and a 12-month phase 2b trial (n=100) — plus a 3-month preliminary nursing-home study in established dementia (n=85).
cards.result: Read together, the record is a complete and common evidence story: a small pilot generated a moderate effect-size signal whose confidence interval reached zero, and the larger, longer trial built to test it found no difference on its primary memory endpoint or its secondary outcomes (the treatment made no difference). Exploratory verbal-memory and inflammation findings in the larger trial are unconfirmed subgroup-style signals, not a rescued positive. The nursing-home dementia study (Pekar 2021) points the other way but is preliminary, subgroup-based and in a different population, so it leaves a research question open in dementia rather than answering the shelf question positively.
cards.watchOut: Spermidine supplements are marketed for memory and longevity on the pilot and on animal data; anyone citing the 2018 pilot without the 2022 phase 2b null is presenting half the record. Higher doses remain a research question, not a workaround available to buyers today.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wirth M et al. Cortex. 2018 (PMID: 30388439); Schwarz C et al. JAMA Network Open. 2022 (PMID: 35616942); Pekar T et al. Wiener klinische Wochenschrift. 2021 (PMID: 33211152).

shelves.title: mTOR inhibition and immune ageing: phase 2 trials improved influenza-vaccine responses by about 20% in relative terms and cut reported infections, but the phase 3 RTB101 trial (n=1,024) FAILED — symptomatic respiratory illness 26% versus 25% on placebo (the treatment made no difference)
shelves.question: In older adults, does low-dose mTOR inhibition (everolimus, or the TORC1-selective RTB101, alone or combined) improve vaccine response and reduce reported respiratory infections versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Antibodies, Viral/immunology · CD4-Positive T-Lymphocytes/drug effects/immunology · CD8-Positive T-Lymphocytes/drug effects/immunology · Cohort Studies · Everolimus · Humans · Immunity/drug effects · Influenza Vaccines/immunology · Placebos · Programmed Cell Death 1 Receptor/metabolism · Protein Kinase Inhibitors/pharmacology · Seasons · Sirolimus/analogs & derivatives/pharmacology · TOR Serine-Threonine Kinases/antagonists & inhibitors/metabolism · Vaccination
shelves.balance: UNLIKELY (benefit) for preventing respiratory illness — the phase 2 positives and the phase 3 failure must be read together. Phase 2a (Mannick 2014; n=218 elderly volunteers): the mTOR inhibitor everolimus (RAD001) enhanced the antibody response to influenza vaccination by about 20% — a relative measure — at relatively well-tolerated doses, and reduced PD-1 expression on T cells. Phase 2a (Mannick 2018; n=264): six weeks of a low-dose TORC1-inhibitor combination (the catalytic inhibitor RTB101, then called BEZ235, plus everolimus) was associated with a significant decrease in infections reported over the following year (p=0.001) and better vaccine responses. But when RTB101 alone was tested at phase 3 scale (Mannick 2021; phase 3 n=1,024), it did not reduce clinically symptomatic respiratory illness: 26% on RTB101 versus 25% on placebo (odds ratio 1.07, 90% CI 0.80–1.42; p=0.65; the treatment made no difference), even though interferon-induced antiviral genes were upregulated. The phase 2b part of the same report was itself split: the prespecified part-2 primary analysis missed significance, and a pooled analysis found fewer laboratory-confirmed infections on RTB101 10 mg once daily (19% versus 28%). Vaccine-response gains remain a phase 2 biomarker finding; infection prevention failed its definitive test.

cards.headline: Mannick 2014 — phase 2a (n=218): everolimus (RAD001) enhanced the influenza-vaccine antibody response by about 20% in relative terms and reduced PD-1 on T cells
cards.summary: Mannick 2014 — phase 2a (n=218): everolimus (RAD001) enhanced the influenza-vaccine antibody response by about 20% in relative terms and reduced PD-1 on T cells
cards.people: 218 elderly volunteers (n as reported for the trial) given the mTOR inhibitor everolimus (RAD001) at low doses or placebo around influenza vaccination, with vaccine antibody responses and T-cell PD-1 expression as the immune-ageing readouts.
cards.result: Everolimus enhanced the response to the influenza vaccine by about 20% — a relative measure of antibody response, not a 20-percentage-point gain and not a reduction in influenza illness — at doses that were relatively well tolerated. It also reduced the percentage of CD4 and CD8 T lymphocytes expressing the PD-1 receptor, a marker that rises with age and inhibits T-cell signalling. No infection or clinical illness endpoint was tested.
cards.watchOut: A vaccine-antibody surrogate in 218 people: a roughly one-fifth relative boost to antibody titres is not evidence of fewer infections, hospitalisations or deaths, and mTOR inhibitors as a class carry metabolic, mouth-ulcer, cytopenia and infection risks that short low-dose courses only begin to characterise.
cards.source: Mannick JB et al. mTOR inhibition improves immune function in the elderly. Science Translational Medicine. 2014. PMID: 25540326. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mannick 2018 — phase 2a (n=264): 6 weeks of low-dose TORC1 inhibition (RTB101/BEZ235 plus everolimus) was associated with significantly fewer infections reported over a year (p=0.001) and improved vaccine response
cards.summary: Mannick 2018 — phase 2a (n=264): 6 weeks of low-dose TORC1 inhibition (RTB101/BEZ235 plus everolimus) was associated with significantly fewer infections reported over a year (p=0.001) and improved vaccine response
cards.people: 264 elderly subjects given study drugs for 6 weeks in a phase 2a randomised, placebo-controlled trial of low-dose TORC1-selective inhibition — a combination of a catalytic mTOR inhibitor (BEZ235, later named RTB101) plus the allosteric inhibitor everolimus (RAD001) — versus other dose arms and placebo, with infections reported over the year after dosing began.
cards.result: The low-dose combination was safe in this trial and was associated with a significant (P=0.001) decrease in the rate of infections reported by elderly subjects for a year after study-drug initiation. Antiviral gene expression was upregulated and the response to influenza vaccination improved in this treatment group.
cards.watchOut: Infections were reported (not uniformly laboratory-confirmed) events collected over a year after only 6 weeks of dosing, across several dose arms in 264 people — exactly the kind of phase 2 signal that requires a phase 3 test, which this programme then received and failed (next cards).
cards.source: Mannick JB et al. TORC1 inhibition enhances immune function and reduces infections in the elderly. Science Translational Medicine. 2018. PMID: 29997249. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mannick 2021 — phase 2b (n=652): SPLIT result — the first prespecified primary analysis missed significance; a second pooled analysis found laboratory-confirmed respiratory infections in 19% on RTB101 10 mg daily versus 28% on pooled placebo (OR 0.60)
cards.summary: Mannick 2021 — phase 2b (n=652): SPLIT result — the first prespecified primary analysis missed significance; a second pooled analysis found laboratory-confirmed respiratory infections in 19% on RTB101 10 mg daily versus 28% on pooled placebo (OR 0.60)
cards.people: 652 adults aged 65–85 years at higher respiratory-infection risk (asthma, type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure, current smoking, or a recent emergency visit/hospitalisation for a respiratory infection) in New Zealand, Australia and the USA, randomised across two parts to RTB101 5 mg or 10 mg once daily, 10 mg twice daily, RTB101 10 mg plus everolimus 0.1 mg daily, or placebo, for 16 weeks during winter cold and influenza season. The primary outcome was the incidence of laboratory-confirmed respiratory tract infections.
cards.result: The first prespecified statistical analysis — RTB101 10 mg plus everolimus versus placebo in part 2 — did not meet statistical significance. In the second prespecified analysis pooling parts 1 and 2, the proportion with one or more laboratory-confirmed respiratory infections was lower on RTB101 10 mg once daily (34 of 176, 19%) than on pooled placebo (50 of 180, 28%) (odds ratio 0.601, 90% CI 0.391–0.922; p=0.02) — an odds ratio, a relative measure; the absolute difference is 9 percentage points. Interferon-induced antiviral genes were upregulated on RTB101.
cards.watchOut: A positive second analysis sitting beside a negative first analysis is a fragile phase 2 result; the dose that looked best here (RTB101 10 mg once daily, alone) is precisely the regimen the phase 3 trial then tested and found ineffective.
cards.source: Mannick JB et al. Targeting the biology of ageing with mTOR inhibitors to improve immune function in older adults: phase 2b and phase 3 randomised trials. The Lancet Healthy Longevity. 2021. PMID: 33977284. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03373903 and ANZCTR ACTRN12617000468325 (phase 2b), from the record. phase 2b randomised trial (mannick 2021) 652 adults aged 65–85 years at higher respiratory-infection risk (asthma, type 2 diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure, current smoking, or a recent emergency visit/hospitalisation for a respiratory infection) in new zealand, australia and the usa, randomised across two parts to rtb101 5 mg or 10 mg once daily, 10 mg twice daily, rtb101 10 mg plus everolimus 0.1 mg daily, or placebo, for 16 weeks during winter cold and influenza season. the primary outcome was the incidence of laboratory-confirmed respiratory tract infections. the first prespecified statistical analysis — rtb101 10 mg plus everolimus versus placebo in part 2 — did not meet statistical significance. in the second prespecified analysis pooling parts 1 and 2, the proportion with one or more laboratory-confirmed respiratory infections was lower on rtb101 10 mg once daily (34 of 176, 19%) than on pooled placebo (50 of 180, 28%) (odds ratio 0.601, 90% ci 0.391–0.922; p=0.02) — an odds ratio, a relative measure; the absolute difference is 9 percentage points. interferon-induced antiviral genes were upregulated on rtb101. a positive second analysis sitting beside a negative first analysis is a fragile phase 2 result; the dose that looked best here (rtb101 10 mg once daily, alone) is precisely the regimen the phase 3 trial then tested and found ineffective. mannick jb et al. targeting the biology of ageing with mtor inhibitors to improve immune function in older adults: phase 2b and phase 3 randomised trials. the lancet healthy longevity. 2021. pmid: 33977284. registry id: clinicaltrials.gov nct03373903 and anzctr actrn12617000468325 (phase 2b), from the record. mesh: aged · aging · antiviral agents · biology · covid-19 · diabetes mellitus, type 2 · everolimus · humans · immunity · mtor inhibitors · pandemics · pulmonary disease, chronic obstructive · respiratory tract infections · tor serine-threonine kinases · treatment outcome

cards.headline: Mannick 2021 — phase 3 (n=1,024): RTB101 FAILED its primary endpoint — clinically symptomatic respiratory illness 26% (134/511) on RTB101 versus 25% (125/510) on placebo (OR 1.07; p=0.65) (the treatment made no difference) — full journal report, not sponsor reporting alone
cards.summary: Mannick 2021 — phase 3 (n=1,024): RTB101 FAILED its primary endpoint — clinically symptomatic respiratory illness 26% (134/511) on RTB101 versus 25% (125/510) on placebo (OR 1.07; p=0.65) (the treatment made no difference) — full journal report, not sponsor reporting alone
cards.people: 1,024 adults aged at least 65 years (excluding chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and current smokers) at 54 sites, enrolled May 2018 to July 2019 and randomly assigned to RTB101 10 mg once daily (513) or matching placebo (510) for 16 weeks during winter season; the primary outcome was the incidence of clinically symptomatic respiratory illness, irrespective of laboratory confirmation.
cards.result: RTB101 did not reduce the proportion of patients with clinically symptomatic respiratory illness: 134 of 511 (26%) on RTB101 versus 125 of 510 (25%) on placebo (odds ratio 1.07, 90% CI 0.80–1.42; p=0.65; the treatment made no difference). Interferon-induced antiviral genes were nonetheless significantly upregulated on RTB101. The drug was safe and well tolerated; one patient in the placebo group had treatment-related serious adverse events, and one death occurred in the phase 3 trial, not considered treatment-related.
cards.watchOut: The phase 3 endpoint (symptomatic illness) was broader than the phase 2b endpoint (laboratory-confirmed infection), and the authors suggest endpoint and population refinement might matter — but as tested, in over a thousand older adults, the clinical claim failed, and a biomarker (antiviral gene upregulation) again separated from the outcome that matters.
cards.source: Mannick JB et al. Targeting the biology of ageing with mTOR inhibitors to improve immune function in older adults: phase 2b and phase 3 randomised trials. The Lancet Healthy Longevity. 2021. PMID: 33977284. Registry ID: ANZCTR ACTRN12619000628145 (phase 3), from the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: immune biomarkers move, illness does not — phase 2 promise, phase 3 failure, presented together
cards.summary: Synthesis: immune biomarkers move, illness does not — phase 2 promise, phase 3 failure, presented together
cards.people: The full programme: 218 elderly volunteers (everolimus, vaccine response), 264 elderly subjects (TORC1 combination, reported infections), 652 at-risk older adults (phase 2b RTB101) and 1,024 older adults (phase 3 RTB101).
cards.result: Low-dose mTOR inhibition reproducibly moves immune biomarkers in older adults — influenza-vaccine antibody responses up by about 20% in relative terms, antiviral gene expression up, PD-1 down — and phase 2 infection counts favoured treatment. The definitive test reversed the clinical story: in phase 3, symptomatic respiratory illness was 26% on RTB101 versus 25% on placebo (the treatment made no difference). No mTOR inhibitor is an evidence-based infection preventive for older adults on this record.
cards.watchOut: This programme is frequently cited in the longevity literature by its phase 2 papers alone. The phase 3 trial exists as a full journal report (Lancet Healthy Longevity 2021) — earlier mining that described it as sponsor-reporting-only was superseded at build — and any honest account of mTOR inhibition for immune ageing must carry the failure beside the promise.

shelves.title: GlyNAC in older adults: one 24-person trial reported broad improvements, the independent 114-person trial missed its primary glutathione endpoint, and an 8-person open-label pilot is the rest of the base
shelves.question: In older adults, does high-dose GlyNAC (glycine + N-acetylcysteine), versus placebo, correct glutathione deficiency and improve oxidative stress, physical function and ageing-hallmark measures?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). Two randomised trials answer this question and they disagree at the primary endpoint. The Baylor (Sekhar-group) trial — 24 older adults randomised for 16 weeks, with 12 young adults as a reference group — reported that GlyNAC improved or corrected glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function, inflammation, insulin resistance, gait speed and strength, but its abstract prints no effect sizes, so none are quoted here. The independent trial (114 healthy older adults, 2 weeks at 2.4–7.2 g/day) missed its primary endpoint: glutathione redox status did not improve in the full cohort (p=0.739 for the high dose), with a signal only in a post-hoc high-oxidative-stress/low-glutathione subgroup. An earlier open-label pilot from the same Baylor group treated just 8 older adults. Single-research-group dominance and the failed independent primary are both on the face of this shelf. Doses in these trials are gram-level and far above typical retail supplement doses, the fetched records do not name a commercial product, and current retail GlyNAC products may differ from what was tested. Surrogate and biomarker outcomes dominate; no trial here measured clinical endpoints such as falls, hospitalisation or mortality.

cards.headline: Randomised trial (Kumar 2023): GlyNAC improved glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function and physical function over 16 weeks — n=24 older adults; the abstract prints no effect sizes
cards.summary: Randomised trial (Kumar 2023): GlyNAC improved glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial function and physical function over 16 weeks — n=24 older adults; the abstract prints no effect sizes
cards.people: 24 older adults randomised to GlyNAC (n=12) or isonitrogenous alanine placebo (n=12) for 16 weeks, studied before, at 2 weeks and at 16 weeks; 12 young adults received GlyNAC for 2 weeks as a reference group. Outcomes spanned glutathione concentrations, oxidative stress, mitochondrial fatty-acid oxidation, inflammation, endothelial function, insulin resistance, ageing hallmarks, gait speed, muscle strength, 6-minute walk, body composition and blood pressure. Registered as NCT01870193.
cards.result: Compared with young adults, the older adults had glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, insulin resistance, multiple ageing hallmarks and impaired physical function at baseline. GlyNAC — and not placebo — supplementation improved or corrected these defects, per the authors, and was reported as safe and well tolerated. The fetched abstract states these conclusions without numerical effect sizes, so no magnitudes are printed on this card.
cards.watchOut: Twelve people per arm, dozens of outcomes, one research group, and a conclusion-only abstract: even taken at face value this is a hypothesis-confirming pilot-scale trial, not a basis for clinical claims. Every positive GlyNAC trial in older adults comes from this single group — the independence problem is structural, not incidental.

cards.headline: Independent randomised trial (Lizzo 2022): primary glutathione endpoint NOT met in 114 healthy older adults over 2 weeks (p=0.739 at the high dose); post-hoc subgroup signal only
cards.summary: Independent randomised trial (Lizzo 2022): primary glutathione endpoint NOT met in 114 healthy older adults over 2 weeks (p=0.739 at the high dose); post-hoc subgroup signal only
cards.people: 114 healthy older volunteers (mean age 65 years) randomised to glycine + N-acetylcysteine at 2.4, 4.8 or 7.2 g/day (1:1 ratio) or control for 2 weeks, with a young reference group (n=20, mean age 31.7 years) for baseline comparisons. The primary endpoint was glutathione redox status (reduced-to-oxidised glutathione ratio and total glutathione). Registered as NCT05041179.
cards.result: GlyNAC did not increase the reduced-to-oxidised glutathione ratio (end of study: placebo 12.49 vs 7.2 g/day 12.65; p=0.739) or total glutathione (903.5 vs 959.6 mg/L; p=0.278) — the primary endpoint was not met in the full cohort. In post-hoc analyses, participants with high baseline oxidative stress and low glutathione who received the medium and high doses showed increased glutathione generation (905.4 vs 819.7 mg/L on placebo; p=0.016). Supplementation was safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Two weeks is far shorter than the Baylor trial's 16 weeks and the doses overlap only partly, so this trial does not refute a longer-course effect — but it is the only independent randomised test, it was adequately sized for its biomarker endpoint, and it was negative. The positive subgroup is post-hoc and hypothesis-generating only.

cards.headline: Open-label pilot (Kumar 2021): 24 weeks of GlyNAC improved multiple measures in 8 older adults, with benefits declining 12 weeks after stopping — no control group
cards.summary: Open-label pilot (Kumar 2021): 24 weeks of GlyNAC improved multiple measures in 8 older adults, with benefits declining 12 weeks after stopping — no control group
cards.type: Open-label pilot clinical trial (Kumar 2021) — no comparator, n=8 treated older adults
cards.people: Eight older adults and eight young adults in a 36-week open-label trial; the young adults left after baseline studies, and the older adults were restudied after 24 weeks of GlyNAC supplementation and again after 12 weeks of withdrawal. Outcomes included red-cell glutathione, mitochondrial fuel oxidation, oxidative-stress and inflammation biomarkers, cognition, strength, gait speed, 6-minute walk and body composition. The record carries no registry ID.
cards.result: After 24 weeks, GlyNAC had corrected red-cell glutathione deficiency, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction and improved inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, insulin resistance, genomic damage, cognition, strength, gait speed, exercise capacity, body fat and waist circumference, per the authors; benefits declined after 12 weeks of withdrawal. The abstract prints no numerical effect sizes, so none are quoted.
cards.watchOut: Eight treated people, no control group, no blinding, and the same research group as the positive randomised trial: this pilot is carded because it is part of the published human base for this question, and it is labelled so it cannot be mistaken for confirmatory evidence. Practice, expectancy and time effects are fully plausible explanations for uncontrolled before–after improvements.

cards.headline: Synthesis: GlyNAC reliably engages its target pathway in one group's hands, missed its primary endpoint in the only independent trial, and has no clinical-outcome evidence — MAYBE, with the N on the stamp
cards.summary: Synthesis: GlyNAC reliably engages its target pathway in one group's hands, missed its primary endpoint in the only independent trial, and has no clinical-outcome evidence — MAYBE, with the N on the stamp
cards.people: Synthesis of the three reports carded on this shelf: the Baylor randomised trial (24 older adults), the independent randomised trial (114 older adults) and the Baylor open-label pilot (8 older adults) — total randomised older-adult evidence N=138.
cards.result: The pattern is a familiar geroscience one: broad, large-sounding benefits in a very small single-group trial; a null primary endpoint when an independent group tested the core biomarker claim at larger N; and no trial measuring anything a patient would feel or survive. Safety and tolerability were good in all three reports.
cards.watchOut: MAYBE (weak evidence): the stamp carries the N because the base is small and split. A positive, independently run trial of at least several months with a prespecified functional endpoint is what this question needs; supplement marketing that quotes the Baylor conclusions without the Lizzo null misstates the record.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 35975308, 35821844, 33783984). No additional source.

shelves.title: Nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) in older adults: it raises blood NAD+, one small clamp study found better muscle insulin sensitivity, and pooled trials show no significant benefit on glucose, HbA1c, lipids, muscle mass or strength
shelves.question: In middle-aged and older adults, does oral NMN, versus placebo, improve insulin sensitivity, muscle function, walking or metabolic measures?
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence). NMN does the biochemical thing it promises — blood NAD+ rose significantly in every randomised trial carded here — and almost nothing clinical follows in the pooled data: the 2026 meta-analysis of 15 trials found no significant effects on body weight, BMI, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid profiles or systolic blood pressure, and no increase in adverse events. The one positive metabolic result is Yoshino 2021's clamp study in postmenopausal women with prediabetes, where muscle insulin sensitivity and insulin signalling increased on NMN but not placebo; its fetched abstract states neither the sample size nor the dose, so none is printed, and a published Comment in the same journal (PMID 34326206) challenged the trial's baseline comparability (hepatic lipid content 6.3% in the NMN group vs 14.8% on placebo, p=0.003, as printed in that Comment's record). Walking results split by trial: Yi 2023 found longer 6-minute walk distances at all doses with no HOMA-IR change; Pencina 2023 (MIB-626, a named microcrystalline β-NMN formulation from Metro International Biotech, as printed in its record) found no change in muscle strength, fatigability, aerobic capacity or insulin sensitivity, alongside reductions in weight, diastolic pressure and LDL cholesterol. Tested products differ by maker — the Yoshino record does not name its product's supplier — and current retail NMN products may differ in content and purity from trial material. Regulatory status has swung in recent years (FDA supplement exclusion in 2022, reversed in 2025, per the commissioning slate); this shelf rules on evidence, not legal status.

cards.headline: Yoshino 2021 (Science): muscle insulin sensitivity by clamp increased after NMN but not placebo in postmenopausal women with prediabetes — sample size and dose not stated in the fetched record
cards.summary: Yoshino 2021 (Science): muscle insulin sensitivity by clamp increased after NMN but not placebo in postmenopausal women with prediabetes — sample size and dose not stated in the fetched record
cards.people: Postmenopausal women with prediabetes who were overweight or obese, in a 10-week randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial of NMN; insulin-stimulated glucose disposal was measured by hyperinsulinaemic-euglycaemic clamp, with skeletal-muscle insulin signalling (AKT and mTOR phosphorylation) and gene expression as supporting outcomes. The fetched abstract does not state the sample size or the NMN dose, so neither is printed here. Registered as NCT03151239.
cards.result: Insulin-stimulated glucose disposal and skeletal-muscle insulin signalling increased after NMN supplementation but did not change after placebo. NMN up-regulated expression of platelet-derived growth factor receptor β and other muscle-remodelling genes. The abstract reports no effect sizes for the clamp outcome, and no changes in body composition, blood pressure, fasting glucose or lipids are claimed in it.
cards.watchOut: The field's flagship positive result rests on a single small trial whose own journal published a Comment (Brenner, PMID 34326206) arguing the groups were not effectively randomised on a key baseline variable — hepatic lipid content 6.3% (NMN) vs 14.8% (placebo), p=0.003, per that Comment's record — with the authors' reply defending the muscle outcome. A surrogate clamp endpoint in one centre, contested at baseline, is not a metabolic indication.

cards.headline: Yi 2023: NMN 300–900 mg/day for 60 days raised blood NAD+ and lengthened 6-minute walk distance vs placebo (all doses p<0.01), with no HOMA-IR difference — n=80
cards.summary: Yi 2023: NMN 300–900 mg/day for 60 days raised blood NAD+ and lengthened 6-minute walk distance vs placebo (all doses p<0.01), with no HOMA-IR difference — n=80
cards.people: 80 healthy middle-aged adults randomised to placebo or NMN 300, 600 or 900 mg once daily for 60 days in a multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-dependent trial; primary objective was blood NAD concentration, with 6-minute walk, blood biological age (Aging.Ai 3.0), HOMA-IR and SF-36 as secondary objectives. All 80 completed the trial. Registered as NCT04823260 and CTRI/2021/03/032421.
cards.result: Blood NAD concentrations rose significantly in all NMN groups at days 30 and 60 versus placebo and baseline (all p≤0.001), highest at 600 and 900 mg. Six-minute walk distance increased significantly more in all three NMN groups than placebo at days 30 and 60 (all p<0.01). HOMA-IR showed no statistically significant difference versus placebo at day 60. SF-36 scores favoured NMN, and no safety issues were found.
cards.watchOut: The abstract gives p-values without the walk-distance magnitudes, so the size of the walking benefit cannot be judged from the record — a statistically significant few metres and a meaningful improvement are indistinguishable here. Participants were healthy middle-aged adults, not the frail older adults of the marketing; 60 days is short; and the insulin-resistance measure was null, cutting against the Yoshino clamp signal rather than confirming it.

cards.headline: Pencina 2023 (MIB-626): NAD+ rose; weight −1.9 kg, diastolic pressure −7.0 mmHg and LDL cholesterol −18.7 mg/dL vs placebo — but strength, aerobic capacity and insulin sensitivity did not change (n=30)
cards.summary: Pencina 2023 (MIB-626): NAD+ rose; weight −1.9 kg, diastolic pressure −7.0 mmHg and LDL cholesterol −18.7 mg/dL vs placebo — but strength, aerobic capacity and insulin sensitivity did not change (n=30)
cards.people: 30 overweight or obese adults aged ≥45 years randomised 2:1 to MIB-626 (two 500-mg tablets of microcrystalline β-nicotinamide mononucleotide twice daily; Metro International Biotech, as named in the record) or placebo for 28 days, with safety, NAD metabolome, body composition, insulin sensitivity, lipids, blood pressure and muscle performance outcomes. The record carries no registry ID in its databank fields.
cards.result: Adverse events were similar between groups, and circulating NAD and metabolites rose substantially. Versus placebo, body weight fell by −1.9 kg (p=0.008), diastolic blood pressure by −7.01 mmHg (p=0.034), total cholesterol by −26.89 mg/dL (p=0.004), LDL cholesterol by −18.73 mg/dL (p=0.007) and non-HDL cholesterol significantly. Muscle strength, muscle fatigability, aerobic capacity and stair-climbing power did not differ significantly, and insulin sensitivity and liver/intra-abdominal fat did not change in either group.
cards.watchOut: Thirty people for 28 days, with many outcomes and no evident multiplicity control: the lipid and weight findings are exactly the size and shape that small short physiologic studies produce by chance, and the same trial's null insulin-sensitivity result is the more decision-relevant finding alongside Yoshino. The authors themselves frame it as rationale for larger trials.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Yang 2026): across 15 randomised trials, NMN did not significantly affect weight, BMI, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids or systolic pressure — and did not increase adverse events
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Yang 2026): across 15 randomised trials, NMN did not significantly affect weight, BMI, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipids or systolic pressure — and did not increase adverse events
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Yang 2026)
cards.people: Fifteen parallel randomised trials of oral NMN or NMN-related preparations versus placebo or control (doses 250–2000 mg/day, durations 14 days to 24 weeks), searched to 13 May 2026, with 10 trials contributing to safety analyses; random-effects models with GRADE certainty ratings. Registered in PROSPERO as CRD420261382497, as printed in the record.
cards.result: NMN did not increase overall, serious, withdrawal-related or system-specific adverse events and did not significantly raise ALT or AST. No significant effects were observed on body weight, BMI, fasting glucose, HbA1c, lipid profiles or systolic blood pressure. Diastolic blood pressure decreased slightly, and HOMA-IR showed a non-significant downward trend.
cards.watchOut: The pooled null is the best current summary of NMN's clinical effects — and it is a null over short durations (at most 24 weeks) in mostly healthy adults, so it cannot exclude slow or long-term effects in either direction. It does exclude the large short-term metabolic benefits implied by retail marketing.

cards.headline: Synthesis: NAD+ goes up; glucose, HbA1c, lipids, weight and strength, pooled, do not move — NMN is a well-tolerated supplement with an unproven clinical claim
cards.summary: Synthesis: NAD+ goes up; glucose, HbA1c, lipids, weight and strength, pooled, do not move — NMN is a well-tolerated supplement with an unproven clinical claim
cards.people: Synthesis of the four reports carded on this shelf: Yoshino's clamp trial in prediabetic postmenopausal women, Yi's 80-person dose-ranging trial, Pencina's 30-person MIB-626 physiologic study, and the 2026 meta-analysis of 15 trials.
cards.result: Every layer agrees on target engagement (NAD+ rises) and tolerability (no excess adverse events). They diverge on the one positive surrogate (Yoshino's clamp result, baseline-contested, unconfirmed by Yi's HOMA-IR or Pencina's insulin-sensitivity measures) and converge on null clinical-metabolic outcomes when pooled. Walking findings are positive in one trial with magnitudes unprinted in its record.
cards.watchOut: MAYBE (weak evidence): the stamp reflects a real biomarker effect without demonstrated clinical benefit. Anyone quoting Yoshino without the meta-analysis — or the meta-analysis as proof of long-term safety, which its ≤24-week trials cannot show — is misusing this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards on this shelf (PMIDs 33888596, 36482258, 36740954, 42514320). No additional source.

shelves.title: Rapamycin for healthy ageing: celebrated in mice, null on human primary endpoints so far
shelves.question: In healthy older adults, does intermittent low-dose rapamycin, versus placebo, improve measures of ageing (body composition, immune function, physical performance)?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Sirolimus/administration & dosage, adverse effects, pharmacology · Male · Double-Blind Method · Middle Aged · Adult · Aged · Bone Density/drug effects · Biomarkers/blood · Aging/drug effects
shelves.balance: The animal longevity data behind rapamycin's reputation have not yet translated. PEARL, the largest and longest human trial (48 weeks of weekly compounded rapamycin in healthy adults, run by AgelessRx, which sells the intervention), was null on its primary endpoint — visceral adiposity did not change (p=0.942) — with positive signals only in secondary subgroups of women. RAPA-EX-01 (n=40, rapamycin with exercise) was likewise null on its primary analysis, and its prespecified sensitivity analyses significantly favoured placebo, with a higher adverse-event burden on the drug (99 versus 63 events, including one possibly related pneumonia). The earlier 25-person pilot found feasibility and red-cell index falls, and no cognitive, physical or metabolic benefit. Clarification exception in full: PEARL tested compounded rapamycin at roughly one-third the bioavailability of commercial sirolimus — nothing here reads across to pharmacy sirolimus or grey-market supply. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence), with the nulls worded plainly on the face.

cards.headline: PEARL 2025 (48-week RCT of weekly compounded rapamycin): primary endpoint null (the treatment made no difference to visceral adiposity, p=0.942); secondary signals confined to women, including a 10 mg subgroup of 8 women reported in the trial's secondary coverage
cards.summary: PEARL 2025 (48-week RCT of weekly compounded rapamycin): primary endpoint null (the treatment made no difference to visceral adiposity, p=0.942); secondary signals confined to women, including a 10 mg subgroup of 8 women reported in the trial's secondary coverage
cards.type: Decentralised double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial — 48 weeks (enrolled N not documented in the record's abstract)
cards.people: Healthy adults with normative ageing receiving placebo, 5 mg or 10 mg compounded rapamycin once weekly for 48 weeks in a decentralised trial; primary outcome visceral adiposity by DXA, with lean tissue and bone mineral content, blood biomarkers and well-being surveys as secondary measures. (The record's abstract does not print the enrolled number; where a paper reports no number, this shelf prints N not documented.)
cards.result: Visceral adiposity did not change significantly (the treatment made no difference on the primary endpoint; p=0.942), and blood biomarker changes remained within normal ranges. Lean tissue mass (p=0.013) and self-reported pain (p=0.015) improved significantly for women using 10 mg rapamycin; self-reported emotional well-being (p=0.023) and general health (p=0.004) improved at 5 mg. No other significant effects were observed. Adverse and serious adverse events were similar across groups.
cards.watchOut: A null primary endpoint with positive secondary signals in sex-and-dose subgroups is the classic pattern of multiplicity, and the trial was run by a sponsor (AgelessRx) that sells the intervention — both facts belong on the face. The tested product was compounded rapamycin, whose bioavailability is roughly one-third that of commercial sirolimus: these results do not read across to pharmacy sirolimus or to grey-market supply.
cards.source: Moel M et al. Influence of rapamycin on safety and healthspan metrics after one year: PEARL trial results. Aging (Albany NY). 2025. PMID: 40188830. Registry ID: NCT04488601, printed in the record's abstract (no databank entry in the record). cards.headline: RAPA-EX-01 2026 (rapamycin + exercise RCT, N = 40): primary analysis null (the treatment made no difference to chair-stand gains, p=0.089) — and prespecified sensitivity analyses significantly favoured placebo
cards.summary: RAPA-EX-01 2026 (rapamycin + exercise RCT, N = 40): primary analysis null (the treatment made no difference to chair-stand gains, p=0.089) — and prespecified sensitivity analyses significantly favoured placebo
cards.people: 40 sedentary adults aged 65-85 (mean 72.2 years; 47.5% female) assigned 1:1 to sirolimus (rapamycin) 6 mg or matched placebo once weekly for 13 weeks, both groups performing a standardised home-based resistance and endurance exercise programme three times weekly; primary outcome change in 30-second chair-stand repetitions.
cards.result: Both groups improved. The intention-to-treat difference (sirolimus minus placebo) was -2.13 repetitions (95% CI -4.61 to 0.34; p=0.089) — the treatment made no difference on the primary analysis. Prespecified sensitivity analyses favoured placebo and reached significance: complete-case -2.46 repetitions (p=0.045) and per-protocol -3.44 (p=0.007). Grip strength, 6-minute walk and SF-36 differences also favoured placebo without significance. Adverse events were reported by 85% in each arm but the total burden was higher on sirolimus (99 versus 63 events), including one possibly drug-related serious adverse event (pneumonia).
cards.watchOut: Exploratory and small (40 patients, 13 weeks), so the placebo-favouring sensitivity analyses are a warning light, not proof of harm — but combined with PEARL's null primary, the human record now has two randomised trials and no demonstrated functional benefit, with a higher minor-adverse-event burden on the drug.

cards.headline: Kraig 2018 (pilot RCT, N = 25): 8 weeks of daily rapamycin 1 mg was feasible and showed no cognitive, physical-performance or glucose-tolerance benefit (the treatment made no difference on those measures) — with significant falls in haemoglobin and other red-cell indices
cards.summary: Kraig 2018 (pilot RCT, N = 25): 8 weeks of daily rapamycin 1 mg was feasible and showed no cognitive, physical-performance or glucose-tolerance benefit (the treatment made no difference on those measures) — with significant falls in haemoglobin and other red-cell indices
cards.type: Pilot double-blind placebo-controlled randomised trial — N = 25 analysed
cards.people: 25 generally healthy older adults aged 70-95 randomised to rapamycin 1 mg daily or placebo; 11 rapamycin and 14 control participants completed at least 8 weeks and were analysed, with laboratory safety monitoring, oral glucose tolerance tests, cognitive batteries, grip strength, timed walks and immune profiling.
cards.result: No changes were noted in clinical laboratory measures other than red-cell indices, nor in cognitive function, physical performance or self-perceived health (the treatment made no difference on those measures); glucose tolerance, insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity were unchanged. Statistically significant decrements occurred in haemoglobin, haematocrit, red-cell count and related indices on rapamycin, without clinical manifestations over the short study. Reported side effects on rapamycin were facial rash (1), stomatitis (1) and gastrointestinal issues (2). Immune parameters were largely unchanged, with increases in a myeloid subset and regulatory T cells detected.
cards.watchOut: A 25-person feasibility pilot: it was designed to ask whether a bigger trial could be run safely, not whether rapamycin slows ageing, and its nulls are as underpowered as its reassurance. Its durable contribution is the red-cell signal and the absence of a glucose signal at this dose and duration.
cards.source: Kraig E et al. A randomized control trial to establish the feasibility and safety of rapamycin treatment in an older human cohort: immunological, physical performance, and cognitive effects. Exp Gerontol. 2018. glucose tolerance, insulin secretion and insulin sensitivity were unchanged. statistically significant decrements occurred in haemoglobin, haematocrit, red-cell count and related indices on rapamycin, without clinical manifestations over the short study. reported side effects on rapamycin were facial rash (1), stomatitis (1) and gastrointestinal issues (2). immune parameters were largely unchanged, with increases in a myeloid subset and regulatory t cells detected. a 25-person feasibility pilot: it was designed to ask whether a bigger trial could be run safely, not whether rapamycin slows ageing, and its nulls are as underpowered as its reassurance. its durable contribution is the red-cell signal and the absence of a glucose signal at this dose and duration. kraig e et al. a randomized control trial to establish the feasibility and safety of rapamycin treatment in an older human cohort: immunological, physical performance, and cognitive effects. exp gerontol. 2018. pmid: 29408453. registry id: none in the record. mesh: aged · aged, 80 and over · aging/drug effects · cognition/drug effects · double-blind method · drug administration schedule · erythrocyte indices/drug effects · female · glucose tolerance test · hand strength/physiology · humans · immunosuppressive agents/administration & dosage · insulin resistance · male · myeloid cells/cytology · physical fitness · pilot projects · prospective studies · sirolimus/administration & dosage · t-lymphocytes, regulatory/cytology · tor serine-threonine kinases/antagonists & inhibitors · texas · walk test

cards.headline: Synthesis: two larger randomised trials, two null primary endpoints, one sensitivity-analysis signal favouring placebo — no demonstrated healthy-ageing benefit in humans — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: two larger randomised trials, two null primary endpoints, one sensitivity-analysis signal favouring placebo — no demonstrated healthy-ageing benefit in humans — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Randomised human evidence in healthy older adults: PEARL (48 weeks, weekly compounded rapamycin; enrolled N not documented in the record's abstract), RAPA-EX-01 (N = 40, with exercise) and the Kraig pilot (N = 25). A 6-person open-label cardiac pilot from the same era sits below this library's reference floor and is not carded.
cards.result: Primary endpoints: visceral adiposity unchanged on rapamycin (p=0.942); exercise gains not enhanced (p=0.089), with sensitivity analyses significantly favouring placebo. Positive findings are confined to secondary, sex-specific subgroups in PEARL (lean tissue mass and pain in women at 10 mg). Safety over these durations was broadly acceptable, with a higher minor-event burden in RAPA-EX-01 (99 versus 63 events) and red-cell index falls in the pilot. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) — in humans, unlike mice, rapamycin for healthy ageing currently has no demonstrated benefit on any primary endpoint, and the honest summary of the carded record is that the treatments tested made no difference where it was prespecified to count.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here concerns rapamycin's licensed immunosuppressant uses, and the everolimus/RTB101 immune-ageing programme is a different drug question homed elsewhere in this library. Longevity itself — lifespan or healthspan in years — has never been an endpoint in a human rapamycin trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Moel M et al. 2025 (PMID: 40188830), Stanfield B et al. 2026 (PMID: 41985884) and Kraig E et al. 2018 (PMID: 29408453), all carded above.

shelves.title: 4AT for delirium: pooled sensitivity 0.88 / specificity 0.88 on 2 anchors + 1 supporting validation — ROC 0.89 even with dementia, weaker in severe cognitive impairment
shelves.question: In hospitalised older adults on wards, in the emergency department and after surgery, how accurately does the 4AT (the 4 'A's Test — alertness, AMT-4, attention, acute change or fluctuating course) detect delirium against a reference standard, how does it perform in patients with dementia and after stroke, and how long does it take at the bedside?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Delirium · Female · Geriatric Assessment · Humans · Inpatients · Male · Mass Screening · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Prospective Studies · ROC Curve · Sensitivity and Specificity · Surveys and Questionnaires · Emergency Service, Hospital · Reproducibility of Results · Sweden
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — good pooled accuracy on a stated base of 2 anchors + 1 verified supporting validation (3 reports in total). The founding validation (236 patients aged ≥70) gave sensitivity 89.7%, specificity 84.1% and ROC area 0.93 — 0.89 in patients with dementia, the population where the test is hardest. The anchor meta-analysis (17 studies, 3,702 observations) pooled sensitivity 0.88 and specificity 0.88 at 24.2% prevalence (ex-stroke 0.86 / 0.89). The one supporting independent validation (Swedish, 200 patients) was weaker — sensitivity 0.70, specificity 0.92, AUROC 0.808, worst on the severe-cognitive-impairment ward. The test takes under 2 minutes. No card implies detection improves outcomes.

cards.headline: Founding validation (Bellelli 2014): 236 patients aged ≥70 on a geriatrics ward and in rehabilitation — sensitivity 89.7%, specificity 84.1%, ROC area 0.93 overall, 0.92 without dementia and 0.89 with dementia
cards.summary: Founding validation (Bellelli 2014): 236 patients aged ≥70 on a geriatrics ward and in rehabilitation — sensitivity 89.7%, specificity 84.1%, ROC area 0.93 overall, 0.92 without dementia and 0.89 with dementia
cards.type: Prospective validation study (founding 4AT study, 236 patients aged ≥70)
cards.people: 236 consecutively admitted patients aged ≥70 years (mean 83.9 ± 6.1 years; 64% women) on an acute geriatrics ward and in a rehabilitation department over 4 months; the 4AT was given by a geriatrician within 24 h of admission and the DSM-IV-TR reference diagnosis within 30 min by a different, blinded geriatrician; delirium in 12.3% (29 patients), dementia in 31.2% (74) and both in 7.2% (17). (The fetched record's article title says 234 hospitalised older people; its abstract reports 236 patients studied — the abstract's number is used here.)
cards.result: The 4AT had sensitivity 89.7% and specificity 84.1% for delirium. Areas under the ROC curve were 0.93 in the whole population, 0.92 in patients without dementia and 0.89 in patients with dementia. The authors conclude the 4AT is a sensitive and specific screening method for delirium in hospitalised older people whose brevity and simplicity support routine use.
cards.watchOut: Performance in dementia (ROC area 0.89) is core content, not a caveat — dementia is the commonest reason the test is hard — and the founding setting was geriatrics / rehabilitation with geriatrician assessors, not an undifferentiated emergency department.
cards.source: Bellelli G et al. Validation of the 4AT, a new instrument for rapid delirium screening: a study in 234 hospitalised older people. Age and ageing. 2014. PMID: 24590568. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Meta-analysis (17 studies, 3,702 observations): pooled sensitivity 0.88 and specificity 0.88 at a delirium prevalence of 24.2%, across acute medicine, surgery, a care home and the emergency department
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (17 studies, 3,702 observations): pooled sensitivity 0.88 and specificity 0.88 at a delirium prevalence of 24.2%, across acute medicine, surgery, a care home and the emergency department
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 4AT diagnostic accuracy (17 studies, 3,702 observations) — anchor synthesis
cards.people: 17 diagnostic-accuracy studies (3,702 observations) in older adults (≥65 years) across acute medicine, surgery, a care home and the emergency department, searched to 21 December 2019; 3 studies assessed the 4AT in stroke; methodological quality assessed with QUADAS-2 and rated moderate to good overall; pooled estimates from a bivariate random-effects model.
cards.result: Overall delirium prevalence was 24.2% (95% CI 17.8 to 32.1%; range 10.5 to 61.9%). Pooled sensitivity was 0.88 (95% CI 0.80 to 0.93) and pooled specificity 0.88 (95% CI 0.82 to 0.92). Excluding the stroke studies, pooled sensitivity was 0.86 (95% CI 0.77 to 0.92) and specificity 0.89 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.93) — the stroke subgroup is thus carded separately in the pooled reading, not merged silently. The 4AT takes under 2 minutes.
cards.watchOut: One of this shelf's two anchors (see the count stated on the synthesis card): a pooled pair across settings with prevalence ranging 10.5–61.9% is an average performance, and the stroke studies pull the pooled estimates, which is why the ex-stroke figures are printed beside them.
cards.source: Tieges Z et al. Diagnostic accuracy of the 4AT for delirium detection in older adults: systematic review and meta-analysis. Age and ageing. 2021. PMID: 33951145. cards.headline: Supporting validation — Swedish 4AT (200 patients aged ≥65, two hospitals): sensitivity 0.70, specificity 0.92, AUROC 0.808 vs DSM-IV-TR, with weaker performance on the severe-cognitive-impairment ward
cards.summary: Supporting validation — Swedish 4AT (200 patients aged ≥65, two hospitals): sensitivity 0.70, specificity 0.92, AUROC 0.808 vs DSM-IV-TR, with weaker performance on the severe-cognitive-impairment ward
cards.type: Independent-setting validation study (Swedish 4AT, 200 patients) — supporting report, not an anchor synthesis
cards.people: 200 patients aged ≥65 years at a university hospital and a county hospital in two Swedish regions, across geriatric stroke/neurology, geriatric multimorbidity, severe cognitive impairment, orthopaedic and urology wards; the translated Swedish 4AT was tested against a DSM-IV-TR reference standard based on the Organic Brain Syndrome scale and patient records, assessed simultaneously and independently by two assessors; applicability was also assessed in the 200 patients and 37 assessors.
cards.result: By the reference standard 18% had delirium and by 4AT 19%; overall percent agreement was 88%, AUROC 0.808, sensitivity 0.70 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.84) and specificity 0.92 (95% CI 0.87 to 0.96). On the severe-cognitive-impairment ward (n = 63) the 4AT was less sensitive and less specific; on the other wards (n = 132) sensitivity was 0.77, specificity 0.93 and AUROC 0.848. Interrater reliability was kappa 0.918; the test took a few minutes, was well tolerated by patients and easy for professionals to use.
cards.watchOut: Labelled as what it is: the one further independent validation beyond the two anchors, in a translated version, with the lowest sensitivity on this shelf (0.70) — concentrated on the severe-cognitive-impairment ward, the population where delirium detection is hardest.
cards.source: Johansson YA et al. Diagnostic accuracy and clinical applicability of the Swedish version of the 4AT assessment test for delirium detection, in a mixed patient population and setting. shelves.title: Morse Fall Scale predicting inpatient falls: cut-off 45 in acute care, 40 in obstetrics / gynaecology — and retrospective design inflates its accuracy by 0.22 Youden points (GAP-E)
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults, how well does the Morse Fall Scale (fall history, secondary diagnosis, ambulatory aid, intravenous therapy, gait, mental status; usual high-risk cut-off ≥45) predict who will fall during the admission — what sensitivity, specificity and discrimination does it deliver at the standard and at locally re-derived cut-offs, how much does the ward type move the answer, and how much of the published accuracy is an artefact of retrospective study design?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls · Female · Humans · Male · Republic of Korea · Retrospective Studies · Accidental Falls/prevention & control · Risk Assessment/methods · Adult · Middle Aged · ROC Curve · Obstetrics and Gynecology Department, Hospital/standards · Obstetrics · Gynecology · Electronic Health Records · Aged · Accidental Falls/statistics & numerical data · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Sensitivity and Specificity · Bias · Evaluation Studies as Topic · Forecasting · Hospitals · Mass Screening · Prospective Studies · Reproducibility of Results · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Geriatric Psychiatry · Hospitalization · Inpatients/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — modest, local, and inflated by design (GAP-E). The Morse Fall Scale (fall history, secondary diagnosis, ambulatory aid, intravenous therapy, gait, mental status) was validated at its conventional ≥45 cut-off in a Korean acute-care sample (66 fallers, 100 non-fallers; the record prints qualitative accuracy descriptors only), while an obstetrics-and-gynaecology re-evaluation (136 fall, 120 no-fall) found the locally optimal cut-off was 40 (AUC 0.772; sensitivity 0.735, specificity 0.808). The core finding is methodological: across 51 tool evaluations, retrospective designs reported Youden indices 0.22 higher than prospective ones, and prospectively the Morse scale, STRATIFY and nursing clinical judgement had comparable accuracy; a cross-instrument meta-analysis likewise found STRATIFY ahead (diagnostic odds ratio 7.64) and in-stay reassessment reducing the Morse DOR (relative DOR 0.75). A psychogeriatric report (Morse sensitivity 50% on only 4 in-stay falls) is carded as a labelled caution, never as evidence. No sensitivity / specificity pair is printed without its design and ward type.

cards.headline: Korean acute-care validation (Sung 2014): in 66 patients who fell and 100 who did not, the optimal Morse Fall Scale cut-off was the conventional 45 points, with acceptable sensitivity and fairly good specificity, negative predictive value and accuracy — as published (the record prints no numeric sensitivity / specificity pair)
cards.summary: Korean acute-care validation (Sung 2014): in 66 patients who fell and 100 who did not, the optimal Morse Fall Scale cut-off was the conventional 45 points, with acceptable sensitivity and fairly good specificity, negative predictive value and accuracy — as published (the record prints no numeric sensitivity / specificity pair)
cards.type: Retrospective validation study (Korean Morse Fall Scale, acute-care tertiary hospital)
cards.people: Medical records of 66 inpatients who fell and 100 who did not fall, sampled from inpatients at a tertiary acute-care hospital in Seoul, Korea (January to November 2009); the Korean version of the Morse Fall Scale (fall history, secondary diagnosis, ambulatory aid, intravenous therapy, gait, mental status). A retrospective case-control-style sampling of fallers versus non-fallers.
cards.result: The optimal cut-off point for the Korean Morse Fall Scale was 45 points — the conventional high-risk threshold — which produced an acceptable sensitivity and a fairly good specificity, negative predictive value and accuracy, as published; the highest peak on the receiver-operating-characteristic curve was at 45 points. The fetched record gives these qualitative descriptors and no numeric sensitivity or specificity values, and this card claims none. The authors called for further research to determine the optimal cut-off in more homogeneous medical or surgical populations, with daily measurement.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective sampling of known fallers versus non-fallers is exactly the design the design-bias card below shows inflates accuracy (Youden index higher by 0.22) — this study's favourable descriptors must be read under that warning, and no numeric accuracy pair may be quoted from it.

cards.headline: Obstetrics and gynaecology re-evaluation (Mao 2024): the locally optimal cut-off was 40, not 45 — AUC 0.772 at 40 vs 0.761 at 45, with sensitivity 0.735 and specificity 0.808 at 40 (136 fall and 120 no-fall inpatients, retrospective)
cards.summary: Obstetrics and gynaecology re-evaluation (Mao 2024): the locally optimal cut-off was 40, not 45 — AUC 0.772 at 40 vs 0.761 at 45, with sensitivity 0.735 and specificity 0.808 at 40 (136 fall and 120 no-fall inpatients, retrospective)
cards.type: Retrospective re-evaluation study (Morse Fall Scale, obstetrics and gynaecology wards) — the locally-derived cut-off card
cards.people: Electronic medical records from an obstetrics and gynaecology hospital and a general hospital (January 2020 to July 2022): 136 inpatients who fell and 120 who did not, scored on the Morse Fall Scale and assessed against the gold standard of having fallen while hospitalised. A retrospective survey.
cards.result: At cut-off scores of 40, 45, 50 and 55, the area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve was 0.772, 0.761, 0.749 and 0.763 respectively. cards.headline: Systematic review and meta-analysis of fall-risk instruments in acute hospitals (Aranda-Gallardo 2013): STRATIFY gave the greater diagnostic validity (diagnostic odds ratio 7.64); reassessment during the stay significantly reduced the Morse scale's diagnostic odds ratio (relative DOR 0.75); the authors warn every instrument behaves differently outside its development setting
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of fall-risk instruments in acute hospitals (Aranda-Gallardo 2013): STRATIFY gave the greater diagnostic validity (diagnostic odds ratio 7.64); reassessment during the stay significantly reduced the Morse scale's diagnostic odds ratio (relative DOR 0.75); the authors warn every instrument behaves differently outside its development setting
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (fall-risk assessment instruments in acute hospitalised patients; Morse among them)
cards.people: 14 studies selected for systematic review, with meta-analysis performed on the Morse Fall Scale, STRATIFY and the Hendrich II Fall Risk Model in acutely hospitalised adults; two blinded reviewers assessed eligibility and methodological quality.
cards.result: The STRATIFY tool provided greater diagnostic validity, with a diagnostic odds ratio of 7.64 (95% CI 4.86 to 12.00). A meta-regression assessed average patient age over 65 and whether risk reassessments were performed during the stay: reassessment showed a significant reduction in the diagnostic odds ratio on the Morse Fall Scale (relative diagnostic odds ratio 0.75, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.89; P=0.017). The authors concluded STRATIFY was the best-performing tool in this analysis, but that the behaviour of these instruments varies considerably depending on population and environment, so their operation should be tested before implementation.
cards.watchOut: A cross-instrument synthesis, not a Morse-only validation: its Morse-specific quantitative finding is the reassessment effect (relative DOR 0.75), and its setting-dependence warning applies to every number on this shelf.

cards.headline: Design-bias meta-analysis (Haines 2007): retrospective evaluations of fall-risk tools reported Youden indices 0.22 higher than prospective ones — the artefact that inflates most published Morse accuracy; pooled prospective evaluations showed Morse, STRATIFY and nursing clinical judgement to have comparable accuracy

cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of design-related bias in fall-risk tool evaluations — the retrospective-artefact card (quantified: +0.22 Youden index)
cards.people: 35 publications containing 51 evaluations of hospital fall-risk screening tools: 20 classified as retrospective validation evaluations, 11 as prospective (temporal) validations and 20 as prospective (external) validations; study design was classified by two blind reviewers and its association with reported Youden index (sensitivity + specificity − 1) examined by regression, with pooling of the prospective evaluations. This shelf's core methodological card, as commissioned.
cards.result: Retrospective evaluations had significantly higher Youden indices than prospective ones — by 0.22 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.33). Pooled Youden indices from prospective evaluations demonstrated the STRATIFY tool, the Morse Fall Scale and nursing staff clinical judgement to have comparable accuracy. The authors concluded practitioners should exercise caution comparing tools whose evaluation has been limited to retrospective designs, and that widespread adoption of either Morse or STRATIFY is unlikely to generate benefits significantly greater than nursing staff clinical judgement.
cards.watchOut: This is the lens for the whole shelf: both primary validations carded here sampled fallers and non-fallers retrospectively, so their accuracy figures sit in the inflated class this analysis quantifies. Heterogeneity between studies was substantial.

cards.headline: Labelled caution — psychogeriatric comparison (Wong 2021): Morse sensitivity was only 50% at the ≥45 cut-off, but that figure rests on just 4 in-stay falls among 183 identified patients (prevalence 2.19%) — carded as a caution only, never as accuracy evidence
cards.summary: Labelled caution — psychogeriatric comparison (Wong 2021): Morse sensitivity was only 50% at the ≥45 cut-off, but that figure rests on just 4 in-stay falls among 183 identified patients (prevalence 2.19%) — carded as a caution only, never as accuracy evidence
cards.type: Multicentre psychogeriatric comparison (Wilson Sims vs Morse) — SUPPORTING REPORT, labelled, never load-bearing (only 4 in-stay fall events)
cards.people: 183 psychogeriatric inpatients aged 65 or older, identified across four Hong Kong hospitals (Shatin, Tai Po, Castle Peak, United Christian) because they had a fall incident recorded between April 2019 and April 2020, and assessed with both the Wilson Sims Fall Risk Assessment Tool and the Morse Fall Scale (high risk at ≥45). Only 4 of the 183 actually fell during the hospital stay.
cards.result: All four patients who fell during the stay were classified high-risk by the Wilson Sims tool, but only two of the four were classified high-risk by the Morse Fall Scale — a Morse sensitivity of 50% on an event count of four. The authors concluded the Wilson Sims tool is the better scale for psychiatric inpatients on sensitivity (100% vs 50%).
cards.watchOut: Four events cannot estimate a sensitivity: the 50% figure would swing by 25 points on a single patient. This report is carded, as commissioned, only as a labelled caution that ward type (here psychogeriatric) can break a general-ward instrument — its numbers carry no weight on this shelf.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the Morse Fall Scale predicts inpatient falls modestly and locally — the conventional ≥45 cut-off was optimal in one acute-care validation and 40 in obstetrics / gynaecology (AUC 0.772, sensitivity 0.735, specificity 0.808) — and much of its published accuracy is a retrospective-design artefact: retrospective evaluations run 0.22 higher on the Youden index than prospective ones, under which prospective Morse accuracy is comparable to nursing clinical judgement

cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: two retrospective validations (166 and 256 sampled inpatients), two systematic reviews / meta-analyses (14 studies; 35 publications / 51 evaluations), and one labelled psychogeriatric caution resting on 4 fall events.
cards.result: Cut-offs: 45 optimal in Korean acute care (qualitative accuracy descriptors only, as published); 40 optimal in obstetrics and gynaecology (AUC 0.772 at 40 vs 0.761 at 45; sensitivity 0.735, specificity 0.808 at 40). Cross-instrument synthesis: STRATIFY's diagnostic odds ratio 7.64 exceeded the other tools', and in-stay reassessment reduced the Morse diagnostic odds ratio (relative DOR 0.75). Design bias: retrospective evaluations inflated the Youden index by 0.22 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.33) over prospective ones, and prospectively Morse, STRATIFY and nursing judgement were comparable. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf only: it proposes no fall-prevention intervention and no card may print a sensitivity / specificity pair without its study design and ward type.
cards.watchOut: Both primary validations are retrospective faller / non-faller samples — the inflated class. The psychogeriatric report (4 events) is a caution, not evidence.

shelves.title: Hendrich II Fall Risk Model: AUC 0.765 and 78.7% sensitivity at ≥5 across nine hospitals, but AUC 0.57 and 29.5% sensitivity at the same cut-off in a single-centre re-validation
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults, how well does the Hendrich II Fall Risk Model (confusion / disorientation, depression, altered elimination, dizziness / vertigo, male sex, antiepileptics, benzodiazepines, and the Get-Up-and-Go rising item; standard high-risk cut-off ≥5) predict who will fall during the admission — what sensitivity, specificity and discrimination does it deliver at the standard cut-off and at locally lowered cut-offs, and how far does its accuracy swing between the large multisite validations and single-centre re-validations?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/prevention & control,statistics & numerical data · Case-Control Studies · Concurrent Review · Hospitals/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Logistic Models · Models, Theoretical · Nursing Assessment/methods · Reproducibility of Results · Risk Assessment/methods · Risk Factors · Sensitivity and Specificity · United States · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Male · Middle Aged · Patient Safety/standards · Psychometrics/standards · Retrospective Studies · Risk Assessment/standards · Risk Reduction Behavior · ROC Curve · Inpatients · Geriatrics · Italy · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — moderate in the large multisite validation, poor at the same cut-off in a single-centre re-validation, and that transportability swing is the content. In 214,358 inpatients across nine hospitals the Hendrich II model at its standard cut-off ≥5 gave sensitivity 78.72%, specificity 64.07% and AUC 0.765; lowering the cut-off to ≥4 raised sensitivity to 90.56% and dropped specificity to 44.43%. In a single Taiwanese centre (303 fall events) the same ≥5 cut-off gave sensitivity of only 29.5% with specificity 86.3% and AUC 0.57, with acceptable discrimination (AUC 0.75) only at ≥2. A small prospective geriatric-unit validation found sensitivity 86% and specificity 43% at its optimal cut-off of 5 (AUC 0.72). The 2003 derivation report is the model originators' own and is labelled as such. No sensitivity/specificity pair on this shelf prints without its setting and cut-off, and nothing carded shows that scoring — or any bundle a high score triggers — prevents falls. PROPOSED STAMP: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — setting-dependent (see proposedStamp).

cards.type: Programme report: derivation / concurrent case-control validation by the model originators (Hendrich II Fall Risk Model)
cards.people: 355 fall cases and 780 controls, randomly enrolled in an acute care tertiary facility and assessed for more than 600 intrinsic and extrinsic risk factors, using standardised instruments and clinician assessments; the model was developed by stepwise logistic regression. PROGRAMME-LABELLED: this is the derivation / concurrent validation report of the model's own originators, not an independent validation.
cards.result: The study produced the Hendrich II Fall Risk Model: an easy-to-use eight-assessment-parameter model for identifying high-risk fall patients, tested in acute care environments. cards.watchOut: Originators' own derivation in a single tertiary facility: derivation-setting accuracy is expected to flatter a model, and here the record does not even print the values — this card establishes what the model is and where it came from, not how well it performs elsewhere.
