cards.headline: Nine-hospital validation (Hendrich 2020): 214,358 inpatients — at cut-off ≥5 sensitivity 78.72%, specificity 64.07%, AUC 0.765; at ≥4 sensitivity 90.56%, specificity 44.43%
cards.summary: Nine-hospital validation (Hendrich 2020): 214,358 inpatients — at cut-off ≥5 sensitivity 78.72%, specificity 64.07%, AUC 0.765; at ≥4 sensitivity 90.56%, specificity 44.43%
cards.type: Retrospective multisite validation (nine hospitals), standard and lowered cut-offs
cards.people: 214,358 adult inpatients consecutively admitted to nine Ascension hospitals (January 2016 to December 2018); fall risk assessed with the Hendrich II model on admission and at least once per nursing shift, in a retrospective analysis of electronic health record data. Overall fall rate 0.29%.
cards.result: At the standard threshold of ≥5, 492 falls and 76,800 non-falls were identified (fall rate 0.36% in that stratum, as published); sensitivity was 78.72% and specificity 64.07%, with area under the ROC curve 0.765 (standard error 0.008; 95% CI 0.748 to 0.781; P < 0.001) — moderate accuracy. At a lower cut-off of ≥4, an additional 74 falls could have been identified, with sensitivity improving to 90.56% and specificity falling to 44.43%. The study also identified 77,292 inpatients with multiple fall risk factors that are typically not actively managed during hospitalisation.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective EHR validation in one US health system, and the first author is the model's originator; even here, the ≥4 cut-off that catches 90.56% of fallers flags so many non-fallers (specificity 44.43%) that most high-score patients will not fall — the base fall rate was 0.29%.

cards.headline: Single-centre Taiwanese re-validation (Hu 2024): at the same ≥5 cut-off sensitivity collapsed to 29.5% (specificity 86.3%, AUC 0.57); acceptable discrimination only at ≥2 (AUC 0.75)
cards.summary: Single-centre Taiwanese re-validation (Hu 2024): at the same ≥5 cut-off sensitivity collapsed to 29.5% (specificity 86.3%, AUC 0.57); acceptable discrimination only at ≥2 (AUC 0.75)
cards.type: Retrospective single-centre re-validation, ROC analysis at standard and lowered cut-offs
cards.people: 303 fall events and 47,146 non-fall events captured from the electronic medical record and patient safety reporting systems of a medical centre in southern Taiwan; retrospective ROC analysis. Wards with the most scores above 5 were internal medicine (50.6%), surgical (26.5%) and oncology (14.1%).
cards.result: At the standard threshold of ≥5, the median score in the fall group was significantly higher than in the non-fall group, but ROC analysis showed sensitivity of only 29.5% and specificity of 86.3%, with an area under the curve of 0.57 — limited discriminative ability in this centre. At a lower cut-off of ≥2, the AUC was 0.75, suggesting acceptable discriminative ability, with an additional 101 fall events identified. The authors emphasise the importance of selecting an appropriate cut-off score when using the model.
cards.watchOut: The direct contradiction of the nine-hospital figures at the identical cut-off is the finding: a ≥5 score missed about 70% of fall events in this centre. Event-based (not patient-based) counting and a single centre limit generalisation in the other direction too — neither validation may be quoted without its setting.
cards.source: Hu CY et al. Validating the accuracy of the Hendrich II Fall Risk Model for hospitalized patients using the ROC curve analysis. The Kaohsiung journal of medical sciences. 2024. cards.headline: Prospective geriatric-unit validation (Ivziku 2011): 179 patients — sensitivity 86% and specificity 43% at the optimal cut-off of 5, AUC 0.72, inter-rater reliability 0.87, about one minute to administer
cards.summary: Prospective geriatric-unit validation (Ivziku 2011): 179 patients — sensitivity 86% and specificity 43% at the optimal cut-off of 5, AUC 0.72, inter-rater reliability 0.87, about one minute to administer
cards.people: 179 patients over 65 consecutively admitted to an acute geriatric unit of an Italian university hospital over 8 months; screened with the Hendrich II model within 24 hours of admission, with falls during the stay registered prospectively. The most frequently reported risk factors were depression, incontinence and vertigo; confusion and depression were most strongly associated with falls.
cards.result: Sensitivity was 86% and specificity 43% at the optimal cut-off score of 5, with an area under the ROC curve of 0.72. Inter-rater reliability was 0.87 (95% CI 0.71 to 1.00) and administration time was about one minute. The authors conclude the findings support using the model to screen older patients at risk of falling in acute care settings.
cards.watchOut: Small (N = 179) and single-unit: the 86% sensitivity comes with 43% specificity, so most patients flagged at ≥5 in this elderly population did not fall; it supports feasibility and reliability more than it settles accuracy.
cards.source: Ivziku D et al. Predictive validity of the Hendrich fall risk model II in an acute geriatric unit. International journal of nursing studies. 2011. PMID: 20926075. cards.headline: Synthesis: the Hendrich II model's accuracy is a property of setting and cut-off, not of the model alone — AUC 0.765 and sensitivity 78.7% at ≥5 in nine US hospitals, against AUC 0.57 and sensitivity 29.5% at the same ≥5 in one Taiwanese centre
cards.summary: Synthesis: the Hendrich II model's accuracy is a property of setting and cut-off, not of the model alone — AUC 0.765 and sensitivity 78.7% at ≥5 in nine US hospitals, against AUC 0.57 and sensitivity 29.5% at the same ≥5 in one Taiwanese centre
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The originators' 2003 derivation (355 cases, 780 controls) produced the eight-parameter model but prints no numeric accuracy in its record. The independent and semi-independent validations diverge: Hendrich 2020 (214,358 inpatients, nine hospitals) found sensitivity 78.72% / specificity 64.07% / AUC 0.765 at ≥5, improving to 90.56% sensitivity at ≥4 at the cost of specificity 44.43%; Hu 2024 (303 fall events, one Taiwanese centre) found sensitivity 29.5% / specificity 86.3% / AUC 0.57 at ≥5 and AUC 0.75 only at ≥2; Ivziku 2011 (179 geriatric patients, prospective) found 86% / 43% at an optimal cut-off of 5 with AUC 0.72 and one-minute administration. Lowering the cut-off always buys sensitivity with specificity. Nothing carded tests whether acting on the score prevents falls.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each validation's setting and limits; this synthesis adds no new data. Distinct from the Morse Fall Scale shelf — a different instrument with a different item set and literature.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: STRATIFY falls tool: pooled sensitivity 67.2% and specificity 51.2% in geriatric rehabilitation — but sensitivity collapsed to 11.3% after stroke at the same ≥2 cut-off, so its accuracy is a property of the setting, not the tool
shelves.question: In hospitalised adults, how well does the STRATIFY falls risk-assessment tool (recent falls, agitation, visual impairment, frequent toileting, impaired transfer / mobility; standard high-risk cut-off ≥2) predict who will fall during the admission — what pooled sensitivity and specificity does it deliver in geriatric rehabilitation, and how far does its accuracy collapse in stroke rehabilitation, nursing-home and general acute-care validations?
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/prevention & control · Aged · Forecasting · Geriatric Assessment/methods · Humans · Inpatients · Middle Aged · Probability · Reproducibility of Results · Sensitivity and Specificity · Accidental Falls/prevention & control,statistics & numerical data · Acute Disease · Adult · Aged, 80 and over · Cohort Studies · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Male · Mobility Limitation · Predictive Value of Tests · Prospective Studies · ROC Curve · Risk Assessment · Stroke/complications · Stroke Rehabilitation · Netherlands · Nursing Homes · Proportional Hazards Models · Risk Assessment/methods · Retrospective Studies · Tertiary Care Centers · Colombia · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — modest at best, and setting-bound. The pooled geriatric-rehabilitation figures (Oliver 2008: sensitivity 67.2%, specificity 51.2%, PPV 23.1%, NPV 86.5%) are the tool's best case, and even there three of four flagged patients do not fall. Transport is the story: after stroke, sensitivity was 11.3% in the first 28 days (Smith 2006) — the tool missed almost nine of ten fallers; in a nursing home, sensitivity was 50% with a relative risk of falling of 2.35 at ≥2 (Wijnia 2006, a relative measure); and in 93,347 general acute-care records, sensitivity was 0.672 and specificity 0.612 with an AUC of 0.69 (Cortés 2023). A single sensitivity/specificity pair for STRATIFY does not exist; every pair on this shelf prints with its setting and cut-off. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf: nothing here shows that scoring patients, or acting on a high score, prevents a fall. Distinct instruments, distinct shelves: Morse is #7650 and Hendrich II is a separate row — no anchor is shared.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Oliver 2008): in geriatric rehabilitation, STRATIFY pooled sensitivity 67.2%, specificity 51.2%, PPV 23.1%, NPV 86.5% — with significant heterogeneity for specificity and predictive values
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Oliver 2008): in geriatric rehabilitation, STRATIFY pooled sensitivity 67.2%, specificity 51.2%, PPV 23.1%, NPV 86.5% — with significant heterogeneity for specificity and predictive values
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective STRATIFY validations (8 studies reviewed; 4 geriatric-rehabilitation studies pooled)
cards.people: Systematic review of prospective STRATIFY validation studies in hospital inpatients: 8 studies eligible for the review and 4 conducted in geriatric rehabilitation settings pooled in the meta-analysis (precision-weighted fixed- and random-effects models).
cards.result: Using a random-effects model in the four geriatric-rehabilitation studies: sensitivity 67.2% (95% CI 60.8 to 73.6), specificity 51.2% (95% CI 43.0 to 59.3), positive predictive value 23.1% (95% CI 14.9 to 31.2) and negative predictive value 86.5% (95% CI 78.4 to 94.6). The homogeneity test was not significant for sensitivity (P = 0.36) but was significant (P < 0.01) for specificity, PPV and NPV; total predictive accuracy across the four studies varied from 43.2% to 60.0%. The authors conclude the relatively high NPV and low PPV and accuracy suggest STRATIFY may not be optimal for identifying high-risk individuals for fall prevention, and that population and setting affect its performance.
cards.watchOut: The pooled pair is a geriatric-rehabilitation figure only. A PPV of 23.1% means most patients flagged high-risk do not fall — print it beside the sensitivity wherever the pooled figures are used.
cards.source: Oliver D et al. A systematic review and meta-analysis of studies using the STRATIFY tool for prediction of falls in hospital patients: how well does it work? Age and ageing. 2008. PMID: 18829693. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Stroke rehabilitation (Smith 2006): STRATIFY sensitivity only 11.3% for falls in the first 28 days (specificity 89.5%) and 16.3% after discharge — the tool performed poorly after stroke
cards.summary: Stroke rehabilitation (Smith 2006): STRATIFY sensitivity only 11.3% for falls in the first 28 days (specificity 89.5%) and 16.3% after discharge — the tool performed poorly after stroke
cards.type: Prospective multicentre cohort validation of STRATIFY in stroke rehabilitation (225 patients, 28-day inpatient study)
cards.people: Prospective multicentre cohort in six stroke rehabilitation units in the North of England: 225 patients contributed to the 28-day inpatient study (of 387 admitted during the study period) and 234 were followed up at 3 months after discharge; STRATIFY was scored on admission, weekly and before discharge.
cards.result: STRATIFY performed poorly in predicting falls in the first 28 days (sensitivity 11.3% and specificity 89.5%) and after discharge (sensitivity 16.3% and specificity 86.4%). Agreement was 'fair' between baseline and discharge scores (kappa = 0.263) and 'good' between the pre-discharge score and the score from the preceding week (kappa = 0.639). The authors conclude STRATIFY performed poorly in a heterogeneous stroke population and that a disease-specific rather than generic falls tool is needed.
cards.watchOut: High specificity with 11.3% sensitivity is a tool that rarely flags anyone — including almost all eventual fallers. Do not average this pair with the geriatric-rehabilitation pool; the collapse is the finding.
cards.source: Smith J et al. Use of the 'STRATIFY' falls risk assessment in patients recovering from acute stroke. Age and ageing. 2006. PMID: 16368736. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nursing home (Wijnia 2006): at STRATIFY ≥2 the relative risk of falling was 2.35 (95% CI 1.22 to 4.52), a relative measure — with sensitivity 50% and specificity 76.2%
cards.summary: Nursing home (Wijnia 2006): at STRATIFY ≥2 the relative risk of falling was 2.35 (95% CI 1.22 to 4.52), a relative measure — with sensitivity 50% and specificity 76.2%
cards.type: Prospective nursing-home validation of STRATIFY (120 newly admitted patients)
cards.people: Prospective study in one Rotterdam nursing home: 120 newly admitted patients (75 women, 45 men, average age 74.5 years) with a STRATIFY score, followed for falls over a 13-week observation period; 36 patients (30%) fell.
cards.result: The risk of falling in patients with a STRATIFY score of 2 or more was 2.35 (95% confidence interval: 1.22, 4.52) times that of patients with a lower score — a relative risk, printed as published. Sensitivity was 50% (95% CI: 32, 67) and specificity 76.2% (95% CI: 65, 87.5). The authors describe the results in their setting as disappointing. During the 3 months, 24 of the 120 patients (20%) had died and 56 (47%) had been discharged.
cards.watchOut: A relative risk of 2.35 on a 30% fall base still leaves the tool missing half of fallers (sensitivity 50%). Single home, 120 patients — the pair belongs to this setting only.
cards.source: Wijnia JW et al. Validity of the STRATIFY risk score of falls in nursing homes. Preventive medicine. 2006. PMID: 16297975. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: General acute care (Cortés 2023): 93,347 hospital records — sensitivity 0.672, specificity 0.612, positive likelihood ratio 1.73, AUC 0.69
cards.summary: General acute care (Cortés 2023): 93,347 hospital records — sensitivity 0.672, specificity 0.612, positive likelihood ratio 1.73, AUC 0.69
cards.type: Retrospective external validation of STRATIFY in general acute care (93,347 hospital records)
cards.people: Retrospective external validation in a Colombian tertiary hospital: 93,347 patient hospital records (mean age 56.9 years, 50.2% women), adults admitted 2018–2020 with a STRATIFY score recorded at admission, assessed for falls during the admission.
cards.result: Overall sensitivity was 0.672 (95% CI 0.612 to 0.723), specificity 0.612 (95% CI 0.605 to 0.615) and positive likelihood ratio 1.73 (95% CI 1.589 to 1.891) — a likelihood ratio, printed as published. The area under the ROC curve was 0.69 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.72), and age subgroups gave similar results. The authors conclude that applying STRATIFY at admission resulted in lower performance for predicting falls and that individual evaluation of fall risk factors is needed.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective record-based validation: the score was taken as recorded at admission in routine care, not administered for research. Its 0.69 AUC in undifferentiated acute care — not the geriatric-rehabilitation pool — is the figure for general wards.
cards.source: Cortés OL et al. Validation of the stratify scale for the prediction of falls among hospitalized adults in a tertiary hospital in Colombia: a retrospective cohort study. cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: one systematic review and meta-analysis (8 studies reviewed, 4 pooled), one prospective stroke-rehabilitation cohort (225 patients), one prospective nursing-home cohort (120 patients) and one retrospective acute-care validation (93,347 records). The modified, re-weighted Canadian version of the tool is a derivative instrument and is not carded as a validation of the original.
cards.result: Every validation agrees the tool discriminates weakly (AUC 0.69 where measured; PPV 23.1% in its best setting), and they disagree on where the errors fall: stroke rehabilitation keeps specificity (89.5%) by sacrificing sensitivity (11.3%), while geriatric rehabilitation balances at 67.2% / 51.2%. Print each pair with its setting and the ≥2 cut-off, and never as evidence that fall-prevention action works — no card on this shelf tests an intervention.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: PAINAD in advanced dementia: reliable between raters (ICC 0.92–0.98 in acute hospitals) but validity unsettled — the blinded placebo-controlled test was null and the largest validation found weak concurrent validity (τ = 0.29)
shelves.question: In people with advanced dementia who cannot self-report pain, how well does the PAINAD scale (Pain Assessment in Advanced Dementia; five observed items, score 0–10) detect pain — what reliability and validity did its derivation study show, what happened when the German version was put to a double-blind placebo-controlled analgesic test of validity, and how does it perform in acute general-hospital inpatients?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Alzheimer Disease · Analysis of Variance · Hospitals, Veterans · Humans · Male · Pain · Pain Measurement · Psychometrics · Reproducibility of Results · Severity of Illness Index
shelves.balance: MEASUREMENT PERFORMANCE — genuinely split, and the split is the answer. The derivation study (the originators' own report; only 19 residents observed) found adequate inter-rater reliability and internal consistency, correlation with the Discomfort Scale, and scores that fell after pain medication. But the one double-blind placebo-controlled test of responsiveness — German PAINAD in advanced dementia — found that neither PAINAD-G nor any of three comparator observational tools separated oxycodone from placebo. And the largest validation, in 230 acute general-hospital inpatients, found excellent inter-rater reliability (ICC 0.92 at rest, 0.98 in movement) beside only modest test–retest reliability (ICC 0.54–0.66) and weak concurrent validity against self-rated pain (Kendall τ = 0.29), with its authors raising concerns about validity in acute hospitals. No card presents PAINAD as settled-valid. Settings print on every card: VA dementia unit, German trial, London acute wards.

cards.headline: PAINAD derivation (Warden 2003 — the originators' own report, VA dementia special-care unit; observed N = 19, printed on the face): adequate inter-rater reliability and internal consistency, significant correlation with the Discomfort Scale (DS-DAT), and scores fell significantly after pain medication in records of 25 residents receiving PRN analgesia
cards.summary: PAINAD derivation (Warden 2003 — the originators' own report, VA dementia special-care unit; observed N = 19, printed on the face): adequate inter-rater reliability and internal consistency, significant correlation with the Discomfort Scale (DS-DAT), and scores fell significantly after pain medication in records of 25 residents receiving PRN analgesia
cards.type: Derivation and psychometric evaluation — the PAINAD originators' own report (programme-labelled; observed N = 19)
cards.people: 19 residents with advanced dementia who were aphasic or unable to report pain, observed in inpatient dementia special care units in a Veterans Administration Medical Center, plus medical records of 25 residents receiving as-required (PRN) pain medications; six professional staff took part.
cards.result: Adequate levels of inter-rater reliability were achieved between rater dyads, and internal consistency was satisfactory with a one-factor solution. PAINAD and the Discomfort Scale–Dementia of Alzheimer Type (DS-DAT) were significantly correlated, and PAINAD detected a statistically significant difference between scores before and after pain medication. The authors themselves noted the development population was a relatively small number of males and that further research was needed before universal recommendation.
cards.watchOut: Small derivation N (19 observed residents, all in a VA dementia unit) — printed here and never hidden. The before/after medication fall in scores came from a quality-improvement activity and records review, not a blinded placebo-controlled test; that test is the next card, and it was null.

cards.headline: Placebo-controlled validity test (Lukas 2019, German PAINAD-G): in a prospective double-blind randomised trial in people with advanced dementia expected to be in pain, NEITHER PAINAD-G nor any of three comparator observational tools (BISAD, CNPI, Algoplus) separated oxycodone from placebo — the null responsiveness result prints beside the derivation claims
cards.summary: Placebo-controlled validity test (Lukas 2019, German PAINAD-G): in a prospective double-blind randomised trial in people with advanced dementia expected to be in pain, NEITHER PAINAD-G nor any of three comparator observational tools (BISAD, CNPI, Algoplus) separated oxycodone from placebo — the null responsiveness result prints beside the derivation claims
cards.type: Prospective double-blind randomised placebo-controlled validity trial, German PAINAD (PAINAD-G) in advanced dementia
cards.people: People with advanced dementia expected to be in pain, in a prospective double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial of oxycodone vs placebo, with pain rated on the German PAINAD (PAINAD-G) and three comparator observational tools (BISAD, the Checklist of Nonverbal Pain Indicators, and Algoplus). The abstract does not state the randomised number, and none is claimed here.
cards.result: The study revealed no difference in 'pain reduction' between the oxycodone and placebo groups on PAINAD-G, and none of the other three observational tools demonstrated a significant difference between the study groups either. Correlations among the four observational tools were mostly moderate to high. The authors discussed possible reasons including sensitivity to change / responsiveness, consistency of the underlying construct, and the analgesic's efficacy in advanced dementia.
cards.watchOut: A null here can mean the scale is unresponsive, the analgesic did not work in this population, or both — the card reports the result, not a verdict on which. What it does remove is any claim that PAINAD's responsiveness to analgesia has been demonstrated under blinded placebo control.
cards.source: Lukas et al. Pain assessment in advanced dementia. Validity of the German PAINAD-a prospective double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial. Pain. 2019. PMID: 30371557. cards.headline: Acute-hospital validation (Dunford 2022, two London acute general hospitals, N = 230): inter-rater ICC 0.92 at rest and 0.98 in movement and internal consistency α 0.76–0.80, but test–retest ICC only 0.54–0.66 and concurrent validity against self-rated pain weak (Kendall τ = 0.29) — the authors raised concerns about validity in acute hospitals
cards.summary: Acute-hospital validation (Dunford 2022, two London acute general hospitals, N = 230): inter-rater ICC 0.92 at rest and 0.98 in movement and internal consistency α 0.76–0.80, but test–retest ICC only 0.54–0.66 and concurrent validity against self-rated pain weak (Kendall τ = 0.29) — the authors raised concerns about validity in acute hospitals
cards.type: Psychometric evaluation in acute general-hospital inpatients with dementia (N = 230)
cards.people: 230 people with dementia (65.7% female, mean age 87.2 years) admitted to two acute general hospitals in London, UK, in a secondary analysis of a longitudinal study; PAINAD tested at rest and in movement.
cards.result: Inter-rater reliability was ICC 0.92 at rest and 0.98 in movement; internal consistency was Cronbach's α 0.76 at rest and 0.80 in movement. Test–retest reliability was more modest (ICC 0.54 at rest, 0.66 in movement). Concurrent validity against a self-rating of pain was weak (Kendall's τ = 0.29), there was no correlation with a measure of behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia, and PAINAD scores were higher during movement than at rest (z = −8.01, P<0.001). The authors concluded the study raises concerns about the validity of PAINAD in general acute hospitals.
cards.watchOut: Raters can agree with each other (ICC 0.92–0.98) while the score agrees only weakly with patients' own pain ratings (τ = 0.29) — reliability and validity are different claims, and this card holds them apart. The setting is acute general wards, not the dementia unit of the derivation study.

shelves.title: Nu-DESC delirium screening on wards: sensitivity 0.98 and NPV 1.00 in the largest validation but PPV only 0.43 at 9% prevalence, and the cut-off is unsettled (Italian optimum 3, not the derivation cut-off)
shelves.question: On hospital wards, how accurately does the Nu-DESC (Nursing Delirium Screening Scale; five nurse-observed items) detect delirium against CAM / DSM reference standards — what sensitivity and specificity did its derivation study deliver, and what do the general-medical-ward and translated-version validations find, including the cut-off disagreement?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Cohort Studies · Delirium · Female · Hospitalization · Humans · Male · Mass Screening · Mental Status Schedule · Middle Aged · Nursing Diagnosis · Psychiatric Status Rating Scales · Psychometrics · Reproducibility of Results · Sensitivity and Specificity · Severity of Illness Index · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: MEASUREMENT PERFORMANCE — high sensitivity in the ward validations, with two numbers that must travel with it: the positive predictive value and the unsettled cut-off. At derivation (the originators' own report, oncology inpatients, CAM reference) sensitivity was 85.7% and specificity 86.8%. On German general medical wards (698 patients aged ≥65, DSM-5 reference, delirium occurrence 9.0%) sensitivity was 0.98 and specificity 0.87 — but PPV was only 0.43 at that prevalence, so most positive screens were not delirium. The Italian validation (101 elderly inpatients, CAM reference) found its optimum at a cut-off of 3, not the derivation cut-off, with sensitivity 100% and specificity 76% and AUC 0.946. No card prints one cut-off as universal. This is a diagnostic-accuracy shelf: no card claims Nu-DESC screening improves outcomes.

cards.headline: Nu-DESC derivation (Gaudreau 2005 — the originators' own report, oncology inpatient units): sensitivity 85.7% and specificity 86.8% against 59 blinded CAM ratings, with DSM-IV and MDAS co-ratings, in 146 consecutively assessed hospitalised patients
cards.summary: Nu-DESC derivation (Gaudreau 2005 — the originators' own report, oncology inpatient units): sensitivity 85.7% and specificity 86.8% against 59 blinded CAM ratings, with DSM-IV and MDAS co-ratings, in 146 consecutively assessed hospitalised patients
cards.type: Derivation study — the Nu-DESC originators' own report (programme-labelled), oncology inpatients, CAM reference standard
cards.people: 146 consecutive hospitalised patients on oncology inpatient units, continuously assessed for delirium symptoms by bedside nurses using the five-item Nu-DESC, against 59 blinded Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) ratings by research nurses and psychiatrists, with DSM-IV criteria and the Memorial Delirium Assessment Scale (MDAS) rated alongside.
cards.result: Nu-DESC sensitivity was 85.7% and specificity 86.8%, values the authors describe as comparable to the longer MDAS; Nu-DESC and DSM-IV sensitivities were similar. The authors concluded Nu-DESC is psychometrically valid and well-suited to widespread clinical use in busy oncology inpatient settings.
cards.watchOut: Derivation population was oncology inpatients and the reference was CAM in 59 ratings — the derivation sensitivity (85.7%) sits well below the later German ward figure (0.98), and the gradient prints rather than being averaged away. The derivation cut-off is not the Italian optimum (next cards).
cards.source: Gaudreau et al. Fast, systematic, and continuous delirium assessment in hospitalized patients: the nursing delirium screening scale. Journal of pain and symptom management. 2005. cards.headline: German general-ward validation (Bergjan 2020, N = 698 aged ≥65, DSM-5 reference): Nu-DESC sensitivity 0.98, specificity 0.87, NPV 1.00 — but PPV only 0.43 at a delirium occurrence of 9.0%, so most positive screens were false positives at ward prevalence
cards.summary: German general-ward validation (Bergjan 2020, N = 698 aged ≥65, DSM-5 reference): Nu-DESC sensitivity 0.98, specificity 0.87, NPV 1.00 — but PPV only 0.43 at a delirium occurrence of 9.0%, so most positive screens were false positives at ward prevalence
cards.type: Prospective validation in general medical wards (N = 698), DSM-5 reference standard
cards.people: 698 patients aged 65 and older on general medical wards (two neurology wards and one cardiology ward) of a German tertiary care hospital, assessed during nursing shifts with Nu-DESC and the Delirium Observation Screening Scale (DOS), with delirium diagnosed against DSM-5 criteria by neurologists.
cards.result: Overall delirium occurrence was 9.0%. For Nu-DESC, sensitivity was 0.98, specificity 0.87, PPV 0.43 and NPV 1.00; for DOS, sensitivity was 0.94, specificity 0.86, PPV 0.40 and NPV 0.99. Predisposing risk factors raised delirium probability (pressure ulcer risk relative OR 17.3; falls risk relative OR 14.0; immobility relative OR 12.7; dementia relative OR 5.38 — relative odds ratios, as published). The authors concluded Nu-DESC is an efficient screening tool that can be integrated into routine care.
cards.watchOut: PPV 0.43 at 9% prevalence is content, not a footnote: a positive Nu-DESC on a general ward is more likely false than true, while NPV 1.00 makes a negative screen the informative direction. This record carries no MeSH terms in PubMed ('none in the record' on its source line).

shelves.title: SARC-F sarcopenia screening (3 syntheses, overlapping primary sets): pooled sensitivity only 0.21–0.39 against most reference definitions beside specificity 86–91% — a negative SARC-F misses most sarcopenia; Ishii (79%) and MSRA (82%) were more sensitive
shelves.question: In older adults, how accurate is the SARC-F questionnaire (five self-reported items; score ≥4 screens positive) as a bedside / clinic screen for sarcopenia — what pooled sensitivity and specificity does it deliver against the EWGSOP, AWGS, IWGS and FNIH reference definitions, and how does it compare with the other screening instruments (Ishii score, MSRA) in head-to-head synthesis? (This shelf rests on 3 syntheses with overlapping primary-study sets, counted as 3 syntheses on its face.)
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Geriatric Assessment · Humans · Japan · Male · Mass Screening · ROC Curve · Sarcopenia · Sensitivity and Specificity · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: SCREENING PERFORMANCE — the sensitivity failure is the headline, printed as 3 syntheses, never as independent-cohort support. This shelf rests on three meta-analyses / systematic reviews whose primary-study sets overlap; the count is 3 syntheses, not 3 independent cohorts. Against EWGSOP, pooled SARC-F sensitivity was 0.21 (specificity 0.90) in the 2018 synthesis of 7 studies / 12,800 subjects, and 32% in the 2021 diagnostic meta-analysis of 20 studies — which also showed how criterion-dependent the estimate is (EWGSOP2 77%, AWGS 27%, IWGS 39%, FNIH 35%, specificities 63–91%). The 2023 head-to-head synthesis of five screening tools (42 studies) found SARC-F specificity 87% but the Ishii score combining sensitivity 79% with the best negative likelihood ratio (relative, 0.25) and MSRA reaching sensitivity 82% — SARC-F was not the most sensitive instrument. A negative SARC-F misses most sarcopenia against most criteria and must never be presented as a rule-out test. Pooled figures are criterion-specific and are never merged into one accuracy pair. No grip-strength data is carded on this shelf. This is a screening-accuracy shelf: no card claims SARC-F-triggered pathways improve outcomes.

cards.headline: Synthesis 1 of 3 (Ida 2018 — meta-analysis, 7 studies, 12,800 subjects; overlapping primary sets with the other two syntheses): against EWGSOP, pooled SARC-F sensitivity 0.21 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.31) and specificity 0.90 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.94), positive likelihood ratio 2.16 and diagnostic odds ratio 2.47 (both relative measures, labelled as such), with similar results against IWGS and AWGS
cards.summary: Synthesis 1 of 3 (Ida 2018 — meta-analysis, 7 studies, 12,800 subjects; overlapping primary sets with the other two syntheses): against EWGSOP, pooled SARC-F sensitivity 0.21 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.31) and specificity 0.90 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.94), positive likelihood ratio 2.16 and diagnostic odds ratio 2.47 (both relative measures, labelled as such), with similar results against IWGS and AWGS
cards.type: Meta-analysis of screening test accuracy (synthesis 1 of 3 on this shelf; primary-study sets overlap across the three syntheses)
cards.people: Older adults in 7 studies totalling 12,800 subjects, pooled in a meta-analysis of SARC-F screening test accuracy against the European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People (EWGSOP), International Working Group on Sarcopenia (IWGS) and Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia (AWGS) reference standards; too few studies used the Foundation NIH (FNIH) standard for meta-analysis.
cards.result: Against EWGSOP, pooled sensitivity was 0.21 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.31), specificity 0.90 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.94), positive likelihood ratio 2.16 (95% CI 1.51 to 3.09), negative likelihood ratio 0.87 (95% CI 0.80 to 0.95) and diagnostic odds ratio 2.47 (95% CI 1.64 to 3.74) — likelihood ratios and the odds ratio are relative measures, labelled as such. Similar pooled sensitivity and specificity were found against IWGS and AWGS. The authors concluded SARC-F's screening sensitivity was poor but its specificity high, making it a tool for selecting subjects for further confirmatory testing.
cards.watchOut: One of 3 syntheses with overlapping primary studies — never counted as independent-cohort support for the other two. Sensitivity 0.21 means roughly four of five people with EWGSOP sarcopenia screen negative; that is the card's headline, not its caveat.

cards.headline: Synthesis 2 of 3 (Lu 2021 — diagnostic meta-analysis, 20 studies; overlapping primary sets): pooled SARC-F sensitivity by criterion was EWGSOP 32%, EWGSOP2 77%, AWGS 27%, IWGS 39% and FNIH 35%, with specificities 63–91% — the criterion-dependence of the sensitivity estimate is itself a finding
cards.summary: Synthesis 2 of 3 (Lu 2021 — diagnostic meta-analysis, 20 studies; overlapping primary sets): pooled SARC-F sensitivity by criterion was EWGSOP 32%, EWGSOP2 77%, AWGS 27%, IWGS 39% and FNIH 35%, with specificities 63–91% — the criterion-dependence of the sensitivity estimate is itself a finding
cards.type: Diagnostic meta-analysis (synthesis 2 of 3 on this shelf; primary-study sets overlap across the three syntheses)
cards.people: Adults aged 60 years and older in 20 studies (sarcopenia prevalence 6.42% to 21.56%), pooled against five reference definitions — EWGSOP (13 studies), EWGSOP2 (4), AWGS (13), IWGS (8) and FNIH (7) — using bivariate and hierarchical summary ROC modelling.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity / specificity by criterion: EWGSOP 32% (95% CI 19 to 47) / 86% (77 to 92); EWGSOP2 77% (49 to 92) / 63% (43 to 79); AWGS 27% (16 to 42) / 91% (85 to 95); IWGS 39% (27 to 52) / 86% (76 to 92); FNIH 35% (23 to 49) / 89% (81 to 93). Areas under the hierarchical summary ROC curve ran 0.67 to 0.75 by criterion. The authors concluded SARC-F's screening accuracy varies by diagnostic criteria, while noting its practicability and specificity, and that accuracy under EWGSOP2 needs further exploration.
cards.watchOut: The EWGSOP2 sensitivity (77%) comes from only 4 studies with a wide interval (49–92%) and a much lower specificity (63%) — it may not be quoted as 'SARC-F sensitivity is 77%' without its criterion, study count and specificity beside it. Each criterion defines a different sarcopenia; the pairs are never merged.

cards.headline: Synthesis 3 of 3 (Huang 2023 — systematic review and meta-analysis of five sarcopenia screening tools, 42 studies; overlapping primary sets): SARC-F specificity 87% (95% CI 82 to 90), while the Ishii score combined sensitivity 79% with the best negative likelihood ratio (relative, 0.25) and MSRA reached sensitivity 82% — SARC-F was not the most sensitive instrument in the comparison
cards.summary: Synthesis 3 of 3 (Huang 2023 — systematic review and meta-analysis of five sarcopenia screening tools, 42 studies; overlapping primary sets): SARC-F specificity 87% (95% CI 82 to 90), while the Ishii score combined sensitivity 79% with the best negative likelihood ratio (relative, 0.25) and MSRA reached sensitivity 82% — SARC-F was not the most sensitive instrument in the comparison
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of screening instruments (synthesis 3 of 3 on this shelf; primary-study sets overlap across the three syntheses)
cards.people: 42 studies of five sarcopenia screening tools, identified from 7,120 screened titles and abstracts, with study quality assessed by QUADAS-2 (moderate to good) and measurement properties by the COSMIN checklist.
cards.result: Three instruments had specificities of 85% or more: the modified SARC-F 92% (95% CI 63 to 99), SARC-F 87% (95% CI 82 to 90) and the Ishii score 85% (95% CI 77 to 90). Three tools had sensitivities of 75% or more: MSRA 82% (95% CI 69 to 90), the Ishii score 79% (95% CI 62 to 89) and U-TEST 76%. Positive likelihood ratios above 5.0 (relative measures) were present for the Ishii score and modified SARC-F, and the Ishii score had the best negative likelihood ratio, 0.25. The authors concluded MSRA and the Ishii score had excellent sensitivity for early screening, while modified SARC-F and the Ishii score had superior specificity.
cards.watchOut: Head-to-head figures come from pooling across different study sets per instrument, not from within-study comparisons alone — read as a synthesis-level comparison. SARC-F's own sensitivity is not pooled in this report's abstract; its specificity (87%) is the SARC-F number here.

shelves.title: MOBID / MOBID-2 pain scale in advanced dementia: total-score reliability good (test–retest ICC 0.81–0.85, smallest detectable change 2.3–3.1 points) and US validity moderate (rho 0.54–0.57 vs expert ratings) — but derivation N = 26 and individual behaviour items unreliable (kappa down to 0.05)
shelves.question: In people with advanced dementia who cannot self-report pain, how well does the MOBID / MOBID-2 pain scale (Mobilization-Observation-Behavior-Intensity-Dementia — pain behaviours observed during five standardised guided movements, inferred intensity 0–10) perform — what reliability and validity did its derivation study show, what are MOBID-2's test–retest reliability, measurement error and responsiveness in nursing-home residents, and does the scale hold up in English-speaking US nursing homes?
shelves.mesh: Aged, 80 and over · Dementia/nursing · Female · Geriatric Nursing/methods · Humans · Male · Nursing Assessment · Pain/diagnosis/nursing · Pain Measurement/methods/nursing/standards · Reproducibility of Results
shelves.balance: A measurement shelf, not a treatment shelf. MOBID observes pain behaviour during five standardised guided movements and infers intensity 0–10 for people with advanced dementia who cannot self-report. Its derivation (the originators' own report, programme-labelled) studied only 26 nursing-home patients — N printed on the face — finding α 0.90 and inter-tester ICC 0.70–0.96 for inferred intensity, but kappa 0.05–0.84 across individual behaviour indicators, a weakness that prints beside the strong total-score figures. MOBID-2's test–retest reliability in 352 Norwegian nursing-home patients was ICC 0.81–0.85, with standard error of measurement 1.4–1.9 and smallest detectable change 2.3–3.1 points, and 5 of 6 responsiveness hypotheses confirmed inside that one trial programme's dataset (labelled as such). In 138 US residents, the overall score correlated moderately with expert clinician ratings (rho 0.54 current, 0.57 worst week; α 0.83) and was completable by trained non-clinical staff. The movement-provocation that makes the scale work is also its burden — guided mobilisation and trained raters are required.

cards.headline: MOBID derivation (Husebo 2007, N = 26 nursing-home patients with severe cognitive impairment — the originators' own report, programme-labelled, N printed on the face): internal consistency α 0.90 for the reduced item set and inter-tester ICC 0.70–0.96 for inferred pain intensity, but kappa 0.05–0.84 across individual behaviour indicators; MOBID disclosed significantly more pain than routine morning-care scoring
cards.summary: MOBID derivation (Husebo 2007, N = 26 nursing-home patients with severe cognitive impairment — the originators' own report, programme-labelled, N printed on the face): internal consistency α 0.90 for the reduced item set and inter-tester ICC 0.70–0.96 for inferred pain intensity, but kappa 0.05–0.84 across individual behaviour indicators; MOBID disclosed significantly more pain than routine morning-care scoring
cards.type: Derivation and validation study — originators' own report (programme-labelled; N = 26)
cards.people: 26 nursing-home patients with severe cognitive impairment; their primary caregivers (5 registered nurses and 6 licensed practical nurses) rated pain intensity during regular morning care and by MOBID — pain behaviour indicators (pain noises, facial expression, defence) observed during standardised active, guided movements — at bedside and from video, with 3 external raters also scoring the videos. The initial 7-item scale was reduced by deleting the at-rest and teeth/mouth-care items.
cards.result: Internal consistency of the reduced MOBID was high (Cronbach's alpha = 0.90). Inter-tester reliability for inferred pain intensity was high to excellent (intraclass correlation coefficient 0.70–0.96), but varied between poor and excellent for the individual pain behaviour indicators (kappa = 0.05–0.84). MOBID disclosed significantly more pain than pain scorings during regular morning care, and video observation demonstrated higher pain intensity than bedside scoring. The authors conclude that registering pain behaviour during active, guided movements is useful to disclose reliable and valid pain intensity scores in patients with severe cognitive impairment.
cards.watchOut: Programme-labelled, and N = 26 is small — it prints here and in the balance, never rounded up by the larger later datasets. The weak item-level kappas (down to 0.05) print beside the strong total-score ICCs: the total score is reliable in a way its individual behaviour items are not.
cards.source: Husebo BS et al. Mobilization-Observation-Behavior-Intensity-Dementia Pain Scale (MOBID): development and validation of a nurse-administered pain assessment tool for use in dementia. Journal of pain and symptom management. 2007. PMID: 17509814. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: MOBID-2 reliability and responsiveness (Husebo 2014, data from a cluster RCT of 352 patients with advanced dementia in 18 Norwegian nursing homes): test–retest ICC 0.81–0.85, standard error of measurement 1.4–1.9 and smallest detectable change 2.3–3.1 points, with 5 of 6 pre-formulated responsiveness hypotheses confirmed — including discrimination of change under a stepwise pain-treatment protocol
cards.summary: MOBID-2 reliability and responsiveness (Husebo 2014, data from a cluster RCT of 352 patients with advanced dementia in 18 Norwegian nursing homes): test–retest ICC 0.81–0.85, standard error of measurement 1.4–1.9 and smallest detectable change 2.3–3.1 points, with 5 of 6 pre-formulated responsiveness hypotheses confirmed — including discrimination of change under a stepwise pain-treatment protocol
cards.type: Reliability, measurement-error and responsiveness study within a cluster RCT programme (MOBID-2)
cards.people: 352 patients with advanced dementia in 18 Norwegian nursing homes, within a cluster randomised trial; test–retest analyses in patients not expected to change (controls) between baseline and week 2 (n = 163) and weeks 2 and 4 (n = 159). The responsiveness evidence comes from inside this one Norwegian trial programme's dataset and is labelled as such.
cards.result: Test–retest ICCs of the total MOBID-2 score were 0.81 (0–2 weeks) and 0.85 (2–4 weeks); standard error of measurement was 1.9 and 1.4 and smallest detectable change 3.1 and 2.3 over the same periods — so change scores of ≥3 points are beyond measurement error. Five of six pre-formulated hypotheses were confirmed: MOBID-2 discriminated (P < 0.001) between change in patients with and without a stepwise protocol for treatment of pain, showed a moderate association with the Cohen-Mansfield Agitation Inventory (r = 0.35) and no association with MMSE, Functional Assessment Staging or Activities of Daily Living; the expected association with the Neuropsychiatric Inventory — Nursing Home version was not confirmed.
cards.watchOut: A measurement row, not a treatment row: that MOBID-2 scores fell under a stepwise pain-treatment protocol shows the scale is responsive to change — it does not show the protocol, or scale-guided treatment, improves outcomes. The dataset is one programme's; no independent responsiveness replication is carded.
cards.source: Husebo BS et al. The MOBID-2 pain scale: reliability and responsiveness to pain in patients with dementia. European journal of pain (London, England). 2014. PMID: 24799157. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: MOBID in US nursing homes (Herr 2019, 138 residents with dementia across 16 homes in four states): overall score correlated with expert clinician pain ratings at rho 0.54 (current pain) and 0.57 (worst week), internal consistency α 0.83, and the tool was completable by trained non-clinical staff
cards.summary: MOBID in US nursing homes (Herr 2019, 138 residents with dementia across 16 homes in four states): overall score correlated with expert clinician pain ratings at rho 0.54 (current pain) and 0.57 (worst week), internal consistency α 0.83, and the tool was completable by trained non-clinical staff
cards.type: Cross-sectional psychometric evaluation in US nursing homes (independent population)
cards.people: 138 older adults with dementia and moderate to severe cognitive impairment in 16 nursing homes in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Georgia and Alabama (four states, as the record's MeSH names them); a cross-sectional psychometric evaluation of the original MOBID (five standardised movements, inferred intensity 0–10) in English-speaking US settings.
cards.result: MOBID overall scores were significantly associated with the expert clinician's rating of current pain (rho = 0.54, P < 0.001) and worst pain in the past week (rho = 0.57, P < 0.001), and also with nursing staff current and worst pain ratings and with the Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia (rho = 0.29, P < 0.001). Internal consistency was acceptable (alpha = 0.83). The authors conclude the results support use of the MOBID in English-speaking staff and residents in the US, and that the tool can be completed by trained, non-clinical staff.
cards.watchOut: Correlations of 0.54–0.57 against expert ratings are moderate, not strong — about a third of the variance shared — and print as such. This card validates the original MOBID in US homes; it does not re-validate MOBID-2's responsiveness, which rests on the Norwegian dataset alone.
cards.source: Herr K et al. Psychometric Evaluation of the MOBID Dementia Pain Scale in U.S. Nursing Homes. Pain management nursing : official journal of the American Society of Pain Management Nurses. 2019. PMID: 31085096. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: MOBID / MOBID-2 measures movement-evoked pain in advanced dementia with good total-score reliability (derivation ICC 0.70–0.96 at N = 26; MOBID-2 test–retest ICC 0.81–0.85 with smallest detectable change 2.3–3.1 points) and moderate validity against expert ratings in US homes (rho 0.54–0.57) — while its individual behaviour items are unreliable (kappa down to 0.05)
cards.summary: Synthesis: MOBID / MOBID-2 measures movement-evoked pain in advanced dementia with good total-score reliability (derivation ICC 0.70–0.96 at N = 26; MOBID-2 test–retest ICC 0.81–0.85 with smallest detectable change 2.3–3.1 points) and moderate validity against expert ratings in US homes (rho 0.54–0.57) — while its individual behaviour items are unreliable (kappa down to 0.05)
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: derivation (N = 26, originators' report), MOBID-2 reliability/responsiveness (352 patients in a Norwegian cluster-trial dataset) and the US psychometric evaluation (138 residents). Cross-point: PAINAD (shelf S21-4-02's row) is a different instrument — at-rest observation of breathing, vocalisation, face, body and consolability, from a US VA programme — with no shared anchor; neither shelf is 'the' dementia-pain shelf.
cards.result: The scale's distinctive claim — that pain must be provoked by standardised guided movement to be seen in people who cannot self-report — is supported by its disclosing more pain than routine morning care, and is also its burden: it requires guided mobilisation and trained raters in every report carded.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. This is a measurement shelf, not a treatment shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Abbey Pain Scale in advanced dementia: good inter-rater reliability (ICC 0.84) and responsiveness, weak criterion validity (kappa 0.42), derivation N not documented
shelves.question: In people with advanced dementia who cannot self-report pain, how well does the Abbey Pain Scale (six observed items — vocalisation, facial expression, change in body language, behavioural change, physiological change, physical change; score 0–18, completable in about a minute) perform — what did its derivation study in residential aged care show, how did the Danish version agree with a verbal rating scale and between raters in severely demented or non-communicative geriatric inpatients, and how did the scale compare psychometrically with the DOLOPLUS-2 and the Checklist of Nonverbal Pain Indicators when the same nurses rated the same residents on all three? (Derivation report: N not documented in its abstract.)

shelves.balance: This is a measurement shelf, not a treatment shelf. The derivation report's undocumented sample size prints on the face ('N not documented'). Criterion validity is the weak limb: agreement with a verbal rating scale was poor (kappa 0.42) in patients largely unable to self-report — the reference standard itself is compromised in this population, which prints as context, not as an excuse. The responsiveness evidence (score halving after analgesia; 88% improving on retest) is uncontrolled before–after observation and prints as such. Distinct from the PAINAD and MOBID shelves: three different dementia-pain instruments, cross-pointed, none presented as 'the' dementia-pain shelf.

cards.headline: Abbey Pain Scale derivation (Abbey 2004, International Journal of Palliative Nursing — residents with end- or late-stage dementia in residential aged care; sample size not stated in the abstract: N not documented): after pain-relief intervention the mean scale score fell by more than half (P < 0.001), with validity and internal reliability judged satisfactory — programme-labelled: the originators' own report
cards.summary: Abbey Pain Scale derivation (Abbey 2004, International Journal of Palliative Nursing — residents with end- or late-stage dementia in residential aged care; sample size not stated in the abstract: N not documented): after pain-relief intervention the mean scale score fell by more than half (P < 0.001), with validity and internal reliability judged satisfactory — programme-labelled: the originators' own report
cards.type: Derivation and initial validation study (originators' report; N not documented in the abstract)
cards.people: Residents with end- or late-stage dementia unable to articulate their needs, identified by the registered nurses who knew them, in residential aged care homes; the abstract does not state the derivation sample size — N not documented, printed as such.
cards.result: Following pain-relief intervention, the average pain score fell by more than half (paired t-test, P < 0.001). Validity and internal reliability (Gamma and Cronbach's alpha) were judged satisfactory. Users considered the scale a useful clinical device completable within one minute (six observed items, score 0–18). Inter-rater reliability testing and examination of limitations were still to commence at publication.
cards.watchOut: The score-halving after analgesia is uncontrolled before–after observation, not a trial of scale-guided treatment. The undocumented N means this report's weight cannot be sized from its abstract — printed on the face.

cards.headline: Danish Abbey Pain Scale validation (Gregersen 2016 — 50 geriatric-ward patients aged 70+ with MMSE <5, delirium, non-communicative aphasia or unconsciousness): agreement with the verbal rating scale was poor (kappa 0.42), inter-rater reliability was good (ICC 0.84), internal consistency was fair (α 0.52), and 88% of retested patients showed a score reduction after expected analgesic effect
cards.summary: Danish Abbey Pain Scale validation (Gregersen 2016 — 50 geriatric-ward patients aged 70+ with MMSE <5, delirium, non-communicative aphasia or unconsciousness): agreement with the verbal rating scale was poor (kappa 0.42), inter-rater reliability was good (ICC 0.84), internal consistency was fair (α 0.52), and 88% of retested patients showed a score reduction after expected analgesic effect
cards.people: 50 old patients (70+ years) consecutively admitted to geriatric wards at Aarhus University Hospital, Denmark, fulfilling at least one of: MMSE <5, delirium, non-communicative aphasia, or unconsciousness. Criterion validity against a verbal rating scale; two independent ratings of the same patient at the same time for inter-rater reliability.
cards.result: Agreement between the Abbey Pain Scale and the verbal rating scale was poor (Cohen's kappa 0.42). Inter-rater reliability was good (ICC 0.84). Internal consistency was fair (Cronbach's alpha 0.52). Pain was observed in 66% of patients, who were retested when an expected analgesic effect had occurred; of these, 88% reached a reduction in the sum score (P < 0.001). The authors consider the Danish version qualified and usable in this population.
cards.watchOut: Journal note: the slate row named the Scandinavian Journal of Caring Sciences; the PubMed record fetched this session gives International journal of palliative nursing — the record governs the source line. Kappa 0.42 against a verbal scale in patients largely unable to self-report cuts both ways: the reference standard is itself compromised here, which is context, not a rescue of the validity limb. The 88% retest improvement is uncontrolled before–after observation.
cards.source: Gregersen M et al. Reliability of the Danish Abbey Pain Scale in severely demented and non-communicative older patients. International journal of palliative nursing. 2016. cards.headline: Comparative psychometric evaluation of three dementia pain scales (Neville 2014 — 126 residents with moderate-to-severe dementia rated by 26 nurses on two occasions): the Abbey Pain Scale and DOLOPLUS-2 both showed good reliability and validity, with the Abbey scale better suited to raters who use pain scales only occasionally or hold lower-level qualifications; the Checklist of Nonverbal Pain Indicators was psychometrically weaker
cards.summary: Comparative psychometric evaluation of three dementia pain scales (Neville 2014 — 126 residents with moderate-to-severe dementia rated by 26 nurses on two occasions): the Abbey Pain Scale and DOLOPLUS-2 both showed good reliability and validity, with the Abbey scale better suited to raters who use pain scales only occasionally or hold lower-level qualifications; the Checklist of Nonverbal Pain Indicators was psychometrically weaker
cards.type: Comparative psychometric evaluation (126 residents, 26 nurses, three scales)
cards.people: 126 people with moderate to severe dementia in residential aged care facilities, rated independently by 26 nurses on two occasions on all three scales: Abbey Pain Scale, DOLOPLUS-2 and Checklist of Nonverbal Pain Indicators.
cards.result: The Abbey Pain Scale and DOLOPLUS-2 showed good psychometric qualities in reliability and validity, including resistance to the influence of rater characteristics; the Checklist of Nonverbal Pain Indicators had reasonable but weaker results. The DOLOPLUS-2 provided more reliable measurement, while the Abbey scale may be better suited to nurse raters who only occasionally use pain scales or hold lower-level qualifications.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the Abbey Pain Scale is reliable between raters (ICC 0.84) and responsive in uncontrolled before–after observation, and compares well psychometrically with DOLOPLUS-2 — but its criterion validity is weak (kappa 0.42 against a compromised reference standard), its internal consistency only fair (α 0.52), and its derivation sample size is not documented in its abstract

shelves.title: Berg Balance Scale for fall prediction: 3 overlapping syntheses split — two say not useful alone, one ranks Berg ≤50 among the best-supported performance measures
shelves.question: In older adults, how well does the Berg Balance Scale (14 observed balance tasks, each 0–4, maximum 56) predict who will fall — what cut-offs have been proposed, why did two systematic reviews conclude the scale should not be used alone to determine fall risk, and where does the scale sit in the posttest-probability synthesis of fall-risk measures alongside the Timed Up and Go and the five-times sit-to-stand? (Base: 3 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — counted as syntheses, never as independent cohorts.)
shelves.mesh: Accidental Falls/prevention & control · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Geriatric Assessment/methods · Humans · Physical Therapy Modalities/statistics & numerical data · Postural Balance/physiology · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: This shelf rests on 3 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — the count prints as 3 syntheses, not 3 independent cohorts. The verdict split is the content and no card resolves it into a single verdict: two systematic reviews conclude the evidence is insufficient / the scale is not useful alone to predict falls, while the posttest-probability synthesis places a Berg score ≤50 among the five most evidence-supported performance measures. Cut-offs are unstable across studies (45–51, and ≤50 in the synthesis) and print with their source. Distinct from the chart-based fall-risk-score shelves (Morse, Hendrich II, STRATIFY) and the preoperative Timed Up and Go shelf: the Berg is a performance-based balance examination. This is a prediction shelf, not an intervention shelf: no card implies Berg-guided exercise or referral prevents falls.

cards.headline: Berg falls synthesis 1 of 3 (Lima 2018, systematic review — 8 prognostic studies): mean Berg scores were high regardless of fall history, proposed cut-offs ranged from 45 to 51 points, only two studies found a score difference between fallers and non-fallers, heterogeneity made meta-analysis unfeasible, and the reviewers conclude the evidence to support using the scale to predict falls is insufficient
cards.summary: Berg falls synthesis 1 of 3 (Lima 2018, systematic review — 8 prognostic studies): mean Berg scores were high regardless of fall history, proposed cut-offs ranged from 45 to 51 points, only two studies found a score difference between fallers and non-fallers, heterogeneity made meta-analysis unfeasible, and the reviewers conclude the evidence to support using the scale to predict falls is insufficient
cards.type: Systematic review (synthesis 1 of 3; primary-study sets overlap across the three syntheses)
cards.people: Prognostic studies or clinical trials assessing the Berg Balance Scale (14 tasks, maximum 56) and falls history in older adults; 8 studies included from 1,047 found; methodological quality assessed with the Quality In Prognosis Studies tool (low to moderate risk of bias). One of 3 overlapping syntheses — never an independent cohort. The review was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42016032309, as published in its abstract).
cards.result: The mean Berg score was high regardless of fall history. Three studies presented cut-off scores, ranging from 45 to 51 points. Two studies reported a difference in score between fallers and non-fallers. Meta-analysis was unfeasible due to heterogeneity. The reviewers conclude the evidence to support the use of the Berg Balance Scale to predict falls is insufficient, and it should not be used alone to determine the risk of falling in older adults.
cards.watchOut: Journal note: the slate row named the Journal of Geriatric Physical Therapy; the PubMed record fetched this session gives Physiotherapy — the record governs the source line. High mean scores in both fallers and non-fallers are a ceiling problem for prediction, not a data error.

cards.headline: Berg falls synthesis 2 of 3 (Neuls 2011, systematic review — 9 studies in older adults with and without neurological pathology): sensitivity and specificity varied greatly with the cut-off chosen, eight of nine studies recommended specific cut-offs, and the reviewers conclude the Berg Balance Scale alone is not useful for predicting falls in older adults
cards.summary: Berg falls synthesis 2 of 3 (Neuls 2011, systematic review — 9 studies in older adults with and without neurological pathology): sensitivity and specificity varied greatly with the cut-off chosen, eight of nine studies recommended specific cut-offs, and the reviewers conclude the Berg Balance Scale alone is not useful for predicting falls in older adults
cards.type: Systematic review (synthesis 2 of 3; primary-study sets overlap)
cards.people: 9 studies in older adults (≥65 years; 5 without pathology, 4 with neurological disorders), each scoring ≥5 of 10 on the Physiotherapy Evidence Database scale; all 9 reported sensitivity and specificity for predicting falls. One of 3 overlapping syntheses — never an independent cohort.
cards.result: Sensitivity and specificity varied greatly depending on the cut-off score and the authors' objectives; 8 of the 9 studies recommended specific cut-off scores, which varied. The reviewers conclude the Berg Balance Scale alone is not useful for predicting falls in older adults with and without pathological conditions, and recommend using it in conjunction with other tests and measures and unique patient factors.
cards.watchOut: Cut-off instability is the finding: when every study recommends a different threshold, no single Berg cut-off on this shelf may be presented as validated.

cards.headline: Berg falls synthesis 3 of 3 — posttest-probability synthesis (Lusardi 2017, Journal of Geriatric Physical Therapy — 59 data-contributing studies of fall-risk measures in community-dwelling older adults): no single test showed strong posttest probability, but a Berg score ≤50 points was among the five most evidence-supported performance measures, alongside Timed Up and Go ≥12 seconds and five-times sit-to-stand ≥12 seconds, on cumulative posttest probability
cards.summary: Berg falls synthesis 3 of 3 — posttest-probability synthesis (Lusardi 2017, Journal of Geriatric Physical Therapy — 59 data-contributing studies of fall-risk measures in community-dwelling older adults): no single test showed strong posttest probability, but a Berg score ≤50 points was among the five most evidence-supported performance measures, alongside Timed Up and Go ≥12 seconds and five-times sit-to-stand ≥12 seconds, on cumulative posttest probability
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis using posttest probability (synthesis 3 of 3; primary-study sets overlap)
cards.people: Ambulatory community-living older adults (≥65 years, sample ≥30, falls tracked ≥6 months; acute / long-term care and significant cognitive or neuromuscular conditions excluded); 95 full-text articles met inclusion, 59 contained data for posttest-probability calculation across history, self-report and performance measures. One of 3 overlapping syntheses — never an independent cohort.
cards.result: No single test or measure demonstrated strong posttest probability values; posttest values could be calculated for only 35 of 119 candidate measures. Five performance-based measures had clinical usefulness on cumulative posttest probability, including Berg Balance Scale score ≤50 points, Timed Up and Go ≥12 seconds and five-times sit-to-stand ≥12 seconds — described as currently the most evidence-supported functional measures for individual fall risk.
cards.watchOut: This synthesis's favourable placement is on cumulative posttest probability among measures with calculable data — it does not overturn the other two reviews' verdicts, and 'among the best-supported' is not 'accurate alone'. The ≤50 cut-off belongs to this synthesis and prints with it.
